en: The *Hetubinduṭīkāloka*, composed by the scholar Durveka Miśra.
[1b] Homage to the Buddha!
Having prostrated before the Tathāgata, who has abandoned the accumulation of obscurations,
I shall explain the words of my venerable teacher Bhaṭṭārcaṭa according to my ability.
For those whose wealth is pride and those people whose wealth is intellect, this effort is not for their sake; therefore, it is by no means useless.

For it is known from scripture that paying homage to one’s own chosen deity is the ground for the production of merit; furthermore, through this, the desired completion of the work occurs free from obstacles. Thus, Dharmākaradatta—who follows the dharma of preserving the conduct of the learned—desiring to compose a commentary on the *Hetubindu*, pays homage at the very outset to his own tutelary deity, preceded by praise.

Regarding the composition of the verse of homage (*namaskāraśloka*), the objections and their refutations should be understood according to the method found in the *Dharmottarapradīpa* and other works.

By means of the distinction between intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*), both types of causal states (*hetvavasthā*) will be shown; and by means of the distinction between the excellence of one’s own welfare (*svārtha*) and that of others’ welfare (*parārtha*), both types of resultant states (*phalāvasthā*) will be shown.
This presentation of the causal and resultant states of the Lord of Sages (*munīndra*) is intended as an act of homage.

For during his state as a bodhisattva, the Blessed One, through the practice of cultivation over many lifetimes and by association with spiritual friends, first brought forth the perfection of a distinguished intention (*āśaya*),
which those who know reality call here the "vow-mind of awakening" (*praṇidhibodhicitta*).
Subsequently, he performed every kind of distinguished application (*prayoga*) in order to accomplish the intended goal.
That which they call the bodhicitta of setting forth—
after that, through the attainment of the excellence of specific application, he obtained the entire fruit of the supreme human goal;
thereafter, he performed various kinds of unimpeded benefit for sentient beings.
For this very reason, he first explicitly stated the state of intention with the words beginning "When this has arisen" (1.5);
thereafter, the state of application with the words beginning "Virtue and knowledge" (1.6);
and subsequently, the state of fruition with the words beginning "In its entirety" (1.7).
Immediately following that, by the words "In the world" (*loke*) and so forth, he indicates the state of benefiting sentient beings.
The grammatical connection is: "I pay homage (*namasyāmi*), that is, I bow down, to that Sun of the Victors (*jinaravi*) who is of such a kind.

And compassion (*karuṇā*)—which consists in the desire to deliver [beings] from suffering or from the causes of suffering—is "great" because it functions equally toward both the benefactor and the beneficiary, arises without interruption, and is endowed with magnanimity.
And compassion has that as its essence;
thus, he who has generated great compassion (mahākṛpā) is so described. When there is an expectation as to what such a person does, he says: "in order to protect" (trātum).
When the question arises as to "whom to protect," he states that the object of the act of protection is "people" (*jana*).
Qualifying that, he says "entirely" (*samagram*), meaning complete or whole. He further specifies them as being "in distress" (*vyasaninam*).

*Vyasana* means suffering; [the term refers to one] who possesses that. This suffix *ini* should be understood as expressing a constant connection (*nityayoga*). Due to the proximity of the word *kṛpā* (compassion), by implication, the meaning established is "to protect from suffering or from the cause of suffering."
Alternatively, there is no status as an ablative (*apādāna*) because the [meaning of] "ablative" is not intended to be expressed.

The state characterized by the perfection of the intention, namely, "I must liberate all sentient beings from suffering and from the causes of suffering," is called the "state of intention" (*āśayāvasthā*).
"Cause" (*hetu*) means the "motive" (*nimitta*).

The phrase "of the state of omniscience" (sārvajñapadasya) is to be understood through the force of the capacity to attain the excellence of its own purpose, which will be explained later. The accusative case ending is used because of its connection with the action of "piling" (citikriyā). To address the inquiry as to what kind [of state it is], the words beginning with "meritorious" (puṇya) are stated to qualify it; these are to be construed later.
This merit and knowledge has merit and knowledge as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Otherwise, he qualifies it as "vast" (*vipula*), meaning extensive and great, up to that point;
for it is indeed the accumulations of merit and knowledge that bring about the state of omniscience.
The very accumulation of the equipment of merit and wisdom is the application for the sake of uplifting sentient beings;
for it is only through the attainment of that state by means of it that the uplifting of sentient beings is possible,
whereas otherwise that state would not exist.
[2a] A state endowed with such a perfection of application is called the "state of application" (*prayogāvasthā*).

Both this application and the preceding disposition (*āśaya*) are causes for the attainment of the supreme state through a continuous succession. Therefore, with the intention of expressing merely their status as causes for attaining that state, and with the intention of expressing them as mere states, the Blessed One designates them as the "causal state" (*hetvavasthā*).
Furthermore, with the intention of expressing a distinction, it is said that these are the states of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*).
"Having accumulated" (*pracitya*), "having piled up" (*upacitya*), and "having made into a heap" (*rāśīkṛtya*) mean the same thing.
In the expression "resorting to such a mountain," the suffix indicating the prior time (*paurvakālika-pratyaya*) is used in view of the act of resorting.
He asks, "Why did he act in this manner? and replies with the verse beginning "In its entirety" (kṛtsne).
The word *yat* ("which") is to be connected here as well, and it will also be connected further on.
Having become what kind of person does one rely upon that [state]? To this he says: "vidhūte" (in the verse 1.6).
One by whom the exertion of effort—consisting of devoted, uninterrupted, and long-term practice—has been entirely cast off; such is the meaning.

This occurs either through pervasion at all times by resorting to both systems (*mata*), because it is dependent on will, or through pervasion by way of fitness, insofar as its entirety has been employed.

Because of the use of the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*), it is that which pervades all objects of knowledge consisting of everything to be abandoned and adopted along with their means; and because of the supreme abandonment of the impurity characterized by obscurations and so forth, it is "stainless wisdom" (*nirmalaprajñā*).
It is likewise [called] "the mountain of arising" (*udayādri*) because it is the locus for the emergence of the welfare of others, just like a mountain of sunrise.

"Resorting to that" (śritaḥ) means having attained it; that is to say, one has become a yogin endowed with that. And this very state, which is the station of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) and the fruit of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), is called the "state of fruition" (*phalāvasthā*) because it is the stage characterized by the perfection of such a fruit.

That which exists in the heart (*hṛdaya*) is "of the heart" (*hārda*). Because it obstructs the discernment between the paths of the existent and the non-existent, it is like darkness; thus it is "darkness" (*tamaḥ*), meaning ignorance (*ajñāna*).
However, depending on a certain perspective—specifically when one intends to express a distinction between the heart (*hṛd*) and the mind (*manas*)—both terms are used.
Or, this may be according to common worldly usage.
It dispels—that is, it destroys—[the darkness] by means of the teaching of the Dharma and in other ways as well; thus [it is said].
Because he has conquered Māra, the Victor (Jina) is the Blessed Buddha. To the question "Where does he dispel the darkness of the heart? he says: "In the world" (loke).
He is the destroyer of that mental darkness which has the world as its object;
that is to say, he is the one who destroys such darkness for the world itself. The term "loka" (world) is so called because it is dissolved (*lupya*).
Because of its proximity to the word "heart" (*hr̥d*), it should be understood as the living being within the heart.
A state that acts in this manner is called a "state of benefiting sentient beings," because it possesses the common characteristic of being a vessel for compassion that protects those in distress.
Because the sun is likewise described as having its purpose [fulfilled] upon its arrival there,
one should understand that at that time there is "calamity" (vyasana) and "disease" (roga),
due to the similarity of its resting upon the mountain of sunrise and its common characteristic of destroying darkness in the world.
Then, the seventh darkness is to be seen;
he is like the sun, a sun.
And here, the poetic figure of *rūpaka* (metaphor) is shown as a quality of poetry (*kāvyaguṇa*).
"I pay homage with my head" (mūrdhnā namasyāmi) should be understood as speech uttered while actually bowing the head;
by this, physical prostration is demonstrated, and not otherwise.
However, by the utterance of the specific sequence of words, verbal prostration is demonstrated.

And since both bodily activity and speech are preceded by the mind that originates them, it is also mental; thus, everything is clear. This salutation is performed by way of explaining the accomplishment of one's own welfare together with its means; therefore, the explanation of the reality [of the title] has not been elaborated upon here, as it would have been redundant and not very closely connected. Alternatively, it is explained in another way.
Indeed, this work characterized as a commentary (*ṭīkā*) is intended for the sake of others.
Furthermore, when there is a suspicion of defects in the subject matter, another person does not apply themselves to listening.

Therefore, since lack of attention is pervaded by the suspicion of defects in the subject matter, [the author], desiring to demonstrate the purity of the subject matter—which is the opposite of that [suspicion]—in order to negate such lack of attention, intends to show the following:
He says: "That which... and so forth.
Furthermore, the subject matter of the commentary is the treatise of the master Dharmakīrti.
And its purity [is established] through the purity of the teaching (*pravacana*),
because the Teacher’s treatise is devoted to supporting the meaning of the teaching and has that alone as its subject matter.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate the purity of the teaching— which is the basis for the purity of the Teacher’s treatise— he shows the Blessed One’s possession of excellent qualities and freedom from faults by means of the instruction on the act of homage.

By describing the Blessed One’s reliance upon the mountain of such wisdom (*tathābhūtaprajñā*) preceded by the demonstration of skillful means (*upāya*), his freedom from all ignorance is shown. Granted that he is faultless due to being devoid of all ignorance, why does he— who has attained the excellence of his own welfare— teach others the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted along with its means, by which...

In response to the expectation that such a teaching might arise from him, [the author] demonstrates his connection with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) by means of the passage beginning with "He who, having become... (*yaḥ saṃjāta-*, 1.5).
Consequently, through the presence of great compassion, he teaches what is correct, and through the application of the excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*), he teaches what is real (*bhūta*).
The word "nam" (reverence) has been explained.
By this, both the absence of instruction and instruction in a contrary manner are excluded. As it is said:
"Out of compassion he teaches what is beneficial; through knowledge, he teaches reality along with its means" (PV 1.284).
Likewise:
"Because of its fruitlessness, He does not speak untruth.

For this very reason, by means of teaching the objects of knowledge and so forth without error, He has become the dispeller of the darkness within the heart (hārdatamopaha); thus, by the very implication of the meaning, His speech is shown to be pure.
And by virtue of having that as its object, the purity of the Teacher’s treatise is established;
and by virtue of having that as its object, the purity of the commentary is also effectively declared.
The remainder is the same as before.
"Let it be that the Blessed One’s teaching is pure due to his faultlessness;

nevertheless, one might suspect that this treatise will not shine forth because of the possibility of defects in the Teacher's speech and mind. Therefore, [the author] demonstrates the Teacher's possession of wisdom that transcends the world, thereby [showing the purity of] his speech and mind."
The absence of deficiency in speech and mind will be demonstrated by the passage beginning with "in the path of logic" (1.13).
For deficiency in speech and mind occurs when there is dullness, and is thus pervaded by it.
And its opposite is the state of possessing an exceedingly exalted intellect;
for [the author] intends to ask how [a commentary] could exist when that [exalted intellect] is present.
Even if the text of the Master is pure, your own commentary will not be clear due to the deficiency of your own speech and mind.
Anticipating this objection, and under the guise of avoiding arrogance, he accepts his own dullness in comparison to the words of the Teacher;
nevertheless, by means of the statement beginning with "even so" (1.15), he will also reveal the deficiency and lack of excellence in his own speech and mind through a gesture of the Vaidarbhī style.

At the outset, how can you— who are engaged in chewing over what has already been chewed by providing an explanation for a text that someone standing nearby has never heard before, or who is disregarded therein— attain that sweetness characterized by the illumination of the excellence of reality which brings internal satisfaction?
Thinking, "Why has this been done? he speaks the words beginning with "varaṃ hi" [1.10] in order to spontaneously unravel the intention behind that haste.
Having refuted the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this proponent of haste, he speaks the words beginning with "nyāyamārge" [1.13] while dispelling those very same doubts.

However, according to the previous interpretation, it is better not to comment on this; let the effort be applied elsewhere where the savoring of a specific aesthetic flavor (*rasaviśeṣāsvāda*) is possible.

Furthermore, regarding the doubt that this [is not the case] because of the impossibility of that here, this [following point] should be applied; however, with the two subsequent verses, Dharmakīrti has merely offered a defense against his own arrogance. These are the words of Dharmakīrti among them.
For that which has had its essence extracted (*ākṛṣṭarasa*) is called "chewed" (*carvita*).

Since these [works] have also been explained by many, they have had their essence extracted; thus, among the "chewed," they are like something already chewed. Chewing (*carvaṇa*)—in the sense of tasting the flavor (*rasāsvāda*)—is a specific kind of activity.

This is understood from the context as being contrasted with the explanation of other texts that have not been explained, which is of the nature of chewing what has not yet been chewed. This is the limit intended for the connection.
Regarding the desire for something [else], he states the indeclinable *varam* [1.10]:
from “Better a pigeon today than a peacock tomorrow,” and “Better death than weakness,” and so forth.
Furthermore, he did not say that there is no chewing of other texts not yet chewed; rather, he spoke thus specifically regarding those factors to be avoided that have been brought to mind.
And because it is understood through implication, he did not explicitly state that which is intended as something to be avoided.
The word "api" expresses a logical possibility.
Others, however, describe the word *vara* as being co-referential with "chewing" (*carvaṇa*), taking it to mean "the very best" (*anipātam eva śreṣṭhavacanam*).
They explain the word *api* as meaning "not only in the case of those not chewed.
[They refer to] the Teacher, who is even greater than the great.

And this should be understood as a designation for the wise person in every respect. Now, one might object: "Since it has already been explained that [the juice] extracted by squeezing lacks even a trace of sweetness due to its internal nature, how can it be called 'better' when it is not even attained? Anticipating this doubt, he provides an answer by means of the figure of speech *prativastūpamā* (parallel simile): [The text continues: Just as a garland made from flowers gathered from various trees, though lacking the specific fragrance of each individual flower, is nevertheless superior to a single flower because it possesses a multitude of fragrances; so too, although the juice extracted from the interior of the sugarcane lacks sweetness, the juice obtained from the exterior is better because it possesses a greater degree of sweetness. Thus, the meaning is established. Furthermore, the word "even" (*api*) is used here to indicate that even if there were no difference in the degree of sweetness, the external juice would still be better simply because it is more abundant. This is because the word "even" is employed to signify abundance, as in the expression "even a single drop of water. Therefore, the sense is that the external juice is better because it is more abundant. Alternatively, the word "even" may be understood to mean "in every respect," signifying that the external juice is better in all ways. Or else, the word "even" may be taken to mean "at least," indicating that the external juice is better at the very least. Thus, the meaning is that the external juice is better in every respect. Alternatively, the word "even" may be used to exclude other things, as in the statement "even a single drop of water is better than a hundred jars of wine," where the word "even" excludes the possibility of anything else being better. In this case, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice alone, and nothing else. Or else, the word "even" may be used to express a concession, as in "even though he is a fool, he is learned," where the word "even" concedes that he is indeed a fool. In this context, the meaning is that although the internal juice is sweet, the external juice is better nonetheless. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote simultaneity, as in "even while he was speaking, he smiled," where the word "even" indicates that the two actions occurred at the same time. Here, however, the word "even" is used to denote a lack of distinction, as in "even the sky is like the earth," where the word "even" signifies that there is no difference between them. In this case, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, which is without distinction. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of expectation, as in "even though he is a king, he is poor," where the word "even" expresses that one does not expect him to be wealthy. Here, the meaning is that although the internal juice is sweet, the external juice is better, and this is not something to be expected. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of connection, as in "even the sky is not connected to the earth," where the word "even" signifies that there is no relationship between them. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not connected. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of pervasion, as in "even the sky does not pervade the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it does not cover it entirely. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it does not pervade it. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of inclusion, as in "even the sky does not include the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it is not contained within it. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it is not included within it. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of dependence, as in "even the sky does not depend on the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it is not reliant upon it. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it does not depend upon it. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of support, as in "even the sky does not support the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it does not hold it up. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it does not support it. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of cause, as in "even the sky is not the cause of the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it is not the origin of it. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it is not its cause. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of effect, as in "even the sky is not the effect of the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it is not produced by it. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it is not its effect. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of similarity, as in "even the sky is not similar to the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not alike. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not similar. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of identity, as in "even the sky is not identical to the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not the same. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not identical. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of difference, as in "even the sky is not different from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that there is no distinction between them. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and there is no difference between them. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of opposition, as in "even the sky does not oppose the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they do not conflict. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they do not oppose each other. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of contradiction, as in "even the sky does not contradict the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not inconsistent. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they do not contradict each other. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of incompatibility, as in "even the sky is not incompatible with the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not mutually exclusive. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not incompatible. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of exclusion, as in "even the sky does not exclude the earth," where the word "even" signifies that it does not set it aside. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and it does not exclude it. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of separation, as in "even the sky is not separated from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not distinct. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not separated. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of division, as in "even the sky is not divided from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not partitioned. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not divided. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of distinction, as in "even the sky is not distinguished from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not differentiated. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not distinguished. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of variety, as in "even the sky is not varied from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not diverse. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not varied. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of multiplicity, as in "even the sky is not multiple from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not manifold. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not multiple. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of plurality, as in "even the sky is not plural from the earth," where the word "even" signifies that they are not many. Here, the meaning is that the external juice is better than the internal juice, and they are not plural. Or else, the word "even" may be used to denote a lack of diversity, as in
Regarding the phrase "niṣpīḍitāpi" (even when squeezed):
*mṛdvīkā* refers to the grape fruit.
Because the interrogative pronoun *kim* is used in a sense of negation (*kṣepa*), the meaning is "it does not abandon [its sweetness] at all."
By this mode of expression, he also indicates a degree of dissatisfaction:

"Surely the predecessors did not explain the entire range of meanings of the profound words of the Teacher exactly as they are; therefore, it must be emphatically stated that there will be a tasting of such flavor [only through this work]."
The particle *hi* is used here in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*) or in the sense of "clearly" (*vyaktam*).
The compound *nyāyamārgas tulā* is a *samāsa* (compound) in which the restriction is internally implied, meaning "the path of reasoning itself is like a scale."
The word "ekatra" (in one place) functions with respect to both sides like the eye of a crow (*kāka-akṣi*).

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the world, which is the object of action, being on one side—that is, existing within one pan of the scale—would be surpassed or rendered inferior by that person whose mind is situated on the other side. The word "jayed" (would conquer) is a term expressing possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
The meaning is that the world’s subjugation is rendered possible by her; or, it refers to the sense of capability—
that she is capable of conquering the world.
The words—such as "concerning objects beyond perception" and so forth—of him who possesses such a view;
by asking "where? he treats them as worthy of being explained by himself.
They are profound because they are difficult to fathom.
For this very reason, he asks "Where?
and says "I, of dull intellect, where? By this, not considering himself capable of explaining them, he distances himself from the task.

Nevertheless, by means of this collection of particles beginning with "tathāpi" (nevertheless), he responds to the subject at hand. "With reference to whom" (*yān uddiśya*) means "with reference to which" or "for whose sake.
"By me also" (*mayāpi*) means "even by me, who am of such a kind."
Regarding the view that this is a direct statement by the author himself, by addressing the Teacher as "one of dull intellect," he has implicitly included the opposite toward the world at large.
[1] Relying on the Tibetan translation, we have conjectured and printed the reading as “for their sake” (*teṣāṃ kṛte*);
however, relying on this commentary, the original reading there should be supplemented as “with reference to whom” (*yān uddiśya*).

"There are some of duller intellect than even I" (1.15)— by this statement of Vidarbha, which gratifies the minds of the wicked— it is explained by me for the sake of the many that, if a wicked person were not to act directly toward me, the intention of the Teacher would not have been properly manifested; thus, this is analyzed specifically for the sake of the multitude.
Otherwise, even that person will understand the meaning of the Master’s treatise from the aforementioned work containing the false explanation;
for there is no rule that an ignorant person understands something only from what was composed by a learned author and not from anything else.
Therefore, he shows: "How could I engage in this great and fruitless effort?"

In the previous explanation, however, it was intended merely to avoid restlessness; this [present explanation] does not have that as its final function, and thus everything is faultless. The "treatise" (*prakaraṇa*) consists of two distinct masses—the expressed and the expresser—existing in a relationship of the delimited and the delimiting (the qualified and the qualifier). It is called a "treatise" because it is "begun" (*ārabhyate*).
By implication, the "purpose" (*prayojana*) therein is the "fruit" (*phala*) of the treatise; such is the meaning.

And this should be understood as stated by relying on the literal sense (*śābdī gatī*). However, according to the implicit logic (*ārtha nyāya*), the purpose of inference—which is the subject matter of this treatise—should be known as the comprehension of imperceptible objects, insofar as it serves the purpose of exposition.
For why else would the author undertake this very exposition of inference?
Since the cognition of an imperceptible object depends upon that [word],
therefore, when one speaks a sentence for the sake of that [cognition], that [word] alone is the meaning of the sentence.
And this will be determined briefly later on by the passage beginning with “[Because the comprehension of an imperceptible object has inference as its basis]” (3.23).
That is the statement of the purpose (*prayojana*). The particle *ca* is used for emphasis and should be understood as following the word "for the sake of engagement" (*pravṛttyarthaṃ*).
The particle *iti* signifies "in this manner."

Some commentators hold that this is the distinction [the word "iti" is to be supplied]. They themselves, introducing another witness who assists that [point], state: "That has been said" (1.20), and so forth.
By the phrase "of someone" (1.21), he includes everything; the meaning is "whether it be small or otherwise.
For this very reason, the word "vā" (or) is used to show that there is no difference from what preceded.

The indeclinable *yāvat* [1.22] denotes a limit (*avadhi*). From the word *noktam* [1.22], the verb *asti* followed by the suffix *bhavantī* (present indicative) should be understood as established in its general sense. *Tāvat*, like the preceding term, denotes a limit.
By whom could that treatise and that activity be undertaken—that is, made into an object of engagement?
Since the interrogative pronoun *kim* is used in a derogatory sense, the meaning is "by no one.
Therefore, it is improper to state the purpose at the beginning of the treatise for the sake of engaging the listener.

One might object: "Surely you have not understood that very intention with which they describe that [activity] for the sake of its engagement; how then can this be refuted? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] reveals their intention with the words beginning with "yataḥ" (1.24).
By the particle *iti* (1.24), he indicates the form of the statement.
Having ascertained that this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) is the means toward that [goal], one would engage in it so that it might come to pass; thus, from the context, [the question arises]:
"What is the use of ascertaining the means for them? To this he says: "anupāya" [1.25].
The term "of the discerning" (*prekṣāvatām*) [2.1] is connected to both sides by way of the maxim of the crow’s eye.
To the question, "Even when there is certainty regarding the means (*upāya*), why does one engage [in it]? he says: "By the desire for that" (*tadarthitayā*), meaning by the longing for that fruit.

To the question, "Where does one engage? he says: "In the hearing of the treatise" (*prakaraṇasya śravaṇam*); by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), reflection (*cintā*) and so forth are also included therein.
The word "iti" (*iti*) is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
"Of that designation" means of the statement regarding its purpose.
"Possession of meaning" (*arthavattā*) means being fruitful; this is what is described by them, as is clear from the context.
If they have described it in such a way with supporting arguments, then it would indeed be excellent; thus he says: "And this is not so. (*na caitad iti*).
The word "co" (ca) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). That designation, which is pregnant with the proof immediately presented hereafter, is not consistent with reason.
"In its means" (*tad-upāye*) means in the means for that purpose.
Its state [2.3] is its being a means;
this is due to the ascertainment of that [2.3].
Consequently, there is engagement with a means for grain and so forth, such as the seed and so on [2.4].
In the word *avadhṛte*, the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇij*) should be understood as being included.
Therefore, it refers to those by whom the state of the seed and so forth has been determined or ascertained.
Even farmers act with prior deliberation regarding seeds and the like; thus, they are cited as examples on the basis of their being discerning persons (*prekṣāvattva*).

One might object: "If, for those seeking a goal (*upeya*), there is a loss of their status as prudent agents (*prekṣāvattva*) when they act without certainty regarding the means (*upāya*), why should there not be such a loss when they act without certainty regarding the goal itself? To this he replies: "But regarding the goal" (*upeye tu*).
The particle *tu* indicates its distinction from the preceding case.
The term "future" (*bhāvini*) is a qualification used in the sense of being the cause.
Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of certainty" (*aniścaye 'pi*), it refers to the "object to be attained" (*upeya*) due to the context.
Since this passage is missing from the manuscript of the *Hetubinduṭīkā*, the word "in the future" (*bhāvini*) has been supplied and was not printed on the indicated page;
nevertheless, that word must certainly be placed there immediately after "but in the case of the object to be attained" (*upeye tu*), in accordance with the *Āloka*. 32. He.

The word "iti" [2.8] indicates the form of a possibility (*sambhāvanā*). This is what is meant: those who act without having ascertained what is ascertainable are to be censured for failing to perform their own duty, but not [those acting toward what is] impossible (*aśakya*).
Regarding the phrase "ascertainment" (*niścayam*):

if it is argued that people will indeed proceed toward this treatise once they have ascertained its status as a means toward a specific purpose and thus desire it, the author says: "And ascertainment" (*niścayaś ca*).
The particle *ca* (and) is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
He asks why this is not the case and says: "[Because of] words" (2.11).
But surely, since there exists a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier, the absence of such a connection is unestablished.
For instance, if the expressive power of the word and the signified power of the object did not exist as real entities (*vastusatī*), then they would be merely human constructs.
Furthermore, if the capacity [of words] were dependent upon human beings, then this observed restriction— that "only the word is the signifier of the meaning,
and only the meaning is the signified,
but the meaning is not the signifier of the word"— would not exist.
Because human desire can proceed unhindered,
there is no loss of restriction;
for even a person who is the author of a convention does not [possess] the expressive power in an object, despite desiring it.
And since a word is capable of conferring the power of being expressed upon its object,

therefore— just as the powers of illumination and being illuminated in the case of a jar and a lamp are real, restricted, and do not experience a reversal of roles— likewise, the power of being expressed and expressing in the case of a word and its meaning is also real and restricted.
If the restriction is propounded with reference merely to the object and the word, then it is unestablished.

For instance, by virtue of convention (*saṃketa*), an object such as a bundle of grass (*tṛṇajūṭa*) is the signifier (*vācaka*) and revealer of another object characterized by the specific action of ownership; likewise, by the power of convention (*samaya*), the word itself certainly becomes the signifier of that object.

For example, in the art of palmistry (*bhūtahastalakṣaṇā*), the fingers beginning with the little finger represent the letters *ka* and so forth, while the lines on their joints represent the vowels *a* and so forth.
Furthermore, for a word as well, there is no so-called "expressiveness" (*vācakatva*) other than the manifestation of meaning and the production of the cognition of that meaning.
Now, if it is argued that the object "jar" is not the expressive [cause] of the word "jar":
Ah!

Who can prevent even that [convention] from having such a status by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*)? As it has been said: "When I show you the object 'pot,' then the word 'pot' must be uttered."
Or else you will know otherwise. In that case, does its being such [as it appears] not exist?
If you are a speaker of truth, you ought not to speak thus; therefore, this is merely something trivial.
Consequently, the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandhābhāva*) is established.
Now, one might object: "There is indeed a necessary connection between a word and the speaker's intention;

and since that intention occurs exactly according to the external reality, who could deny the validity of the word based on this indirect connection with the external world? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"[Regarding] the desire to speak" (2.11), and the particle "api" (2.12) is used in the sense of admitting a specific intention to speak.

The inclusion of the term "restriction" (*niyama*) indicates that [the cognition] occurs in some cases even without exceeding the actual object. Therefore, in the sense of "from that" (*tataḥ*), it means from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, from the word (*śabda*).
This might be the case: those speakers who apprehend an object in accordance with their intention (*vivakṣā*) represent it exactly in that way.

Regarding the statement "they act for the sake of an object," one might suspect: "If there is certainty that the performer's intention will result in exactly such performance, how can there be a lack of certainty? Anticipating this, he says: "For not... (2.13). The particle *hi* means "because.
To explain why there is no rule regarding such performance, he says: "...in case of contradiction" (2.14).
“On the riverbank, a cartload of gravel lies overturned;

come now, let us go!”—even after saying this, one observes that people in the world act otherwise. Thus, because there is no confidence even in the words of every author of treatises, there is an absence of reliance upon them.

Because the purpose (*prayojana*) of the treatise is stated, there arises for those seeking it a doubt regarding whether the subject matter is indeed a means to that purpose; this doubt is a factor for engagement (*pravṛtty-aṅga*).

Consequently, since seekers will engage with the treatise [only when such a doubt exists], the opening statement was spoken to establish a doubt concerning the treatise’s status as a means toward its specific purpose—a point which Dharmottara and others have also demonstrated by implication.
Casting a glance at them, he says: "In the purpose" (*prayojane*), and so forth.
The word "of the treatise" (*prakaraṇasya*) should be connected first. That which has as its object the state of being that, or the means for that, or the fact of being that—such is the meaning.

[3] We have printed the reading "tadupāyatāviṣaye," having conjectured it; however, relying on the Āloka, the reading "tadupāyatāviṣayaḥ" should be adopted. As for the partial expectancy, "Of what is this the means?", it should be understood from the fact that it is heard [in the text] as "of the treatise" (prakaraṇasya) at [2.17]. [At 2.18,] "is produced" (janyate) means "is born" (jāyate).

For this very reason, the ablative case is used before that which has acquired the designation of *apādāna* by the rule "the source (*prakṛti*) of the agent of the verb 'to be born' (*janiḥ*)" [Pāṇini 1.4.30].
This is because doubt arises thereafter [at verse 2.18],
and for the sake of determining the means to ascertain its nature [at verse 2.18].
A farmer is a plowman; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), others besides him are included.
A seed is that which is suitable for producing sprouts and the like.
The opposite of that is "seedless" (*abīja*). For the sake of determining that— that is, for the purpose of its restriction—

the reading of the *Ṭīkā* accepted as authoritative here is "for the determination of the seeded and the seedless" (*bījābījāvadhṛtaye*), and not as it appears in the printed edition, "for the determination of seeds and so forth" (*bījādyavadhṛtaye*).
The word "if" (*cet*) is used everywhere to indicate the opponent's own admission;
"no" (*na*) negates the activity that is intended to be logical.
He states the reason: "because of a purpose" (*prayojane*).
To the question, "In the absence of a statement, how can there be a possibility [of understanding]? he says: "By that which establishes it" (*tatsādhake*). Regarding "that," namely doubt:

having raised the objection—"If its purpose is stated as 'the elucidation of inference' (*anumānavyutpattiḥ prayojanam asya*), then how can the treatise be understood here by a wise person as a means toward that specific purpose when it is still doubted?"—he says:
"From seeing" (*darśanāt*) means from perceiving (*upalambhāt*).
By implication, the meaning should be understood as "from hearing them.
This is the intention of the venerable Ācārya Arcata here: that for one who seeks proficiency and for whom there exists the possibility of a text concerning those means having been heard.

Upon seeing a certain treatise, even without [hearing] such words, one who does not perceive any means of valid cognition— either proving or refuting— the fact that it is a means for the object of his desire, being impelled merely by that desire and suspecting whether it is indeed a means for the object of his desire,
will proceed to engage with that treatise out of a mere wish to know, just as if he were encountering a treatise that lacks an introductory statement.
He will engage in the activity characterized by hearing its recitation and so forth;
otherwise, there would be no engagement with a vast treatise that lacked an introductory statement.
And whatever serves as the basis for engagement in that case will likewise serve as the basis here.
Nor is confidence appropriate even when an introductory statement exists,
for we observe that those who have made one promise proceed to teach something else; as in the case of "atha ataḥ" (or simply "atha").
Having made the promise, "We shall explain *dharma*" [VS 1.1.1], Kaṇāda proceeds to set forth the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthī*).
Therefore, if that initial statement were not described as being for the sake of engaging the audience by generating doubt regarding its subject matter, it would be entirely fruitless;
otherwise, how indeed would a listener be prompted to engage even with the initial statement?
By means of this very same line of reasoning, one may also raise an objection against the system of Dharmottara and others.

For instance: if the subject matter and so forth are stated in the opening sentence in order to produce a doubt regarding the purpose (*artha*) as a necessary factor for engaging with the treatise, and if the fruit of that [treatise] is described precisely because of that production [of doubt], [then...]

If that is so, how is it that listeners engage with that very initial statement? To the question, "In the absence of another statement that expresses the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and other elements of that initial statement," let Dharmottara and others explain:
what is the engagement with the initial statement?
It is its reading, its hearing, and the comprehension of its meaning.

Otherwise, the same objection applies: what is the motivation for engaging with a treatise (*prakaraṇa*)? If it is argued that engagement with it occurs because of the words of an expositor, then what harm is there in the case of a treatise as well?
If you say that his words might also be possible for other reasons, such as for the sake of sport and so forth;
This is the same elsewhere as well:
if one were to proceed with the desire to know [the meaning], the opening statement would be rendered useless;
for by proceeding with the treatise even if it lacked an opening statement, the effort required would be minimal.
In this regard, the reply that "its occurrence is there [in the case of doubt], but not elsewhere" has been refuted.
Therefore, even if one were to go to great lengths, he must ultimately admit this very point which we ourselves maintain; so what is the use of such persistence, and why inflict so many faults?
Showing the actual nature of doubt, he says: "What is this... [2.22].

By the phrase "or nothing at all," the seed for following another [treatise] out of certainty is shown. Having first demonstrated that doubt regarding whether this treatise serves as a means toward a specific purpose— which arises logically prior to its exposition— by means of stating that [purpose], there now follows the doubt as to whether it is a means even with respect to the mere purpose, which is why that [purpose] is stated.

Showing that the engagement with the treatise remains unimpeded even after what has arisen previously, he states the reason for the further elaboration right there with the words "Moreover" (api ca) [2.23].
The phrase "thus for one who desires to know" [2.24] means "from the desire to know" (jijñāsātaḥ).
"Devoid of purpose" (niṣprayojana) means lacking a purpose useful for engagement; its opposite is "possessing a purpose" (prayojanavat).
The word "uta" indicates an alternative position.
By this, [the author] demonstrates that [the treatise] is motivated by the state of being one who acts with prior deliberation (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*).
The purpose has been shown.
The underlying intention is that, in pursuing the question of its utility, it is possible that even the purpose favored by us might be found.
For this very reason, he clarifies: "or by that which is favored by us" [2.24].
By the word *itihā* [2.25], the nature of the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is shown.

[The objection: "The introduction of the opening sentence of the treatise [2.26], which states its purpose, is useless (*vyarthaḥ*), that is, fruitless. Anticipating the question, "If the presentation of the meaning of the sentence is thus useless, then for what purpose was it composed by the author of the *Vārttika*? he demonstrates its utility under the guise of a conclusion with the words beginning with *tasmāt* [2.27].

Because the meaning is connected in this way, for that reason, it is "not undertaken"—that is, it is not commenced or performed; this is the connection according to the respective order. He states the examples for those two things to be proven in that very same order.

The particle *iti* [3.2] expresses the form of the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), which is characterized by the performance and execution of the instrument for that which is to be negated. [3.2] Of one who "opposes" (*pratyavatiṣṭhamānasya*), that is, of one who is making a counter-objection (*pratyavasthānaṃ kurvataḥ*),
there is the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of that [non-apprehension].

The "purpose" (*artha*) is that which constitutes its manifestation and demonstration; this is an adjectival qualification of the act of presentation, meaning "so that it may come to be. It is called the "beginning" (*ādi*) because it is taken from this; [it occurs] therein.
Indeed, it is by taking up this very point again and again that [the arguments] are explained.
One might object: "Since this statement lacks authority regarding an external object, how can one understand its non-establishment through that statement?

If it is argued that a doubt regarding the object arises from another person and becomes a factor for activity, then that very position has already been reached; so what is the use of following this practice of the "ink-smeared rooster" maxim?

To this he replies: It is for the sake of a specific cognizer— one who, when there is a purpose and so forth, necessarily regards the author at the outset as one who acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*) and, not seeing a statement to that effect even from him, understands that the purpose and other factors are inherently included in the fact that [the work] was produced by one who is not lacking in foresight— it is for such a specific cognizer that the author of the *Vārttika* composed this statement beginning with "not made" (*akṛta*) and so forth.
Otherwise, how could he have stated so unequivocally that "if this were purposeless," and so forth?
However, since the engagement of the first [position] proceeds without obstruction according to the principle already stated, everything is perfectly clear.
In this matter, the venerable Arcata’s view is challenged by all those who follow the opinions of Dharmottara and others. We have presented this [position] in such a manner;
whether it is correct or incorrect, the virtuous themselves will discern it with an impartial mind.
Previously, the statement of the purpose was explained in general terms; now, delimiting it specifically, he says "therein" (tatra) [3.5] as an introductory phrase to the sentence.
Since this [purpose] is possible for both the nature of the meaning (*artha*) and the nature of the treatise (*prakaraṇa*), he specifies it as being of the nature of the treatise.
As it has been stated in the *Kāvyālaṅkāra*: "Poetry consists of word and meaning together" [Kāvyā. 1.16].
But how is there an exposition? Anticipating the objection that the purpose of this treatise— consisting of words such as "regarding an object beyond the senses" (parokṣārtha)—

is not established, he begins with the verse starting "according to their respective [objects]" (yathāsvam) [3.6], first presenting the purpose common to all words and then demonstrating how this [treatise] is connected to it.
The meaning of the phrase "that which belongs to whom" (*yasya yadātmīyam*) is as follows:

regarding a sentence [3.6], when a single meaning is to be conveyed as the primary sense, there is a collection of words existing in a relationship of mutual dependence through the medium of their respective meanings, standing in a relation of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*).
The particle *hi* [3.6] is used in the sense of "because."
He says "that very thing does not exist here" with the words "tac ca" (and that).
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "because.
"Of the words" (padānām) refers to the words ending in nominal or verbal suffixes that are contained within subordinate sentences.

In relation to the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) known as the *Hetubindu*, there is a mutual dependence (*vyapekṣā*) among the sentences contained within it by way of their respective meanings. Because of this mutual connection, [the commentary] is designated as the *Hetubinduṭīkā* (from here onwards, the name *Hetubinduṭīkā* should be understood for the printed portion).

[Objection: Even by this much, it is not yet known what the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) here is, that which is to be established in which these [words] function through their mutual connection. To this he says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*). This collection of particles (*nipātasamudāya*) is used everywhere in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
"Is explained" (*vyutpādyate*) means it is established by way of refuting misconceptions (*vipratipatti-nirākaraṇa*). "Thus" (*iti*) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

If that [word] were referred to by the pronoun "that" (tat), then its denotation would have been stated as something to be explained; however, since it is not referred to by the pronoun "that," he says: "of that very [thing]" (tasyaiva) [3.9].
The particle "ca" is used in the sense of "because" (yasmāt).
And it should be understood as a difference in syntactical construction (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: "because there is a connection with that [word], i.e., its acceptance, by means of the word *tat* (that), therefore [it is so] from that connection" [3.9].
Furthermore, following the light of the commentary (*āloka*), the reading of the *ṭīkā* should be: "and of that very [object] by means of the word *tat*."
In the *Mudrita*, however, the reading "tu ca" is omitted.
This might be the case: indeed, this word "tat" (that) is observed to refer back to the primary subject immediately preceding it;
and inference (*anumāna*) pertains to the general [meaning] (*sāmānya*).
[The object] has become subordinate.
How, then, can there be a conceptual apprehension (*parāmarśa*) of it by means of that [subject]? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though... [3.9].
And this collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) is everywhere accepted as denoting a specific meaning;
it is "subordinate" (*guṇībhūta*), that is to say, secondary or non-primary,
because in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, another referent is indeed primary.
[7] Since the manuscript (prati) is missing here in the *Ṭīkā*, the reading "guṇabhūtam" has been established as a conjecture; however, the reading "guṇībhūtam" is supported by the *Āloka*.
Nevertheless, this is stated as a specific qualification (*viśeṣokti*) based on the prior admission [at 3.10].
The "function" (*vṛtti*) of a word is its "activation" (*pravṛtti*), that is, the denotation of an object;
the "contact" (*saṃsparśa*) with that primary [object] means its acceptance, which is to say, its connection.
He says "[of] words" [3.12] because, through a real connection with that [primary object], there would be a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it.

"By way of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) means by its own form, without the intervention of linguistic convention; this is the meaning. Alternatively, thinking, "What is the use of such a great exertion, which is like drawing a sword against a mere gnat? he says "In the case of... (*pakṣe*) and so forth, demonstrating precisely that [intrinsic nature] which is intended as primary.

This is his intention: although it is impossible to reflect upon [the meaning of a compound] when it is subordinate to the sense of the whole compound, nevertheless, because it is the subject under discussion in the treatise as that which is to be explained, it is grasped by a different act of cognition and, being independent, is then reflected upon— just as in the case of the command, "Bring that house which is this."

The realization of the non-erroneous intrinsic nature is to be understood as residing within the mental continuum of the disciple. It must be emphasized that this is "precisely because it is something to be accomplished" (sādhyatvāt).

If this is so, one might ask: what is the purpose of using the causative suffix (*ṇic*) when it should simply have been said, "for the sake of its cultivation"? To this he replies: "Precisely for this reason" (ata eva).

Since the purpose of the treatise is precisely the instruction in inference (*anumānavyutpatti*)—and not otherwise—it is for this reason that its function, namely the expression of its subject matter, is shown. To show what kind of form that [subject matter] has, he says: "In inference" (*anumāne*).

That whose object is the instruction in inference because it is the goal to be accomplished is so described; "to show that" means, in short, to show the activity of the author which has the instruction as its object.

The teacher explains this by implication; he shows that the form "ākāram" belongs specifically to the causative suffix (ṇic). Having supplied the word "pratipādayitum" (in order to demonstrate), the reading of the commentary is completed.
Nevertheless, it is precisely correct to say, "It is shown in accordance with the common usage [of others].
By explaining it in this way, he demonstrates that the treatise functions as the cause for the student's mastery of inference,
because one observes such usage in the world, namely, that "a word conveys its meaning."
And by implication, he intends that the teacher also possesses such a state.
This being the case, the purpose of the instrument for the agent and the listener is also indicated.

Now, if the relationship between the probandum and the probans were not stated, how could there be a cognition of it, by which its purpose might attain fulfillment? To this he says: "And therefore" [3.17].
Since the function of the treatise has been stated to have as its object the instruction in inference (*anumāna*), for that reason—
and because the word "ca" [at 3.17] is stated [to mean] restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and has been explained [as such]—
the sense is that otherwise it would be impossible for the function of the treatise to have that as its object.

But surely, it is said that one speaks in order to convey the meaning residing in the author's knowledge; it is not by means of the uttered nature of the word or the context that its expression must be performed.
For otherwise, one would not be able to convey that meaning.
The operations (*kṛtya*) can be demonstrated;
likewise, the function of the causative context (*prayojaka-prakaraṇa*) here is precisely the denotation of the meaning (*arthābhidhāna*),
and that [function] is what is expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Therefore, the designation of the treatise is precisely its exposition;
consequently, it would follow that this [work] is undertaken solely for the purpose of designating it.
But this is not tenable.

In order to refute the objection that "this [treatise] is commenced for the sake of explaining inference (*anumāna*), and not for the sake of defining it [the word]," he says, "Even though... [3.18], while accepting that point.
The "functioning" (*vṛtta*) of a word means its occurrence, its engagement, or its operation (*vyāpāra*).
The meaning is that, by this verbal logic, the operation of the context (*prakaraṇavyāpāra*) is primary.

This is what is being said: for the operation of the prompter (*prayojakavyāpāra*), which is the object of the word’s derivation, is the primary denotation; therefore, its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) should be understood.
Anticipating the objection, "If this is already accepted, then for what purpose was it stated in this way?", he provides the resolution with the words, "Even so" (*tathāpi*).
"By the actual state of things" (*vastuvṛttena*) means "in consideration of the actual state of things," that is to say, by the objective principle.
He asks: "How is it that, even from the perspective of the actual state of things, derivation (*vyutpatti*) has primacy? and answers with the words "of that" (*tasyāḥ*).
This is the intended meaning: for every activity of an instigator (*prayojaka*) is for the sake of the action of the one being instigated (*prayojya*).
For it has been said: "In the case of the root *pac*, the primary meaning is softening (*viklitti*), with moistening (*vikledana*) being subordinate.

Therefore, the phrase "for the sake of derivation" means "for the sake of derivation [of the word] just like the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*). However, if it were stated as "for the sake of deriving that," then—just as in the case of eating and so forth—it would be understood as having other purposes.

The prompter (*prayojaka*) would be said to be the same [as the agent] in terms of place and so forth, because his activity consists solely in that [the agent’s] purpose; yet, he does have a unique activity (*asādhāraṇa-vyāpāra*). How, then, could this be understood? It is therefore logical to prescribe the suffix *ṇiṅ*.
Having relied upon the verbal mode of cognition (*śābdī gati*) and intending to show that the discourse proceeds by stating the purpose and context of the treatise,
[the author], demonstrating that the portion beginning with "parokṣārtha" expresses its meaning as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*) precisely through the verbal mode of cognition,
says: "parokṣārthe" (3.23).

If the purpose of the treatise has been stated in terms of its verbal form (*śabdātman*), one might suspect that nothing is achieved by stating its purpose in terms of its meaning (*arthātman*); anticipating this, he says: "For not... [3.24].

By explaining in this way through the demonstration of the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), he shows that this sentence is actually engaged in stating the purpose of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) according to the proper method.
The phrase "as in [4.5]" serves to indicate the scope of this which was stated in general terms.

Regarding the word *bhūtam* [in 4.5], it means "true. When the expectation arises as to what that is, although the feminine gender is understood when the word *brāhmaṇī* is uttered, the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is not applied there; the meaning is that this should be seen as applying everywhere.
"Āvapanam" (the sower) is that by which one sows all around; when there is the expectation of "what is it?", the answer is "this," namely, a small leather bag (*uṣṭrikā*) or a basket (*piṭakikā*).

Now, an objection might be raised: since the comprehension of objects beyond the senses relies upon inference, if that [inference] is being explained, then why is verbal testimony (*śabda*) and so forth not also explained, given that it too is a cause for that [comprehension]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By this" (anena) [refers to] the statement that the comprehension of that [object] is based on a logical mark possessing the three characteristics; "and" (ca) has the sense of "because."
"Having become a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇabhūtā*) means having the nature of a means of valid cognition, that is to say, non-erroneous.

Why is it stated thus? He says: "from another" (*anyasmāt*). This is because it is impossible for there to be a non-erroneous comprehension of an imperceptible object—that is, a comprehension of the object from another source than the aforementioned three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), since such a source would not be employed.
If there were no restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), from where would this meaning arise? To this he says: "From restriction" (*avadhāraṇāt*) means "from the rule" (*niyamāt*).
The particle "iti" shows the form of the restriction.
"Thence" (*tataḥ*) is because the comprehension of an imperceptible object depends precisely upon inference.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and so forth is intended;
that is to say, provided that they possess the status of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) as inference (*anumāna*) by a manner other than what has been stated.
"Of these" refers to those [means of knowledge], such as verbal testimony and the rest.

It might be argued: "Even a cognition of an imperceptible object that does not arise from a logical mark (*aliṅgaja*) may be non-deviant; so how is it that words and the like possess such validity even though they are means of knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*), [verse 4.13].
By the word "all" (*sarva*), he demonstrates the inclusion of everything without exception.
"Independent" (*svatantrā*) means self-reliant, that is to say, not dependent on a logical mark (*liṅga*). He states the reason for this with the words "of that" (*tasyāḥ*):
that which is determined by it is its own object (*svārtha*).
"Let it not be that it is non-contradictory; why then should it not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
He replies: "Non-contradiction (*aviṣaṃvādana*) is the state of being non-deceptive (*aviṣaṃvādakatva*)."
That which has that very characteristic as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—the state of being so is reality (*tattva*); therefore [4.15].

The root text accepted by Āloka reads "because it has non-contradiction as its characteristic" (*avisaṃvādanalakṣatvāt*), and not as printed—"because it has non-contradiction as its characteristic" (*avisaṃvādalakṣaṇatvāt*).
This is because an independent [definition] would be untenable.
"It will arise from something else; what does it matter that it is an inference?

[The author replies: "For the property of being a *pakṣadharma* (a property of the subject) alone is not the defining characteristic (*rūpa*) of a logical mark (*liṅga*), such that its offspring would necessarily possess that same nature. Thus he says: "Even in another case" [4.15], meaning "from that which is unrelated" [4.16], i.e., from that which is not connected to the intended object of proof (*siṣādhayiṣita*).
[10] Since this portion is missing here, we have supplied it with "yadi syāt" (if there were).
Following the *Āloka*, the reading "yadi syāt" should be supplied to connect the text.
Let it be that there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), but not the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Then, fearing that even a word or other sign which possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) would not be inference—because it does not have the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) yet leads to the unerring cognition of an imperceptible object—he says: "Even when there is no connection with the subject" (4.16).
If this is so, let it be that the cause of that cognition also possesses the property of being a characteristic of the subject.
He asks, "What follows from this? and replies: "In this way" (evam) [4.18].
That which is of such a form [11] is connected with the probandum (*sādhya*) and connected with the specific property (*viśiṣṭadharma*).
The particle "iti" indicates the reason (*hetu*).
"Entirely" (sarvā) means all-inclusive; "not divided" (na bhidyate) means it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is the reading accepted as the "light" (*āloka*).
"Sevambhūtaḥ":
the word "iti" is used here to indicate the completion of the sentence's meaning;
however, where it refers to a specific meaning, that is generally stated.
It might be argued: "This meaning you have explained is contrary to the sūtra; this was not what the Teacher intended here. To this he says: "And this" (4.19).

The word "and" (ca) [in 4.20] has the sense of "because. Now, one might object: "Surely, because of the connection with the subject at hand, this meaning is desired [by the Teacher]; [otherwise, in the context of the ultimate view, this meaning would be irrelevant]."
Thus he says: "the thesis" (pakṣa) [4.20].
And "only pervaded" (vyāpta eva ca) [4.22] is an emphatic restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) joined with the preceding.
At the beginning, he himself gave birth to two sons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa alone.

Thus, the intention is as follows: "Even when it is not employed, its meaning is understood through the speaker's intention," and because of the restriction expressed by those who say, "from the determination [of the speaker's intent]. (4.22)
Since the inclusion of the word "object" (*artha*) is possible even in the phrase "for the purpose of explaining that," he says "here" (*atra*). The reading is:
"In this case, there is the inclusion of the word 'object'. [The variant is:
"With the inclusion of the word 'object'."

The word *itiḥ* [4.24] indicates the form of the term; "having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object" means having a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, not having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object— this is the implied meaning.
How is it that by stating that inference has an object as its domain, it is said that its object is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)? He says: "In the object" [4.25].
He says "For this very reason" [4.26] in order to show that the Teacher’s statement is consistent only in this way and not otherwise;
that is, precisely because the validity of inference has the particular as its object.
The intention is that it would have been stated as a specific qualification—“otherwise, there would be no establishment of perception”—rather than in general terms.

In this regard, since validity has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, it cannot be established by another mode, namely, by having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, in respect to that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). [4.27]
The point is that it is not logical for activity directed toward one object to arise from a cognition whose object is something else, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
[Objection: But surely even a universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity (*vastu*).

He says—“of the universal” [5.1]—because activity would be justified solely by the desire for that specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). By the word “also” (*api*) [5.1], he shows the acceptance of its being a real entity (*vastutva*). He says—“and of that” [5.2]—to show that activity will occur toward that very same causal efficiency.

"At its very arising" (tadutpattāv eva) means precisely at the arising of the cognition that has the universal as its object (*sāmānyālambana*). [The opponent objects: "In that case, since the universal 'cowness' (*gotva*) is perceived precisely through the desire for purposeful action such as riding or milking, one will act toward that universal. To this he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*).
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.
He states the reason with the words "of that" (*tasya*).
The intended meaning is that, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), its operation is determined to reside in that [object] alone.

[14] Because there is no relation other than the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for that which exists as distinct, namely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, [the author] says "[because it is not assisted]" (*anupakāryatayā*).
[15] [The variant reading is] "by way of not assisting" (*anupakārakatvena*).
Having even granted the existence of a relationship, he now says: "Even when [it exists]" (5.5).
The word *ca* (5.5) is used for the conjunction of another point to be stated.

Since it would follow that even one seeking smoke would have a cognition of fire (*dhūmadhvaja*) upon the cognition of smoke, this is an "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*), meaning a logical consequence that transgresses what is desired; for that reason.
"Undetermined" (*anavasita*) means not ascertained;

"by whom there is distinction" (*viveka*)—that is, otherness—refers to such a person [5.6]. To the question "Why is there precisely that lack of ascertainment? he says: "Of inherence" (*samavāyasya*) [5.3].
For it is the view of the Naiyāyikas and others that the universal (sāmānya) is connected by way of inherence (samavāya).
[The phrase] "due to the determination of that universal" (5.7) means due to its superimposition (samāropa).
"Therein" (tatra 5.7) refers to the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
[16] The reading is "regarded as light because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that. (Note: *avasāyāt* in manuscript S).
Now, what is intended by this "subtlety" (*sūkṣmatva*) of inherence (*samavāya*)? If it means possessing a particular dimension (*parimāṇa-viśeṣa*),...
That is not possible for it.
Furthermore, even if its lack of a form capable of producing a cognition were the case, then because of that very absence, let it simply not be perceived;
however, it is not tenable to claim that there is no perception of the distinction between the universal and its cause by virtue of its possessing such a nature.

Nor is it the case that inherence (*samavāya*) is not perceived, because in the view of the Naiyāyikas its perception is accepted by way of its being a qualifier of that which is inherent, and because that view is what is being questioned here. This is not so, however, due to a failure to understand the intended meaning.
For here, the subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) of inherence (*samavāya*) is intended to mean its incapacity to be perceived as distinct from the two relata of inherence (*samavāyin*).
This indeed is the greatness of inherence, by which it does not cause the two relata to be perceived as distinct, like [the perception of] a cloth and its threads;
otherwise, any other explanation would be mere temerity.
To this, the rebuttal is: "In that case, then... [5.7]. He says: "Since you too must necessarily admit error here, let there be only error" [5.8].

For conceptual construction, bound by two types of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), while cognizing its own appearance as excluded from non-cows, [also cognizes] the external object as being excluded from non-cows.

Being unable to penetrate the distinction [between the particular and the universal], one conceives the thought, "I have perceived an external cow"; thus, by its very nature, it arises as a form of error.

Error itself is mere error (bhrāntimātra), for it is devoid of any real universal (sāmānya) and is accepted as being based on its own momentary particular (svakṣaṇa) and as the basis for inferential cognition.
And because it exists between those two and is useless, it is like a goitre (*gaḍu*)—a mass of flesh situated between the forehead and the skull;

thus it is "goitre-like" (*gaḍurūpa*). By that [conceptual construction], which is accepted as having that [external object] as its object, what [is achieved]? The meaning is: nothing at all, according to the context.

This is his intention: if conceptual construction were unable to engage the world by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object, and if even upon accepting that [unification], error were not the cause for engagement.
In that case, a universal (*sāmānya*) might indeed be useful for such activity,

provided it were established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, even if accepted like a goitre (*gaḍu*) as being useless, one would still desire to act upon it once it has been so accepted.
To the extent that all of this is indeed impossible:
surely, the superimposition of one thing upon another without a basis is not tenable;
and there is no cause whatsoever for the superimposition of a conceptual appearance of a recurring form upon individuals that are entirely distinct from one another.
With the intention of showing how the postulation of activity through delusion is superior, he says: "In the absence of a seed" (5.8).
The answer is: "Those very [particulars]" (5.9).

Those individuals which have arisen in such a way from their own causes produce a single effect—such as the cognition of an object or a single reflective awareness—by virtue of the capacity of their own causes; those [individuals] are "those which have that [single effect]."

This is what is meant: by the exclusion of what does not produce that effect, the fact of producing that single effect—which is common to all members of the same class—is present in those [individuals]. Why should this not be the seed for the superimposition of a corresponding form upon the appearance in cognition?
It might be argued: even though the individuals are of such a nature due to their commonality in producing that single effect, they are nonetheless established as the seed for such an error.

Considering that there is no evidence whatsoever for our position—that [the universal] is a generality—he says "[in the case of] color" (varṇe) in order to uproot the mutual designation of them as universals.
"Color" (varṇa) refers to white and so forth;
"shape" (ākṛti) refers to configuration, which is a particular kind of conjunction.

That which has a common, non-distinct form or appearance (*ākāra*) from those two is described as such. This means it has an appearance identical to color and an appearance identical to shape; that is to say, an appearance of color and an appearance of shape.
This is because the universal (*sāmānya*) is dependent upon color and shape.
He states that it is not illogical for the cognition of that [object] to be likewise [of that nature], saying: "And not... [5.11].
"That form" [5.11] refers to a form endowed with color and shape. As it has been said:
"Indeed, 'cowness' is described as being devoid of the forms of color, shape, and syllables" [PV 2.147].
Therefore,

that which appears as being associated with color and shape would be the seed— that is, the basis— for the error regarding another thing that is actually endowed with that color and shape; the point is that nothing else could be so.

Even if there is indeed a dissimilarity between the universal (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) due to their association with color and other qualities, one might ask: why does the universal not serve as the basis for error in that case? To this he says: "In the case of similarity" (*sādṛśye*). For there is indeed a certain kind of error which occurs when an internal disturbance is possible; intending this, he says "by others" (*paraiḥ*). If this is so, one might ask: what is the similarity between the external object and the universal appearing in cognition, by virtue of which an error arises? To this he says: "The individuals" (*vyaktayaḥ*).

[17] That cognition which has a universal as its object possesses an aspect (*ākāra*) that is a form excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*). [5.13] The phrase "excluded from what is of a different class" [5.12] is a qualification used in the sense of a reason;
thus, the meaning is "because it is excluded from what is of a different class.
Alternatively, the intention is that the appearance in cognition manifests precisely by way of being turned away from what does not possess that [universal's] nature.
[17] The reading is "ālokasammataḥ sāmānyālambanajñānākārasarūpāḥ"; in manuscript S it is "sāmānyākārajñānasvarūpāḥ". [18] The reading is "ālokasammataḥ vijātīyavyāvṛttāḥ".
"Excluded from those of a different class.

Having demonstrated that even those such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*) must necessarily accept, according to the aforementioned principle,
that the validity of inference has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, [the author] now addresses the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
He begins with the words "by which... [5.16] and so forth.
