The particle *tu* [5.16] has the sense of specification (*viśeṣa*).
It is the universal (*sāmānya*) appearing in inference that is the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*).

The intention [of the opponent] is that since that [object] is the very nature of the individual (vyakti), its validity necessarily falls within the domain of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Anticipating the objection that "if this is so, then this view is as excellent as your own," he says: "In the case of the particular characteristic" (svalakṣaṇe).

[This is because] there is the undesirable consequence that, just as in sensory perception, it would appear [in consciousness] from a word as well, due to being produced by the proximity of that [particular] location.

The point is this: if the manifestation were not perceived, then since that would entail the uselessness of the visual faculty and so forth, how could the universal—which is of the nature of that manifestation—possibly appear?

Now, one might object: "If inference is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then how is it distinct from perception? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "[19] 'Inconceivable' (*parokṣa*).
The word "but" (*tu*) shows that inference is indeed distinct from perception.
[19] Since the manuscript of the *Saṃjñakahetubinduṭīkā* is fragmentary here, the absence of the root text (*mūlapāṭha*) is to be understood.
The meaning is: because [the sign] does not arise directly from the object, it requires a mark (*liṅga*) in order to arise, and it does not directly perceive the object; therefore.
The existence of "being" (sati-bhāva) has the sense of a substratum.
It might be thought: if its object is also a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), then there must be another universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
[Otherwise], the *Nyāyabindu*—which states that "this is the object of inference" (NB I)—would be contradicted; thus he says: "that very [thing].
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because.
To the question, "How can it be stated in such a way? he replies: "it is characterized."

The meaning is as follows: "Generality" (*sāmānya*) is that which has exclusion from what is not its own form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*) as its definition and as its designator—that is, of the real entity (*vastu*) excluded from what is not its own form.
Furthermore, those very particulars (*bheda*), when their distinctions have not been analyzed, are the generality; this is the sense.
The phrase "fear of repetition" (*punar uktāśaṅkā*) should be understood as the fear of repetition in terms of meaning (*arthapunaruktāśaṅkā*).
Because there is no possibility of suspecting a verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*) precisely due to its direct perception [in that context],
for tautology is indeed of two kinds.
Verbal tautology occurs when the very same meaning is expressed by another word in the absence of a desire to specify a distinction or similar purpose.
Verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*), however, occurs precisely when that same word is uttered again in the absence of a desire to state something further (*vidhitsā*) and so forth.

When there is a desire to state a distinction and so forth, that very [repetition] becomes twofold, consisting of the nature of a restatement of meaning (*arthānuvāda*) and a restatement of words (*śabdānuvāda*).
If it is argued that, in that case, there would be a lack of skill on the part of the Teacher (*ācārya*) in the *Vārttika* and other works:
No; for that [work] was composed with reference to those of dull intellect.
The suffix *tas* should be understood as following the instrumental case-ending of *pramāṇena*.
The analysis of the compound is: "the instruction of persons by means of the ascertainment of that [object], that is, by means of the ascertainment of its distinctions."
The phrase "the exposition of the divisions" is to be connected [to the previous].

Furthermore, the division is to be seen as twofold: by way of the distinction between non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and so forth, and by way of the nature of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.
If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines the distinctions such as the effect (*kārya*) and so forth has been stated here, [then...]

Anticipating the objection that, in that case, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated to determine the specific nature of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, he says "threefold" (*trividha*). That is,
by way of the three modes consisting of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
"Of that which is distinguished by excellence," meaning that which has attained differentiation;
and it is precisely because of this designation that we have explained it in that manner here regarding "this subdivision," for otherwise it would not be consistent.
This might be the case: there would be an exposition of the nature of inference characterized by the mark (*liṅga*) if the definition were indicated as the object to be defined (*lakṣya*).
Furthermore, there would be a distinction [of categories] only if there were an explicit definition (*nirdeśa*) of it;
however, since no such term exists here, he says: "when the threefold classification has been established.

Thus, it should be understood that this is merely a demonstration of the definition for the sake of others, and not a presentation of a prescription of the definiendum (*lakṣya*) by way of restating its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The word "hetu" (reason) refers back to the definiendum (*lakṣya*), while the definition (*lakṣaṇa*)—namely, "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth—is that which is to be enjoined and understood.
By the particle "iti," the form of the restriction is shown. The mention of "existence" (*bhāva*) serves as an indicator for what is to be established.
Therefore, the meaning is "in regard to entities" (bhāva), that is, those things which are denotable;
it would not be so in regard to non-entities (abhāva).
In this context, however, introducing Kumārila as a witness for his assistance, he says: "It has been stated."
The persistence of cognition is its continuity, which is to say its stability or its state of being a continuous stream.
However, where the cognition of the absence of opposing factors, though arisen once, is not firm—
He indicates this by the phrase "not there, as has been determined," because [it pertains to] a portion (or factor) of the existence of the sense faculty.
It is not conjunction itself;
by the word "conjunction," a relationship is intended,
but not merely a quality such as action belonging to one of the two factors.
Because it would follow that universals and the like could not be perceived.
To the question "Why is that [the sense organ] also [not capable of perceiving them]?", he says: "Because of its capacity.
According to the Mīmāṃsaka view, the sense organ is capable when it is connected with the positive aspect (bhāvāṃśa) [of the object].

The meaning is that a relation is possible only when [the object] exists. "Having that as its object" (*tadviṣaya*) means that which has that as its object; the state of being so is "thatness" (*tattā*).
In response to the expectation "Of what is this?", he says: "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*).
He asks "Why? and says: "Because of the object," etc.
It is "contradictory" and "unestablished" in four ways, that is, by four modes.
For [it is said in the Ślokavārttika, Abhāva 18]: "The connection with the positive aspect alone [is the cause], such as the suitability of the sense organ. [20]
He says "therein" (*tatra*) because that [reason] will serve as its proof precisely by way of being non-common (*asāmānyatayā*).
That whose nature (*svabhāva*) is the form (*rūpa*) mentioned [in verse 6.9] is "of such a kind.
What is to be expressed is the form already mentioned—that is, introduced—as having the characteristic of being associated with a single cognition and possessing equal capacity.
He says that another reason (*hetvantara*) will likewise be so, anticipating this with the words "yadi" [6.9].
The particle *hi* [6.9] has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
It follows from the context that "it would be of such a nature" (*syāt tathārūpam*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), time (*kāla*) is included;
the intended meaning is "like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*).
This mode [of proof] is characterized by cause and effect, as well as by the pervaded and the pervader.
Therefore, because of the absence of the relation of cause and effect and so forth,
those two— namely, the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the pervader—
it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to have existence when its causes are complete; such is the meaning.
This is the method:
[22] "That" — S {p.
253} — now, having admitted the possibility of these [entities], he provides the refutation: "And if there were possibility... [6.14] 5. Thus.

[23] To the question, "How is this restriction established?", and anticipating the objection, "Why is this 'unaccomplished' state being mentioned when it is not a factor for establishing the restriction?", he says: "He thinks thus" (6.18).
That is, what is about to be stated.
Here, in verbal discourse (*vāṅmaya-vyavahāra*),
by its opposite (*tadviparyayeṇa*)— that is, by the opposite of that which is being restricted—
and by the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of its counter-correlate (*tadvipakṣasya*)— the counter-correlate of the object of that restriction.
[6.21] When it exists:
by the perception of that which is contradictory to the nature of the probans (*hetu*)—namely, the state of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsatva*)—which is what is to be negated.
[6.25] But surely, one who desires the cognition of the characteristics of a reason as they have been stated...
One may understand the nature of the reason itself;
however, how is their contradiction understood through their mutual exclusion? To this he says: "tadātme" [7.1].

Because of that cognition—the awareness or perception of the appearance restricted to the nature (ātman) of that reason—one understands by implication that which is its opposite as being other than it, that is, as not having that nature.
And this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Its appearance as such is due to the ascertainment [of that appearance] through the force of its cognition.
Therefore, he asks "What happens from that? and says: "Mutually" (*parasparam*).

It might be argued as follows: there is no apprehension of contradiction with anything whatsoever regarding an absolutely non-existent alternative cause, by virtue of which the cognition of its absence would arise from the perception of a contradictory factor. Furthermore, in that case, how could causality—which is absolutely non-existent—be negated? Anticipating these two prior positions (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: "And those... (7.4).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Nor should it be connected with the idea that the causal status being negated by him is accepted as being absolutely non-existent.
Then, what is the reality here? He says: "merely" (*kevalam*).

Elsewhere—in the effect and so forth—it is well-known and certain; however, due to delusion or ignorance, it is superimposed upon that object which lies outside the three types of causes, and established as existing.
"Śaṅkita" means that which has become the object of doubt, namely, "does it exist or not? Therefore, it is asked: "Why is it being manifested through its own capacity?
Since this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), one should also consider how its negation is established.

[Objection: Is it not the case that one must first understand how the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) in another reason ceases because of the presence of the state of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsatva*), so that its contradiction by this [present reason] may be stated? To this he says: "And not... (7.8).
Now, even while accepting absolute non-existence, he speaks in order to demonstrate the absence of any fault: "Nor also... (7.10).

Anticipating the objection, "But how is it that there is no comprehension of that very thing in that very place? he says: "For not... (na hi). Fearing that a contradiction might be perceived there, he asks, "How is there absolute [non-existence] of that which exists elsewhere? and replies: "Everywhere" (sarvatra).
[24] Here, the reading is uncertain;
however, in accordance with the context, it is understood as: "But there is contradiction everywhere.
The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of things (*vastu*) is their distinct form.
"That which has this as its purpose" is thus [stated].
The collective meaning is that the very cognition of a fixed form is, for him, simultaneously the cognition of its contradiction with everything else.
[7.15] This is technical (lākṣaṇika).
The movements of those of evil intellect have been explained;
regarding them, concluding the section, he says: "Thus it stands" (iti sthitam etat).
The word *iti* refers back to the manner of reasoning just mentioned.

The word *iti* [7.20] shows the form of the intended object as it has been made the object of an intention. Because there is a duality of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it was stated [in 7.25], "by which of the two," when both display an indeterminate form. By the word *upagata* ("accepted"), he expresses superimposition (*āropa*).

With the intention that the affirmation of the remainder is obtained through the negation of specific alternatives, he says: "Even though the presence of the property in the subject (pakṣadharmatā) exists" [7.27].

To the question, "Granted that there is an absence of inseparable connection (avinābhāva), why is it a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa)? he replies: "Because of the absence of inseparable connection" [8.2].

[The author], by means of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*)—that is, a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—now excludes this proof [from the category of fallacies] by specifying its name, saying "iti" (thus), and so forth.
But how is it that the very absence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) constitutes a failure of proof? To this he says: "And the absence of inseparable connection" (8.5).

Regarding those things distinct from the [five categories] beginning with intrinsic nature (svabhāva), [the phrase] "by the non-perception of the pervader" (vyāpakānupalabdhyā) means by the non-perception of the pervader that will be described later. As for the question "Why is there precisely that non-perception of it? he says: "In three ways" (trividhe).
The point is that, since it would necessarily be included within one of the three types [of valid cognition] if it were to exist, it could not possibly be distinct from them.

He asks: "How does one establish its existence through the non-perception of its pervader? and answers: "For instance" (tathāhi), [verse 8.6], meaning "either by way of identity (tādātmya) or by way of origination (tadutpatti)."
This is what is intended;
it is not by means of both [factors] alone.
Therefore, "arising from that" (*tad-utpatti*) should be understood as intended to mean either arising from that [cause] or the arising which has that [cause] as its cause.

He asks, "How is there a pervasion of that by those two? and answers with the words "[of those two]" (tayoḥ) [8.7]. In that context, "[therein]" (tatra) [8.7] means in the case of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*);
"[of that]" (tasya) [8.8] means of that inseparable connection.
[The effect exists] only when those two exist.
Why does its existence depend on those two alone?
Furthermore, why is it that it does not exist otherwise? To this he says: "Because it does not have that as its intrinsic nature" (atatsvabhāvasya).

By the negation of arising from what was previously mentioned, it should be understood that "for whatever there is no arising from something, or for whatever reason there is no arising from that cause, because of its not arising from that" (8.8). Here, with the desire to abandon the notion of independence, he introduces the Vārttika, saying: "This has been stated" (8.9). It might be argued: "It is observed that there is an invariable concomitance of one thing with another that is neither of the same nature nor arisen from it, such as the concomitance of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth with taste (*rasa*) and so forth. To this he says: "With color-form and so forth" (8.15).
Thus:
"The inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of taste and so forth" means its non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*).
To the question "By what?", he says: "By color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), touch and so forth are included.

By stating "only its arising from that cause" (*tatkāraṇotpattir eva*) [in verse 8.16], he clarifies that by the term "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), two types [of causes] were intended previously.
He confirms this very point with the words "otherwise than this" (*etad evānyathā*) [in verse 8.17] and so forth.

The absence of a distinction (*viśeṣābhāva*) is unestablished; thus, the author raises an objection with the words beginning “ekārtha” [8.19], intending that the very fact of inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāyitva*) constitutes the distinction.

Regarding the term *ekārthasamavāya*, there are two possible etymological analyses (*vyutpatti*): either "inherence in one object" (*ekasminn arthe samavāyaḥ*) or "the inherence of one object" (*ekārthasya samavāyaḥ*).

But here, what is intended is that there is a co-inherence (*samavāya*) of two things in a single object; that which is the cause of such inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is described as such. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), about to offer a rebuttal, raises an objection with the words "Now, [8.20]..."

In passages such as, “Inherence is that relation which, being the cause of the cognition ‘it is here,’ pertains to things that are inseparably established and stand in the relation of the supported and the support” (*Praśastapādabhāṣya* p. 696), it is described by including the terms "supported" and "support.
To the question, "Let it be so for those two; what is the harm? he says: "And that... [8.20].
Because of which [reason]:
since it would entail the fault of over-extension (*atiprasakti*) regarding the nature of that which is intended to be the denotable object (*abhidheya*), it is not established;

for the status of being a substratum (*ādhāra*) by means of performing functions such as abiding and so forth has been refuted elsewhere—this is the sense. The particle *iti* [8.21] indicates the reason.
This was stated having accepted the existence of inherence (*samavāya*);
however, now demonstrating that such [inherence] does not exist at all, he says: "[27] And just as... and so forth.
Furthermore, in the phrase "and in the case of identity" (*tādātmye*), it should be construed precisely with "together with that" (*tena saha*).

[27] Since this portion is missing from the manuscript, the reading has been supplied by conjecture as “-samavāyo ’vaseyaḥ. However, according to the context, it should rather be: “-samavāyo ’vaseyaḥ / yathā ca samavāyaḥ.”
[28] Or rather—S {p.
256} those things which are the very nature of entities (*vastu-svabhāva*) are such that they are non-deviating from being thus; if so, what do they do? To this he says: "merely" (*kevalam*).
"Perceivers" [9.3] refers, according to the context, to those who discern the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things as they truly are.
The word "akasmāt" signifies "without cause"; therefore, the meaning is that arising "without cause" (*akasmāt*) means being causeless.
Thus [9.4], for that reason, the intrinsic nature of no thing whatsoever could ever cease.
The meaning is that everything would have the nature of everything else.

However, for the proponent who maintains that there is no restriction of place or time for an existent that is causeless—just as in the case of [the directions] space and so forth—the mention of "place and time" should be understood as being for the sake of an illustration.
By this, the meaning is that just as there is no restriction of place or time for that which lacks a cause, likewise there would also be no restriction of substance.
He establishes this very point with the words "For that indeed is that" (9.5) and so forth:

because that indicative thing (*vastu*), acting as the agent, might be presented in some locus (*dharmī*) as something to be cognized—either as fire or as not fire—or it might be the opposite of that. (9.5)
Regarding the statement, "Of which object, in whatever that is to be understood, some substance is dependent or not," its explanation is "not dependent.
In the printed edition, the reading is correctly completed as "in some cases" (*kvacid*).
Having stated it by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he establishes it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth.
In the printed edition, the reading is completed as "tataḥ."
Regarding the phrase "stretching out the feet" [9.9],
this should be understood as an illustration of remaining in a state of ease;
the actual reason must indeed be stated.
But he says "And that" [9.10] to show that this is not what you intend;
"iti" [9.10] means "therefore"; "deficient in that" [9.11] means lacking inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
Connecting this very point with the words of the Teacher, he says: "And so it has been said" [9.11].

This might be the case: even in the absence of an essential identity (*tatsvābhāvya*) or a causal relationship (*tatkāryatva*), some other entity (*arthāntara*) is indeed observed to be non-deviant, such as the shadow of a tree in relation to the heat of the sun, or the lowering and raising of the near side of a scale in relation to the lowering and raising of its far side.
Thus, this has been explained in detail by us in the *Dharmottarapradīpa*; let it suffice for now.

It might be argued: "The cause for the non-deviation of inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) from identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) is not, first of all, identity and causality themselves;

for if that were so, then just as this [instance] is such, any other [instance] would also be non-deviant from it, yet it would neither possess its nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*) nor be its effect (*tatkāryatva*)."
To this it is replied:

that which is called "inseparable concomitance" (*avinābhāva*) is not something distinct from the nature of that which possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and is inseparable;

it is merely described as if distinct from it by virtue of some particular perspective. However, for that reason, it is not actually distinct in reality. Furthermore, the nature of that which is inseparable is not some separate entity distinct from the non-deviating [cause].
There is no difference in meaning [between the two types of relation];
for that [effect], the necessary connection exists precisely by virtue of being its effect, whereas for the non-different [identity], it exists by virtue of identity (*tādātmya*).
Precisely because of this existence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the conventional usage of "identity" and "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*) is established.
But when that [cause] is absent, it is established that even that form does not exist; thus, everything is clear.
In this regard, [at 9.15], for this purpose, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is a proof-statement consisting of two members.
However, in the case of the theory of production from that (*tadutpatti*), there is also the phrase "and by its cause."

This might be thought: "Just as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), even in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), is non-deviant from the probandum (*sādhya*), why should another [reason] not be so as well? Anticipating this, he says "in its own nature" (*svabhāve*). The intention is that it is because it establishes the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahārayogyatā*). That which has identity as its characteristic or basis is described as such.
Showing that this too is the Master’s intended view, he says: "As it has been said" (9.22).

Now, wishing to explain this very verse beginning with "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) in another way, he says—"Thus, therefore" (9.25)—in order to enumerate all the points indicated by this [verse].
[31] *Tasya* refers to the logical justification (*upapatti*) for that restriction of number (*saṃkhyāniyama*).

“And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that demonstrates it”—this is the reading accepted by Āloka as “and its logical proof. Showing yet another way of explaining this verse, he says: “Alternatively, [9.28]...”
Previously, however, [the text] was intended to be focused on prescribing a definition by way of restating the object to be defined (*lakṣya*);
it was not made with the intent of considering a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*). Therefore, this present explanation is distinct from that.
With the thought, "How is this restrictive determination justified?", he asks.
What is the reason? It is because of the context here. He asks "what" as a general inquiry regarding the reason.

With the intention of providing a concise (śliṣṭa) explanation, he says "because of the existence of inseparable connection" (avinābhāva), and then states "and of the threefold [reason]" (trividhasya).

For when it is stated that "because of the restriction due to the necessity of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), and upon the question "of what?", since the threefold [reason] has been mentioned, it is appropriate to say "of the threefold. Thus, by means of this twofold restriction— [namely, the restriction of the reason to the three types and the restriction of the three types to the necessity of inseparable connection]— it is established.
He says "by that" (tena) [10.3] to show what specific excellence is revealed by the explanation already given.
The two words "also" (api) have the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Thus, this is what is being stated:
Therefore, those who apply the conventional designation of "reason" (hetu) to things excluded from the three types of reasons are refuted.
Why? Because of the absence of inseparable connection (avinābhāva).
Furthermore, those who declare the threefold reason to be non-reason (ahetu) are likewise refuted.
Why? Because here the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) necessarily exists [10.8]. The reading accepted as "light" (*āloka*) is correct, and not as it has been completed.

[34] The state of being causeless (*ahetutva*)—in this commentary, while formulating the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) to explain the statement "the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those," he says [35]: "And thus this... [10.11]. For the absence of pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is twofold: because of the pervasion of the opposite (*viparyayavyāpti*), and because of the absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite. With this intention, he says "regarding the opposite" [10.17], and so forth.

Those [reasons] established in the intellect—namely the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—are indeed understood as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) due to their deficiency in the characteristics of a valid reason.
However, the mention of "unestablished" and so forth is merely a restatement of their actual nature;
there is no purpose in designating them by those specific names once they have been recognized as such.
Because the purpose is fulfilled by the mere knowledge of their being causes;
or even if they are known as "wisdoms" (*prajñā*), there is no fault whatsoever.
Regarding this, it is said: S.
Establishing this very point by way of demonstrating a general principle, he says: "For instance" (tathāhi) [10.19].
In this explanation as well, making a distinction between the meanings presented through the relationship of constituent parts and the whole, he says: "In that regard" (tad atra) [10.27].
Of those two, the threefold reason alone—

The reason for these two restrictions—namely, that "the cause is indeed threefold" and "there are two types of proof"—is because of the meaning of the word *śliṣṭa*, which is connected with both the genitive and the locative cases;
this is indicated by the statement: "due to the necessity of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)."
The three meanings just mentioned, together with these two meanings characterized by the two causes and the two presumptive implications (*arthāpatti*), constitute six meanings.
In this very verse, without abandoning the previous explanation, he offers another interpretation by way of repetition, saying "furthermore" (*kiñca*) [11.4].
Now, in the first explanation itself, it was said: "in three ways indeed... (*trividhaiva* / *tridhaiva*).

By stating, “This is the exposition of the divisions,” it has already been made clear that this reason is threefold, being divided by the distinctions of effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); if one asks,
“How then is this a different explanation?”— that is true.

Regarding the statement "only 'in three ways indeed is he' [is the case]," this alternative explanation (*vyākhyānāntara*) is to be formulated; and that becomes well understood if it is presented after first showing its previously established explanation. With this intention, that previous explanation has been restated. However, with reference to this, one should understand that the alternative explanation which is shown by the word "or" (*athavā*), illuminating the sense of the particle "moreover" (*kiñca*), is precisely what constitutes this alternative explanation.
This distinction should be understood as being precisely the same as the distinction between "not abandoning the effect" (*ajahatkārya*) and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning is this: each [reason] is indeed threefold in nature—consisting of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—and is differentiated by the distinctions of "effect" (*kārya*) and so on.

By this, having rejected six positions through the exclusion of one or two terms, he demonstrates that the author of the *Vārttika* intends the definition of inference by adopting the seventh position.
Since there are three positions by the inclusion of one term and also three by the inclusion of two terms, making six;
by the exclusion of those, the seventh [position] is established.
[This is] for the purpose of inclusion.

For if it were stated simply that "the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is the reason" (*hetu*), then even that which lacks concomitance with the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and occurs in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) would be a reason;
for example: "Sound is eternal because it is produced."

If it were stated that "it is that which has positive concomitance (anvaya) in the similar class (sapakṣa)," then a reason that functions in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) and is not a property of the subject (apakṣadharma) would become a valid reason—for example: "Sound is eternal because it is visible, like a universal.

Likewise, if it were stated that "it is that which lacks [concomitance] in the similar class," then that which is not a property of the subject and does not exist in the similar class would also become a valid reason.

For example, [if one were to argue] that "sound is impermanent because it is non-existent," when it is stated that "that which exists in the subject (pakṣadharma) and in the similar instances (sapakṣa) is called a reason," then the reason "sound is permanent because it is knowable" would become a reason that occurs in dissimilar instances (vipakṣavṛtti). Conversely, when it is stated that "the reason exists in the subject but does not exist in the similar instances," then the reason "sound is permanent because, while possessing genus, it is audible" would become a reason lacking occurrence in the similar instances (sapakṣavṛttihīna).

If it were merely stated that "it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)," then the reason "atoms are impermanent because they are produced" would be a reason that lacks the property of the subject (apakṣadharma).
To prevent all such [faults], this is the purpose of employing the term "composite" (samudāya).
Having kept all of this in mind, we stated in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra* (Dharmottarapradīpa): "By one who declares 'from the mark possessing the three characteristics,' etc."
Now, one might object: "In the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the nature of being a property of the subject has indeed been expressed;

but by what means are the two forms consisting of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) denoted, such that [the definition] is explained in this way? To this he says: "In its part" (*tadaṃśe*).
Demonstrating here itself how [the other two forms] are delimited by implication (*sāmarthya*), he says: "Not when sublated" (*nābādhite*), and so forth.
Because this particular distinction is intended without abandoning its previous subdivisions,
he refers to both by means of that [single] term.

Since the very existence of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) constitutes the existence of the condition of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), it is not a different form from that.

Furthermore, because two contradictory natures cannot exist in a single entity, the impossibility of another [nature]— which would be concomitant with that which is contradictory to it— occurring within that same thing which is concomitant with the former, is itself included under the term "non-contradiction. However, for those who maintain that this [non-contradiction] is distinct from that [concomitance], the mention of "distinct" (*vyatirikta*) is made according to their intention.
The "occurrence" (*sambhava*) of another form is its "existence" (*sadbhāva*);
[the author] establishes this with the words "for there is no absence of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvābhāvam eva na hi*), and so forth.

He says that its existence is unestablished because even when there is a connection with another form, an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is impossible; thus he says, "In that which possesses it" (tadvati), meaning "possessing an invariable concomitance based on a necessary connection. If there were another form even in that [subject], this would merely be called "without proof"; therefore he says, "And just as... (yathā ca). This will be explained by the reason [in verse 11.15]. It is made manifest by the logical reason (hetu).
[36] He will state:
"The thesis (*pakṣa*) is the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*).
The sense is that it is impossible to apprehend everything as having that property because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish such an aggregate."
Now, if by some means that property were established [11.19], or if there were certainty regarding it, then because its purpose would already be accomplished, that reason would be redundant.

With the intention that "this very person is 'another' (para) because he has fallen into the position of another," it is Īśvarasena himself who is intended as "the other" (para). [12.6] Adhi(vyadhi)...

[The reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) by virtue of having a locus distinct from the locus of the probandum (*sādhyādhikaraṇa*), because both [reasons] are unestablished in that subject (*dharmin*) which has long been the basis [of the discussion].

If it is asked: "How is it determined that 'this is unestablished in its own nature' (*svarūpāsiddha*), whereas 'this is unestablished due to being in a different locus' (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*)? [the answer follows:]
This is true;

however, in that case, even though the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), it is presented as residing in another locus (*dharmī*); such a reason should be understood as "unestablished due to a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*).

In response to the doubt as to why one should not suspect that this was stated for the sake of establishing a connection with that [other property], it must be explained that it was not stated by him because it was already manifest through that [previous statement].
For when it is said that "the property (dharma) is the reason, being pervaded by a part of that [subject]," everyone indeed understands this;
it is not intended to mean that it is pervaded by a part of its own self.
"By the Teacher" means by Ācārya Dignāga.

Since a property of the subject (dharmin) of the thesis (pakṣa) is untenable, it cannot first be a *karmadhāraya* compound; nor can it be a *dvigu* compound, because it does not have a numeral as its prior member.
Furthermore, it cannot be an *avyayībhāva* compound because [the word] is not indeclinable (*avyaya*).

It cannot be a *bahuvrīhi* compound because the referent denoted by the word "yat" is impossible; for there is a contradiction in meaning in saying that the substratum (*dharmin*) is the very same as the attribute (*dharma*), and furthermore, it would entail the application of the suffix *-anic* at the end of the compound.
It is not a *dvandva* compound because the term is neuter, because it would entail a dual number, and because the sense of "and" (*ca*) is impossible here.

Furthermore, since the word *dharma* is not included in the rule for locative compounds (*saptamī-samāsa*), even if such a compound were possible through a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), there is no difference between the genitive and the locative cases; with this intention, he says: "[37] From a genitive *tatpuruṣa*...
Furthermore, in a genitive compound such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"), the exclusion of other owners is observed, meaning that the man is the king's and not anyone else's.
Similarly here, the connection is that there is an exclusion of association with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), namely, "this is a property of the subject (*pakṣa*) and not of anything else.
And from the genitive compound—S.
Now, one might object: "The flame is fire;

and by the word 'etcetera,' cognition and so forth are intended as being accepted as momentary. Therefore, how can there be an absence of a thesis (pakṣābhāva) with respect to that proponent who maintains non-momentariness?
To this he says: "Even that which... [15.21].

The intention of one who says "not through direct perception" [15.22] is as follows: if the moment were perceived by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the search for an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would reach its conclusion.
But when it is known through inference (*anumāna*), how could that inference of theirs possibly be without an example? Thus, the proof is difficult to establish.

And this has been stated while provisionally accepting the momentariness of some other [entity]. However, it should be understood that for those who maintain that destruction is caused by a cause, momentariness—defined as the fact that even cognition and so forth exist only at the very moment of their arising and not in a second moment—must be accepted; for it is intended that the term "momentary" (kṣaṇika) applies to things that perish very rapidly.

In that regard, even if the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the fuel is established by means of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*), the intention is that its conceptual nature (*kālpānikatva*) would be understood— on the grounds that, despite their difference, one must still depend upon its occurrence in this very [fuel]. "Understood" (*pratipanna*) means accepted or admitted.
*Sva* (in 15.26) means the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum;
*anyatra* (in 16.1) refers to the *Viniścaya*.
When a thing such as smoke is observed and ascertained in some place, such as a mountain, then, regarding that smoke and so forth, in relation to fire and so forth—

Invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is the state of being invariably connected (*pratibaddhatva*). For a person who knows that—that is, one who knows the invariable concomitance—the indicator (*gamaka*), which is the inferential mark (*anumāpaka*) such as smoke, leads to the cognition (*iti*) of that object of the concomitance, such as fire, on that locus, such as a mountain;
"leads" (*gati*) means power or capacity (*sāmarthya*).
The statement "its presence in what is similar to it" has this as its ultimate purpose and this as its primary aim.

That which has that as its property (*taddharmā*)— meaning that whose property is the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmī*) by way of being real through the reason (*hetu*), even though the reason itself is conceptually constructed— is that [subject].
That which arises from the power of real entities (*vastu-bala*) is real.
Since it is excluded from being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by virtue of its status as the subject (*pakṣa*), he says "by way of being the probandum" (*sādhyatvena*).
By this, its unreality is shown, because its definition is established merely by [subjective] desire.
The connection is as follows: "Therefore, there is a deficiency in strength because the state of being inseparable from the probandum lacks inseparability.
In response to the expectation of why that is its basis, he says: "Otherwise" (anyathā).
This means because that state of being inseparable from the probandum would be impossible, that is, unworkable.

Regarding this, [the phrase] "because it does not follow here" is answered with the words beginning "True," and so forth. "Of something" refers to such things as *śiṃśapā*-ness, which establishes the conventional usage of "tree-ness" and so on.

Even when an effect arises from such a cause through a well-established necessary connection (*pratibandha*) despite its difference [from other causes], how could it be faulty for not following [the same pattern] elsewhere? To this he says: "For then... (tadā hi).
If it is argued that even a contradictory [reason] is a correct reason in the opposite case, this expresses the fact that its occurrence is not ascertained in the opposite case;
thus, it would be a reason for doubt regarding that subject (*dharmin*).
[The opponent objects: "By implication, [the subject] refers to the presence and absence of the probandum (*sādhyabhāvābhāvayoḥ*).
Since there exists another alternative mode, the locus (*dharmī*) will be entirely free from both the presence and absence of the probandum;

how then could it be a cause for doubt in that regard? Anticipating this, he says: "Because it is impossible for it to exist outside of those two" (16.19); for if the occurrence of the probandum were excluded, the presence of fire would be impossible.
To the question "Of what? he says: "Of its subject" (*taddharmiṇaḥ*), meaning of the locus of that reason.
Why, then, must it possess either the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) or its absence?
He says "in the probandum" (*sādhye*) because another alternative is also possible.
The point is this: since things that consist of mutual exclusion (*anyonyavyavaccheda*) entail the affirmation of the other when one is negated, how could another alternative be possible?

It might be argued: "From the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), there arises the knowledge that the subject under dispute possesses that property."
How is it that the Venerable Dharmākaradatta did not perceive the extreme futility of the fundamental reason (*maula-hetu*), even though it was so clearly evident?
Oh, what a display of ignorance regarding the intended meaning!

For one who speaks thus, this is the underlying intention: [the thought] that if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were grasped by means of a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*) and without restriction of properties, both in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*) and in the subject-to-be-proven (*sādhya-dharmin*), then the probandum would be established from the fundamental reason alone.
How could there be futility?

Otherwise, if one were to admit that the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) also operates against the opposite [of the probandum] in the case of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), how indeed would the fundamental reason (*maulo hetuḥ*) not incur futility?
For in that case as well, that [proof], by apprehending the generality of the subject (*dharmisāmānya*), establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And thus, even for that which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), its possession of the property sought to be known is established from that very [reason].

Now, it might be argued: "Even if existence (*sattva*) establishes momentariness by the power of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), why is the reality of things such as a rabbit's horn not also established?
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that [existence] consists in the exclusion of those [non-existent things], the subject must necessarily be qualified as 'this is existent' (*saṃścāyam*)."
The meaning “sound and so forth” is to be supplied [to the conclusion].
From this very reason of existence (*sattva*), even when not yet fully integrated, the understanding of the momentariness of sound and so forth arises; thus, in our view, the reason is not redundant.
[Objection: But is this not the same for us as well?

For instance, even though the cognitive activity proceeds from the means of valid cognition that apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it does not grasp a specific locus (*dharmiviśeṣa*), the activity arises as something floating in form, grasping the identity (*tādātmya*) between momentariness and existence;
however, it is not yet a factor for [specific] activity.
But when it is shown that "this [is] existent," the cognition arises as a factor for activity in the form: "This—sound and so forth—is momentary."
Since [the cognition] proceeds toward a distinguished place and so forth,
how can it be said— with such a lack of modesty— that the fundamental reason in our view is futile?
Even though this position has been censured by Dharmottara and others, this interpretation has been described by us.

However, something must be said regarding this point as well; we have already demonstrated that in our own investigation of the internal [Buddhist] schools (*svayūthya*). But it is not stated here so that there may be no lack of interest (*virasībhāva*).
Now, one might object: "Does the particle (*nipāta*), when uttered together with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), exclude non-connection (*ayoga*)?
For there is the statement: 'By means of both the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣya*')."

And here, since the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) that performs the exclusion (*vyavacchedaka*), the restriction must be expressed with that very [subject]. Thus, if one says "the property of the subject alone" (*pakṣasyaiva dharmaḥ*), the fault remains as before.
If this is argued, it is not so.

In the phrase "by means of the qualifier and the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyābhyām*), the intended meaning of "qualifier" and "qualified" is based on their functional relationship (*ārtha*), rather than relying on the literal grammatical process (*śābdī gati*); for [the former] is a qualifier because it is that which is supported, and [the latter] is the qualified because it is the support. And this being so, the subject (*pakṣa*) is not the qualifier.

However, because it is the substratum (*āśraya*), the locus (*dharmin*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); whereas the property (*dharma*), being that which is supported (*āśrita*), is only the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not the qualificand.
Therefore, since the particle is uttered together with that [property], it excludes only non-connection (*ayoga*); thus, everything is clear.
A certain person named Caitra:
since he is already known in that very form, it is illogical to pose a question for the sake of knowing him.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth is intended.
That which has its application (*vṛtti*) in a preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*), unique (*ananyasādhāraṇa*) quality or excellence (*atiśaya*) is [described] as such.

This has been stated: "For it is not merely the proximity of a particular (*viśeṣa*) that is the cause for general terms (*sāmānyaśabda*) to be established in a particular sense; rather, context (*prakaraṇa*), capacity (*sāmarthya*), and so forth, also contribute.
He supports this very point with the passage beginning "In the case of Pārtha... and so on.
Pārtha is the offspring (apatya) of Pṛthā, who was Kuntī; this is a term based on both etymological derivation (yoga) and conventional usage (rūḍhi), and therefore it denotes Arjuna alone.
"Of the listener" means, by implication, of the questioner—that is to say, of the person to whom the teaching is addressed.
When such an extraordinary proficiency in archery (*dhānuṣkārya*) is denied to others,
it is correctly regarded as "light" (*āloka*) by virtue of its capacity and other qualities. [38]
But it is not as it was sealed [in the previous section], namely, "by means of the force of the context (*prakaraṇa-sāmarthya*) and so forth.

Why is there only the status of being an archer (*dhanurdharatva*) in that case? To this he says: "with respect to what is to be established" (*pratipādye*). It is "referred to" (*parāmṛśyate*), that is, it is grasped as the expressed meaning (*vācyatvena*).
It is explained:
"He negates what is not intended, but not the property (*dharma*). To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the property (*dharmasya*)."
Now, what kind of verbal formulation is this, that "there is no possibility of attributes (dharma) for a dharma"?
Is it because smoke and the like, being substrates, lack such attributes as "smokeness" (dhūmatva) or "earthiness" (pārthivatva),
that it is stated thus?
This is true; however, one should simply exert effort toward awakening.
Here, by the word "dharma," what is intended to be established is fire and so forth; and since that [fire] does not possess a "dharma" [in the sense of a property], what is the fault?
Now, if it is asked, "By what is 'dharma' denoted here, such that it is appropriate to establish the state of being a dharma for a dharma?", he says: "And a part" [17.22].
"In what sense [is it a part]?

A 'part' (*aṃśa*) is like a portion; just as a portion is a qualifier of a whole (*aṃśin*), so too is a property (*dharma*) a qualifier of the property-bearer (*dharmin*); this is the intended meaning.
Since the word 'thesis' (*pakṣa*) denotes the whole, it must be stated that a 'part' is only one portion of that; thus he says: 'by the word "thesis"... [17.22].
To the question, "Why is not just a single part of that [nature] stated? he says: "And of that" (*tasya ca*).
Although the reading found in the printed edition lacks the word "ca," the reading supported by the *Āloka* is "of a single part of that" (*tasya ca eka-*).
It should be understood from what precedes that it is because it is impossible for phenomena (*dharma*) to be the substratum (*ādhāra*) of phenomena.

Since pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists precisely in the necessary presentation of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) when the pervaded (*vyāpya*) exists—because it is that which effects this—the cognition of the pervaded alone as being "pervaded" is the cognition of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*). To the question, "In dependence upon what does that cognition occur?", he says: "In the pervader" (*vyāpake*).

It depends upon the state of being a pervader (*vyāpakabhāva*); by the rule “*īkṣi-kṣamibhyāṃ ñ ca*” [Vārttika 1981], the suffix *ṇa* is applied when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a governing word (*upapada*).
The meaning is that, having depended upon—that is, having reflected upon—the form of the pervader’s state as the object of a restriction, such a cognition arises.
This alone is the correct reading, and not that which was previously proposed by us: “because there is no other property among properties” (*dharmāṇāṃ dharmāntaratvābhāvāt*).
[42] Regarding the reading "ālokasammataḥ ‘vyāpakabhāvāpekṣā’," this is correct and not as we have imagined it.

In that context, having demonstrated the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) intended by the phrase "bhāvam eva" (only the entity), he says "na tv i... (but not... while refuting what is not intended.
Nor is it "only there" (nāpi tatraiva);
the word "is determined" (avadhāryate) carries over from the previous context.
"Common" (sādhāraṇaḥ) means common to both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (asapakṣa).
The particle *ca* has the sense of adding another fault. The word *vā* indicates an alternative position with respect to the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*).
Regarding the restrictive term *tatraiva*, the author says "here too" (*atrāpi*) in order to negate an intended restriction that might otherwise be understood differently by the opponent.

Harmonizing this very point with the words of the author of the Sūtra, he says: "That has been stated" [18.17]. When the mark (liṅga) exists as the means of proof, the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), which is the probandum (sādhya), necessarily exists.
By this, the pervasion (vyāpti) residing in the pervading property (vyāpakadharma) is demonstrated.
Furthermore, the other type of indicator (itaraliṅga) exists only in that which possesses the indicator (liṅgin), namely in the probandum (sādhya) itself.
By this, the pervasion residing in the pervaded property (vyāpyadharma) has been stated.

In the manner described, regarding the reversal or inversion of the restriction or determination—wherein "reversal" consists in the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda) with respect to one [term] as a qualifier—[the following applies].

In the other case, by way of excluding connection with anything else, when that misconception exists, the meaning is that the non-connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*).
By this, through demonstrating the negation of the apprehension of a single form in both [the positive and negative instances], [the pervasion is established].
And this objection was raised by the Teacher against those who maintain that smoke is the probans (*hetu*) by virtue of being in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but not against the Naiyāyikas;
for they accept smoke as a mark (*liṅga*) on the basis of its inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*).

For they, having established as the subject (*dharmin*) either the whole consisting of smoke or a particular location, take as their reason either "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) or "possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattva*)— which are universals— with the desire to prove the presence of fire.
By this, it is explained— that is, revealed— that the capacity to produce cognition (*sadgamakatva*) is like pervasion (*vyāpti*).
He establishes this very point with the words beginning "for thus" (*tathāhi*).
Connecting this also with that statement, he says "and so" (*tathā ca*).

Having raised the objection—"Since a relation resides in both [relata], how could there not be a pervasion by a single form in both places?"—he responds with the phrase "even though," thereby accepting the relation as something real (*vāstava*) even while it resides in both.
He provides a response.
To the question "Of which two is this? he says: "In the member" (*aṅge*) [19.2].
[This is derived from] *aṅg* [in the sense of] "knowing" (*jñāna*).

Because it is grasped (*grahaṇāt*), it is inferred (*aṅgyate*), marked (*liṅgyate*), or understood (*pratīyate*) by means of this [sign] regarding an object that is beyond the senses; thus, *aṅga* is a sign (*liṅga*).
Therefore, the meaning is "of the sign and the bearer of the sign" (*liṅgaliṅginor*).
He asks: "Of what nature is it? and says:
Because it is precisely those two that are under discussion as occurring simultaneously;
and by the very admission of their being located in two [different things], the admission of their coexistence also follows.
Although the word "even though" (*yady api*) is present, it should be understood in meaning as "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
The "occurrence" (vṛtti) of that relation is its functioning;
[this refers] to those two, namely the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin), as is understood from the context.
To the question "Of what two is it like?", he says: "As of the container and the contained"—the suffix *vati* is used here after a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*).
Just as the relationship characterized by the nature of the container and the contained, although residing in two things, does not subsist in both through a single mode of existence—

since, even when joined by the same relation, the container does not possess the state of being the contained, nor does the contained possess the state of being the container— so too the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), such as in the case of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) and so forth, is otherwise.
Otherwise, this would apply to "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) and so forth as well.
For this very reason, it is only "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*) and the like that serves as the indicator by way of being the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and not "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and the like;

it is only "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) and the like that is the indicated by way of being the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and not "grass-fuel-originated-ness" (*tārṇatva*) and the like; nor is smoke the indicated and fire the indicator.
Since its function is thus, for that reason—
by the words "thus" (*iti*) and so forth, there is a conclusion of the section.
"Elsewhere" (*anyatra*) refers to the *Nyāyabindu*.
In the *Viniścaya* as well, it is stated: "From a mark possessing the three characteristics," and so forth.
A *kakṣā* is a position established through competition.
One whose *kakṣā* is equal is [a *tulyakakṣa*].

The state of being that is *tattā* (thatness); its indicator is its manifestation, which is precisely the meaning or purpose of the word "or" (*vā*). By stating and establishing this through the phrase "because of identity in the ultimate sense," it is shown that the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is intended when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) leads to the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and when negative concomitance leads to the understanding of positive concomitance.
Therefore, whatever has been proposed by some— namely, that "for one who desires the capacity [of words], the determination of duality is lost"— should be regarded as having been brushed aside.
[44] By way of a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*), from the nature of certainty, and from the context;
because of the statement, "The reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that is pervaded by a part of it (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*)," according to the sequence and order of the Sūtra.
The phrase "of all" (sarvasya) must be understood as an emphatic restriction meaning "of every single one.
Regarding the phrase "by means of perception and inference," it should be understood as a denial of [the existence of] the whole, and not of any part;
for other than these two, each exists by means of its own respective [means of knowledge].
[44] Here, one leaf of the manuscript *S* is lost.

Anticipating the objection—"Since it is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpanatvāt*), how is it possible for a certain determination (*niścaya*) regarding it to arise from perception (*pratyakṣa*)?"—he says: "By means of perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*).
The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmād*).
"Because it generates a conceptualization of a universal" (sāmānyavikalpajananāt) is stated with the intention of referring to the perception of a mark such as smoke;
"metaphorically" (upacārataḥ) means that it is said to be a determination through perception metaphorically.
In manuscript S, the word "prati" does not appear.
"Now, since the universal (*sāmānya*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*), how can its ascertainment be through perception? To this he says: "Even though... (*yady api*).
With the words "But as for... (*yas tu*) and so forth, the view of Uddyotakara is anticipated. "Connected with fire" (*agnisambandhī*) means possessing fire (*vahnimān*).
The intention is that this region [of space] is imperceptible because the lower region possesses that same nature. Anticipating the question, "Does such a sky exist?
or "If it does exist, does it have parts?", the opponent speaks of "light" (āloka) to demonstrate precisely what is intended by the Buddhists.
By the mention of "the first" (ādi), darkness (tamas) is included;
thus it is said: "Light and darkness are space"—this is the intended meaning. In a particular location, [the proof] is based on actual similarity (sādharmya).
It should be understood as "dhāra.
Anticipating the objection that, in that case, inference would be utterly destroyed, he says "therefore" (tasmāt) while re-establishing the system.
To the question, "How can that very same subject (dharmin) be that very same reason (hetu)?", he says "possessing fire" (sāgni).

By this, he shows that the specific smoke (*dhūmaviśeṣa*) possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*), while smoke in its general form (*dhūmasāmānya*) possesses the status of the reason (*hetu*).
Through the means of demonstrating an objection that applies equally, the proponent (*siddhāntin*) begins his rebuttal with the words "of that which is likewise" (*tulyāpi*) and so forth.

For one who holds such a view, the phrase "to that extent" refers to one who possesses the distinction between the visible and the invisible; thus, this [objection] applies equally to smoke as the subject (*dharmin*) in the manner already stated. This is the intended meaning of the opponent's conceit of equality.
Regarding this, he says: "And [it is] only in a particular location" (*pradeśa eva ca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to distinguish this from the position of others.
To the question, "How can that which is perceived in one place be an indicator with respect to another location?", he replies: "In terms of place and time" (*deśakāla*).
Demonstrating that this is also the intention of the Teacher (Ācārya), he says: "When [he] said... (yadāce...);
and showing that it must therefore be accepted in this way, he says: "...on the path" (pathe...).
It is an inference because it is the cause of inference, such as [the reason] "being differentiated by the difference in conditions" (pratyayabhedabheditva).
Or rather, one should apply the argument: "How even the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substratum (*dharmin*) is possible.
The apprehension of the relation between those two, characterized as that of locus and located (*ādhārādheyalakṣaṇa*), is what is meant.
The particle *iti* shows the form of the objection being raised.
Anticipating the question, "How is it known that he [Kumārila] has thus countered [the objection]? the author says: "For by him" (*tena hi*).
For (*hi*) because of this, by that Kumārila, dharma is to be understood as the means for achieving the highest good (*śreyas*), such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth.
As Śabarasvāmin said: "What is dharma? It is that which is the means of achieving the highest good" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2).
For this very reason, Kumārila also said:
"The fact that these [Vedic injunctions] are the means of achieving the highest good is also eternally understood from the Veda" (Ślokavārttika 2.14).

This is the commentary (bhāṣya) by Śabarasvāmin on the Jaiminisūtra [at 21.17]. And when it is referred to as "this commentary," it is spoken of by way of its meaning; however, the actual text of the commentary is not exactly like this.
When the intention is to refer to "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the term used is "inference and so forth" (*anumānādi*).
To the question "When is that preceded by that?", he says: "When...
[referring to] "the sensory cognition which is non-conceptual," meaning devoid of mental construction (*kalpanā*).
To the question, "How is that so?", he says: "Because of memory" (smṛteḥ).

Or rather, the word *yat* should be understood as having the sense of *yasmāt* ("because"). To the question, "Why is there no apprehension in that way even without conceptualization? he says: "And not... (na ca).
Because the logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth are proximate, it should be understood that one must indeed conceptualize (*avikalpya*) the logical mark itself.
Likewise, "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means apprehension by way of being related.
The particle *iti* shows the form of the implication (*ākṣepa*).
In response to the expectation of whose [object] there is non-apprehension by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: "of the sign (*liṅga*) and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says: "because of the absence of conceptualization (*avikalpanāt*).
The word "that" refers to the non-apprehension.

"No," he negates [this], because even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is accepted [as a means of knowledge] in this context, as indicated by the word "by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*). Anticipating the objection that conceptual construction might arise in that way merely by itself, he says: "in the object" (*arthe*).
If that which has the form of the object is beneficial [to cognition], then there must also be something beneficial to it; thus [it is said].
But surely, this can only be said when there is a duality between the cognition of the object and the object itself, distinguished as non-conceptual and conceptual respectively.
And since this is not possible, he says: "It exists" (*asti*).
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because.

Because it exists prior to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that is, first or initially, cognition—since such conceptual constructions are not admitted in the case of infants and others—is accepted as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"Arising from a pure object" means arising from an object devoid of the recollection of words.
"Thereafter" means at a later time following the cognition of mere observation (*ālocanājñāna*). "Again, not for the first time."
The word "also" (*api*) implies that the cognition by which an object qualified by genus and so forth is determined is not merely a non-conceptualizing awareness (*ālocanājñāna*).

The intention of one who speaks thus is as follows: although, at first, the dual-natured object is grasped through non-conceptual cognition due to its connection with the sense organ, it is nevertheless not grasped as having entered into the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*).
Because it directly perceives both the universal and its possessor as being like an iron pin,
this is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By the use of "iti" [at 22.1], he demonstrates its cognitive aspect (*ākāra*).
It was stated [22.3]: "This is stated by implication;
however, it was not stated by him directly.
Because this was revealed by implication by him who spoke thus, therefore [22.3] "for that reason."
In order to refute the fault pointed out by Kumārila— namely, that "for the Buddhists alone, there is no apprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth through perception"—
it has been described.

In order that his disciples may easily understand, [the author], demonstrating the collective meaning of the passage beginning with "for it is accompanied by smoke" (sadhūmam), says: "This is here" (ayam atra).

Now, one might raise this objection: "Since non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is not capable of performing such a range of functions, how can a determination based upon it be said to exist? Why, then, does this statement—'for it is accompanied by smoke,' etc.—not collapse? In response to this doubt, he says: "This is here."
The particle *hi* [22.5] is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

It has been stated that because one [of the two] is produced directly and the other through implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it generates a pair of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consisting of affirmation and negation [22.9].
This was said with the intention that it sometimes generates a conceptual construction of affirmation and sometimes a conceptual construction of negation.
"Thus it is" (*evam etat*) indicates the conceptualization of affirmation (*vidhi-vikalpa*) as appropriate;

"not otherwise" (*nānyathā*), etc., indicates the conceptualization of negation (*pratiṣedha-vikalpa*) as appropriate. Does the arising of conceptualization occur with respect to an experienced object?
To show that this is not so, he says: "according to habituation" (*yathābhyāsam*), which means "according to experience" (*yathānubhavam*).
If conceptual construction were to arise without being restricted by experience, then it would follow that it could arise with respect to every aspect [of an object]; therefore, he says "habituation.

It should be understood that "of those having habituation and so forth as auxiliary causes" (*abhyāsādisahakāriṇām*) means "of those having habituation and so forth as their auxiliary conditions" (*abhyāsādisahakārikāṇām*).
But the beginning of the arising conceptual construction is not a cooperative cause for [the memory],
whereas it is so for the experience.
Indeed, some [cognition],
namely experience, generates a conceptual construction (vikalpa) in accordance with its auxiliary cause, which is the repeated observation characterized by practice.
The meaning of this is as follows: experience does not produce conceptual construction merely by being experience;
rather, it is a certain [experience] that, arising repeatedly therein, becomes such [a cause], as is the case for those who examine jewels and the like.
But some [cognition] produces [the memory] by depending on proficiency characterized by an excellence of its own nature.
The meaning of this is as follows: some experience arises as inherently more proficient, being capable in that regard, just as is the case for yogins with respect to everything.
In some cases, for people such as ourselves, [the mind] is capable [of discerning the truth] regarding a certain object;

however, in other cases, due to the persistence of ignorance and being deceived by the production of successive similar moments, its clarity is always obscured, and it is simply not capable of that [discernment],
as is the case for those of limited vision regarding [doctrines such as] momentariness.
Regarding the phrase "due to proficiency, etc. (*pāṭavādī*), the mention of "etc. (*ādi*) includes proximity, degrees of intensity, and so forth.

As for the expression "in accordance with experience": one might object, "Since there is no experience of a definitive cognition that 'this is a relation,' how can it be said that the determination of the relation is based upon that? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "For instance" (*tathāhi*).
By that aforementioned method, there arises the conceptual construction of affirmation and negation regarding the subsequent [object].
Now, one might ask: since the relation characterized as the locus and the located is not experienced, how can its ascertainment—which is said to be based upon it—be described? To this he says:
"And not... (na ca). Thus, having relied upon—that is, having grasped—the two objects situated in a vertical relationship (auttarādharya).

If there is nothing other than these two such entities, then how is it that there is the conventional usage: "this is the relation between these two, and these two are the relata"? To this he says: "by that" (tena).

Because a relation is superimposed based on the experience of those two such entities, for that reason the verbal convention—"this is the property-bearer (dharmin), this is the property (dharma)"—is intended; and this instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇā*) [indicating the cause of the designation as property and property-bearer].
He states the reason for this conventional usage [in the phrase] "due to another distinction" (*bhedāntara*).
The meaning is that this is not a conventionality pertaining to ultimate reality (*paramārthika*).
Now, one might object: since there is no relation other than the two such entities, how can this be?
And since that [relation] is ascertained through perception, it is produced by two such entities;
but how can the ascertainment of the universal of the logical mark (*liṅga*) be produced by that [perception],
given that the universal of the logical mark is not apprehended by perception?
Nor can a particular (viśeṣa) be the mark (liṅga); anticipating this objection, he says "in the universal" (sāmānye).
The word "also" (api) is intended to show that the conventional usage of the universal is not superior to the conventional usage of the relation.
This might be asked: if there is no persisting entity, how could a persistent cognition be without a cause? To this he says "of those very [particulars]" (teṣām eva).

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not have a direct function in producing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because that [conceptual construction] does not have that [particular characteristic] as its object; thus he says: "In experience" (*anubhave*).

Even if those [particular characteristics] possess natures that are of a different class (*vijātīya*), how can they be the cause of that [single] cognition? To this he says: "In the case of the heterogeneous" (*vijātīye*).
This refers to the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a single form—that is, a non-differentiated form.
And that is also a condition (*pratyaya*) because it serves as a cause therein. Connecting this with the words of the Teacher, he says: "And thus it has been said" [22.25].
The reflective awareness (*pratyavamarṣa*) of a single, undifferentiated thing—namely, the synthesis (*sambandhāhāra* or *samanvāhāra*) of the form "this is that very same thing"—[is what is meant].

Thus the analysis (vigraha) should be made, and not as "this is both one and a reflective awareness" (ekaś cāsau pratyavamarṣaś ca). For if it were so, since this reflective awareness would also be divided, how could there be oneness?

If it were said that [the determination of reality] occurs through another subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), then the reality of that [subsequent awareness] would likewise depend on yet another, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And thus, as long as the suchness of the final [awareness] is not known, there can be no establishment of the reality of even the first one.

And if that [cognition] were non-existent, it would be impossible to attribute non-difference even to the individuals by virtue of their being the cause of a single cognition; enough of this elaboration here.
Since this conceptual construction is produced by them, therefore:
"Memory is a cognition whose object is what has been previously experienced."

But here, one might ask: "By what was this universal experienced, such that it could be grasped [by this cognition] and thus possess the nature of memory? To this he says: "[It is] that which appears therein" (tatpratibhāsina). The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), excluded from those of a different class, has been perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But he says "not exclusion" (na hi) [23.3] because [concepts] do not touch upon external objects due to their grasping at what is not an object. One might ask: since conceptual cognitions grasp what is not an object and thus do not contact external things, how can they possess the nature of memory, which is defined as grasping what has already been grasped? To address this wonder, he states the conclusion by way of a summary: "Therefore" (tasmāt) [23.4].

If this is so, and both types of conceptual construction (vikalpa) are called "recollection" (smṛti) because they grasp an external object as determined by the cognizer’s own ascertainment, then from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), what is their object? To this he says: “In reality” (vastutaḥ). Since this conceptual construction, although ultimately devoid of an object, is intended to be recollection in accordance with the cognizer’s ascertainment, therefore (tasmāt): [he says] “from that.”
Regarding this which is about to be stated, someone such as Kumārila and others asks:
"What does he say? He replies: "With respect to the universal (*sāmānya*)," etc.

If a Buddhist were to say that this cognition—which has a non-differentiated form due to its lack of distinction—is of the nature of memory (*smārta*), being of the form of recollection; [then the following applies].
For one who speaks thus, let there indeed be the capacity—the efficacy—of that recollection even with respect to the son of a barren woman;

that is to say, let it be that he is capable of remembering even the son of a barren woman. To the objection, "How can his capacity for the recollection of an absolute non-entity be postulated?", he states the justification in the prose commentary: because the universal has not been experienced, that is, due to its being unexperienced.
Even for one who speaks thus, the implication is this: memory occurs only with respect to what has been experienced.

If, however, recollection were possible even regarding what was not experienced, then why could a memory-cognition not be postulated even for the son of a barren woman, since there is no difference in their both being unexperienced?
The word *aṅga* is used for addressing someone;
the word *kiṃ* is used for a general question;
however, the word *punaḥ* is used for a specific one.
Therefore, the meaning is this: "Having requested you alone, we ask this both in general and in detail.

A human lifespan consists of a hundred years. Here, wishing to avoid the appearance of acting on his own authority, he introduces the verses that express that [point], saying: "And so it is said" (tathā cāha).

According to the view of that Buddhist, the connection should be made as follows: "For him, there is no comprehension (*gati*) even in many thousands of aeons regarding that which possesses a single characteristic (*ekaliṅgin*).
The reason is "due to infinity" (*ānantyāt*).
The entire [preceding] passage is a justification for that very point.
He says "And not" (*na ca*) [at 23.21] to show that inference will indeed be non-derived from a logical mark (*aliṅgaja*);
the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because."
"Free from a mark" (*liṅgavinirmukta*) means devoid of a mark.

He says "and not" (*na ca*)— the word "and" being as before— to address the objection that a mark, even if it is entirely unknown, will produce the cognition of the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*), since the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not a universal (*asāmānya*).
The meaning is that it lacks the capacity to be an indicator because it is not a manifest light.
