"Of that" refers to the mark (liṅga) which has the nature of a universal.
"The arising of another inference" refers to the birth of that other inference which apprehends the universal of the mark.
From what kind of mark (*liṅga*)? From one accompanied by the cognition of the universal—that is, conjoined with the cognition of the universal, or in other words, known in its universal form.

And the meaning is that this universal mark, while being cognized, is the object of inference (*anumeya*), because according to your own view, the universal is not grasped by perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"The emergence of that mark (liṅga), which is a universal, is 'its emergence' (tadudbhava)" [23.26]; this means by another mark.

With the intention that even that [mark], being of the nature of a universal, must likewise be established through yet another inference known [by that means], he says: "known through yet another inference" [23.27].
To the question, "Let it be so; what is the harm? he replies: "And thus" [23.27].

If it is objected: "In that case, there would indeed be an infinity of inferences of the mark (*liṅga*), but not of the inferences of the marked (*liṅgin*); so how can it be said 'of the inferences of the marked'?"—[the reply is:

True; however, because that very first mark, by virtue of being under the heading of a "reason as a signifier" (*jñāpaka-hetu*) and by its nature as a cognized universal, becomes the "marked" (*liṅgin*) when it is ascertained through inference.
There is no fault at all, because the intention is that [the reason] is intended to depend on a mark even while depending on its own mark;
[this occurs] in a single substratum (*liṅgin*), that is, in the factual base (*dharmin*).

Now, one might object: "If the universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*), and that is apprehended only by inference and not through perception, then how is it appropriate for the Teacher to describe its ascertainment through perception in the passage beginning with 'possessing smoke' (*sadhumat*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "He thinks as follows" (*evaṃ manyate*).
"By nature" means "due to delusion," that is, because of error.
For a universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*).

The meaning is this: since there is no universal other than the exclusion of heterogeneous things, the cognition of the universal is nothing but the cognition of the exclusion of heterogeneous things.

Furthermore, conceptual construction (vikalpa), bound by two types of latent impressions (vāsanā), necessarily perceives its own internal reflection as having an external form and as being common [to others]; it thinks, "I am perceiving an external object through the exclusion of dissimilar things.
This is because the universal (sāmānya) is, by its very nature, an error.
It has been stated that this very non-difference, whose distinctions have been analytically separated, is what is cognized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Now, if this conceptual construction is inherently erroneous, how can it possess the quality of reliability (*saṃvādakatva*), characterized by its capacity to lead one to an object that is excluded from what it is not? To this he says: "And of the conceptual construction of the mark (*liṅga-vikalpa*)" [24.2].
Why, then, is the universal (*sāmānya*) appearing as a conceptual construction considered to be the logical mark (*liṅga*)?
But [it is] not so for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth; thus he says, "For not... (*na hī*).
With the words beginning "Of that" (*tasya*), he states the logical justification.
Showing the supporting reason (*upacayahetu*) for this very point, he says, "In the probandum" (*sādhye*).
This is the intended meaning here:

for one who necessarily desires to infer something, after the perception of the specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) such as smoke, one must synthesize [the cognition] that "this is the probandum" and "this is the probans.
And when this synthesis exists, there is no perception of the real entity because of its momentary destruction.

Furthermore, the designation of the visible object (*dṛśya*) by means of the perceiver (*viṣayin*), which is the act of seeing, implies that there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the visible object because its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is absent— this is the meaning. Consequently, how could there be a relationship of the cognized and the cognizer (*gamyagamakabhāva*) based on the perception of a particular characteristic, such that the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer would not be mediated by imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*)?
[48] P reads *dṛśyasya liṅgam*; N has *prateḥ* here as the correct reading; for this very reason, that [reading] alone has been established in the root text (*mūla*).

Now, one might object: "If a universal is indeed apprehended by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then would this not contradict what was stated in the *Nyāyabindu*: 'The other, the specifically characterized (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), is the object of inference'? Anticipating this objection, he says: "As for what was said... [24.9].

The phrase "of the other" [24.11] refers to another independent conceptual construction—such as the form "there is fire here"—which arises subsequent to inference and whose status as a valid means of knowledge has not yet been established.
He asks, "Even so, for what purpose is this determined? and replies with the words *svalakṣaṇa* [24.12].
The meaning is that it is in order to demonstrate that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist as an object in the sense of being an apprehended entity (*grāhyatvena*).

Having explained the general meaning of the passage preceded by the two opposing positions (*pūrvapakṣa*), he begins to explain the meaning of the individual parts with the words *tatra* [24.13], etc.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of [theories] such as the destruction of all [atoms] upon the destruction of one is intended. He states the intended meaning of the phrase "by one who has seen through direct perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa dṛṣṭavataḥ*) with the words "but not... (*na tv i*);
and he explains why such a conception is untenable with the words "for not... (*na hī*).
The qualification "arising from the power of the thing itself" (*vastubalabhāvini*) is an adjectival attribute used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
It might be argued: "How can there be a cognition of isolation?
If it is a cognition of the thing alone, then that is all the more impossible without the awareness of non-existence; so how can it be described as being grasped by perception in such a manner?
This is incorrect.
For instance, even by one who maintains that non-existence is distinct [from existence], the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of things must necessarily be admitted as not entering into others;

otherwise, it would be impossible for non-existence itself to possess its own specific individuality (*prātisvika*). Therefore, apprehension without entering into others is indeed apprehension in its absolute sense (*kevalagraha*).
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

For indeed, as long as there is no apprehension of the bare locus (*kevalagraha*), there is no cognition of absence (*abhāvasaṃvitti*), just as there is none of that [locus] itself; and as long as there is no cognition of absence, there is no apprehension of the bare locus.
Furthermore, just as a solitary absence is cognized without another absence, why should an entity not likewise be measured in its solitude without another absence?
Otherwise, if this were not admitted, an infinite regress would result.
Thus, Prajñākaragupta says in the *Vārtikālaṃkāra*:
“Cognition through the exclusion of others is the apprehension of the thing alone;
but how can there be cognition of the thing alone without the cognition of non-existence?”
That [object] also does not exist without pure consciousness; thus, there is equality.
"Just as a mere non-existence is cognized without [another] non-existence, so too is existence;
if it were not thus, an infinite regress would result. Thus [it is said].

How can it be said that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which lacks an object and consists of distinctions as they are perceived, has the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as its object? To this he says: "By ascertainment," and so forth. By this, it is shown in consideration of the logical justification (*upapatti*).
The connection with the word *paramārtha* was demonstrated by the author of the *Ṭīkā* regarding the author of the *Vārttika*;
this is also observed to be the intention of the Master (*Ācārya*).
"Just as" (*yadvat*) means of such a kind; "as seen" (*yādṛśaḥ*) means as it has been observed; "according to what was seen" (*yathādṛṣṭaḥ*).
And that very differentiation is the ultimate reality (paramārtha);
that which has this as its object by virtue of determinative cognition (adhyavasāya) is "such" [i.e., having that as its object].
Otherwise, however, it would have no object at all from the perspective of ultimate reality.
"How could the author of the *Vārttika*, employing the term 'ultimate reality' (*paramārtha*), not be guilty of negligence?"—
we do not understand why Umbeka and Arcata did not explain it in this way.

Having demonstrated the connection [of the definition] with the general characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says "existent" (*sat*) while demonstrating the connection of the specific means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), with its own characteristic.

The plural number in "of the sense-faculties" (*indriyāṇām*) is used with the intention of referring to individual instances. However, in the application of this text in relation to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it refers to the sense-faculty as a whole (*avayavin*)—namely, the ocular ray—which is established through inference; when there is a conjunction or connection with a portion of its constituent parts (*saṃbhāra-daṃśena*), then for this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
"Because the impermanent has been brought under the category of self.

{p. 272-278} Based on their own conceit, the opponent has cited the sense faculty as an example of perception, citing such statements as: "Or rather, the sense faculty would be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and its contact with the object [is the perception]" [Ślokavārttika 4.60].
Furthermore, an example cannot be a domain of intellectual consensus between the proponent and the opponent,
because the Buddhist does not accept this [consensus] and because it would involve stating a refutation.
The word division at "prathamam iti" (in the phrase *prathamamitī*) is indeed easily understood.
Explaining the word "first" (*ādya*), he says "at the beginning" (*ādau*).
When there is the inquiry "In what sense 'at the beginning'?", he replies "of the arising of conceptual construction" (*vikalpapravṛtteḥ*).

Since it means "that which exists at the beginning," by the phrase "of whatever object... and so forth, he explains that because the unique characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is characterized precisely as the non-common, the unique characteristic has the non-common as its object.
He establishes the very point already stated by means of the passage beginning with "tathā hi" (for instance).
"In its unmixed form" means in a nature that is not contaminated [or touched] by another.
But is it not the case that its unmixed nature does not arise from itself, but rather from the existence of the portion consisting of non-existence?

Anticipating the objection, "How can it be stated in this way?", he states the reason with the words beginning "For it is thus" (*tathāhi*). Otherwise—that is, by way of its being mixed with the form of another—it would follow that the very portion consisting of non-existence (*abhāvāṃśa*) would not be established as the non-existence of the other, just like the nature of the other itself; such is the meaning.
Right here he states the reason for the further elaboration with the words "And not...
[25.28]. To the question of how that "mixed nature" [26.1] is not logical, he replies with "by the power of its own causes" [26.2].
This is a qualification of that which has arrived through the power of its own causes by virtue of being their cause.
The exclusion of [the entity] from conjunction is due to its non-conjunction with that object, by implication.

Now, it might be argued that since that [non-existence] destroys that [entity] which has a mixed nature, and because of the absence of anything else, all entities would indeed cease to exist after the moment of their arising; thus the world would become of a single flavor consisting solely of non-existence.
This consequence, however, is not tenable.
"Therefore, rather than the destruction of a mixed form, it would be better for things that possess unmixed forms to arise from their own causes alone.
This is true,
according to the scriptural tradition.
This might be a fault;
however, one must simply exert effort to understand its intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).

For here, although all phenomena (*bhāva*) are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*), there exists a cognition regarding the continuum of things (*vastusantāna*) due to the arising of successive moments that are similar [to their predecessors], and not a cognition whose object is non-existence (*abhāva*).

Therefore, an obscuration arises in the form of a distortion of reality. Furthermore, how could a cognition whose object is the actual thing be possible immediately after its arising, if that very non-existence were to exist without the previously established mixed nature [of the thing], or if it were to destroy another?
One might propose that [non-existence] produces a scattered form;

and if this were so, it would be better to say that such a state arises from its own cause alone. For, since being a cause consists in performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), which is the very nature of a real entity (*vasturūpa*), the status of non-existence as a non-entity would be lost. This [objection] must be disregarded.
And this which was stated should be understood as follows:

regarding destruction, it would be better—first, to accept the arising of things with mixed forms, and subsequently to arrive at the emergence of things with unmixed forms. Anticipating the objection, "What loss is there in this?", he says "What [then]... and so forth.

It is said that once a certain wandering mendicant, picking up a sweetmeat that had fallen into an impure place, was asked by someone with a sneer, "Why are you taking a sweetmeat from an impure place?
Being thus questioned, he replied to him, "I shall wash it and discard it right here."
This is the logic for the wandering mendicant’s purpose of seizing the sweetmeat; what is gained by accepting that?

And just as their opinion there was, "This very [body] must be abandoned right here," then what is the use of taking food that has been preserved [only to become] impure? It is better that this [food] remain in its previous state; such is the censure applied here as well.

The intention is this: if one must admit that things which are by their very nature unmixed arise only subsequently, then it would be better to admit from the very beginning that such things arise as they are.
Therefore, this intended criticism should be understood as being directed toward the establishment of such a [theory] through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The conclusion of the subject at hand is introduced with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth.
Demonstrating the intended meaning of the phrase "by the force of direct perception" (*pratyakṣabalena*), he says: "If, however" (*yadi tu*).
Here, the word *yadi* expresses possibility, while *tu* serves to distinguish [the two cases].
"Having exclusion as its object" means having as its object a form that is excluded—that is to say, having as its object a form that is turned away from what is not that [form].
If this were the case, there would be no memory;

the point is that [memory] would involve the apprehension of a specific, uncommon form residing in a particular place and so forth, which was not previously apprehended by the valid cognition grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

“‘This is not of another form’—by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this apprehension of non-existence intended [to be established], such that its validity is refuted by the Teacher? Anticipating this question, the author, clarifying the Teacher’s intention, says: “[It is] not [a means of valid cognition] regarding non-existence. Why, then, is there no other means of valid cognition called ‘non-existence’ that produces this apprehension?

And he says that this is its result with the words "for not" (*na hi*). An *ākāra* is that which is formed or determined; it is a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) consisting precisely of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
To the question "Of what kind? he says: "In proficiency" (*pāṭave*).
"Acuity" refers to the sharpness of the intellect, according to the context;

by the word "etcetera," proximity, degrees of intensity, and so forth are included. Because a subsequent cognition [of acuity] depends upon its own ascertainment, it is said to be "dependent on that."
Establishing this very point, he says: "For not... [26.22].
Regarding the phrase "because of non-apprehension" [27.10], it should be understood as meaning that the object is not grasped as a qualifier;
however, it should not be said that there is no apprehension whatsoever.
This is because he accepts that apprehension is independent, like iron rods [that do not touch one another];
otherwise, it would contradict such statements as: "Even though an object has a dual nature, it is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition" (Ślokavārttika, p. 118).
And how could the arising of the cognition of perception, which depends on the connection with the sense faculties (*indriya*), be brought about by a mere undesirable [consequence]?
By stating "it is described again" at the beginning [of the second chapter], he demonstrates that [the opponent's position] is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
*Prakhyā* means manifestation, illumination, or appearing;
that which has such a manifestation—like the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) and so forth—is described as such.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that it is "similar to that."
Now, one might object: "Let it be that the universal is not the means for accomplishing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); however, the particular (*vyakti*) certainly becomes such a means.

And since the affirmative conceptual construction (*vidhi-vikalpa*) functions precisely by determining that [particular], why should it not be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Anticipating this, the connection with the distant phrase "there is no validity therein" (*na tatra prāmāṇyam*) must be made;
for the context concerns "of that," namely, the affirmative conceptual construction.
One might wonder how there could be invalidity;
this should be addressed by stating that it is because that object of non-conceptual perception is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition.
The particle *ca* is used here in the sense of "clearly" (*vyaktam*).

"I do not assert that it is the determiner (*adhyavasātṛ*) of the object of non-conceptual perception, which is the means for accomplishing purposeful action (*arthakriyāsādhana*), such that you would speak in this way," he says with the words "thereafter" (*tataḥ param*) and so forth. The word *ca* [at 27.21] has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Therefore, this is the meaning: since it is stated thus by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin), it follows by implication.
Anticipating the objection—"Even if it is expressed in this way, how does the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [universal] come to be stated?"—he says "therein" (*tatra*).

Anticipating the objection—"The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of this [cognition] will belong to one who apprehends a universal (*jāti*) as something distinct"—he repeats the very same point for the sake of further elaboration, saying "but of the universal" (*jātes tu*).
The word "api" [in the verse] refers to intolerance (*akṣamā*).

This is because it is non-beneficial (*anartha*) due to its lack of capacity to accomplish purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), whereas only that which accomplishes purposeful action is considered beneficial (*artha*).
It was stated that there is no validity because the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, being a cognition of an object not previously known—is absent.

By this, it is shown that the general application of the definition of a means of valid cognition to the conceptualization of an injunction (*vidhivikalpa*), which was demonstrated by the opponent through the passage beginning with “In that case, there is a cognition of an object not previously known,” does not exist.

Furthermore, demonstrating that even the specific application of the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) to it, as shown by the passage beginning with “Contact with an existing [object]” (*satsaṃprayoga*), does not exist, he says: “For this very reason” (*ata eva*).

Therefore—precisely because a universal (jāti) is useless due to its lack of capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsādhanatva)—its perceptibility is also impossible for this conceptual construction (vikalpa). To explain why it is not possible, he says: "causal efficiency" (arthakriyā).
Because of the absence of that conjunction— that is, the connection— of the sense faculties with it;
for according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, it is always connected with the sense faculty.
The intention is that [the sense organ] does not have power over the non-existent.
This has been stated by Kumārila:
"For the connection [of the sense organ] is indeed with the aspect of existence, because of its [inherent] capacity" (Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa 18).

Of this cognition—which has as its object the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—the phrase "because it is a factor for engagement with the entity that accomplishes purposeful action" means, in short, "because it brings about the attainment of the object presented.
This is to be connected with the statement: "it does not declare anything other than valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

"The other" refers to that which does not have as its object the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Because it is the opposite of that, it is not a factor for engagement in the accomplishment of purposeful action. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
"Non-deceptive" means that which brings about the attainment of the object as it has been demonstrated.
The word-break at "loke 'pi" is indeed clear; "in the world" refers to among people who engage in worldly discourse.

[The word] *api* [is used] in the sense of "this is clearly evident. [Regarding the passage: "In that case, [the suffix] *S* [is applied]. Now, one might object: "Even if it does not function as an instigator toward the accomplishment of that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), nevertheless, why should it not be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its being a 'conveyor' (*prāpaka*) and thus being non-contradictory (*avisamvādaka*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which... [yac].
Regarding the phrase "not attaining" (*anadhigacchan*) [in the verse],
it functions here as a present participle (*śatṛ*) because it is prescribed as such when expressing a cause;
thus, "due to non-attainment" (*anadhigamāt*) is stated as the reason.

{p. 281} By virtue of being that which is to be established, it is accepted as being produced from a common origin—that is, characterized by non-differentiated cognition and designation—because of the statement: "A universal (*jāti*) has the nature of producing what is similar."
Regarding the phrase "to be accomplished by the individual" (*vyaktisādhyām*), it should be understood as "accepted as being accomplished by the individual.

By this, the position that "the very same causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) which is accepted by you as being accomplished by the individual will be what is accomplished by that [universal]" is also refuted.

The intended meaning is that in both cases, it is through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the capacity of the individual alone—both directly and indirectly—to produce that [result] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that while it is appropriate to say "after the apprehension of the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇapratipatter ūrdhvam*) in response to the question "At what time does one act?", it is not so in response to the question "Of what nature is it?", we reply: True; however, it should be understood that because it is perceived at a time subsequent to the apprehension of the specific characteristic, the word "after" (*ūrdhvam*) refers to a later time in a figurative sense (*upacārataḥ*).
Demonstrating that it is indeed perceived subsequent to the apprehension of that [particular], he says: "by its power" (*tatsāmarthya*).

Alternatively, having first asked "of what kind?", one should connect it with "by its power. Furthermore, is this state of being graspable by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by its power only after the apprehension of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), or is it for some period of time?
In response to the expectation of what [the basis] is, it is said: "after the realization of that"; thus he speaks.
To the question, "What kind of generality does he proclaim as suchness?", he says "through vision" [28.27], explaining why this expression is used even from the perspective of another's intention.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the universal alone is not capable of accomplishing purposeful action (arthakriyā), such that you speak thus merely because others have stated so? Anticipating this, he provides an answer by way of admission, saying: "Everything indeed... [28.29]. Of what kind is it? S... [52]

If this were so, then because the universal (*sāmānya*)—which is grasped by inferential conceptualization—is likewise [unreal], the inferential conceptualization that has it as its object would also lack validity. Consequently, one might fear that upon the entry of the word, the situation would become like "the eyes being pulled out through the ears. Anticipating this, he says: "But even though... (yat tv api).
The particle *tu* (but) is for the sake of distinction.

Regarding the question of what kind of universal (*sāmānya*) it is that brings about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), he says: "that which has not been previously apprehended" (*anadhigata*). This means:

that whose object is a means for accomplishing purposeful action which has not been previously apprehended—that is, not determined by a prior cognition—and which functions through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) based upon that [object].
This qualification is made by way of its being a cause (*hetubhāva*).

By this, it is shown that although the universal appearing as a conceptual construction (*vidhivikalpa*) has the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as its object, it does not have the accomplishment of an unapprehended purposeful action as its object; thus, there is no validity for that which has such [a universal] as its object.

To the question, "From what does it have that as its object? he says: "Connected" (*sambaddha*). That which is connected to purposeful action... [29.2] ...is that which is connected to purposeful action.
By virtue of its nature as a battle, because of its connection with that, because of its being mounted upon that— that is to say, because of its being established therein.
When there is the expectation of where such a state of being connected through a connection (sambaddhasambandha) of this [subject] occurs, the phrase "in the cause," etc., should be applied.

Because it is cognized by way of the ascertainment of a mark (*liṅga*) that has become such [as a cause or a pervader], it should be understood as having arrived through the door of the ascertainment of a mark connected to a cause or a pervader.

The point is this: the effect (*kārya*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*), when determined in such a manner, cause one to understand their own cause and their pervader as being excluded from what does not possess that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*).

By all of this, the following is stated: for in reality, it is precisely the fire and so forth—which are the means of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsādhana*)—that are apprehended by inferential conceptualization (*anumānavikalpa*) as delimited by specific locations and so on.
A universal (*sāmānya*) is that which is delineated by being excluded from one side;
since it is nothing other than this, the validity of that [cognition] which determines it is established.

Now, is it not the case that for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising after perception—which grasps an object as having a specific location and so forth—it is precisely that [object] which accomplishes purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)?

Because of such determination (*adhyavasāya*), even a universal (*sāmānya*) that is grasped by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of affirmation, being an object that accomplishes a telic function (*arthakriyā*) not yet attained, will cause the conceptual construction that grasps it to be endowed with validity. Thus he says: "This... [29.4].
The particle *tu* indicates its difference from the previous case.
"It is cited" means it is made into an example;
and the underlying intention is: "What is the reason for abandoning the subject under discussion?"
The phrase "is cited in order to refute" (*nirākartum udāhriyate*) should be supplied [to the text].
He begins with the words "But which... (*kāṃ punar...*) in order to explain the very example.
For, through their mutual exclusion (*parasparavyāvṛttyā*), individual manifestations (*vyaktayaḥ*) would indeed produce distinct cognitions.
Anticipating the objection, "But how can it produce both a cognition and a verbal designation that are not distinct?", he says: "In this way" (evam).
That single effect, such as carrying or milking, is the specific determination (*pratiniyama*) therein.
It is described as such because its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the state of being specifically determined, which necessarily entails having existed previously.
It should be understood that [the cause] is to be assisted and made manifest, but not produced,
because its nature as such is admitted by the opponent due to its permanence.
Furthermore, if one does not rely on the opponent's own admission, it is impossible for this to function as an example.
Therefore, "another universal" (*aparaṃ sāmānyam*) than the intended one is that single universal called "manifestation" (*vyañjakatva*).
Otherwise—that is, by way of connection with another universal in the form of manifestation—[the argument would fail].
To manifest that [universal] as well, another universal—called the "manifestor of that single universal" or the "manifestor of universals"—must be accepted.
Likewise, to manifest that too, yet another would be required; thus, there is the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because it never reaches a conclusion.
This is because they will establish [their existence] by their very nature, without connection to the intended universal, as is understood from the context.

"Now, why do you exert such effort in denying an object perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that you speak in this way? To this he says: "What [is the point]? (29.6). Or rather, must that which lacks a known means of valid cognition necessarily be non-existent, such that its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is entirely cut off? To this he says: "And by that which is not sublated by a means of valid cognition" (29.26). He begins with the words "For instance" (29.27) in order to demonstrate the lack of sublation by a means of valid cognition to some extent; by saying "we do not perceive" (29.28), he shows the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) consisting in the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*).
"Non-manifestation" (*avibhāvana*) means non-comprehension through differentiation, like an embryo that has not been extracted.

Intending to show that if there were a difference between form (*rūpa*) and the possessor of form (*rūpin*) due to their non-difference, then only the possessor of form would undergo differentiation, he says: "because it would entail the admission of two distinct categories of entities.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), sound and cognition are included.

Now, one might object: "The difference between entities arises from their connection with distinct universals (*sāmānya*), and not from a difference in appearance. Anticipating this, [the author] provides a single refutation of the universal, even though a hundred faults might occur here, out of fear of overloading the text: {p. 283} [30.7].

He thinks as follows: if the difference between entities arises from the difference between universals, then just as there is a difference between a cow and a horse, so too there must be a difference between "cowness" and "horseness" due to the difference between other universals belonging to them; thus, there would follow an infinite regress of universals for each universal. To the objection, "Let this be so; what is the harm? he replies: "Of that which is devoid of a universal" (niḥsāmānyasya).
"Of this" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*).
"By this" refers to the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), which has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "I do not perceive anything of that kind.
But how is the non-perception of the perceptible established, such that this [universal] would be refuted by it? [The answer is: "Because... [as follows].
"In that case, it is unestablished" (tadāsiddham)—

this should be understood from the context as referring to the fact that cognition depends upon a subsequent following (*anvagam*). In this regard, "because it is not perceived" (*anupalakṣaṇāt*) means because it does not appear in sensory cognition (*indriyabuddhi*).
It is intended here that a general cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*), which does not possess distinct forms such as blue and so forth, is what is experienced; for,
setting aside the form of the particular (*vyakti*), nothing else is desired [as the object].

Anticipating the objection that "that very form which has been approached appears there, and that alone is the universal for us," [the author], intending to show that even that does not exist, says: "Even of the distinct...
This is to be connected with the phrase "because of non-perception."

Now, having provisionally accepted the second [type of inference], that which has a clear form, as an illustration, he says "And if that exists" (*tad-bhāve ca*) in order to refute its conformity with the [logical] mark (*anvaya*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is used here to signify the acceptance of the statement of a specific meaning.

By this, what is meant? Does that second, manifest form not pervade the space between the two individuals, the *sābaleya* and the *bāhuleya*? Having presented these two alternatives—"does it pervade? and "does it not pervade?"—the author demonstrates the fault in the position that it does not pervade: for that which does not pervade the intervening space—that is, the gap between the two individuals—and which does not connect with it by means of its own existence (*svasattayā*).

How is there "following after" that? Following after another individual instance means pervading other individual instances; however, because it is inactive, movement is impossible and thus such an operation cannot occur. Even if it were so, it would entail the consequence of being separated from its previous location, and yet it is not joined to that [new location]. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the second alternative as well, he says: "And if there were pervasion... [30.18].
In that regard, concerning the interval [between the two cognitions], he says "no" because its form is not manifest there due to the absence of a manifestor, and thus it is not perceived.
For the point is this: since on the surface of the ground it must necessarily be manifest by some means, it is impossible for it to have an unmanifest form.

Demonstrating that this meaning is also intended by the author of the *Vārttika*, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Since only the portion relevant to the subject at hand ought to be recited, he recited only these two quarters of the *Vārttika*. By the reasoning already stated, if a single manifest form were possible, then this other [point] would also [be established].
Demonstrating this, he says: "Even in one place" (*ekatrāpi*). The particle *ca* is used for the conjunction of another statement.
The word "entirely" (*sakala*) is said with reference to the proponent who maintains that [the quality] is omnipresent in all things.
But for one who maintains that [the universal] is omnipresent within its own substratum, [the phrase] "in its own substratum" [is used].
The word "name" (*nāma*) indicates impossibility.
Even by this part—that it resides in only a single substratum—this is not a valid example; rather, it is like [the case of] momentariness.

Just as there is no determination of seeing even for that which is seen by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-bodha*), so too there is no determination of seeing despite the manifestation of the form of its entire locus; this is precisely what [the opponent] means.
"In that case, let there be a determination of the form existing in all worlds."
Or rather, what harm is there if [the universal] resides in all its substrata? To this he says, "From that" (tataḥ).
"From that" means from such a determination of form;
by the word "that" (tat), the universal is referred back.
And by the word "sahacārin" (co-occurring), that which is connected [to it] is intended.

Therefore, the meaning is this: [of that which is] co-occurring with it, connected with its universal, and—so to speak—having its inherence as its object. This has been stated in response to the Naiyāyikas and others.
He addresses the Mīmāṃsaka, saying: "And of that which has an essence non-different from it" [31.1].

The two alternatives—whether the appearance of the universal is in sensory cognition or in conceptual cognition consisting of inference—are contained within the word "or. Having set aside one alternative, he says "Now then" [31.3] in order to refute the other.
By the word "etc. (ādi), sound and so forth are included. The phrase "intending only the previous [state]" is to be connected here.
Therefore, there is the mention "the cognition of inference and so forth" using the accusative case.

Just as a distinct form of the individual (*vyakti*) or the form of the object (*artha*), being perceived, exists as something experienced, so too the manifestation of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—that is, the form of the individual—is not perceived; this is how it should be construed.
Why is this so? He says: "In the absence of that" (*tadabhāve*); that is, in the absence of that particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), those [cognitions], namely the cognitions of universals (*sāmānyabuddhi*).

Right here he states an additional reason by way of another aspect (*ākārāntareṇa*), namely: "And [because] in its own cognition" (*svajñāne*). This refers to the cognition produced by the sense organ.

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) possesses two forms: a distinct and an indistinct one. Therefore, it appears in the sensory cognition with a distinct form, whereas elsewhere it appears with an indistinct form; thus he says "many" (*aneka*).

Regarding the phrase "because of the over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgāt*): even when there is the appearance of a jar, there would have to be the conceptualization of the appearance of a cloth, because the cloth possesses both the characteristic of a jar and the characteristic of a cloth; the intention is that the subsequent argument beginning with "because of the cloth" could be easily stated here as well.

This [cognition], which has an undifferentiated appearance and a universal form, arises from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, being "arisen from a particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇodbhavā*), it does not appear as something that grasps differentiated objects—that is, as something that grasps excluded entities.
Rather, it is [said to be] "beginningless" (*anādi*).
By stating, "because of the firmness of cognition at all times," if the firmness of cognition was intended, then examining even that, he says: "And as for this firmness... (31.10).

In the position of those who maintain that destruction has a cause, it should be understood that "because of the acceptance of momentariness" (i[31.10]) means because of the acceptance of extremely rapid perishability.
"Of this" (asyāḥ [31.11]) refers to the cognition of a universal.
"That" (tad [31.10]) refers to its being uncontradicted.

The word *syāt* expresses non-exclusivity (*anekānta*), and because it is fixed [in this sense], there is the doctrine of "perhaps" (*syādvāda*). Alternatively, [it refers to] such statements as "perhaps it is non-momentary" or "perhaps it is momentary"; thus, *syādvāda* is the doctrine of "perhaps. Its refutation (*bhaṅga*) is its rejection (*nirākaraṇa*).
Therefore, for that very reason, it must be understood as the subverter (*bādhaka*), since that is the subject under discussion.

The ablative case here should be understood as occurring after the elision of a verbal root ending in *lyap* (the gerund suffix), following the expression "having studied the refutation of the *syādvāda*.
He says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, concluding what was introduced by the passage beginning with "he thinks thus" (*evaṃ manyate*).
The connection is: "but that which is the fault in falsity" (*yas tu mithyātve doṣaḥ*).
It was stated [at 32.1] "by the opponent," which means implicitly.

Having done what was he so stated? He says: "having formulated the prima facie argument" [at 31.19]. The section beginning with "the universal" [at 31.22] and ending with "will be" [at 31.22] constitutes the text of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The word "iti" indicates the form of this very prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Of that universal (*sāmānya*), it is the regulator— that is, the delimiter— of its occurrence, meaning its functioning.

In the case of Sābaleya and others, although they are mutually distinct and share commonalities such as being white (karka) and so forth, the cause is that "cowness" alone subsists in them and not "horseness.
Just as Karka is distinct from one Sābaleya, so too is Bāhuleya;
thus, even though their distinctness is equal, the subsistence of cowness occurs in some—namely, Sābaleya and others—while its non-occurrence means its absence in those where it does not exist.

In response to the expectation—namely, "of what [property], with respect to which [entities], is there occurrence and non-occurrence? regarding horsehood (*aśvatva*) as subsumed by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is stated: "of cowhood (*gotva*) and so forth.
The term "without a cause" (*animitta*) is connected, according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), to both occurrence and non-occurrence, even within the context of the cognition.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: just as in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, a cognition that appears undifferentiated may occur with respect to only certain individuals—due to the capacity of beginningless impressions (*vāsanā*) of that kind—even though it lacks a cause for its occurrence and non-occurrence, and even though it is devoid of a regulating universal (*sāmānya*), so too will such a cognition arise with respect to only certain things. (31.22) Thus ends the section on the refutation of the universal (*sāmānya*). Now, the refutation of the particular (*viśeṣa*) follows. For some maintain that there exists a particular (*viśeṣa*) which is the ultimate limit of differentiation (*atyantavyāvṛtti*), and that this is the cause of the cognition of difference. To refute this, he says: "The particular (*viśeṣa*) is not perceived by the senses," and so forth. This is because it is not established that the particular is the cause of the cognition of difference; rather, the cognition of difference arises from the very nature of the objects themselves, just as the cognition of difference occurs with respect to two hairs, even though no particular exists there. Furthermore, since particulars are not perceived by the senses, they cannot be the cause of the cognition of difference. Moreover, if particulars were the cause of the cognition of difference, then the cognition of difference would have to occur with respect to all things, because the particular is omnipresent (*sarvagata*). Alternatively, if one were to say that the particular is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal (*nitya*), because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the cognition of difference would occur everywhere, because the particular would be present in all things. Therefore, the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference. Furthermore, since the particular is not perceived by the senses, it is not established that it exists. And since it is not established that it exists, it cannot be the cause of the cognition of difference. Thus, the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference. (31.23–31.24) Now, the following objection might be raised: "If the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference, then what is the cause? To this he replies: "The cognition of difference arises from the very nature of the objects themselves. This means that the cognition of difference arises from the specific characteristics (*svabhāva*) of the objects themselves, just as the cognition of difference occurs with respect to two hairs, even though no particular exists there. Furthermore, if the particular were the cause of the cognition of difference, then the cognition of difference would have to occur with respect to all things, because the particular is omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the particular is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal, because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the cognition of difference would occur everywhere, because the particular would be present in all things. Therefore, the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference. (31.24–31.26) Now, the following objection might be raised: "If the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference, then how can one explain the fact that the cognition of difference occurs only with respect to certain things and not others? To this he replies: "It occurs only with respect to certain things due to the capacity of beginningless impressions of that kind. This means that the cognition of difference arises only with respect to certain things due to the capacity of beginningless impressions of that kind, just as the cognition of difference occurs with respect to two hairs, even though no particular exists there. Furthermore, if the particular were the cause of the cognition of difference, then the cognition of difference would have to occur with respect to all things, because the particular is omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the particular is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal, because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the cognition of difference would occur everywhere, because the particular would be present in all things. Therefore, the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference. (31.26–31.28) Now, the following objection might be raised: "If the particular is not the cause of the cognition of difference, then what is the cause of the cognition of identity (*abheda*), which is the opposite of difference? To this he replies: "The cognition of identity arises from the very nature of the objects themselves. This means that the cognition of identity arises from the specific characteristics of the objects themselves, just as the cognition of identity occurs with respect to a single hair, even though no universal exists there. Furthermore, if the universal were the cause of the cognition of identity, then the cognition of identity would have to occur with respect to all things, because the universal is omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the universal is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal, because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the cognition of identity would occur everywhere, because the universal would be present in all things. Therefore, the universal is not the cause of the cognition of identity. (31.28–31.30) Now, the following objection might be raised: "If the universal is not the cause of the cognition of identity, then what is the cause? To this he replies: "It arises from the very nature of the objects themselves. This means that the cognition of identity arises from the specific characteristics of the objects themselves, just as the cognition of identity occurs with respect to a single hair, even though no universal exists there. Furthermore, if the universal were the cause of the cognition of identity, then the cognition of identity would have to occur with respect to all things, because the universal is omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the universal is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal, because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the cognition of identity would occur everywhere, because the universal would be present in all things. Therefore, the universal is not the cause of the cognition of identity. (31.30–31.32) Now, the following objection might be raised: "If neither the particular nor the universal is the cause of the cognitions of difference and identity, then how can one explain the fact that these cognitions occur at all? To this he replies: "They occur due to the capacity of beginningless impressions of that kind. This means that the cognitions of difference and identity arise due to the capacity of beginningless impressions of that kind, just as the cognitions of difference and identity occur with respect to two hairs and a single hair, respectively, even though neither a particular nor a universal exists there. Furthermore, if the particular or the universal were the cause of these cognitions, then these cognitions would have to occur with respect to all things, because the particular and the universal are omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the particular or the universal is not omnipresent, then it would follow that they are not eternal, because they would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if they were eternal and omnipresent, then these cognitions would occur everywhere, because the particular and the universal would be present in all things. Therefore, the particular and the universal are not the causes of the cognitions of difference and identity. (31.32–32.1) Now, the following objection might be raised: "If the particular and the universal are not the causes of the cognitions of difference and identity, then what is the basis for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'difference' and 'identity'? To this he replies: "The conventional usage of 'difference' and 'identity' is based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). This means that the conventional usage of 'difference' and 'identity' is based on the exclusion of others, just as the conventional usage of 'tree' and 'non-tree' occurs with respect to a *śiṃśapā* tree, even though no universal 'tree' exists there. Furthermore, if the universal were the basis for the conventional usage of 'identity', then the conventional usage of 'identity' would have to occur with respect to all things, because the universal is omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the universal is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal, because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the conventional usage of 'identity' would occur everywhere, because the universal would be present in all things. Therefore, the universal is not the basis for the conventional usage of 'identity'. Similarly, if the particular were the basis for the conventional usage of 'difference', then the conventional usage of 'difference' would have to occur with respect to all things, because the particular is omnipresent. Alternatively, if one were to say that the particular is not omnipresent, then it would follow that it is not eternal, because it would be subject to production and destruction. Or else, if it were eternal and omnipresent, then the conventional usage of 'difference' would occur everywhere, because the particular would be present in all things. Therefore, the particular
Therefore, because there would be no arising of cognition in the absence of an object, they maintain that this universal (*sāmānya*) is certainly eternal;
or rather, for that reason, they maintain that this universal is certainly and definitively [existent].
He asks: "What fault is there in the arising of cognitions whose nature is to conform [to an object] even without an undifferentiated object?
He says: "For those...
[31.26]. Those are the general cognitions that have an undifferentiated appearance.

By this, the opponent has stated a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the production of such a cognition in the case of a universal non-existence (*sāmānyābhāva*). Refuting that very point which has been taken captive, he says: "But not... [31.27].
From the context, it follows that "occurrence" (*vṛtti*) means "restricted."
For one who says that "it does not become faulty," this is the implication: in the arising of such a cognition in the absence of that [universal], there is no subverting fault of falsity.
But as for a universal, what subverting factor exists in its occurrence in only some particulars by means of another universal, such that I would have to admit another universal therein?
This fault of falling into falsity does not invalidate or afflict us and others—those whose intellects are purified by the realization of the Tathāgata’s established doctrine.
Why is this? He says: "In regard to the universal," and so forth.
Although, as before, a measure of the proof for establishing the falsity of the cognition of a universal has been shown.
Nevertheless, in order to demonstrate that there is indeed abundant evidence establishing its falsity,
[the author] uses a gentle approach; the term "hump" (galakambala) includes the hump and so forth by virtue of the word "etcetera" (ādi).
[55] It is not unique, because that would entail the loss of its nature as a universal;
nor does it possess the property of arising and passing away, because that would entail the absence of permanence—this is what is present in the mind.
The word *iti* [at 32.8] refers back to what has just been stated.
To the question "Why is it not logical?", he says: "Because they are contradictory" (*viruddha*).
He states this point at greater length through verses, speaking by way of another, beginning with "He says" (*āha*) and so forth.
The word "destruction" (*nāśa*) should be understood from the context as referring to the manifest (*vyakta*).
The term "unbornness" (*ajātatā*) is to be connected with the word "by what" (*kena*), with the gender changed;
that is, by what cause?
Just as in the case of the individual (*vyakti*).
Lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*) means not following after other individual instances.
The fault of the consequence of falsity;
"without cause" (*animittā*).
[55] And this is not so—S:

But surely, because of the statement, “Moreover, these universals are imperishable due to the destruction of their substrata” [Ślokavārttika, p. 380], the Mīmāṃsakas indeed accept that there is destruction when the individual is destroyed; why then is it said that there is no destruction when the individual is destroyed?
The point that "keneṣṭe" refers to the established Mīmāṃsaka position is true.

The intention of such a speaker is merely this: if a single universal could logically be both distinct from and non-distinct from its instances, then it might indeed be said that it perishes in the form of the individual while persisting in a form separate from it; however, this would be nothing more than a mere consumption of a mental sweetmeat.
This will be established below at the appropriate occasion.
For this very reason, some Naiyāyikas have explained Kumārila’s statement "not non-existent" (*na-āsan*) as meaning "perceptible" (*upalabhyāni*).

Showing that this critique of the universal (*sāmānya*) arises when one rejects its birth at the time of the birth of the individual (*vyakti*), he says: "In the case of the individual," and so forth.

The feminine gender in the term *jātiḥ* is used with reference to what will be explained hereafter; intending that the universal (*jāti*) is devoid of activity, he accepts that it is "not yet arrived" (*nāgatā*). "Prior" (*prāk*) means before the arising of the individual manifestation (*vyakti*).
And with the intention that [the entity] is not perceived despite being visible, he asserts "it did not exist. The word "if" (*cedi*) is also connected here.
Regarding that manifestation as it arises, its "place" (*deśa*) is stated to be its substratum (*ādhāra*), in the sense that "in this [place] it is directed" (*diśyate*).
By this, he shows the following:
it might exist either through a connection with that or by way of being bound to it; however, even that [connection] does not exist as a single entity.

That universal (*jāti*) is conjoined with—that is, connected to—that individual (*vyakti*); how? In no way whatsoever. For if the production of that [individual] by that [universal] is asserted, then identity (*tādātmya*) is first of all not tenable because of their difference; even mere connection (*sambandha*) between them does not cohere. Such is the intended meaning of the one who speaks thus, which is to be understood.

Otherwise, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, since no relation other than identity is accepted, it would follow—via such arguments as "from another substratum" and so forth—that the negation of all relations whatsoever would be rendered useless; yet that very view is what is currently under discussion. Furthermore, if the universal were held to be imperishable even when the individual is destroyed...
Showing what the fault would be, he says "the individual" (*vyakti*).
With the intention that [it] is devoid of activity, he says "not in the future.
And with the intention that there is no perception of what is visible in that which is empty of it—that is, devoid of a vanished individual—he says "not present."
The phrase "Where? (kva) is employed as a rhetorical question (kāku); how does it demonstrate the impossibility [of the objection]?

If one accepts that the universal (*jāti*) has the individual (*vyakti*) as its essence, then upon the arising and passing away of that individual, the persistence and passing away of the universal would not occur.

Having established that these two faults arise when that [universal] is accepted as residing [in the individuals], he says— demonstrating that even when those [faults] are accepted, the acceptance of the identity (*tādātmya*) of the universal with them is the most inferior position—
that "the state of having that individual as its self" means that the individual is its essence or nature (*svabhāva*).
"Of those whose minds are unassailed"—that is, those whose minds have not been brought to a state of unease by sounds and other such objects.
How is this intended? This use of *kimaḥ* (the interrogative pronoun) is employed for the purpose of censure.
This has been shown by implication to be the position of those Mīmāṃsakas whose minds are overwhelmed [by dogmatism]:

that "pramāṇa" is said to be the most excellent instrument (*kāraka*) for the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-siddhi*). The underlying intention is: since there is no production of any excellence (*aviśeṣādhāyitva*), how could this [intrinsic validity] possess the status of being the "most effective means" (*sādhakatamatva*), which is the defining characteristic of a *pramāṇa*?
By stating "not at all" (*naiva*), he indicates that the particle *eva* functions as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

This refers, according to the context, to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) existing at the time of perceiving the mark (*liṅga*). It is thus revealed that it is a universal (*sāmānya*) because it appears within that conceptual construction.
The phrase "due to a connection with what is connected" (*saṃbaddhasambandhāt*) and so forth refers to the manner previously explained.
To the question, "If that [cause] has the nature of a manifest individual (*vyakti*), how could it not be an agent? he says: "of that" (*tasya*).
This means: of that which has as its nature (*svabhāva*) a form (*rūpa*) that is conceptualized (*kalpita*)—that is, constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*).
Because that is impossible, the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) of coloring and so forth is untenable.
Here, collecting the objections common to all [theories of] eternalism, he says:
"And otherwise" (anyā). This is to be understood as characterized by the cognition and designation of non-difference, which is accepted as being produced by that [single cause].

Thus, the author of the *Vārttika* intends this meaning; and by saying "thus," it should be understood that he is placing it in his mind. The word "or" (*vā*) refers to the fact that the opponent has shown the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the verse as being "a means of valid cognition whose object is an unapprehended thing. Demonstrating this, he says: "In that regard, 'unprecedented'... The act of performing [an action] out of a desire for self-aggrandizement is called *āhopuruṣikā*.

By that [cognition], acting as the instrument, it imitates that specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by way of having an unclear form; thus, what is intended is that it "imitates that. Making this clear, he says:
"imitating the unclear specific characteristic of blue" means "appearing as the unclear specific characteristic of blue."
For every conceptual construction (vikalpa) indeed has the appearance of an unclear particular characteristic (aspaṣṭasvalakṣaṇābha).
However, the conceit of a clear manifestation of the object that arises for one who is both seeing blue and so forth and simultaneously conceptualizing it,
is due to the clarity of the non-conceptual [cognition] produced at the same time as that conceptual construction.
And how this is so, as well as both [the points] being correct, should be understood from that very source, namely the *Ācārya-viniścaya*.

Furthermore, how is it that this [cognition] conforms to the non-clear particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue, and does not, like a non-conceptual [perception], conform to a clear particular characteristic? Having raised this doubt, the following should be applied: "directly" (*sākṣāt*), because it does not arise through mediation from that particular characteristic—this being the context.
If it were not produced from that, [it would not be a perception].
Then, having raised the doubt as to where the apprehension of that [cognition’s] fixed form, such as blue, comes from, one should apply the following: "In perception" (*darśane*).
"The cultivated impression" (*hitaḥ saṃskāraḥ*) means latent predisposition (*vāsanā*); its "impulse" (*vedha*) is its projection, and "by its power" (*tadvaśāt*).
The word "clearly" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "this is evident."

[57] Objection (S): Is it not the case that what appears therein is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), by virtue of which it is said to "resemble the clear particular characteristic of blue"? To this, he says: "In the visible... [33.28].
This is because of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized.
The meaning is that [the cognition] proceeds by unifying the two objects—the perceived and the conceptualized.
Furthermore, this unification of the perceived and the conceptualized should be understood as arising precisely from its production in that manner.
The intention is that because that which appears [to consciousness] is not external, this [consciousness] does not imitate an object;
that [consciousness] is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Having raised the doubt as to how, with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*), it possesses the nature of memory (*smṛtitva*)—defined as apprehending what has already been apprehended—he says: "For instance" (*tathāhi*).
Demonstrating that conceptual inference (*anumāna-vikalpa*) has the very nature of recollection (*smṛti*), the opponent says: "For instance," and so forth.
Because it is not delimited by a specific form such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*), he says it is "the mere thing excluded from non-fire. "Kitchen" (*mahānasa*) refers to a cook's workshop;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of a smithy and other such places is intended.
"Previously" (*prāk*) means at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*); this is the intended meaning.
"In a specific location" (*pradeśaviśeṣe*) refers to such places as a mountain.
"Like that" (*tadvat*) means like the conceptual cognition (*anumānavikalpa*) [of inference].

One might object: "Since the validity of this [cognition] as well has already been indicated by demonstrating the validity of the inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*) of the cognizer regarding what has been apprehended, what is the point of stating this again, which does not surpass what has already been said? Anticipating this, he says: "He thinks thus" (34.14). Even when the proponent has stated this, one who speaks in such a manner necessarily "thinks"—that is, he fixes in his mind—that which is about to be stated.
With the words beginning with "yad" [34.14], he demonstrates precisely that which is to be reflected upon;
by the word "ādi" [34.15], time is included.
That which grasps the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is that which grasps the mountain and so forth [34.17].

"Grasping the subject of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntadharmigāhi*) means grasping the subject such as a great mountain (*mahānasādi*). In that regard, by the perception that grasps the subject of the example, a thing qualified by a mountain or the like is not grasped as being excluded from what is non-fire; nor does it say "not a mountain."
Even by one who perceives such a subject possessing the property to be proven, yet does not perceive the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth—

because there would otherwise follow the consequence of non-disagreement regarding its being thus— it is shown that the object qualified by that [property], as excluded from non-fire, is apprehended; this is due to the two-fold observation (*darśanadvaya*).
It has been stated that it is not apprehended.

By means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), there is the elimination of the relation; because it is the opposite of that, namely, because it is the opposite of inferential conceptualization (*anumānavikalpa*). Therefore, as when...
Because it is determined precisely by that which is being perceived.

Now, [the opponent] intends [to argue] that because [cognition] has a real entity as its locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and a real entity as its object (*ālambana*), [it would follow that] inference is not included [among types of perception]. To this, he says: "And [as for] having a real entity as its locus... [34.23].
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "however.
The operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its "attainment" (*prāpaṇa*); it is with reference to that object (*viṣaya*) that this is said.
It should be connected as follows: "It is not with reference to an object characterized as an objective support (*ālambana*) that this is said."

The characteristic of the object (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*) is the form of the apprehended (*grāhya-rūpa*). In a manner other than what has been stated—that is, otherwise—it would be non-pervasive and not included within any valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That [cognition] whose object is remote, being separated by space, time, or intrinsic nature, is described as such.
The rebuttal beginning with "Even there" [35.1] and so forth is as follows:

because only a thing (*vastu*) in the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*), and because it is precisely that [conceptual object] which is the probandum (*sādhya*) in the sense of not being based on that [external reality], such as its being primarily characterized by that [conceptual form].

The collective meaning here is that even in that case, for the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that very form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the real object as its basis.
The context under discussion is that among the conceptual constructions of affirmation and negation regarding perception, validity belongs to perception alone and not to the other two.
And it has been stated: "In that regard, only the first one... [25.11], and so forth.

Anticipating the objection, "How then can there be the establishment of the production of an object through the demonstration of the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on a real entity (*vastu*)," he begins with the words "And this... [35.12] in order to show the connection.
This refers to the lack of proof for that [means of cognition] which is characterized by its capacity to apprehend the nature of an object not yet apprehended.
Its "manifestation" (*udbhāvana*) means its disclosure; for that purpose.
"Of that very" means of that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Even for a universal (*sāmānya*), there is causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Anticipating the prima facie argument that "because it possesses the characteristic of being an object, even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) directed toward it does not lose its status as a valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇya*)," he says, "of the universal" (*sāmānyasya*), [35.21],

meaning because it is the opposite of that— namely, the opposite of the characteristic of possessing causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). And how that [universal] lacks the possibility of performing causal action has already been explained previously.
And it should be understood that he who possesses a hidden intention thinks thus. Furthermore, the connection is: "because a person's activity occurs only with respect to a real entity (*vastu*).

And this is the statement of the reason (*hetupada*) for the thesis (*sādhya*) that "the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) born from the power of that [perception] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
He asks, "How does activity occur? and replies, "By the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that.
He asks, "Why is activity postulated by means of the determination of that? and replies, "Otherwise...
In this regard: [4/...
[35.24] Since the previous argument and this one are equal in their logical validity regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), why is this restated? To this he says, "The former...
[35.27]. This distinction should be understood as being shown by relying on the verbal expression (*śābdī gati*).

Alternatively, if there is an insistence that since there is no difference in meaning, what is the point of showing a distinction merely through a difference in formulation, then with the intention of saying that for that very reason it is stated, he says, "Or rather... [36.1].
The compound of particles *kim iti* functions in the sense of "for what reason" (*kasmāt*).

One might think: "Even though it operates upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the object of non-conceptual cognition, by virtue of experiencing that, it will attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) while having another object of cognition as its domain. Anticipating this, he says: "This is his intention" (*ayam asyābhiprāyaḥ*).
"In that very same case, one should cause it to function toward another object of cognition, namely its own object"—
this is a statement of possibility,
or it expresses capability.
To the question "What would it cause one to engage in? he says: "Its form is that which is to be accomplished" (*rūpaṃ tatsādhyam*).

Having in mind that its object is merely another object of cognition (*prameyāntaramātra*), it was stated that one would engage in that very thing in order to attain the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it. However, it is now said that "or rather not at all" (*naiva vā*) if that other object of cognition is characterized as a mere capacity (*sāmarthyalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, it does not function at all—not with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), nor with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), nor anywhere else; thus, by the negation of mere activity, it is established.
Let it function, O S; let it perform the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it.

Alternatively, what was previously stated—beginning with "in that very [case]" [36.13]—was said without having taken into account the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by a universal;
but now, however, it has been stated after taking into account the causal efficiency to be accomplished by that [particular], namely, "not at all" [36.14].
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "In its object" [36.15].
Thinking that [the opponent] will act for the very sake of establishing that [distinction], he says "in conceptual construction" (*vikalpe*).
This is because of the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by non-differentiated cognition;
and by implication, also because of that characterized by non-differentiated designation—the non-distinction (*abheda*) is thus to be understood.

[Objection: "But surely, even a cognition whose object is another cognizable thing, by causing one to act toward that [original] object, or by causing one to act somewhere where its own objective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has already been accomplished, would also attain the status of valid cognition.
To this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*), etc.
By the plural number in the word *pratyayāḥ* ("cognitions"), he demonstrates totality.
"Established" means accomplished; "those whose causal efficacy regarding their own objects has been established" refers to such things,
and the connection with the preceding clause is that they do not function toward anything at all.

"Specifically" (viśeṣeṇa) means that this is the opinion of those Mīmāṃsakas who explain it in this way by means of specific [arguments], as is understood by implication. "Of the dual nature" (dvyātmakasya) means of that which consists of both the universal and the particular.
Because desire and so forth have causes non-different from those of consciousness, they are of the nature of consciousness.
Having intended [the word] *siddha* (established), it should be understood that the connection with validity (*prāmāṇya*) is made;
[the phrase] "the number of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām iyattā*) refers to their delimitation (*vyavaccheda*).

According to the view of Kumārila, the [doctrine that there are] only six means of valid cognition—namely perception, inference, analogy, presumptive testimony, verbal testimony, and non-apprehension—would thus be shattered or broken. [The things] are characterized by the nature of becoming, having the habit of flowing by way of a stream or current.
"Indeterminacy" is the reason characterized by the identity of acquisition and preservation with that [subject], according to the context.
The proponent [of the theory of convergence] maintains that multiple means of valid cognition—whether of the same class or of different classes—converge and operate upon a single object.
The connection is as follows: [it is argued that the object] differs at every moment. Of what [moments]? Of the specific moments.
A desire arises regarding an object to be accomplished.
If it were argued that such [desire] cannot arise for people like us simply because we do not perceive objects in that way, he says: "of the yogins" (yoginām).
Yoga is one-pointedness of mind; those who possess this are the yogins.
The suffix *ya* should be understood here either in the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*) or in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).
Yoga is either calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), or it belongs to those who possess them.
One might ask: "Since the welfare of others is impossible for them [the Buddhas], with what intention does this desire arise? To this he says: "For others" (*pareṣām*).

Now, one might ask: since those who act for the benefit of others should simply benefit others, why do they desire to attain or avoid an object that must be accomplished through a specific moment? To this he says: "of someone" (*kasyacid*).

This is because there is some utility—either directly or indirectly—for a certain object to be accomplished through a specific moment, owing to its being something that serves a purpose (*upayujyamānatvāt*).
The phrase "in some case" (*kvacit*) should be understood from the context as referring to a living being (*prāṇini*).
By this, its status as a limb of assistance to others is demonstrated.
At that time, it should be connected with the phrase "there is no commonality of acquisition and preservation" (*nānāyogakṣematvam*).
The punctuation at the word *tadā* is indeed clear.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "yathā" (just as).
The meaning of the word "yathā" is that just as this has been shown in the presentation of the object for the purpose of refuting the universal (*sāmānya*), so too should other cases be understood.
By excluding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said to be the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*). These are:
receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).
The receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding suffering,
the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering; the receptivity to dharma-knowledge regarding origination, [the dharma-knowledge regarding origination].
Dharma-knowledge regarding origination;
receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding origination; and subsequent knowledge regarding origination.
Receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation, the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation;
