receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
Subsequent knowledge regarding cessation;
receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path, and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.

The receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*)—thus, these fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). As it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "Because of seeing what was not seen before, the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments" (AK 6.28). Within that path of seeing, there are the five aggregates of affliction (*saṃkleśaskandha*) which constitute the fruit.
The truth called suffering;
regarding that suffering, the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the fitness for the knowledge of its own nature.
It is the direct realization of suffering.
"Wholesome" (*kuśala*) means, in short, that which is capable of producing right knowledge (*jñāna*).
Regarding this, one seeking further detail should consult the *Visuddhimagga*, page 359.
He asks: what does that moment do? He says:

The five—attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, and doubt—and the views characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—these are the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). He explains how one suppresses and destroys their latencies (*vāsanā*):
"How does one do so? he asks.
This mental state (*āśaya*), which is a particular state of the continuum of consciousness (*cittasaṃtati*), is opposed to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) because it brings them to cessation.

Having demonstrated the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), he says "regarding suffering" (*duḥkha*) in order to show that the moment of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) has a distinct causal efficacy from that:
"the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the intrinsic nature of suffering.
Regarding "active knowledge" (*pravṛttajñāna*):

by the etymology "that through which nirvāṇa, i.e., liberation (*mokṣa*), is attained," or by the etymology "that from which the attainment of nirvāṇa arises," the state of being free from afflictions (*kleśaviviktatā*) is expressed by the term "attainment of nirvāṇa."

Among the thirty-two afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because he has brought about the cessation of exactly ten afflictions, he has established himself in the state of being pervaded by the isolation from those ten burnt afflictions.

The state of being far removed from the nature of nirvāṇa—which resembles the abandonment of afflictions that are to be abandoned through the knowledge of the origin [of suffering] and so forth—is established because [the state of being a non-percipient being] is a stage of accomplishment; otherwise, this would be inconsistent.

Alternatively, by the word "nirvāṇa," Arcata does not mean the ultimate supreme bliss (*paramaniḥśreyasa*), for which he spoke thus; rather, it refers to an intermediate form of supreme bliss of that kind, and thus there is no fault whatsoever.
How does one act accordingly? He says: "it underlies" (*anuśayati*).
When that [underlying tendency] exists, those [defilements] do not arise again even slightly;
rather, there is only a continuous stream of moments devoid of them. Thus, at that time, the firm establishment of that [state] is his intention (*adhyāśaya*).
By the preceding moment, the afflictions are eliminated; by the subsequent one, however, one acts in such a way that they do not enter again.
This is the purpose of the activity of these two.
For this very reason, it is shown in the *Abhidharmakośa* as "like the expulsion of a thief and the closing of the door" (AK 6.28).

Regarding the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) concerning suffering, which are to be understood as the antidotes to the afflictions of the desire realm: [the author] uses the plural number in the phrase "of these" (*eṣām*) to indicate that the examples of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of phenomena concerning suffering are merely illustrative in direction, since others are likewise distinguished in that same way. He states "graspers" (*grāhakāṇi*) and "apprehenders" (*ālambakāni*); and as to what those graspers are, he says "others" (*pare*).
The knowledges that have the minds of others as their object are "knowledges of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding the reading *damānāṃ S*, this is stated incorrectly.

For one who attains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the moments beginning with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arise sequentially. When these sequential moments are taken as objects by subsequent knowledges (*jñāna*) through a different application (*yogāntara*) for the sake of the welfare of others, those knowledges directed toward those same objects—arising from that different application—are indeed distinct; they are strictly differentiated from each preceding knowledge.
Having established that the yogic cognitions which have as their objects the moments realized through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) possess validity (*prāmāṇya*) individually,

[the author], now wishing to establish in general that all yogic cognitions— having as their objects moments capable of distinct purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)— are indeed valid, says: "For the benefit of others" (*parahita*), etc.

[Regarding the phrase] "of the Blessed Ones" (*bhagavatām*), because the direct perceptions (*adhyakṣacetas*) of those who possess various [types of] yoga are secure (*yogakṣema*), their status as valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is distinct; this is either the remainder of the sense or is obtained from the context.
Furthermore, this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
The meaning is: "of those cognitions which, directed toward direct realization, are perceptions related to that Blessed One.
To the question, "Of what kind of Blessed Ones? he says: "of all" (*sarveṣām*). This means:
of those who perceive, seeing at every moment all phenomena through knowledge born from the power of meditative cultivation.
To explain how these [cognitions] possess different *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation), he says: "In their object" (*tadviṣaye*).

This means that because those moments which are distinct from the objects of those direct perceptions belonging to the Blessed One are employed—that is, they function—within distinct causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*), one should understand that the nature of the subject is stated here by virtue of the nature of its object.
But why do they observe things at every moment? He says: "only someone" (*kaścid eva*).
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
It follows by implication that this is for the purpose of acting in accordance with what is beneficial or obstructive.
[62] — While they are observing for a moment:

"But even so, why do the Blessed Ones, though having accomplished their own purpose, continue to observe all phenomena at every moment— even if it be for a mere instant or for the sake of some living being— whether to bestow favor or to act as an obstacle?"
Anticipating this objection,

he states the qualifying term for the Blessed One with the words "for the benefit of others" (*parahita*): that which is beneficial for another— that is, wholesome for the future— is its "establishment," meaning its production.
For those who possess that [knowledge], there is a rule that this very initiation must be performed;
furthermore, this suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of a constant connection (*nityayoga*).

Knowledge itself—because it effects the discrimination between the existent and the non-existent—is like light; for those whose inner self (*antarātman*) is illuminated or made radiant by that [knowledge], [the term] "inner self" is used as a designation for the world.

However, the meaning is that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), [the term is used] for those who possess the light of knowledge of things as they truly are (*tathābhūtajñāna*).

If it is argued that this usage—*vastuvistara*—is grammatically incorrect because the suffix *ghañ* cannot follow the root *stṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* when the word to be expressed refers to expansion (*prathana*) within a domain that is not a linguistic object (*aśabdaviṣaya*), then [we reply]: [it is not so].
But that is not quite accurate;
for in the Sūtra, "extension" (prathana) is intended to mean "extensiveness" (vistīrṇatva).
Thus the author of the Kāśikā says: "Extension is extensiveness."
And here, by the word "vistara" (extension), the vastness of objects is not intended, but rather their abundance, as in the expression "an extension of grass.
For this very reason, the counter-example "What is the meaning of 'prathana' (spreading)? An extension of grass" is provided.
And even the author of the *Arthabhāgavṛtti* has clearly explained its meaning:
"The meaning is 'the expansion,' that is, the abundance, of grass. How, then, can the suffix *ghañ* be applied to this verbal root when it is functioning in the sense of non-expansion?

For this very reason, Prajñākaragupta also stated at the beginning of the *Vārtikālaṅkāra*: "Generally, speakers do not indeed venture to speak extensively on a subject already under discussion. Having thus presented the two alternatives—whether you state this reason as being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to omniscient beings, or rather with respect to people like ourselves—and having provided a rebuttal to the first alternative, he now intends to respond to the second one as well; therefore, he concludes with the words "If that... (*tad yadi*), and so forth.

It begins: "The distinction (*viveka*) of moments is their separateness (*pṛthaktva*); this is said with reference to those whose nature it is to perceive that. From the context, the reason—"because [the subsequent moment] shares the same acquisition and security (*abhinnayogakṣema*) as the preceding one"—is declared to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Then, "that reason is not inconclusive" follows from the context; the meaning is that there is no occurrence [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
With the words "Now, however" (*atha*), he introduces an alternative position.
Those for whom the purpose is practical activity (*saṃvyavahāra*), characterized by engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*), and performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
Regarding the statement that "from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the cause of differentiation is due to being the cause of one thing and another" [38.5],
in that context, only the first [type of cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In order to establish that even correct cognitions are not directed toward external objects, he begins with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

The proof of that consists in the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-sādhana*), which is the attainment of that [object]. In this regard, those whose intellects are "not weak and free from error" (*aklībāvidyamānaviplavā dhīḥ*)—meaning those who act with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*)—are such [persons]. The "action" (*kriyā*) of the object is its successful production (*niṣpatti*).
Its "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) is that which brings it about; its "division" (*bheda*) is due to its distinctness.
"Kindling" (*saṃdhukṣaṇa*) means inflaming; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of fanning, sweating, and so forth is intended.
Regarding the phrase "of those with undaunted intellects," the reading accepted as authoritative is *aklībadhiyām*.
Regarding the objection beginning with "if this were so" (i[39.18]) and so forth, concerning those of unimpaired intellect,
it must be stated that it has been said: "perception is a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) when it is non-erroneous."
It follows precisely from the set of reasons just stated.

Furthermore, since the definition of perception has not been stated—and thus perception itself has not been mentioned—even though it has been shown that all cognition of the non-evident is included within inference, how can the duality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be explained?

Moreover, by explaining that "only perception is a means of valid cognition," it is demonstrated that the senses and so forth are not themselves the means of valid cognition, as they are merely forms of cognition.
But how can there be a non-performance of the first [category] when it has been distinguished?
Furthermore, that for which the treatise is primarily intended is said to be its subject matter;
it is not said to be its subject matter simply because it explains something through implication or incidental connection.

And even if one accepts that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is being explained, since this [work] is engaged in explaining it in its primary sense, how can it be said to be for the purpose of explaining "correct knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*) in a general sense?

Otherwise, even if its purpose were the explanation of inference (*anumāna*), the demonstration of fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*) would follow by implication, as would [the discussion of] conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhin*), and those directed toward external objects (*parāñca*).

Why is it not stated that the demonstration that conceptual cognitions (*vikalpajñāna*) are pseudo-means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is for the purpose of distinguishing between inference (*anumāna*) and its fallacies, or for the purpose of distinguishing between the valid and the invalid means of cognition? Even if something else were intended as the purpose for the exposition of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*),
therein too [conceptualization] is active.

Since there is also an exposition of false cognition (mithyājñāna) by way of implication, why is it not said that this too is for the sake of explaining right cognition (samyagjñāna)? This [objection] is trivial.

Likewise, if its primacy is asserted because such [an object] is ascertained through inference, then why is the primacy of perception (pratyakṣa) not also asserted, since without the apprehension of the locus (dharmin) and the apprehension of the pervasion (vyāpti) through perception, there is no engagement with inference?
Nor is it better to assume its primacy on the basis of its posteriority.

Furthermore, even that inference which ascertains reality is subordinate, being an auxiliary to the perception that has been set in motion toward the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that ascertains all reality. This is what [the author] intends to say.
How can those who know reality be mistaken if they hold that the primary factor ought to be so?
Furthermore, since the determination of reality for anyone is in every respect impossible without the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), why is its very primacy not postulated?
For it is the object of false cognition within the scope of perception.
Therefore, a corresponding certainty has been produced, and no dispute regarding it is possible such that a certainty concerning it would have to be sought through inference.
If it is argued that its status as such is asserted because doubt arising at a later time is eliminated by inference,
then that [status] should be asserted with even greater force for perception.

This is because the non-arising of such doubt— which is based upon direct perception— is frequently observed. Now, if at that time that direct perception is not fit for the designation of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, and inference is likewise [not fit], then what is the point of saying this?
Furthermore, momentariness and such are not the object of perception, such that its primacy could be postulated based on its ascertainment through inference; enough of this prolixity.
Why would perception not possess primacy, given that it is sharp and prompts action?

For capacity (*yogyatā*) is not something other than the capable object itself, which—being imperceptible (*parokṣā*)—could not be ascertained by that [perception] but must be ascertained by another means; if the cognition that ascertains it were a distinct means of valid cognition, it would be inference.
However, fitness (*yogyatā*) is simply the state of being fit;
and just as there is a single mode of apprehension regarding an object of direct perception, so too has the Teacher himself demonstrated elsewhere.
Now, although fitness is the very nature of the fit object, it is nonetheless "remote" (*parokṣā*) because it depends upon a remote result.
Now, if the fruit is imperceptible, is it imperceptible in the ultimate sense, or is it merely quasi-imperceptible?
In that regard, if it is held to be imperceptible,
then it must be distinct [from perception], because the identity of the perceptible and the imperceptible is untenable.
Just as for the Mīmāṃsakas, [the cognition] is established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding an effect;
if it is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*),
how then can it be of a direct (*pratyakṣa*) nature while being indirect?
If it is argued that this is because such a certainty cannot be produced:

even if it is indeed impossible to ascertain [the object] prior to practice, why should it not be ascertained by a sharp perception that has reached the stage of practice—a perception from which the causes of error have been spontaneously removed?
Furthermore, its result, such as burning and so forth, is not entirely imperceptible, since it is experienced many times elsewhere as being produced by that [perception].
For this very reason, it has become more acute through practice;
however, prosperity and so forth have not been ascertained by anyone as being the effects of the volition to give, such that there might likewise be an ascertainment of them through practice.
Up to the point that it is indeed absolutely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*).
Therefore, with respect to that [future result], it is logical that there is no certainty regarding the capacity of the volition of giving (*dānacetanā*).

Thus, the meaning is this: one who has repeatedly experienced burning and so forth from fire and the like, even when the fruit is imperceptible at that time, certainly ascertains through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that "this [cause] is capable of producing burning and so forth."
Just as in the state prior to practice,
although a person depends on the instruction of others to recognize whether pearls and the like are artificial or natural— since such recognition is impossible for him by himself—
even when practice has been mastered, that same person, independent of any other person, recognizes the artificial or natural nature of pearls and so forth entirely on his own.

Likewise, even if there is an inherent ascertainment of its fitness [for perception] during the state of non-habituation, why is it not accepted that through habituation and so forth, a clear perception will itself ascertain that very fitness?
Regarding this, Bhartṛhari has said: "The cognition of gems, silver, and the like, for those who know them, is not inferential.
Furthermore, inference does not proceed without the recollection of a pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Furthermore, when one perceives an object such as fire and acts out of a desire for the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it, the proponent of truth cannot claim that there is a recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) prior to that action—based on the thought "whatever performs such purposeful activity is that [real] object, as seen in the kitchen and so forth. Therefore, how is it not sheer audacity to imagine that inference functions as the motivator in that case?
And thus, since perception does not depend upon inference when determining the nature of an object, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would otherwise result.

Just as its proficiency in determining the identity [of an object] is to be described as having fulfilled its purpose, why is it not likewise described as fulfilling its purpose in determining suitability? Enough of this excessive detail.

As for the statement that "this does not exceed the status of being inferable," that was said with reference to cognitions occurring within one's own and others' mental continua, because of the expression "except for objects previously experienced."
And in all these cases, the resolution must be formulated by the wise themselves:
the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the relationship between the cognized and the cognizer.

In the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, the ultimate non-difference between the probandum and the probans does not take as its object—nor does it rely upon—a distinct form in the locus (*dharmin*).
To the question "Why does it not apprehend [the object]? he says: "[Because of the absence of a relation]" (sambandhe).
For if there were no relation between things that are ultimately distinct and do not stand in the relation of cause and effect, it would follow that they lack such a state [of being related].

Here, "inherence in a single object" (ekārthasamavāya) is intended to mean the inherence of two [properties] in one and the same object; this refers to that which begins with "producedness" (kṛtakatva) and "impermanence" (anityatva).
"Producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is the beginning of that group of probans properties such as "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*);
"impermanence" (*anityatva*) is the beginning of that group of probandum properties such as "having parts.
"Of that" refers to inherence (*samavāya*).
Right here he states the reason for the dependence: "because of inherence" (*samavāyāt*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of space, direction, time, mind, and atoms.
But how is it that when [properties] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) reside in sound and so forth, their residence in the self (*ātman*) and other [substances] is precluded? To this he says:
Regarding the phrase "for that very...
[42.3], it refers to that *samavāya* (inherence).

This is because of the statement: "And it is not manifold like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because there is no difference in its marks, and because there is an absence of any mark of distinction; therefore, like existence (*bhāva*), inherence is one everywhere" [Praśastapāda Bhāṣya, p. 172].
[The opponent claims: "It is the acceptance [of the whole] as a unity.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Existence does not occur by means of inherence (*samavāya*), but rather inherence itself is existence. That too is flawed;
for since there is no relation [between them], the conceptualization that "this existence is an occurrence" is untenable.
Furthermore, if one were to postulate another relation [to connect inherence], there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Moreover, if inherence is its mode of existence (*vṛtti*), since it exists in [substances] such as the self (*ātman*) as well, why would it not have a mode of existence there too? Thus, the fault remains as it was.
The word "now" (*atha*) indicates an alternative position.
Showing that in this approach, the incident of the axle-pin emerging when the wedge was inserted has occurred, he says: "In that case, then...
[42.8]. It is possible that the word "self" (*ātman*), which was marked by doubt in the previous context, occurs here as well.

That which, having not existed, does not come into being, and having existed, does not perish—its opposite form is that which is superimposed upon it; the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that superimposition is the object (*viṣaya*) of that [cognition].
Why must this necessarily be accepted, such that the acceptance of another [alternative] is negated? To this he says: "That very [exclusion]" (*saiva*).

By implication, this means that there is a difference from the subject (*dharmin*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*); furthermore, the fact that the possessor of the property (*tadvat*) possesses a difference in the ultimate sense should be understood as stated according to the opponent's own intention.

The meaning is that [the two properties] would apply even to things considered eternal if there were no dependence on their being properties of a subject (*dharmi*), such as sound (*śabda*). Because the "goitre" (*gaḍu*)— so called because it is like a goitre, namely a lump of flesh located between the forehead and the head, which exists in the interval between the conceptualization of the property of arising and perishing and the conceptualizing mind— is fruitless, for that reason [it is rejected].
"Exclusion" (*vyatireka*) means difference;
this is the intended meaning:

if properties such as "being produced" were established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in your subject (*dharmin*) as being excluded from it, then even if that thing possessed such a nature, those properties would be useless, like the teats on the back of a goat.
By whom indeed would these not be accepted?
For the intrinsic nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*) is not subject to questioning;
it is only that such establishment by valid cognition (*pramāṇa-siddhatva*) is impossible, as it is clearly characterized by being sublated by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).

Now, one might raise the following objection: "What purpose do properties such as 'being produced' (kṛtakatva), which reside in conceptual construction, serve in making known the property to be proven (sādhyadharma)? Since the very nature of having the characteristics of arising and perishing—which must necessarily be accepted—is itself the basis for such a cognition, what is the use of anything else? Anticipating this doubt, the author, intending to provide the answer that it is indeed through acceptance [of the logical reason], says: "For instance" (tathāhi), and so forth.

"By mere existence" (sattāmātreṇa) means by its own nature, independent of the cognition that ascertains it; this should be understood to apply "at all times," from the very moment the entity arises. "Uninterruptedly" (anavaratam) means constantly; [the author speaks thus] because of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that there would be a continuous perception of that property—the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
To the question, "How indeed could that [entity] be the basis for the perception of that [property]? he says: "But rather... (kiṃtv i-).

[Objection: But if conceptual construction does not touch the real entity (*vastu*), how can there be a cognition of the real entity’s form as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth? To this he says: "And that" (*sa ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because.
Even though there is no contact with—that is, no grasping of—the form of that [entity], namely the form of being produced and so forth.
To the question, "How can there be a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [external object] by one who does not grasp it?", he says: "By way of a succession" (*paramparayā*).

This is because it has that as its material cause (*upādāna*); that is, because it has as its material cause an external form such as "produced-ness" (*kṛtakatva*), etc. "Of that conceptual construction" (*vikalpasya*) follows from the context.
But surely, properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth are not intended as the basis for such a cognition by virtue of their being causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*);

so how could there be such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) from which [the cognition] might arise? [The author] says, "[But those] distinct from that," in order to show that each of those properties would be redundant.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "because.

Therefore, because the subject—which possesses the property of coming into being after not having existed, and which possesses the property of ceasing to exist after having existed—is distinct from that conceptualizing cognition, its arising is merely the cause (*nimittamātra*) of that [cognition];
such is its nature.

This is what is meant: if "producedness" and so forth were not distinct from the subject (*dharmin*), then the cognition of "producedness" and so forth—which is established by experience—would be without a basis.
But this is not the case; therefore, there exists that which produces this cognition, namely "producedness" and so forth.
That is a conceptual construction;
therefore, it is more appropriate to conceive of [the agent] as being constituted solely by that [construction].
Nevertheless, one might argue that those other things [the causes] should be postulated as the basis for such a state; to this he says, "It is better," and so forth.
Because that which was just mentioned is thus, therefore, there is the postulation of that [property], such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*).

"Let that very nature of being something that did not exist before and then coming into existence—which is the basis for the thought, 'This property of being produced and so forth belongs to this very thing, and not to the self and such'—be the cause for the production of such conceptual constructions;
that would be better. He states "of that" (*tasya*) because he does not accept it as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Even if that were accepted, how could it be useless? To this he says:
And regarding the phrase "if that is accepted":

[the reasons would be] "fulfilled in purpose" (caritārthā), meaning their function has been accomplished by something else; "possessing exclusion" (vyatirekavantaḥ), meaning they are distinct from that [other thing]; and let them be "constructed by conceptualization" (kalpanānirmita).
By this, it is implicitly indicated that there is no contradiction whatsoever in that case.

It might be argued as follows: even if a thing possesses distinct properties such as impermanence and so forth, if speakers nevertheless represent the very entity itself as having the nature of persistence and the like, then—given that it is admitted to possess the property of having come into being and ceased to be, and given that this admission makes it logical for it to be the basis for the cognition "this"—the distinct properties would have fulfilled their purpose and thus cease to exist; for, as long as [impermanence] exists as something distinct, it is that very [entity] which speakers perceive.

Anticipating the objection, "How is it that what is being stated—namely, 'that which is the basis for that conceptual construction' and so forth—actually nourishes the opponent's position? he says: "And necessarily" (*avaśyaṃ ca*).
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*), or it has the sense of "this is clearly evident" (*vyaktam etat*).

Furthermore, the mention of "the apprehension of impermanence" (*anityatāgrahaṇa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by means of it, they likewise understand and ascertain that cognition in respect to "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, as appropriate to each case.
This is because of the context: "from being produced, they infer the state of impermanence."

To the question, "Why do they perceive that which is non-substantial as having such a nature? he says: "Because they act out of a desire for that purposeful action (arthakriyā) which is appropriate, correct, and fitting for a non-stable intrinsic nature;
that is, because those inferents [act] in that way. This is the meaning.
Regarding this, he states the subverting argument for the opposite case with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

If there were a separate impermanence [distinct from the entity], then because that entity—namely sound and so forth, as the context implies—would possess permanence and thus stability, it would follow that it is eternal.

The intention of one who asserts "because of its eternality" and so on is this: even if a separate impermanence were joined to the entity, the entity would not undergo change, because that [separate impermanence] would have no effect upon it.
Or, because the faults of difference, non-difference, and so forth would follow in the case of any action whatsoever;

and even if there were difference, since that [entity] such as space is excluded from that [action], its status as eternal is established—just like space itself. Thus, because the entity is eternal, when it is logically established that one desires the comprehension of that eternity of the entity, [the following applies].

Since this person seeks the purposeful activity (arthakriyā) that is the probandum—namely, impermanent objects such as sound and so forth—therefore, one who suspects that sound and the like are permanent cannot engage in inference because inference is impossible when there is no doubt.
Thus, being in doubt, for what reason would he have directed his interest toward an investigation of the impermanence of an entity? This is the intended meaning of the composition.

The meaning is that since impermanence is distinct from that [object], and because one has ascertained its stable nature, it is impossible for there to be an investigation into impermanence preceded by doubt regarding it.
[65] *avagamārthitvena* is not in S; [66] *nāsti* is not in S.
In some versions, the reading is *vyatiriktānityatayā*.
In that case, the instrumental case is to be understood as referring to the reason (*hetu*) when "permanence" (*nityatva*) is the property to be proven (*prayojya*).

Having established that such an investigation of an entity is not tenable if impermanence is distinct [from it], he says, "And if [impermanence] were distinct," pointing out yet another fault in that position.
In that very context, it is indicated by implication that when impermanence is realized, one has not failed to realize the entity itself;
this is by way of that— that is, by way of impermanence as distinct [from the entity]—
because realization consists in knowing the suchness of the entity.
That by which a thing is obstructed, such as impermanence and so forth, is an "obstruction" (*vyavadhi*);
or rather, the act of obstructing is the "obstruction. What [is gained] by that?
Let there be comprehension precisely of that which is unobstructed—that is, of that which is devoid of the obstruction of distinct [qualities] such as impermanence and so forth; this is better.
He states the specific reason with the words "by that very [means]" (*tenaiva*).
Anticipating a hundred such objections— such as how the cognition of a thing's actual state is possible even when proving a distinct impermanence— he says with a touch of irony,
"this very [point]" (*tad etad*), meaning that the fault just mentioned does not occur.

By virtue of having that as its intrinsic nature—that is, by being its cause—if one were to admit some kind of difference in any form whatsoever, we do not perceive even the slightest benefit; indeed, we do not see any such thing.

He says "sādhye" (in the case of the probandum) to show how the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), which is based upon difference, would otherwise be untenable if there were no difference in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, he states the plausible conclusion arrived at through the force of reasoning:

having demonstrated that if the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) were admitted to be identical in nature to the proving property (*sādhanadharma*), there would be no result whatsoever in admitting their difference, he now shows that a distinction between the single-natured probandum and the proof is simply not possible.
How, then, does he demonstrate that "it is not approached by cognition"? He says: "And not...
[43.11]. Any distinction whatsoever—by any intrinsic nature—between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), that is not tenable.
He asks "Why? and replies: "From one" (*ekasmāt*).
This refers to that single nature (*svabhāva*) by which their non-difference is intended; "from that one" means from the single nature, because the context concerns those two properties (*dharma*).
Even by that nature through which their non-difference exists, there is indeed no difference such that this fault would arise.

However, even from that very nature, there is some kind of both difference and non-difference between those two— producedness and impermanence— such that it is neither difference alone nor non-difference alone.
For, by that nature through which they are held to be non-different, even though they possess difference from that single nature as they are being differentiated,
there is some kind of cause for non-difference by means of that nature which serves as the limit of their difference.
If non-difference is not accepted, then there must be absolute difference;
and this being the case, the aforementioned fault would follow—this is what was stated for the most part.
By that very non-differentiated nature which serves as the cause of non-difference, it should be understood from the context that there is somehow a cause of difference; thus,
the imperceptible must be accepted.

In this case as well, if there were indeed no difference between those two by virtue of that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then there would be absolute non-difference; and consequently, the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*)—which is based on a difference appearing through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—would be undermined. Thus, one should understand the underlying intention to be that such a consequence would lead to the undesirable result of falling into our own [opponent's] position.

Thinking that when a distinct nature (*svabhāvāntara*) is postulated as the cause of non-difference or the cause of difference, there might not be absolute non-difference or difference, it follows by logic that one must again postulate such a further distinct nature; and since this applies there as well, the word "iti" indicates the reason for this intention, stating: "it would be infinite" (*anantatva*).
(The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason.)

The term "buddha" does not apply only to the non-conceptual state; rather, it refers to a lineage or tradition. Through that conceptualization—that is, through the conceptualization of a nature that is both different and non-different—they deceive, meaning they mislead.
Bringing forward another objection here, he says:
"And in some way" (*kathaṃcit*).

How could there be no occasion for those faults, such as the impossibility of the relationship between the probandum and the probans due to the absence of a connection that would exist on the side of the position of difference?
"Vasara" means "opportunity" or "scope.
For this reason as well, he states in brief with the words "And that which... that the two properties of being both different and non-different are impossible.

"Purodhāya" means "placing before" or "taking as an object" by means of a conceptualizing mind (*vikalpabuddhi*). He says "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*) because he is negating that which is constructed by conceptualization.
The word *iti* indicates the form of the triad (*tritaya*).
That which has three parts is a triad.
Because it is non-different from its own nature (S).
[68] Concluding the section, he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth.
And that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is of the form already described.
Because it is contradictory and therefore untenable for that [entity].
And how its non-connection [is established] will be determined later, in the section on auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-parvan*).
By the words "the entity (*bhāva*) is that from which there arise the designation and the cognition," he clarifies that very point through the phrase "it is an effect" (*kāryatvam*), and so forth.
Demonstrating that it indeed conforms to its specific cause, he says "In the case of sandalwood," and so forth.
*Ūrṇā* means sheep's wool; *bheda* means a distinction or particularity.
By this he means: if its cause were invisible, how could it conform to the distinction of fuel and the like, which are themselves without a [visible] cause?

Having established that smoke conforms to the differences in its fuel, he says "alpa... [45.27] while establishing that it also conforms to the differences in fire: "small and large" (*alpamahāntau*) refers to those two transformations of the fuel which are the causes of it.
For when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, there is no mention of its suffixal extension.
The substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel of the first member of a compound] as prescribed by the rule *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.3.46) does not occur here.
The connection is that this is because one perceives smoke that is either small or large, corresponding to that [fire].

This is stated with reference to the fact that, setting aside the necessary presence within the causal complex of fire and so forth—which is itself invisible—smoke is the effect of fire and the like alone.
Having stated this proof with its supporting arguments, he now says "na ca" (and not) in order to show that it is not logical for that [effect] to have a fixed proximity to it [the cause].
The word "ca" (and) serves to connect another point to be stated.
The effect of that fire and so forth is its result; its cause is its producer; its existence is its being; and "tattā" (thatness) refers to its essential nature.
The meaning is that because that very invisible thing exists immediately thereafter, smoke would not occur.
The word "ca" (and) connects the fact that the effect such as smoke possesses an equal means of proof (*tulyopāyatva*) with being an effect of something visible.
Of that which is invisible...
"Conformity with its existence" (*tadbhāvānuvidhānam*).
The particle "ca" is used for emphasis and should be understood as following the word "samāna" (in the preceding verse).
Here too, even in the case of the tree and the fuel, if one imagines their existence in that manner, the same response applies.
Regarding the perception of that [fuel], it is perceived as having been previously perceived when it met the conditions for perception;

thus, in the presence of trees and so forth, there is the existence of some fuel whose nature is invisible due to its fixed proximity. Furthermore, concerning the first objection: the opponent’s own statement—that because fuel conforms to the distinctions of the tree and so forth, it is logical that fuel, though invisible by nature, has a fixed proximity when the tree and so forth are present—is [the response].
"Because there is no obstruction, and even if there were an obstruction," and so forth.

The rebuttal is that the causality of that tree with respect to the tree and so on arises from the very cause of that tree—the seed and so on—because its existence is observed [to follow from them]. Even in that case, because there would be an endless succession of objections and rebuttals such as "due to the constant presence of an invisible nature," there would be no final conclusion.
Consequently, the intention is that even a single [cause] would not have a restricted effect.
Or rather, if that [effect] exists despite being invisible, why is another invisible cause— not merely one whose presence is restricted— not postulated?
Because the logic is the same;
thus, here too, by saying "it is likewise," the meaning is that there would be no established causal relationship due to an infinite regress.

Alternatively, even in that case—regarding trees and so forth—if the opponent were to conceive of their existence in that manner, namely, by conceiving of them as being visible, then that very [objection] applies, because fuel and the like follow the distinctions of trees and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not logical that there should be a fixed concomitance [of sound] with the presence of trees and so forth;

nor is it the case that trees and the like are the cause [of sound], because we observe the existence of trees and such from their own causes, namely seeds and the like, which are themselves imperceptible in nature.
This is the "answer" (*uttara*), so called because by means of it one moves away (*uttīryate*) from an undesirable position (*aniṣṭapakṣa*).

Furthermore, regarding the objection beginning with "because of the restricted proximity in the state of being seeds and so forth" [46.6], our response— stated immediately prior as "precisely that [is the cause], because it conforms to the distinctions of seeds and so forth"— is the refutation of the opponent's challenge. Moreover, the infinite regress has been explained just above.

By this [statement], through the force of the words "because the existence of fuel and so forth is seen to arise from its own cause, namely the tree and so forth," it is established that whatever is seen to exist from something else has that as its cause;
for it is from that very same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) from which fire, fuel, and so forth arise, that their visibility (*taddarśyatva*) comes into being.

The dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*)—which is the cause for their fixed proximity—is also refuted and rejected; for the establishment of something as an effect is only possible when that very thing is known to exist upon the presence of the cause.
The point is that if one were to imagine something to be an effect when it is not perceived upon the presence of the cause, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
While stating this, he says "that" (*tad*) in order to add another point to be discussed in this very context.
That is imperceptible, and that is the conformity with presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka). Stating precisely the absence of a cause, he says: "the effect," etc. [46.10].
When other causes are present and capable, the fact that the effect does not come into being indicates that another cause must be awaited for its production;
it does not, however, [indicate] that [it will] exist.
"Thus" (iti) is the collective meaning;
even there, it is that very same [S]. S. [70] It is that very same S.

[71] Or, even if it were admitted that the bond (*bandha*) is currently the cause of that [suffering], there would be no impairment whatsoever of our thesis; thus, in order to demonstrate this, he says: "But as for form... (*rūpaṃ tu*), meaning "let it be so" (*bhavatu*).

Since fire and so forth would lose their status as causes, there would be the existence of something else—such as smoke—even when fire and so forth are present. [One might ask: "How is it that fire and so forth do not lose their status as causes with respect to smoke?

And how is it that there is no discrepancy when one acts based on the certainty of that [cause]? Anticipating this, he says: "Of that... (referring to the opponent's position). Then, strengthening this point by means of an accepted example, he says: "For not... and so forth.
The abandonment of a perceived cause is its non-existence; for there is no abandonment of causality in that which is cognized as being non-causal—this is the meaning.

The effect of that perceived cause follows from the observation of it. "Non-attainment of that" means the non-attainment of the perceived cause. It is called a *prasanga* (reductio ad absurdum) because it is brought about by this; an excessive *prasanga* is an *atiprasaṅga*. "Enough with that" means it is of no use at all.

But surely, existence when that exists and non-existence when that does not exist—these two are properties of the effect (*kāryadharma*). How then can this alone be called the "relation of cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)? It would be more appropriate to say "the existence of the effect. This is true; however, when this property of the effect is stated, the property of the cause is also implied: existence when [the cause] exists, and the bringing into being (*bhāvanā*).

Existence (*bhāva*) is the state of being a bringer-about (*bhāvayitṛtva*), the state of connecting [something] with existence (*sattā*). And non-existence (*abhāva*) is the absence of that [existence], the state of not being a bringer-about (*abhāvayitṛtva*), the state of not producing. That which has such a characteristic is easily understood; thus it was stated by the Teacher himself, and this [author] has also explained it in this way.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: when there is a difference in entity (*arthāntaratva*), that which exists previously is [the cause].
That which conforms to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the cause;
and that which follows after it, characterized by the conformity to positive and negative concomitance, is the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Alternatively, this very [relation] is so called because it is the cause for ascertaining the causal relation.

For it is precisely through the presence and absence of the effect— namely, its occurrence when that [cause] is present and its non-occurrence when that is absent— that the causal relationship between those two is discerned;
for if causality did not exist, its presence...

[The opponent might argue: "In that case, the existence and non-existence of those two entities would simply not occur. Anticipating this, he says, "For that... (sa hi), meaning "because" (hi) in the sense of "since" (yasmāt). This very nature of being a cause is not such [as described]; rather, there exists another relation residing in both [entities]. To address this, he says, "For that... (sa hi). The word *hi* is used in the sense of *yasmāt* (because/since).

Regarding those two— namely, the presence of the effect when the cause is present and the absence of the effect when the cause is absent— he says "and by its own nature" (*svabhāvena ca*), seeking another refutation of fire and smoke whose causal relationship has not been accepted as their own inherent form.
Of that previously non-existent form being produced by it;
from those two, namely the forms of cause and effect;
for there is no establishing of a different entity [apart from them].
Therefore, because that [fire] is a different entity from that [smoke],
fire exists prior to the form of smoke, being produced by way of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in relation to the preceding [cause].

"That state" (tadbhāvaḥ) [47.13] refers to the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Even though those two possess that same nature, he says "in the effect" (*kārye*) [47.13] because this [causal relation] is employed in the cognition of the cause; thus, it is not redundant. Furthermore, with "also" (*api*) [47.14], he demonstrates its logical possibility. To the question, "How is it determined that [the cognition] is not caused by something else? he says "of that" (*tasya*) [47.14].
By the power of that [cognition], there is the manifestation (*vyakti*) of such another object (*arthāntara*) which does not appear as distinct from those two;
this is what is meant by the word "manifestation" (*vyakti*) in this context.
"Everything is apprehended everywhere"—this is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that transgresses the accepted principle (*dharma*).

Because that [object] has reached the condition of being unapprehendable (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*), this reason is unestablished due to its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*); thus he says "unapprehension" (*anupalabdhi*).
One might ask: "Must that cause of the cognition of those two necessarily be perceived, such that this is being said? To this he says: "For not... [47.18].
"The cognition of those two" [47.18] refers to the cognitions of cause and effect.
"Of these" [47.19] refers to that distinct entity; "of those two" [47.19] refers to the cognitions of cause and effect.

Furthermore, it is established that for one who is ignorant [of the object], the two cognitions—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—do not occur with respect to that [object].
While presenting another argument for this very point, he says "And not...
[47.19]. And [the cognition] is based on a cognition qualified by itself (*sva*).
The basis for the cognition of being colored [by another] refers to the cognitions of cause and effect, which are conceptual in nature; this should be understood from the context of the discussion.
To the question, "Even if that [object] is the basis for those cognitions, why must it necessarily be perceived? he says: "For not... and so forth.

This is to be stated as a conjunction of other points. Here, between the words "kāryakāraṇābhyām" and "atra," the reading "yato vahnyādeḥ kāraṇatvahāneḥ" fits before the subsequent phrase "visaṃvāda ity āśaṅkyāha."
Due to a lapse, the word "prāgāyātaḥ" appears [here],
whereas the subsequent word "tasya?"— marked by a query— is what should appear in this context.
And thus, the phrase "in its existence" (*tadbhāve*) [at 46.13] is an explanation of the expression "when that exists" (*tasya bhāve*).

He asks: since there exists another relation—namely, the existence consisting of the nature of cause and effect—between fire and smoke, which are distinct entities (*arthāntara*), how is it not established? To this he replies:

Therefore, when one asks how this [relation] is connected with another relation that is distinct from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), a further relation must be postulated; and when that is questioned again, yet another must be postulated in the same way—thus there would follow an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Yet, no such further relation is postulated.

What then? He says "in the effect" (*kārye*) to show that the relationship between the things that constitute cause and effect and the relationship termed "cause and effect" is actually a non-causal relationship.
This is because that state—the causal relationship—which is distinct and conceptually constructed, does not coexist with them;
for at the time of the cause and effect—that is, at the time of the entities such as fire and smoke that function as cause and effect—[the conceptual relationship] is absent.
And from what would their simultaneity arise, by which there could be a single productive cause?
In this regard, it should be understood that this was said while closing one's eyes like an elephant;
and that is the determination of cause and effect.

"Let it be that this [object] has a constructed (kalpita) nature; nevertheless, why should its occurrence not be distinct? To this he says: "In the constructed" (*kalpite*). This refers to the determination of that [relation], namely the determination of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) between those two distinct things, the cause and the effect.

The point is this: let it not be that this determination is an object of conceptual construction; for its conceptualization is precisely that. If such a thing is sought after, what is the use of it? What is the nature of this entity being conceptualized—is it produced by both cause and effect together, or by each one individually? Refuting the first of these two positions, he says: "kārya... [48.5];
if it were produced by an effect, it would have the nature of an effect.

Intending to show that the state of being a cause is that which is produced by a cause, he asks "How? [48.6]. Then, while defining the cause even in the case of each individual thing being produced, he says "And when... [48.6].
However, with regard to the word "afterwards" [48.8], the phrase "of its own effect" should be construed by changing the case-ending.
Therefore, since the sixth case (genitive) would result from its connection with an object and a condition (*artha-pratyaya*),
for that reason, the existence (*sadbhāvam*) of both— the effect (*kārya*) and its cause (*tad-bhāva*)— is established.
[75] Its [genitive case ending].
[76] Regarding the rule "The sixth [case ending occurs] after a word ending in a suffix having the sense of *atas* (Pā. 2.3.30)":

if it is argued, "Surely the very fact that these two depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*) constitutes their relationship; so how can it be said that they lack a mutual relationship?"

No; since this causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is under discussion as a relation even with respect to the effect, this [objection] is well-stated. Furthermore, if one accepts that [the cause and effect] depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), then prior to its arising, the cause would not be a cause.
In your view, because of that [dependence], the cause would lack a fixed status; thus, the fault should be seen in the argument that "it is so because of non-attainment" (*aprāptatvāt*).
How can there be the activity—that is, the production—of an effect such as smoke?
[The phrase] "dependent on that" means dependent on the activity of that smoke and so forth. Since this [cause], such as fire, does not exist [at that time], let it not produce that [effect].
"What would be our loss? he asks; [the answer is] "and its existence" (tadbhāva).
Its existence is the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
And because of the absence of a cause, it is unarisen—and thus not [a horse].
The intention is: "Just as a hare's horn does not exist for us, how could a relationship with its existence be possible?
Now, having accepted the position that [things] are non-momentary, he says: "Even in the case of non-momentariness."
The causal condition (pratyaya-hetu), or the cause for the cognition of cause and effect, does not transcend [the object].

For if it were dependent upon that [object], then it would produce such a cognition therein; otherwise, since there would be no spatial distance, it would either produce that cognition everywhere or not produce it anywhere at all—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, this is seen here as correct:
this causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), existing between two entities—the effect and the cause—does not exist partially, like a bamboo staff, because it is of an indivisible nature;
for otherwise, it would follow that the absence of the effect is the absence of the cause, and there would be the undesirable consequence of it assuming multiple forms.

Furthermore, if [the cause] exists as the effect of each individual [cause], then just as it produces the cognitions of "cause" and "effect" for the pair of cause and effect, it would likewise produce them individually.

If this were the case, the cognitions of "cause" and "effect" would necessarily apply only to fire in relation to smoke, and similarly, such cognitions would necessarily apply to smoke only in relation to that fire; or else, let there be no such cognitions of cause and effect at all.

We do not understand how the venerable Arcata, despite having subjected this very relationship— which has been refuted by that single method— to such subtle scrutiny, failed to point out this gross error. Furthermore, the reading "kāraṇabhāva" (the state of being a cause) is also encountered.
Now, this might indeed be appropriate for one who maintains that two entities attain the state of cause and effect by virtue of some other relation characterized as cause and effect;
but for us— who maintain that causality consists in inherence in the effect and being an effect consists in inherence in the cause— the faults just mentioned do not apply.

Anticipating the Nyāya claim that "something [the effect] inheres [in the cause]," and thereby uprooting even that conceit, he says: "the inherent cause" (*samavāyin*). This refers specifically to the potsherd and so forth, which are the inherent causes;
for it is precisely therein that the effect, such as the jar, inheres.
That for which [something exists] is the purpose;
the instrumental cause is the potter and so forth;
the non-inherent cause is the conjunction of the potsherds and so forth.
Since there is no inherence in the effect for those two, they would not be causes; consequently, it has been shown by implication that non-pervasiveness is a defect of the definition.
In the phrase "of that [effect] or of what is not an effect," the word *vā* (or) has the sense of *api* (also).
"Inherence in that" means inherence in the cause.

Inherence (samavāya) and the state of being an effect (kāryatva) reside only in the inherent cause, such as the potsherd, and not in the efficient or non-inherent causes; thus, these two words ending in the locative case should be connected here,
because it is accepted that the arising of the jar and so forth occurs only in that which inheres in the potsherds and the like.

Furthermore, in the case that an effect such as a jar would not exist because of the dependence on a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) for its mark (nimitta), here too the very same lack of pervasion (avyāpti) has been shown. Now, pointing out a common refutation, he says "and of that" (tasya ca). The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin another point to be stated. Regarding "of that," it refers to inherence (samavāya).
The explanation [of the term] as "alteration" (*anyathātva*) is not even mentioned here, as it would be reckless;
for the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is employed in every instance of an effect intended to express a distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*),
that is, in every case regarding a thing that exists in the relation of cause and effect.
Because there is no distinction— that is, because their forms are indistinguishable—
smoke would be the fire and fire would also be the smoke for one another; thus,
each would be both cause and effect.

The intention of one who says that because of the distinction of inherence—which is characterized by being both effect and cause—both [the universal and the particular] would either possess that nature or not possess it, and thus they would not be equal, is as follows:
Alternatively, at all times, even with respect to an entity that is neither effect nor cause;
or everywhere, down to the ultimate level, because of the existence of inherence in the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya), namely Being (sattā), the state of inherence is not clearly manifested.
However, it should be understood that the non-distinction itself is what is being restated.

One might object: "In our view, inherence (samavāya) is not intended as being characterized by the nature of effectness and causeness; rather, it is characterized by the existence and non-existence of prior and posterior states. Anticipating this, he says "pūrva... [and so on].
The two entities delimited by prior and posterior time are referred to as "prior" and "posterior."
Regarding the existence and non-existence of those two:
the very existence of the former is the existence of the latter;
and its non-existence is precisely that non-existence which consists in not being a producer.

Furthermore, the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the prior entity which constitutes its existence (*bhāva*), its being brought into being (*bhāvanā*), and its connection with existence; and likewise, the very nature of the non-existence (*abhāva*) which constitutes its non-being (*abhāvanā*) and its state of not bringing about existence—Inherence (*samavāya*), characterized by such qualifications, is defined as the relation between cause and effect. What is meant is this: that which causes another object to conform to its own positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

And that inherence (*samavāya*) which possesses qualifiers whose positive and negative concomitances strictly follow the positive and negative concomitances of another entity— that inherence has those as its qualifiers. Since it is intended to be characterized by the nature of cause and effect, there is no undesirable consequence of such a state occurring everywhere.
An alternative interpretation is not even mentioned, as it would be reckless due to the difficulty of construing the word "non-existence" (abhāva).
Refuting this, he says:
"It is improper."
He states the reason with the word "tad" (that):
because there is no connection with that entity characterized by existence and non-existence in prior and subsequent times, since its connection is non-existent;
this is the meaning: a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which performs exclusion (*vyavacchedaka*).

In that case, by what relation would this inherence be delimited within such a thing so that it might serve as its qualifier? And if it were indeed so [unrestricted], everything would become a qualifier of everything.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the very relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is the connection? And it is not wise to pursue yet another connection by means of a connection. Anticipating this, he says: "of that which is without further excellence" (*niratiśayasya*).
That from which excellence (*atiśaya*)—that is, a distinction (*viśeṣa*)—has departed from its established form, or from which excellence has departed, is "that which is without further excellence."
The meaning is that it cannot be surpassed by anything whatsoever.
Furthermore, its state of being unsurpassed follows from its eternity; this is what is present in the mind [of the author].
And one who speaks thus intends this: first of all, there must necessarily be something to be surpassed by means of a qualifier; otherwise, everything would become a qualifier for everything else.
In that case, something might indeed be a qualifier by imparting some excellence (*atiśaya*) to an impermanent thing;
yet, even there, one must ask whether that excellence is distinct from it or non-distinct.

If it were distinct, what would happen to the original thing? And if it were non-distinct, then it follows that the very thing itself is being produced—so no one should fail to raise such an objection.
But it does not belong to that which is eternal, whose nature remains unchanged throughout preceding and succeeding times.
Now, if you insist that these two qualifications must necessarily be accepted for this [entity], then, demonstrating that this is the more appropriate view, he says: "Or rather, of those two alone.
The word "or" (vā) indicates an alternative position that has been accepted.

The intention is as follows: let the definition of cause and effect belong to those two alone—the positive and negative concomitances—which follow the positive and negative concomitances of those two [entities] that follow them, and which are intended as qualifiers of that [concomitance] by virtue of being qualifiers of its inherence; for these two are established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the other [inherence] is sublated by them.
The particle *iti* refers back to what has just been stated.
Since the author of the *Vārttika* intends this according to the context,

a compound must be formed with the restriction internalized (*antar-nīta-niyama*), such that "fire, fuel, and so forth" themselves constitute the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For this very reason, anticipating the view of one who maintains a distinct causal complex (*bhinnasāmagrīvādin*) and being unable to tolerate this restriction,
he says "na ca" (and not), while refuting that position.
Otherwise, how could this treatise on refutation have arisen?
"By its very nature" means by a form that is independent of any other causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
This is because, when an effect is to be produced, there would be a contradiction of its capacity (*śakti*).
The particle *anya* (other) has the sense of "different"; thus, the meaning is "something else.
Furthermore, does the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), while producing an effect, produce it by depending on another causal complex, or without depending on one?

If it depends on another causal complex, then that [subsequent] complex alone would be the producer according to the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and the productivity of the initial complex would be like saying that a medicinal fruit (*harītakī*) purges only after reaching a deity.
This would be equivalent [to the following]:

if [an effect] were independent of that [cause], then why does non-existence (*abhāva*)—which likewise possesses the capacity characterized by its own cause—not produce it independently as well? This refutation should also be understood here.
Furthermore, no causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is perceived as distinct from that [non-existence].
Furthermore, it is not logical for this [non-existence] to have reached the condition of being unperceivable (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatā*); this and other points should also be understood as before.

That which has both positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—which consists of the state of being a concomitant (*anvetṛtva*) and the state of being that which is concomitant (*anvīyamānatva*)—and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—which consists of the state of being a separator (*vyatirecayitṛtva*) and the state of being that which is separated (*vyatiricyamānatva*)—is such [a thing].
Those who [hold this view] are the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
Regarding that positive concomitance (*anvaya-niścaya*),

by stating that "it occurs through the non-deviation from its own cause," he demonstrates that whatever object has a positive concomitance with another object witnessed by all the world must necessarily be produced by it, or else produced by the same cause as it; for this very reason.

Regarding the phrase "or because of the relation of cause and effect," it should be understood that this means "because of the relation of cause and effect with that [the probandum] itself, or with its cause. In that context, regarding the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*) and so forth, only the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) operating by way of the contrapositive has been shown. Anticipating the question—"How then is the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) stated?"—he says "In the case of the essential nature... (*svabhāve...*) and so on.

In the case of the contrapositive (*viparyaya*), that is, when there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which gives rise to the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaye*), it functions because the establishment of the probandum and the probans is based upon that [proof]. This refers to the "ascertainment of the positive concomitance" (*anvayaniścaya*), as is clear from the context; the same should be understood for what follows as well.
Because its existence is established—that is, because its occurrence in that alone is established—it has that as its cause.

For when the occurrence of the linguistic convention "non-existent" is established as residing in the mere non-perception of the perceptible, there proceeds the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) to the effect that: "In whatever place and at whatever time there is non-perception characterized by [the object's] being perceptible, in each such case there is fitness for the linguistic convention 'non-existent'."

It has been stated that this is because the existence of that [absence] is established by means of a pramāṇa that proves the non-existence of other causes (*nimittāntarābhāva*), since that [non-existence] is the cause for its establishment.
These two are the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which establish the absence [of the object].
And because it is the cause for establishing the absence of that [S]:

"of that" means of the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent. [80] "Establishing its presence" means establishing its identity (tatsvabhāvatā). This is because there is certainty regarding the nature of the necessary connection—that is, the state of being connected—which is based on the two grounds characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).
Therefore, "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) is intended to mean either arising from that [cause] itself, or arising from its cause.
Regarding the two types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the context refers to the non-apprehension of the cause and the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
To the question, "When, then, can that qualification not be disregarded?", he says: "When... (*yadā*).
"Accepts" (upādatte) means that the proponent takes it upon himself as something to be demonstrated, according to the context.
"Because of being unestablished" (asiddhatvāt) should be understood as "because of being doubtful-unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddhatvāt).
That [verse 52.12] is the demonstration of the absence [of the probans] when the probandum is absent.

For the intention is that, once identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are established, there arises the cognition of the absence of the probans in the absence of the probandum—a cognition whose form is floating [in the mind].
He establishes this very point with the words beginning "for" (*tathā hi*).

Since the word *kārya* used in the sense of "result" (*phala*) is neuter in gender, and since it does not retain its original gender when it is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the designation *kāryam* [in the verse] is to be understood as the view of the author of the *Vārttika*.
[80] "The state of being that" (*tadbhāvatā*) is "non-beneficial" (*anupakārikā*), meaning it is ineffective (*akiñcitkarī*).

"Merely from non-observation" means from the mere non-observation in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) which lacks a necessary connection. "The impossibility of that" means the impossibility of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
He establishes that very point with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathāhi*).

One might suspect: "Since there is no other cause for its non-perception apart from the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), even if it exists in one place, its non-perception occurs; therefore, why should it not be considered simply absent? Anticipating this, he says "place," etc.

By the word "etc.," time is included. In that case, even though the locus (*dharmin*) exists—that is, even while the reason (*hetu*) is present—there is merely non-perception, which is to say, a mere absence of perception.
He says, "of such a kind," because it is not that kind of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) which is intended. [Objection:

But has it not already been shown by the aforementioned reasoning that the impossibility of that [negative concomitance] follows for those who desire negative concomitance based on mere non-observation?

[Response: However, for those who desire positive concomitance (*anvaya*) based on mere observation without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), its absence has not been established; rather, it must necessarily be demonstrated.

And fearing that this might be contradicted by the statement in [Dharmakīrti’s] *Pramāṇavārttika* (3.30), “This rule of invariable concomitance is neither from non-perception nor from perception,” he says, “the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) also,” in order to show that this very point has just been stated immediately prior.
By that [phrase], namely, by the expression “ascertainment of positive concomitance based on the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).”
Regarding the phrase "based on observation" (*darśananibandhana*) [53.8], it should be understood from the context as "based merely on observation in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, regarding this positive concomitance (*anvaya*) [53.9]: we do not accept positive concomitance based on mere observation, such that it would be stated in this way.
However, anticipating the objection that [the negative concomitance] is established from repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), he says: "And not... [53.12].
Since this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), it should be understood that we do not desire the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, but rather from repeated observation;
for it is said: "For [the negative concomitance] is to be understood through repeated observation" (Ślokavārttika, Anumāna 12).

Since it is impossible to understand this [pervasion] even through the indication of its remainder (*śeṣanirdeśa*), one should see that pervasion consists of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). To the question, "Even for you, what other cause of pervasion exists besides frequent observation and non-observation in places such as a kitchen or a great lake? he says, "If it were non-existent" (*asati*).
By this, it is shown that it is established by those two [observations] precisely when they are based on a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and not otherwise.

In some places, as is abundant—that is, as it occurs frequently—among those things such as the *āmalaka* fruit that have been observed through their concomitance (*sāhacarya*) with properties like astringent taste, there is the possibility of another state, such as the condition of having a sweet taste due to the sprinkling of milk and so forth.
To demonstrate the scope for such a possibility, he says: "in the absence of that."
When that "otherwise-ness" (anyathātva)—its possibility—is absent, that is, non-existent;

thus, because this [absence] is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), even if there is frequent observation (*bhūyodarśana*) of the presence of the probandum (*sādhyabhāva*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established.
This is because, even when one observes that things are frequently absent in the absence of the probandum, the possibility of "otherwise-ness" remains.
It should also be understood that this is because there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the impossibility [of such a relationship].

For instance, in the case where the absence of sweetness implies the absence of the probans-property "being water" (ambhatva), this absence is observed everywhere except in the case of sea-water, which is the subject possessing the property to be proven (sādhyadharmin). Thus, even though there is frequent observation [of the concomitance], a deviation is seen specifically in the salt-ocean.
Otherwise, even the state of being water would have to be understood as a valid reason for establishing the sweetness of the waters of the great ocean;
for, in the absence of a subverting factor,
it would [function] when there is the absence of the non-existence of the effect-pervader.

Since it is impossible for those who do not see the truth directly (*rvāgdarśin*) to reach a certain conclusion regarding this, it lacks the defining characteristic [of a valid reason]; thus, "for in the absence of the probandum... and so forth—enough with this prolixity.

The ascertainment of the two types of necessary connection (*pratibandha*), characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), is itself the means; that [connection] exists in the case of the opposite [of the probandum].
Because of the statement, "the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition," and because of the statement, "established by perception and non-perception," [this] has been shown.
Thus, it was not stated separately; that is, it was not stated as a distinct [category] by the Teacher, according to the context.
