Having raised the doubt, "Even when the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established, how are the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the non-perception of the cause and the pervader established?", he says "For instance" (*tathā hi*), etc., while demonstrating this very point.

When there is the absence of that which is pervaded by the effect (*kāryavyāpyābhāva*), one asks: "Of what nature is that [absence]? To this he says: "Having that as its characteristic" (*tallakṣaṇa*).

The intended meaning is that, because the negation of a negation is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpatva*) when it pertains to the essence of the effect or the nature itself (*tatkāryasvabhāvātman*), [the absence] is excluded—that is, it is impossible [for the negation of the negation to be of the same nature as the initial negation].
He asks, "In what way is it distinguished?
and says, "Otherwise" (*anyathā*); that is, if it were not distinguished when there is no exclusion from that.
This refers to the definition of its existence (*tadbhāvalakṣaṇe*).

Following that, one might ask: "Previously it was stated that 'identity and causality pervade inseparable concomitance' (tādātmyatadutpattyor avinābhāvavyāpakayoḥ); how then can it now be said that 'because identity and causality are pervaded by inseparable concomitance'? Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The meaning is that both [identity and causality] pervade [concomitance]."
"It was stated previously" means that it was already said earlier by the passage beginning with "and because of the deficiency of invariable concomitance" (avinābhāvavaikalyāt).
With the words "or if," he shows another logical argument (*upapatti*).
Because of the context of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), it is stated that "there is something other than the effect" (*anyat kāryāt*).

The proximity (*āsatti*) of Rohiṇī—that is, the nearness of the Rohiṇī constellation as it is about to rise—is its "determination" (*klṛpti*), which means to say, "the knowledge of conceptual construction" (*kalpanājñāna*).
That too—meaning that conceptual construction—has been stated [as refuted] because it has already been discussed; the meaning is that this kind of thing has been stated by way of refutation.
Because of being produced (*kṛtakatvāt*)... S.
But how is it that its arising immediately after the arising of that [other factor] is necessarily established? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) by way of a conclusion:
"of the circle of constellations" (*nakṣatracakrasya*)—this should be understood from the context as referring to the group of seven stars known as Kṛttikā;
"transit" (*saṃkrāntiḥ*) is the movement from the place of its previous location, or the attainment of the state of manifestation. Of that...

"The cause itself [is connected] by an interval of time" means that it should be understood as occurring after the lapse of some period of time; it should be conceived as such a cause according to the context.
By this, the existence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) even in that case is demonstrated.
When there is no damage to the nest, one observes the movement of ants carrying their eggs toward a single direction while remaining unafraid;

the inference of rain drawn from this is also possible provided there is no obstruction. Therefore, in that case as well, he shows by means of the word "yathā" [at 56.17] that this very same principle applies.
Otherwise, since this [subject] is a living being under dispute, how could its status as an example be established?
The "disturbance" (*saṃkṣobha*) of the elements—earth and so forth—is a particular state.

The meaning should be understood from the context as follows: that very cause which produces such a disturbance among ants is itself the cause of the rain that occurs at a later time, separated by a certain interval of time.
And the cause should be understood as the "cause of the cause," for otherwise a cause that has long since passed away would have to be accepted or desired.

Therefore, by means of that cause— the rising of Kṛttikā— one infers that property [of the cause] which consists in its capacity to produce [the effect], either by way of transmitting the power to act as the material cause for the rising of Rohiṇī after the lapse of some time, or otherwise.

This third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is expressed in the feminine gender because of its connection with the word "imagination" (*kalpanā*), as in the phrase "the imagination of proximity to Rohiṇī.
Non-apprehension that is not delimited by the qualification of being perceptible is mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhimātra*).

Regarding the phrase "because of the impossibility of non-existence" (*abhāvāyogāt*), it should be understood as "because of the impossibility of having non-existence as its object. This is by way of that, namely, through the door of the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*). One who speaks thus [means that] the very same non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) which operated at the time of grasping the contradiction is now the means of proving non-existence while being remembered. And because it serves as a reminder of that [non-existence], this perception—being unqualified by any other object associated within a single cognition—has the nature of non-perception. For this very reason it was said: "The formal application (*prayoga*) alone is different; in all cases, the meaning is the same."
"He is not divided" (Pra.vā. 2.90)—this is the intended meaning.
And regarding this point, just as Prajñākaragupta has exerted himself [in his argument], so too have we [done] in the *Dharmottarapradīpa*.
This has already been demonstrated, so it is not stated here.

Otherwise, if the application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) by way of that [other thing] were not accepted, then the meaning would be as follows: when the existence of another is not negated, there is a perception that is itself unnegated and unobstructed; even when that other thing exists, such [perception] occurs in reality.
This means that because non-existence is not established, there is no certainty regarding non-existence, and thus non-existence is untenable.

Since the whole (*samudāya*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), he asks how that [whole] is the object of proof; he replies with the word "part" (*avayava*), because no other related entity has been mentioned.
To the question of whose nature that [reason] is to be determined, he says: "In the probandum" (sādhye) [57.6].
Its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is also possible based on that alone;
therefore, he says "he who... [57.17] in order to distinguish it from that.

Even if there is indeed no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), why then is the qualification not tenable? To this he says: "Possibility" (*saṃbhava*). It is "dependent on another's view" (*paramatāpekṣam*) because it depends upon the opinion of others; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to Pāṇini’s Vārttika 470: *īkṣikṣamibhyāṃ ca*, when a direct object is present.
"Are others not also seekers in this way, such that this [statement] is made in consideration of their opinion? To this he says, "The Naiyāyika," etc.

By means of a substance possessing the *saṃskāra* known as velocity (*vega*), such as a mallet or similar object, there arises a quality called conjunction (*saṃyoga*). From that, actions (*karman*)—that is, movements—arise in the parts, such as the potsherds, which are the constituents of substances like pots.
By using the plural form "actions" (*karmāṇi*), he demonstrates pervasion (*vyāpti*), and not merely the number of plurality.
Since conjunction is unitary, action must also be unitary; for example,

as in the case of a swift needle or similar object striking a blue lotus petal or an unbaked clay pot— nevertheless, through the sequence of actions, the destruction of the substance certainly occurs.

From those actions, there arises in the parts—which are the constituents that initiate the substance—a quality called disjunction, which is the opposite of the conjunction that initiates the substance.
From that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction; that is, the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance.
Then, from the destruction of the conjunction:
by that conjunction of parts, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the substance that was produced is destroyed.
For the destruction of a substance is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others to be twofold: through the destruction of its substratum (*āśraya*) and through the destruction of its non-inherent cause.
And here, because of the destruction of this conjunction which is the non-inherent cause,
the actual nature [of the effect] is restated by the mention of the "effect"; however,
there is no such thing as a non-effect produced by that [conjunction] which would need to be excluded.
And if it perishes precisely by virtue of being an effect,
then the mention of "effect" (*kārya*) is intended to establish that whatever is an effect necessarily possesses the nature of perishing.
The use of the accusative case is due to its connection with the verb "he says" (*āha*).
When [the property] occurs by virtue of the force of inherence (*samavāya*), because it possesses a single form, the absence of distinction is intended.

To the objection—"If producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) were one, how could there be the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*), since that [relationship] is possible only when there is difference?"—he says: "Because of perception" (*darśana*).

That conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in which there exists the appearance (*avabhāsa*) of the difference—that is, the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*)—between the two properties, producedness and impermanence, is so described.
Or, it is "thus" because it manifests a distinction between phenomena;
and it is "thus" because it is both that [manifestation] and a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Having thus performed the grammatical analysis of the words:

The analysis of the compound should be made as follows: "that conceptual construction which manifests the distinction between the properties of being produced and impermanence, and which arises from the power of perceiving an entity that possesses the property of having existed after not having existed, and having existed after not having existed.
That itself is the "door" (dvāra), meaning the means (upāya).

The intended meaning is that such a conceptual construction is not logical, because there is an absence of any proving evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) and the presence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
Thus, even if the relationship between the probandum and the probans were established, let that [relationship] be postulated; yet,
if that very distinct entity such as impermanence and so forth is conceptualized by those desiring to attain or avoid the purposeful action (arthakriyā) to be proven,
he says— [29b] "even having postulated"— in order to show that even that does not exist, [referring to] the nature of the thing (*vastvātman*).
Thus, it is precisely that nature of the subject (dharmin) which is to be considered, because it is the object of rejection or acceptance, that is, because it is to be investigated.
To the question, "In what way is that very thing to be considered? he says: "by causal efficiency" (arthakriyā).
He states that it must be considered by some: "by those seeking that" (*tadarthibhiḥ*).

They are so called because they seek that causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*); and since causal efficacy depends upon that [reality], it is precisely for this reason that indifference (*upekṣā*) should be maintained toward other things.
"Those who seek [the goal] follow only the means.
Corroborating this very point with the words of the Master, he says: "That has been stated [at 58.29].
Since it is exactly thus and not otherwise, therefore it was stated by the Master.
For the position that "the meaning of a word is indeed *sat* (being), and its function is the exclusion of non-*sat*"—
by taking that specific distinction of the thesis as the reason, those who do not deny the meaning of words [hold that] it is simply a real entity (*vastu*), namely, the word itself and so forth.

Even for those proponents who maintain that the meaning of a word is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is nevertheless the case that the object itself, as excluded from others, is what is communicated; thus, even they must reflect upon the reality of the thing.
Alternatively, even by those who do not deny the referent of a word, there is always a dependence on [the distinction between] identity and difference (*abheda* and *bheda*).
The meaning is that an entity alone is contemplated, whether as existent or non-existent.
Therefore, he asks why an entity alone is contemplated, and says "by way of expectation" (āśaṃtyā).
"Having abandoned the body" has been stated;
"hir" means "because";
"atra" refers to this matter.

Even if, in this case, the arising of the result is not obstructed within the nature of a non-implicative negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha)—whether in the form of a positive injunction consisting of a universal and so forth, or in the form of an exclusion—nevertheless, why should it be considered as such? To this he says: "The object," etc.

Regarding the eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*)—one incapable of practicing sexual pleasure, a third nature—the compound *rūpaṃ ca vairūpyaṃ ca* (beauty and ugliness) is a singular collective dvandva. In that regard, what is the use of examining—that is, deliberating upon and determining—the beauty of a lustful woman who desires a man? [84] Seeing that...

Now, one might object: "If, in reality, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*), then upon the ascertainment of a thing's being produced, its impermanence must also be ascertained due to that very identity; so how can there be the application of inference? Anticipating this, he says by way of a conclusion: "Therefore... [59.6].
Because the very object [of cognition] must necessarily be accepted as that which is to be heated (or afflicted), therefore the connection is as follows:
even things already seen and determined by one aspect are determined by another aspect through inference.
"Seen" means directly perceived; the entities such as sound and so forth are the subjects (*dharmin*).
By some form such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and so forth;
by what kind?
By that which is excluded from the unproduced, which is other than that which is produced.

"In some way"—that is, by means of such modes as proficiency in practice and so forth, and by that which is other than those, namely impermanence and so on; [it is] "excluded from that" which does not possess that form, i.e., the form of impermanence.
By this non-difference of exclusion, the difference of the exclusions is shown.

If they could be ascertained by that very nature [of being produced] just as by the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), then how could they be ascertained through inference? To this he says: "because they are not ascertained.
Why is there indeed no ascertainment? He says:
because of the existence of the cause of error—that is, of delusion—namely, the continuous production of successive similar moments and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, if at that time the necessary connection between that determined form and an undetermined form has not been established, then how can its determination arise from the perception of something unrelated? In response to this doubt, he states the specific nature of inference with the words "in the case of the determined" [59.8].

[59.8] "From another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarataḥ*) means from a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the contrary case. "The determination of the necessary connection" (*pratibandhāvasāya*) refers to that inference for which the preceding [determination] is prior; therefore, because destruction has a cause other than itself and thus lacks concomitance with that [destruction] alone, its existence (*sattā*) or inherence (*samavāya*) in such a manner constitutes impermanence. For this very reason, the sense is that in the case of the Self (*ātman*) and so forth, there is an absence of such existence and inherence.

Now, one might think: "Let it be so; what is lost by this qualification? We have already declared that destruction is not of the same nature as the thing itself (*atatsvabhāvatā*); our purpose is fulfilled by that much alone. Anticipating this objection from the Buddhist perspective, the opponent—who suffers from the delirium of being confused by his own habitual adherence to his own tenets—says: "And as for 'destruction'... (59.16).
The word *iti* refers back to the term "destruction" (*vināśa*);
thus, the meaning is "by that term 'destruction'.

Since existence and non-existence are of many kinds due to distinctions such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, he specifies [it] as "characterized by the non-existence of destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāvalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, suspecting that you also consider "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) to be of that very same nature, and thus objecting that it is incorrect to demonstrate its lack of that intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāvatā*), the opponent himself says: "But we consider 'producedness' to be distinct"— this is how the sentence is to be connected.

Of such a kind—that is, characterized by non-existence through destruction—it is untenable because of its contradiction with having a cause. To the question "How, then, is there a contradiction?", he says: "by itself," etc.
By speaking thus, he demonstrates the reason for not stating that proof:
those who desire to understand and those who are intent on practice [observe that],
even though [the jar] arises from such things as a hammer, there is the non-existence of its destruction [subsequent to that].
Regarding "in existence" (*bhāve*): destruction occurs in a real entity (*vastu*).
Because it is useless (*anupayogāt*), that is, because it lacks causal activity (*avyāpārāt*); and because it does not serve that purpose, there is instability (*anavasthā*).
The meaning is: since its nature remains in that very same state, how can there be impermanence?

Even if it does not deviate from the form established in its prior state when that [cause] exists, nevertheless, its impermanence is established through the existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*) which qualify it. To this he says "unwavering" (*avicalita*):

the sense is that for that whose form is unwavering—that is, has not undergone change—there is existence; and because generality (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are unitary, the implication is that even the self (*ātman*) and so forth would likewise be subject to such [impermanence].

Having demonstrated that what was stated by the opponent—“we consider ‘destruction’ to be the non-existence of an entity characterized by annihilation”—is flawed, he now refutes what was said [in verse 5d], “but that which is produced,” by stating, “in its own cause.

The intention is that because inherence (*samavāya*) is a single entity, it would follow that even the self (*ātman*) and other such things would likewise exist [as effects]; thus, this [definition of destruction] cannot be established even for one who does not desire it.
Establishing this very point by way of affirmation, he says: "It is described as having 'not previously existed'... (60.8). The words "by the world" (*lokena*) are to be supplied.
By this, he demonstrates that the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) is indeed the ground for determining the meaning of words;
and it is precisely such a meaning that is expressed by the word "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) by the elders.
Previously, a refutation was stated by accepting that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) take on the nature of qualifiers for that [object].
Now, however, he says "And not... [60.8], while dismantling even that [position];
and this has already been largely explained above.
Let that very coming-into-being after not having been, which is the state of becoming and the state of being produced, be [the definition of impermanence].
In this way, by parity of reasoning, for one who does not accept non-existence (*abhavanam*), impermanence is not established.

Or, with the intention that impermanence might consist in the very nature of stability when there is the occurrence of becoming after having been [non-existent], it was said: "and the state of having a non-stable nature.

Alternatively, since it was concluded following the statement regarding origination that one must infer from this that the entity itself has a non-stable nature, it was stated thus with that same intention.
The deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of "being produced" [60.16] means, in short, its occurrence in the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhya*), which is its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

The perception of that dependence on another cause, which is pervaded by "not being necessarily present"—the latter being the opposite of the "necessity of presence" belonging to the object of negation—is called "perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). And this refers to the two types of pervasion by the contradictory.

It should be understood that there is no consequence of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is established through the opponent's own admission.
For where the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is real while the property of being a feature of the subject is established by the opponent's admission, that is a *prasaṅga* (reductio) reason;
whereas where all three [factors] are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is an independent (*svatantra*) reason—this is the intended meaning.

And for that limited cause, namely the support of that—such as a cloth which is the support for dye—a destructive condition (*upadhātaka-pratyaya*) is a counteracting condition (*vidhura-pratyaya*); because of the occurrence of such a condition, it is not necessarily present, meaning it is not inevitable. By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), he distinguishes destruction from passion (*rāga*).
"Prior to the presence of the cause of destruction" means before the presence of the cause of destruction.
His intention is that those very things which are harmful would be the destroyers; and therefore, destruction is established as having a cause.

And for those things that lack a cause, [the phrase] “because their presence depends upon their own causes” is connected [to the argument]. Furthermore, even when destructive causes are present, there may be opposing factors—such as yogins, piśācas, and so forth—that obstruct their power; since these too are infinite, [the argument holds]. “In their existence” means in the actual presence of those opposing factors.
"Because of the obstruction of its power" means because of the impairment of the power that is the cause of its destruction.
He says "not necessarily" in response to the argument that if those are its causes, they must necessarily produce their effects.
For even though sleep and so forth are dependent on other factors, [they do not necessarily produce their results]. Just as [the color] on a cloth dyed with turmeric and so forth [does not remain].
To the question, "Why might it not also depend on a substance? the Buddhist statement would be: "If they were perceived in such a way.
"In such a way" means "by way of being omnipresent.
"If that were so," says the opponent.

The doubt or suspicion regarding the non-occurrence of change (*anyathābhāva*) in any instance—that is, the uncertainty—should not be entertained or produced by you; this is understood from the context. By this, the opponent shows: "For a discerning person like yourself, it is simply not reasonable to suspect the change of anything that has been perceived in every case. Rather, under this mere pretext, you are surely only causing mental distress for yourself because the other's system is faultless."

The proponent [of the established doctrine] asks, "What more? The question is presented by the word *kiṃ punar*, which is a compound of both a particle (*nipāta*) and a non-particle (*anipāta*), through the two aspects of generality and particularity.
He is one for whom there exists a light of knowledge that pervades the full extent of all things—that is, it pervades the vast multiplicity of all entities.
However, how the establishment of the word "vastu" (entity) occurs in its full extent has been explained previously.

Regarding the state of being thus—namely, the seeing of all entities—if the destruction of anything whatsoever were seen to be caused by a specific cause, then the possession of that same nature by everything would be unavoidable; therefore, he says: "of anything whatsoever."

The word *tu* is used for emphasis. Because things whose birth depends on other causes—such as the dyeing of cloth and so forth—are seen to arise otherwise [than their cause would suggest], and because destruction is perceived even when the object is not yellow (*apītate*), there arises in a person a suspicion that the nature [of the object] has changed;

thus, being one who possesses a doubt regarding the non-existence of destruction due to the context, he states by this that "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, since destruction is here being proven as something that follows upon another entity.
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "And this [sound], though produced" (61.9), he demonstrates that it is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to being common to both sides.
By the term "existence and non-existence" (*bhāvābhāva*), the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is intended.
Because that very thing is produced (*kṛtaka*) by virtue of depending on the operation of another for its own accomplishment, and because it is intended as being such;
he states the reason for accepting its permanence [in the following]: "its destruction" (*tadvināśa*).

Because there would follow the consequence—that is, the attainment—of the re-emergence, or the manifestation, of that entity which has been destroyed, characterized by its annihilation; for if it were so, there would be the consequence of its eternal existence and so forth, and thus the emergence of things could not be without a cause. Or rather, what else could this be? It would be as follows: through the consequence of its eternal existence, the emergence of entities would not be uncaused.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the destruction of a thing such as a jar is understood—through positive and negative concomitance—to have that [destruction of the destruction] as its cause; rather, it is the potter and so forth who are so understood.
Therefore, how could it be that upon the destruction of the destruction, there is no emergence of that [jar], which would otherwise be expected?
This [objection] is flawed.

For instance, the exclusion of the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāvavyāvṛtti*) is precisely the jar, and the destruction of the jar is the exclusion of the absence of the jar; thus, since the absence of the absence of the jar results in the emergence of the form of the jar, this is indeed the superior position.
Regarding this very point, he states the supporting reason: "And not... (*na ca*).
How could that destruction, being causeless, arise for that non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)? It ought not to be produced.
This property called "destruction" is necessarily inherent (*aikāntika*) and inevitable (*avaśyaṃbhāvī*) in all things that have come into being.

By this, he shows the following: we do not state "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) as a probans without qualification, such that [the objection] would apply; rather, it is distinguished by the qualification "being an entity" (*vastutva*). Therefore, the meaning is that when something is an entity, its producedness necessarily entails perishability. The proponent answers with the words beginning "From what, then? (*kutaḥ punar*); since the interrogative pronoun *kim* is used in the sense of negation, the meaning is "from nothing at all."
"This" refers to the fact that the destruction of entities is inevitable;
this is determined from the context because no alteration—that is, non-destruction—of those entities is perceived.
"Even while existing" means even while being present.

[The reason] which does not exclude the existence of the self and so forth, and which does not prove the non-existence of the self and so forth, how could it elsewhere negate— that is, exclude— the state of being otherwise (anyathābhāva) or the non-perishing (avināśitva) in other things? By the mention of the "self" and so forth, he demonstrates this.

If the non-perception of non-destruction establishes the absence of non-destruction, then, since there is no difference [in the nature of the argument], the non-perception of the self (*ātman*) and so forth would also establish their absence; yet this is not the case. Anticipating the opponent’s objection that this [example] is thus undermined, he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Of that—namely, the self and so forth—the existence of the self is established by inference from such grounds as its being the object of uncontradicted recognition, which proves the unity or plurality of cognitions of form, taste, and so on.
And as for the directions and so forth included by the word "etcetera," they are established through inference based on cognitions such as "east" and "west"; this is present in the mind.
By the particle *iti*, the form of what is to be stated has been expressed.
In that case as well, it is within the inference that proves their existence.

[87] Regarding the state of being otherwise (*anyathābhāva*): surely, for one who asserts that "that which is not perceived is indeed non-existent," what is this objection? For even if the presence of a reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not observed, there is no contradiction in establishing its non-existence.
"But as for the self (*ātman*) and so forth, non-perception itself is unestablished; therefore, there is no proof of its non-existence.
You have spoken well, yet you did not correctly discern the intention of one who says, "In that case too... and so on.
Indeed, this is his underlying thought:
As long as the non-observation of a reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is not capable of establishing its absence,
so long it is not established that "whatever is not perceived here does not exist.

And this being the case, how could the self (ātman) and so forth— which, though unperceived, would thus be established as non-existent— be an object of inference, since they are refuted by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)?
Thus it has been said: "The non-abode of the reason is pervaded [by its absence].
Alternatively, how could mere non-perception—being devoid of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—establish the existence of things remote in space and time?

For, by means of that [non-perception], one would have to infer the existence of the self (*ātman*) and so forth through the exclusion of the reason from the opposite of what is to be proven (*siddhivipakṣa*).

"By the very manner of the formal argument" (*prayogabhaṅgyaiva*) means by the arrangement of the formal argument itself; that is to say, by way of a consequence (*prasaṅga*), a further implication (*anuṣaṅga*), or an introductory context (*prastāva*).

A formal argument is "possessing common properties" (*sadharmā*) when it has as its object of demonstration a property characterized by the presence of a reason that is "common"—that is, similar—to both the subject of the thesis (*sādhya*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*). This is because the term *sadharmā* is derived through the grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) of the word *samāna*; specifically, while one might expect the rule to apply to the phrase "of the common [property] in the case of the thesis and so forth," the term is accepted here as it is. Thus, the state of being such is established on the grounds that from this [property], both the verbal expression and the cognition arise for you.

[31b] 1. A specific feature of form (*rūpaviśeṣa*). The state of that which has as its property to be demonstrated a dissimilar cause—characterized by the presence or absence of those two very [causes]—is the intended pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) in all other cases, whether it be in every instance of the subject possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), or in the subject itself, provided it is not the property to be proven. This is what is intended to be expressed.

But "external pervasion" (*bahirvyāpti*) is not that pervasion which is grasped by means of a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) through its occurrence in an example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) other than the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*); it is the rejection of that [type of pervasion].

Now, one might object: "In the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) characterized by existence, pervasion can indeed be grasped even within the subject of the thesis itself by means of the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite.
This is not so; for there is nothing here that would necessitate this [rejection], since it does not depend on the reason occurring elsewhere [than the subject].
However, since every effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and every [reason] whose domain is an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) necessarily requires occurrence elsewhere,
why do you not explain that "occurrence elsewhere" (*anyatrānuvṛtti*) was intended for that purpose?

Fearing that his own explanation might be characterized as a misinterpretation because the Master, immediately after presenting the reason based on existence, showed the example "just as jars and so forth" (62.9), [the author] anticipates this censure and, revealing the Master’s different intention, says: "Just as jars and so forth" (62.9).
"For which man" (yasya puṃsaḥ).

Furthermore, why is there a statement of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the purpose of establishing mindfulness (*smṛtyādhāna*) therein, rather than for the purpose of merely presenting an example? To this he says: "In the example" (*dṛṣṭānte*).
By this, he shows that there is nothing faulty in our explanation, namely that "this [was said] by the Teacher" refers to a specific person;
he shows this very connection through the transformation of case endings in the phrase "in all [cases]" (sarvasmin).
"External pervasion" (bahirvyāpti) is pervasion that occurs externally.
The connection is: "they are refuted.
The phrase *yady api* is a collection of particles used to express an admission for the sake of stating a specific distinction.
The term *tāvatā* means "merely by the observation of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the property of the probans with the property to be proven."

The meaning is that there is an absence of the concomitance (*anvaya*) of this probans-property (*sādhanadharma*), namely its "being thus" (*tathābhāva*), with the probandum (*sādhya*); for, in the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there is no contradiction in the absence of the latter even when the former is absent.

The word *iti* [62.25] is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). It serves for the recollection of that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). "Qualified by a property" [63.4] refers to the subject (*dharmin*), such as sound and so forth, which is qualified by the property intended to be proven (*siṣādhayiṣita-dharma*). [63.5]
Regarding that [cognition], which is the realization of the subject as qualified by the property to be proven:

having stated the demonstration of the property of the subject preceded by the demonstration of pervasion, he also says— referring to the case where the demonstration of pervasion is preceded by the demonstration of the property of the subject— "and when it is preceded by that" [means] when the pervasion is being demonstrated with the demonstration of the property of the subject preceding it.

And this is the remainder: since there is no difference between the two cases regarding the cognition that takes the form of a floating [generalization] when the pervasion is grasped through a universal synthesis (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), it should be understood that this was stated merely as a distinction of perspective.
For the sake of remembering that, [the letter] *S*.

The statement of the probandum (*sādhyanirdeśa*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*). Its "application" (*prayoga*) means its employment; that has not been shown here, meaning that the statement of the probandum has not been made.

The mention of "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) should be understood as an illustration for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); by this, there is also inclusion of one who, at night when everything is obscured, determines a specific smoke from a specific scent such as camphor or wool in a distant place like the east, and subsequently infers a specific fire through inference.
The phrase "from that which is devoid of the application of a thesis" (*pratijñāprayogarahitāt*) is a demonstration of the result of this restriction.
It has not been shown by S.
Here, it is said that the very desire (*arthitā*), having come to the ear, reveals what is in the mind; she is indeed the *karṇapiśācikā* (the ear-demoness).

The "following" (*anusaraṇa*) of the *liṅga*—which consists of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—is its ascertainment.
The word "iti" is used here as a causal particle. He mocks [the opponent] by ascending to the very essence of that [position].
To the question "What does he mock? he says: "That which... (yat tad...); this is a common worldly expression.
To the question "How is rivalry with that attributed to him? he says: "Because of its similarity to that" (tat-tulyatvāt);
"of him" (asya) refers to the inferer.
Regarding the sequence [65.15], there is indeed a genitive of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Having previously stated the reason himself with the words “of that statement” [65.23] and so forth, he begins with a question directed at the opponent in order to show the reason stated by the Teacher: “Why? [65.13].
Anticipating the objection, “If that doubt persists even when the thesis (*pratijñā*) is employed, then what is the use of it?”, the opponent himself says: “Impermanent,” and so forth [66.13].

Then, by the word "but" (*tu*), he specifies the position regarding the formulation of the thesis (*pratijñā-prayoga*); it is connected precisely with the phrase "in the absence of the statement of the probandum" (*asati sādhya-nirdeśe*).
There would be no cognition—that is, no ascertainment—of those [logical reasons] that are contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This very point is what is combined [with the previous argument] as a refutation by him.
Gathering another fault in this very context, he says,
"And because of the reason" (*hetoś ca*).
Showing the specific distinction of his own position, he says:

Regarding the phrase *sati tu*: the word *yāvate* is a particle (*nipāta*) resembling a form ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*), but it functions here in the sense of "provided that" (*upapatti*), because it is bound to that [condition]. In that [sense], it means "as if" (*tasminn iva tadvat*).

The object (*viṣaya*), which has the characteristic of being the probandum (*sādhyalakṣaṇa*), is "presented" (*upasthāpyate*) or "brought near" (*upanīyate*) by that [means]. This is the explanation of the meaning. That person by whom it is presented is "thus"; the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is "that which is thus with respect to the object."
In response to the doubt—“How, then, can that which is unspecified by any particular attribute establish the probandum?”—it should be applied as follows: “By means of the thesis (*pratijñā*). (Note:
The word *tu* does not appear in manuscript S.)
[91] "By way of the statement of the thesis," so it has been explained by this [commentator].
However, some others explain this in another way as well.

That by which [an object] is established or revealed—without that speech, this [statement], "without the presentation of the object of cognition" (*prameyasyopadarśanam antareṇa*), will explain the word *upadarśana* as referring specifically to speech and not to a person.

Furthermore, since that [speech] is intended to be unspecified in form—such as "fire is here," "this possesses fire," or "this has fire"—it was stated [by the author]: "by someone" (*kenacid*), meaning by one who is an agent or a petitioner.
The state of being a petitioner (*arthitva*) is to be understood through such factors as the failure to obtain a Brahmin of the same lineage (*anvaya*).
"Price" (*mūlya*) means a ransom (*niṣkraya*); he "seeks" (*mṛgayate*) it, that is, he requests it.
A twice-born man who eats at the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and other such occasions here and there is a "parvan-Brahmin" (*parvabrāhmaṇa*).
Explaining this very example, he says "just as" (*yathā*).
Here, "dakṣiṇā" (the sacrificial fee) should be understood from the context as the gift given immediately after the meal.
"At another time" (*anyadā*) means at a time other than when a specific purpose has been attained.
The practice of wandering from here to there for food based on prior requests is the conduct of one who is like a *parvan-brāhmaṇa* (a Brahmin at a festival).
Regarding the phrase "at *śrāddhas* and so forth," the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*) encompasses festivals such as the initiation (*upanayana*) and the graduation (*samāvartana*).
Since it is not possible that this statement applies to him even when he is merely seeking [food], the author specifies him by saying "one who is full of faith" (*śraddhālu*).
"Faithful" means possessing faith.
By this, the author of the *Vārttika* shows that he intends by the word "purpose" (*kārya*) a purpose permeated by faith.
"Ghee-filled cake" (*ghṛtapura*) refers to a particular kind of food. Regarding him:

He indicates by way of a metaphor that "he too should be given much to me. Silver (*rūpya*) is a specific kind of object composed of a greater amount of copper and a smaller amount of silver. Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth: [93]... at the beginning of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇādau*).
And generally, the usage is by means of a metaphor.
The accusative case is used because of its connection with "gives.
By that Parva-brāhmaṇa who spoke thus.
[92] A follower of the higher chariot (aurdhvarathika), S; [93] a coin (rūpaka), S;
[94] you give, S.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Has it not already been stated that in an inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*), the logical mark (*liṅga*) must be understood from the other person alone? Therefore, you have not yet refuted that. Anticipating this doubt, he begins with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) and so forth, in order to explain what was said in the passage beginning with "even from our own statement" (*asmadvacanād api*). By using the word "moreover" (*ca*), he certainly intends to include another point to be stated.

This shows that [the point] is intended by the Teacher (Ācārya) through the force of the context, but it does not mean that this [word] is used for the purpose of adding another statement to it; furthermore, the employment of the word "kiñca" is appropriate because it is clear that [the passage] beginning with "yad api bravīṣi" is devoted to explaining another statement of the Teacher, namely, "asmadvacanād api.
Alternatively, this is a collection of both particles and non-particles, where the word "kiñca" is intended to express this [meaning], while the particle "ca" is used in the sense of the word "api."
By this, it is said that "something" [is meant].
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "whatever you say, even if it is something insignificant.
And by speaking in this way, a common worldly expression is imitated.
Of that statement [67.18], i.e., of the statement regarding the gender;
"it will follow" [67.20] because that very gender is the subject under discussion.
The word *aṅga* is used here as a term of address or entreaty.
The word *kiṃ* is used for a general inquiry, whereas the word *punar* is used for a specific one.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Having requested you, we shall ask both in a general and a specific manner.
Furthermore, this request for instruction should be understood as being made in jest, according to the context.

[95] Because, by our statement as well— by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)— there is the inclusion of the formal argument based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat-prayoga*), as well as the fallacious reasons (*hetu*), contradictory reasons (*viruddha*), and inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*), and the three characteristics of the reason (*trairūpya*). Previously, by the word "cognition" (*pratīti*), the Teacher [Dignāga] [referred to] the formal arguments based on similarity (*sādharmyavat*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat*), and the fallacious reasons, contradictory reasons, and inconclusive reasons.

Intending that the comprehension of the reason's own nature and its three characteristics (trairūpya) is what is intended to be expressed, he explains that there is "comprehension" [of the reason] through the formulation based on similarity (sādharmyavat-prayoga) and so forth.
For this very reason, all of this will be demonstrated in due order.

One might object: "Is it not necessary that there be both the presence [of the reason in the subject] and the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), such that what is being said here would be appropriate? Anticipating this, he says: "He thinks thus" [68.9]. Having connected the statement "that is impermanent" [68.18], one should connect it with the doubt: "Is that understood by the mere statement of that [property] alone? To which the response is: "when there is the statement of the property of the subject" [68.18]. As for the passage beginning with "whatever... [69.5] and so forth, its explanation has already been provided previously.
In this context, the time of practical usage (*vyavahārakāla*) is intended as precisely the time of inference;
it follows that the comprehension of the real object does not depend upon the apprehension of conventions such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
This was stated by "the venerable teacher" (*ācāryapādaiḥ*), referring specifically to the teacher Vasubandhu.

The meaning of the statement "the observation of an inseparable effect is inference for one who knows it" is as follows: that object which does not exist without something else is "inseparable" (nāntarīyaka).
And here, by implication, it should be understood that whatever object does not exist without a certain other thing, that [other thing] is its inseparable [cause].
And since it is both that [cognition] and the object, at that time there is the perception of it;
and by means of the perceiving subject, there is the designation of that very object which is being perceived.
Thus it is demonstrated that this very object, while being ascertained by that [perception], becomes the cause for an imperceptible object.
"Of one who knows that" (*tadvidas*) means "of one who knows its invariable concomitance" (*tannāntarīyakatām*);
and it is called "inference" (*anumāna*) because it serves as the cause for inference.
Thus, in the treatise titled *Vādavidhi*, he demonstrates the essential nature of the mere form of the indicator (*gamaka*).
Regarding that as well, in the definition [provided] by the Teacher,
one should apply the phrase "by their own wisdom" in response to the doubt: "But why are these faults, which do not even exist, proclaimed by Uddyotakara and others?"
The word "tu" (*but*) serves to emphasize that this is a fault or error of one's own intelligence;

for it is said by Uddyotakara in his *Anumānasūtravārttika*: "But others say: 'Inference is the perception of an object that is invariably concomitant [with another], by one who knows that [concomitance]'. (Nyāyavārttika, p. 54).

Having recited it and explained its meaning with moderation, he stated the refutation with that same moderation, saying, "In this case, the inclusion of the word 'artha' (meaning) is superfluous," and then further elaborated: "The compound term is *nāntarīyakārtha*.
In that regard, if it were a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound, it would mean 'the meaning of the inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*). "
First of all, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not necessarily concomitant with that;
is its "object" (*artha*) a property (*dharma*) or a purpose (*prayojana*)?
If, first of all, the object of being produced is a property, [then...]
It follows that [the object] must be an inference based on such properties as existence, being an object of cognition, and being denotable.

Now, if the purpose is the realization of impermanence, then the logical reason (hetu) is established. Furthermore, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyaka*) with its object."
In that case as well, whatever has "being produced" (kṛtakatva) as its inseparable concomitant (nāntarīyaka) is established as the logical reason (hetu).
And that "being produced" belongs either to the jar and so forth, or to the sound's impermanence.
If [the reason were] from a jar or the like, then a jar or the like would be obtained as the reason:
"Sound is impermanent because of a jar."
Now, as for the word [itself], it follows that the word would be the reason:
"Sound is impermanent because of sound."

Furthermore, if "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is the property (*dharma*) that constitutes both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) of impermanence (*anityatva*), then it would follow that "sound is impermanent because of impermanence. Alternatively, if the meaning of impermanence is producedness,
then in every respect, producedness would not be the reason for impermanence.
Now, [the opponent might argue that] it is "sāmānādhikaraṇa" (having a common substratum) and "nāntarīyaka" (invariably concomitant), and this is also an "artha" (object).
Even so, the compound is incapable [of expressing the intended meaning] because there is no restriction between the qualifier and the qualified.

A compound of the *sāmānādhikaraṇa* type occurs when both words deviate [from their specific referents], as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). This is because the word "blue" (*nīla*) applies to many objects, and the word "lotus" (*utpala*) likewise applies to many; thus, through this co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the compound functions].
It occurs;

however, in this context, when "inseparability" (*nāntarīyakatva*) has been stated, there is no ambiguity regarding whether it is a meaningful or meaningless object, such that the inclusion of the word "meaningful" (*artha*) would be necessary.

Anticipating the objection that "co-referentiality is observed even when there is deviation in one term," as in the case of "earth is a substance," it is stated: "Otherwise, [one would say] 'that is earth' or 'that is a substance';
in this case, there is deviation in both terms."

Due to the distinction between the primary and subordinate aspects of the term *pṛthivī*, it denotes both the substance (*dravya*) and the universal *pṛthvītva*. And by the word *dravya*, when there is an intention to express both the primary and subordinate aspects, it denotes both the substance and the universal *dravyatva*. For this very reason, because of the deviation of both terms [from their respective universals], it is rightly said that "earth is a substance. However, in the present case, it is not appropriate to say "the observation of the inseparable property" (*nāntarīyakadarśana*).
Why? Because the employment of words has the purpose of conveying meaning—for they maintain that the employment of a word is for the sake of conveying meaning.
Furthermore, when it is said "it is inseparable" (*nāntarīyaka*), the meaning is understood;
therefore, the use of the word "meaning" (*artha*) [in the compound *arthāpatti*] is not appropriate.
Therefore, it is not correct to say "one who knows that," nor is it correct to say "one for whom there is no non-invariable concomitance" (*nāntarīyaka*).
For indeed, a resident of a coconut island does not possess the knowledge that [fire] is invariably concomitant with smoke upon seeing smoke.
Consequently, one should not even say "one who knows that."
(Nyāyavārttika, p. 54–55) By asserting that "the defects are simply non-existent," he intends this very point:
first, the defects arising from the position of other compound types are struck down by a single blow merely by not being admitted;
however, a coordinate compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-samāsa*) is not untenable, since it is observed even when there is deviation within a single word.

For in that case, an object might be characterized by impermanence even if it is not invariably concomitant [with it], and it might be characterized by permanence even if it is not invariably concomitant [with it].
Therefore, due to the deviation of even a single term, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not contradictory.
Now, according to your view, there certainly exists what is called "permanent," at least insofar as it persists through the cycles of kalpas.
Therefore, this will be understood from that very [source];
otherwise, what would this term "impermanent sound" exclude?
For momentariness of that kind, as accepted by the Buddhists, is not denied by anyone.
In a formulation such as "there is no non-momentary cognition because of the exclusion of what has become thus," what would this term "non-momentary" exclude?

Furthermore, since it was previously stated that [the reason] is "inseparable" (*nāntarīyaka*), the meaning is already understood; why then use the word "meaning" (*artha*) such that one would consider such a compound?

Alas! Since the nature of substance and so forth is already understood by the preceding word "space" (*ākāśa*) and the like, what is the purpose of the word "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth, such that a similar compound might also be applied there?
Thus, the claim that "the very same solution [you] have for the initial case will also apply to mine" is trivial.

As for the statement that "earth is a substance," after demonstrating the deviation of both terms therein, it was shown that a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) occurs precisely because there is a deviation of both terms in every such instance.
That [is] the conjunction (or: that is more evil);
[namely] the substance space, the substance direction, the substance time, and the category of generality.

In cases such as "the category of particularity" (*viśeṣapadārtha*), "the category of inherence" (*samavāyapadārtha*), "the six categories," or "the beggar man" (*yācakapuruṣa*), even Brahmā would be unable to demonstrate a deviation of both terms [from their respective referents], because we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For no one can perceive or establish a commonality (*sāmānya*) among these— such as ether (*ākāśa*) and so on— by virtue of which the words "ether" and the like could apply to multiple referents, such as ether and the property of etherness (*ākāśatva*), such that there would be a coreferential compound despite the deviation of both terms.
There would have to be a compound; nor is there any commonality among the six [factors] by the designation of which this deviation of both members could be described.
Nor is either the action or its genus denoted by the word "beggar";
and since the proof for this has been stated elsewhere, it is not mentioned here.
Nor is it the substance space (ākāśa-dravya).
The compound *yācakapuruṣa* ("begging man") and others, being *karmadhāraya* compounds, are not observed to have a "common category" (*sāmānyapadārtha*) as their referent.

Furthermore, just as the word "earth" denotes both the earth and the universal "earth-ness," because there is a deviation regarding both terms, it is appropriate to say "earth-substance" (*pṛthivīdravya*).
Likewise, [the compound] *nāntarīyakatva* consists of both *nāntarīyakatva* and *nāntarīyaka*;

and by the word *artha*, both *arthatva* and *artha* are expressed. Thus, because both members of the compound are subject to deviation [in their referents], the compound has precisely the meaning already stated. However, in your view, neither *arthatva* nor [the other properties] exists.
Even if it does not exist in reality, it nevertheless exists as a conceptual construction;
since the establishment of the word is possible by that much alone, this has already been largely stated—what need is there for more?
In terms of the actual state of things, smoke is not an inseparable property [of fire] due to its non-existence.
The perception of that [sign] is also the perception of an object that is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).

In this regard, if one were not to say "one who knows that," then for someone born on an island of coconuts (*nālikeradvīpa*), the perception of smoke would result in an inference; therefore, it must indeed be stated "one who knows that.

Furthermore, the cognition of an invariably concomitant object is not simply called the "cognition of an invariably concomitant object" merely because it is a cognition of an object that is invariably concomitant.
By which it might be said thus;
however, it is the perception of that object which is not in fact inseparable [from another].

"That too" means: enough with this mode of expression for those whose intellects are purified by the meaning of words. The connection is that "the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not logical.
To the inquiry, "In what way is it illogical? there follows the statement of the reason, beginning with "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).
[98] By virtue of being the means of proving impermanence, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is the property (*dharma*). *Nyāyavārttika*, p. 54.
In the phrase "doubt and so forth" (*saṃśayitādika*), the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*) signifies the comprehension of one who has not yet understood and one who desires to know.

Regarding the expression "having set aside the act of existence established by general logical principles" (*sāmānyanyāyasiddhām astikriyām apekṣya muktvā*), the suffix indicating the prior action (*paurvakālika-pratyaya*) is to be understood.
In the phrase "doubt, desire to know, and so forth" (*saṃśayajijñāsādika*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes [the factors such as] purpose (*prayojana*) and the rest.
Likewise, by that very same inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the employment of a reason ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*) must also be included;
for if the thesis (*sādhya*) were not stated, there would be no expectation for a reason at all, such as "from what [is this]?

How could the wise fail to reject one who utters the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), which expresses the reason's status as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) in the establishment of the thesis? How indeed could they not refute him?
"Kṣīraṇṇ" means:

when the example itself is brought to the state of being the object of the statement, that is the "application" (upasaṃhāra); it is the bringing forward (ḍhaukana) or the demonstration of the presence [of the property] with reference to that. And it should be understood from the context as "of the reason whose capacity has been observed in the example."
By the term "sādhya" (the probandum), the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) is intended through metaphorical usage.
Furthermore, because there is no distinction between the genitive and locative cases, the meaning should be understood as "in the subject of the probandum.
Thus, [the text] states the essential nature of the definition; the phrase "the definition of the proposition (*pratijñā*)" is understood to follow from the context.
The conviction regarding that object which has been established by the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the exclusion of any possibility of its being otherwise;
it occurs for that purpose if the operation of the means of valid cognition is concluded by the final member (*nigamana*).

Then this [objection] would be appropriate to state: "But this is not so. Anticipating this, he says "because of the remainder" (*aśeṣe*), where the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
By the word "activity" (*vyāpāra*), the fruit of the activity is intended.
Now, one might raise the objection: "What indeed are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here, by the force of which this synthesis of the meaning [of the treatise] is described?

Anticipating this, [the author] begins with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*) in order to explain how these very members (*avayava*) have been described by others as having the nature of valid cognition.
The word "above" (*upari*) should be understood as referring to the name of a work composed by another, distinct from the present context (*prakaraṇa*).
For instance, having heard the name given by another person of similar status to some prince or high official, they— impelled by self-aggrandizement and the hope for wealth—

create a different name intended to increase their own enthusiasm and apply themselves to writing it down; it is for this very reason that [the term] "writing of names" (*nāmalekhana*) is indicated with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

The statement that [the thesis] is fruitless due to being illogical is a factual restatement that is relevant to the subject at hand; furthermore, the description of its various utilities serves to deceive the ignorant. Thus, by virtue of its definition, it follows from the connection that "there would be futility and so forth" regarding the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*). This is what was stated.

[99] Regarding the writing of the name—S [100] "api" is not present—S: [The opponent asks] "But surely there is a purpose for this as described by Uddyotakara; how then can it be useless? To this he replies: "As for what was said... [71.22].
"The answer has been given" means it was stated because it was already expressed by the passage beginning with "by that very [example] which was shown," and so forth;
and regarding what was thus stated, he himself provides the answer with the words "and whoever," etc.
"In its absence" (tadabhāve) means in the absence of the initial determination of the object characterized by the probandum (*sādhyalakṣaṇakarma*).

And because the opponent has stated—beginning with "as seen in inference for oneself" (*svārthānumānadṛṣṭaś ca*)—that which is intended to justify the application (*upanaya*), [the author], desiring to refute that, says: "And he who [sees] fire," and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).

"Sometimes" (*kadācit*) means when, having seen smoke and recollecting its pervasion by fire, one recognizes it after having reflected upon it as it truly is. This refers to the meaning of the term "reflective cognition" (*pratyavamṛśya-pratyaya*). Now, if one were to say that this [reflective cognition] serves no purpose because the object of the thesis (*pakṣārtha*) is not established even without it; [we reply: no.
One should understand that this same point applies to the present case as well, for one who speaks thus has it in mind.
Furthermore, regarding what was said [at 101] for the sake of establishing the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says [at 72.7]: "But as for that which... and so forth.

By stating that "it is not recited in any scripture" (na kvacid āgame paṭhyate), those who explain that "scripture is called a thesis because scripture and the thesis have the same object" are refuted.
For if the very same meaning that is stated by the thesis were also stated in the scripture, then that would be the case;
but since it is not so, they are refuted.
321} By the word "reason" (hetu), the statement that makes [the object] known is to be expressed; and that which makes it known is the logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics.

Nor is the three-fold nature of the logical mark (liṅga-trairūpya) expressed by that word ending in the fifth case; rather, it expresses merely its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatvamātra) and its status as a cause (nimittabhāva). Such is the intention of the speaker;
by this, that which is asserted by certain logicians who consider themselves clever is also refuted.
The logical mark (*liṅga*) that is capable of establishing the meaning of the thesis and must be presented as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is inference (*anumāna*);

the word expressing that [inference] is the reason (*hetu*). Furthermore, because it is the cause for the restriction of the object to be expressed, it is an external factor. And there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the expression and the expressed, because—whether directly or indirectly—they intend to express non-difference and share a single objective domain.

For smoke and such things are not a logical mark (liṅga) as long as they are not ascertained to be invariably concomitant (anantarīyakatā) with fire and so forth, nor as long as they are not subsumed under a particular subject (dharmin).
Only when they are ascertained as being invariably concomitant and subsumed under a particular [subject] does the capacity to prove the probandum (sādhya) exist, and not otherwise.
Nor is its invariable concomitance with that [probandum] and its presence in the subject (pakṣa) stated by the word "from smoke" (*dhūmāt*) and so forth, which ends in the first case;
for that would entail the redundancy of the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, how can that word be said to be "the statement of the mark (liṅga) capable of proving the meaning of the proposition," such that it is called "the word expressing that is the reason"?

Thus it is called an "external member" (*bāhyāṅga*), and the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "the reason is inference" should be understood accordingly. Since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans is apprehended therein by means of perception, the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is intended here as a perceptual one.
For this very reason, it is not every kind of perception that constitutes it.

It is not the case that in every instance the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans is grasped through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For example, in your own view, regarding the argument "the self is eternal because, while being related to existence, it is non-dependent,

like an atom," the intention is that the pervasion between the two properties— eternality and the state of being non-dependent while related to existence— is grasped in the example by means of inference (*anumāna*).

By this, the following point is also refuted, which is asserted by those very preeminent Naiyāyikas: "The example is the locus [of the inference] due to the pervasion (vyāpti) between the probandum and the probans;
having grasped that pervasion through perception, one subsequently provides the illustrative instance (udāharati).
Therefore, perception serves as the determiner."

The example (*udāharaṇa*) is also merely another part of the statement; because the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception does not have everything as its object, [the pervasion] exists only in some cases. If one were to express it in that way, then for that very reason, the example would be called "inference" (*anumāna*), since it lacks the apprehension of an object distinct from that [pervasion]. With this intention, he says: "But comparison (*upamāna*) is not even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [72.13]
And since this has been stated at length elsewhere, it is not repeated here;
rather, the established point is merely restated.

And by this very same door, that which is stated by those [logicians]—namely, "The cognition of similarity between the example and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) as being 'just so' (*yathātathā*) is analogy (*upamāna*);
the statement of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which grasps the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is the application (*upanaya*).
Here too, analogy is the cause of restriction (*niyamahetutva*)"—[is refuted].

As for the claim that "the application (*upanaya*) is also a distinct part [of the syllogism] because it possesses a restrictive cause (*niyamahetu*), namely, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which, by making known the presence of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) in the subject (*dharmī*), excludes its absence"— that too must be rejected,
precisely because this two-fold comparison (*upamāna*) described above lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge; how, then, could it be a restrictor?
By means of which the application (*upanaya*) would be established as a distinct component through its accomplishment based on the cause of restriction;

and since perception or inference, having determined the presence of the probans in the subject (*dharmin*), excludes its absence, here too there exists a restrictive factor in the form of perception— thus it must be said that the application, like the example, is [established by] perception.
Since in some cases inference (*anumāna*) is also of such a nature, it may be called "inference" as well; enough, then, with this insistence on the words of those who are not logicians.
Its operation (*tadvyāpāra*) is the operation of the application (*upanaya*) in the form of analogy (*upamāna*); that very thing is indeed the application itself.
It might be argued as follows: when it is stated that "sound is impermanent," an expectation arises in the listener as to "from what [is this known]?
However, there is no such expectation regarding the presence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the subject (*dharmin*).
Therefore, immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), there is the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) which is required by another; rather, [there is the cognition of the cause of that cognition].

The employment of a word denoting that [reason] ending in the ablative case is intended for the purpose of establishing [the reason], and not for the purpose of establishing the existence of the mark (liṅga) in the subject (dharmin).

Therefore, since its purpose is not to establish the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), how could he demonstrate that very property of being a feature of the subject? Thus, it would not be appropriate to say that "nothing at all is expressed by that. To this, it is replied: [The opponent says: It is for the purpose of establishing [the reason]; the use of a word denoting it ending in the ablative case is not for the sake of establishing the existence of the mark in the subject. Consequently, since its aim is not to establish the property of being a feature of the subject, how could he show that very property of being a feature of the subject? Thus, it would not be fitting to say that "nothing at all is expressed by that. To this, it is said:

Even when the proposition "sound is impermanent" is stated, immediately thereafter, if one says, "Whatever is produced is all impermanent, just like a jar, and this [sound] is likewise produced," is there no cessation of the expectation for the reason (*nimitta*) once the object to be proven (*sādhya*) has been understood?
For if there were, then one would have to describe the purpose of that cessation as belonging only to the expression of the logical mark (*liṅga*) ending in the ablative case.
If you are a speaker of truth, you ought not to say this.
Furthermore, whatever depends upon something as its cause does not depend upon that thing as being like a rabbit's horn; rather, it depends upon that which actually exists therein.
Therefore, how could existence not have been required by one who has depended upon some cause for the proof of the impermanence of sound?

If it were argued that a word expressing a cause (nimitta) does not possess the capacity for a universal (sāmānya) because it cannot establish an existence that is independent of [the specific instance], then one must necessarily accept that the purpose of employing a logical reason (*hetu*) is to establish the existence that serves as the basis for proving the probandum (*sādhya*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*), such as sound;
and since this can also be accomplished by means of the application (*upanaya*), it was rightly said: "What is the use of that? [72.17].
[102] There is nothing [to be gained] by that; now, regarding the conclusion (*nigamana*), he states the refutation according to the literal text: "In which [case], of the proposition (*pratijñā*)...
[103] Even so, this word "again" (*punaḥ*) does not refer to what is not the first time, but rather to similarity (*sādṛśye*).
As in the case of the statement, "The lightning-flash issues forth once again," there is indeed a certain degree of similarity. Alternatively,
even though the restatement of what is already established is the conclusion (*nigamana*) and the statement of what is to be proven is the proposition (*pratijñā*), [the two are distinct].

Nevertheless, since that very thing which was the probandum (*sādhya*) in the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the established (*siddha*) in the conclusion (*nigamana*), the conclusion is metaphorically designated as the "proposition" by virtue of having the same object, based on its reliance upon that single entity possessing distinct states. Thus, the repetition [of the meaning] is also justified. Furthermore, one should not suspect this conclusion to be purposeless.
This is because its purpose is to negate the undesirable consequence that is the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
As it has been said: "The conclusion (*nigamana*) is for the purpose of excluding doubt regarding the opposite of the *sādhya*.

And although the logical mark (*liṅga*), along with its locus and its invariable concomitance with the *sādhya*, has been stated by the members [of the syllogism] beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), nevertheless, without the conclusion, there might still be a suspicion of a consequence contrary to the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-prasaṅga*).
For indeed, the property to be proven (*sādhya*) in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) was one that pervaded the proving-property (*sādhanadharma*);

yet the impermanence in the [actual] subject (*dharmin*) is quite different, and it does not pervade the proving-property. Thus, thinking he has established something that does not pervade, the dull-witted person—due to the absence of any distinction [between the two cases]—regards permanence as being non-pervasive, which is contrary to the property to be proven.
It might also [be argued that the reason] would entail [the presence of the probandum] in the subject (*dharmin*) itself.

That being the case, when there is a suspicion of the reason's occurrence in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), one must state precisely that subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans as they reside in the example.

For this very reason, by the pronoun "therefore" (*tasmāt*), the mark (*liṅga*) which is connected [to the probandum] is referred back—being the topic at hand—in order to dispel the suspicion of its being contrary to the probandum.

"Therefore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) serves to establish a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that removes the suspicion of the opposite, for the purpose of negating the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
This is nothing but the graceful display of the lapse of the intellect of this eminent Naiyāyika.

For it is as follows: once the probandum has been pointed out, the reason (*hetu*) stated, and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) cited—[and] when the capacity [of the reason] has been observed in the example...

Furthermore, when the reason has been presented in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), what conscious person would either ascertain or even suspect that "whatever property does not exist without X, its existence also establishes the absence of X," such that a conclusion (*nigamana*) would have to be stated in order to dispel the suspicion of an undesirable consequence (*viruddhaprasaṅga*)?

And this person is not insane to hate (or perceive) impermanence in such a way that he would consider the impermanence to be established as something entirely different in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmi*) and something else entirely in the subject-to-be-proved (*sādhyadharmi*), and [thus] think he has proven a non-pervasive [property], since that impermanence does not pervade the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*).
Because there is no distinction [between the two] due to their being co-extensive, one would also entail impermanence in the subject;
yet he did not apprehend the pervasion by means of the specific [property], because a pervasion by means of a specific property is impossible.
And so it has been said: "Pervasion [occurs] between two general properties.
Otherwise, even if that [pervasion] were present, the suspicion regarding it would not be dispelled.

By this, it should be understood that the explanation offered by some— that the purpose [of the *siddhānta*] is the refutation of the suspicion that there might be a counter-argument— is also set aside.
If it is argued that such a thing might still be possible due to the power of delusion (*moha*),
then the five-membered structure of the syllogism must be abandoned.

It may happen that some person of extremely dull intellect, even when a five-membered syllogism has been employed, does not necessarily understand the impermanence of sound without the statement "nor is it eternal. Furthermore, there is a misconception among the Digambaras [Jainas] to the effect that "sound may be eternal" or "it may be impermanent. To exclude that possibility, [the word "not"]...

"Why is it not also said 'and so on'?"—enough of this excessive detail, as it serves no purpose. Since the status of the conclusion (*nigamana*) as a constituent part of the syllogism has been refuted, the position previously presented by both parties has become like weeping in a vast forest; what, then, is the point of discussing it further? "Jyāyān" means more excellent or superior.

That which possesses the five members—thesis (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*)—is thus; it consists of those [members]. This negation should be understood as a negation of the whole.
