Regarding the term "reason" (*hetu*), one should understand it as the word that expresses the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), either by intending the non-difference between the designation and the designated, or because they share the same object directly or through a succession.

Furthermore, when the reason is presented in its nature as something to be restated (*anuvādya*), it becomes for the proponent a form of the pervaded (*vyāpya*); thus, it is expressed by a word ending in the nominative case that designates it.

Therefore, it is logical that only a word ending in the nominative case should express that [proposition]. However, the Master’s refutation of the restriction regarding priority and posteriority should be understood as being made solely with respect to words expressing the reason (*hetu*). And where there is a proposition (*pratijñā*)... [103] ...S.

"It is precisely because the property of the means of proof (sādhana-dharma) has the nature of the property to be proven (sādhya-svabhāva-tā)"—this was explained under the heading of the essential reason (svabhāva-hetu).
Anticipating the objection that there might be deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of an effect-reason (kārya-hetu), he says "of the effect" (kāryasya) at [74.6].
By that [74.7], he refers to the necessary connection (pratibandha).
Of the two, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
"the manifestation of its absence" means the cognition of its absence; and this is the intended meaning for one who makes such a manifestation certain.
When it is stated that "it exists only as similar to that," there arises the contingency that non-existence— defined as its absence everywhere else, whether it be dissimilar, other, or contradictory—

is a separate characteristic. To preclude this, the author of the Sūtra stated "only when it is non-existent" (*asaty eva*), in order to show that non-existence is the third form [of the reason], and not merely its absence in what is contradictory or elsewhere.

Regarding the term "contradiction" (*viruddhatā*): it is contradicted by contradiction characterized precisely by coexistence. To the question, "How is it not [contradictory] even with that which is neither hot nor cold? he replies: "Because it would follow that there is no exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from other opposing factors (*vipakṣa*).
By this, he demonstrates the nature of the fault.
The phrase "of that non-existence" (*tasya tadabhāvasya*) is to be connected with "those who desire another" (*anyam icchatām*).
Likewise, it should also be understood as being "contradictory" by way of contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇa*).
The manifestation of the absence of a cause is also designated as having the characteristic of [non-existence]; furthermore,
it is intended as a specific kind of conjunction with a substance possessing velocity.

The two cognitions of destruction arise solely from the contact with the fire that expresses it; their presence [is required]. Without that, destruction does not enter into a state of conjunction with the jar and other things.
This constitutes a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) characterized by independence from those [factors].
It is established through a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), by means of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as accepted by the opponent.

By stating "in order to elaborate," it is shown that what has already been said for the sake of providing further explanation is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and not a true repetition (*punarukta*).
The mention of space and time (*deśakāla*) in reference to eternal substances such as space (*ākāśa*) should be understood as being for the purpose of an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntārtha*).

By this, the meaning is as follows: just as there is no restriction of place or time for these eternal things, so too a restriction regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such as being a quality of sound (*śabdaguṇatva*), is not tenable; this is the purpose of the illustration.
However, the Dārṣṭāntika [position] is untenable because it lacks the restriction of the nature of place;
for it is deficient in one member, namely, the member consisting of the characteristic of a sentient being.
This is with respect to its having that as its essence—that is, with respect to the uncreated, eternal essence of momentariness, which is the subject under discussion.
The term "the author of the treatise" (śāstrakāra) should be understood as referring to Kīrti on account of the context.
The connection is that he will demonstrate the momentary nature of existence (*sattva*).
By the phrase "by the very state of things" (*vastusthityaiva*), the meaning is: by the actual mode of being of things, and not by the force of another's admission.

"By way of the consequence of non-existence" (abhāvaprasaṅgena) [77.9] should be understood as "by way of the consequence of the existence of destruction" due to the context of the treatise. It should be connected thus: "He begins [77.12] in order to demonstrate that independence with respect to what was stated by the former masters, namely, what was stated by the venerable Dignāga.
"With respect to that" (taṃ) [77.12] means with respect to what is desired by others.
Regarding the apprehension of a thing (*vastugati*), its nature (*tadātman*)— that is, its established and stable nature—
is subject to the consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cause that it would otherwise become something different (*anyathābhāva*).

Because it is impossible for that very thing—which has arisen from its own causes with a stable form—to undergo change; and because, since the cause does not apply to that which possesses a stable form, it is impossible to conceive of the operation of a cause there, its nature as "otherness" cannot be produced. That destruction is its very own nature (*tatsvabhāva*).
The word *lakṣaṇa* is based on form (*rūpa*),
and its establishment is made by means of its own characteristic (*svaliṅga*).
Of that [characteristic], which consists of the nature of other entities and the emptiness of other entities.
The meaning is this: for non-existence, which is devoid of all form, the presence of a cause is contradictory, but not so for this [existence].
If this is also accepted by you, then why is our own position not admitted? To this, he says: "But rather... [78.19].

Regarding "its arising" (*tadutpattau*): this refers to the arising of another entity in the form of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). Even when speaking thus regarding the opponent's intention, the author of the *Vārttika* necessarily considers what is about to be stated; and by implication, the "suchness" (*tathābhāva*) of all things such as fuel is their state of being destroyed (*pradhvastatva*), while the "suchness" of cows and so forth is likewise [their state of being destroyed].
It should be understood that its nature is that of total destruction.
Regarding both of these points, the opponent has stated as follows:
Regarding the phrase "when that exists":

by this, it is shown by the opponent that since all fuel and so forth are excluded by way of the visible state of charcoal and so on, it is not the case that everything has been utterly destroyed; nor, because fuel and so forth are excluded when a cow or the like exists, is it the case that the cow and so forth consist of the nature of utter destruction.
Of this—[referring to] the embers and so forth. "They perish" (*dhvaṃsante*) means they undergo destruction (*dhvaṃsam upayānti*), that is to say, they vanish.
Their unmanifestness is in relation to the lamp; [it is not unmanifestness] of the substance (*dravya*).

By contrast, he states that the self-nature (*ātmabhāva*) is the absence of unmanifested existence (*bhāvarūpāvyaktatābhāva*). Thus, let it be established that its nature is the absence of such a self, because the cognition [of it] consists solely of non-existence.
He thereby demonstrates that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the occurrence of unmanifested existence in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

Demonstrating this very point, he says "yadi hi" and so forth. Here too, in the phrase "in the case of attaining a nature devoid of fitness for perception," the explanation of the term "by way of exclusion" (paryudāsena) is given as "from that which is intended."
Having attained the sphere of awakening, it has come within the range of supernormal knowledge (*avadhijñāna*); in the absence of that [awakening], it perishes when fire and so forth are present.
The suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of cause, according to Pāṇini 3.2.126: *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*.
This is a statement of the reason by way of formal proof.

One might object: "Since, according to the principle already stated, it is logical that destruction is the effect of that [cause], why did the Master say this? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The intention is as follows" [80.16]. It might be thought: "Even though it is an object of cognition, it does not perform the purposeful activity (arthakriyā) characterized by cognition therein."

Just as the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which consists in the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent, is perceived by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) yet is not [produced] by that conceptual construction,
how can it be called its "agent" (*kāraka*)?
For an object cannot be non-causal, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This is not so; for that statement was made with the intention of referring to knowledge that functions through direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), and thus there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case.

Furthermore, by this [statement] as well, there must necessarily be an object of such knowledge; otherwise, how could the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which is based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), be established? For this very reason, he says: "Or how [could there be] its object... [tadviṣayasya].

Or, it is the understanding of the possession of a cause; that is, the state of being endowed with capacity (*sāmarthya*), the state of possessing capacity, existence (*bhāvatā*), or substantiality (*vastutā*).
"Always beyond perception" (*atyantaparokṣāṇām*) means, from the perspective of one who is not omniscient, they are forever imperceptible.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *tarhi* (then/in that case) here should be understood from the context of the treatise.
By the phrase "as the cause of cognition" (*jñānaheturūpatayā*), what is intended is "by means of establishment through inference.
By this, the opponent has shown that these [entities] appear by way of appearing as the cause of cognition, and by their established form.
With the word "no" (*na*), he negates the position held by the opponent that there is no appearance of a non-existent thing as an established form.

The proponent has also demonstrated that appearing as having the nature of an existent is, in comparison with things such as a rabbit’s horn, precisely what constitutes the appearance of a stable form.
Furthermore, while adducing another fault in the case of non-existence characterized by the absence of all causal capacity, he says: "And of the exclusion of all forms" (sarvarūpavivekasya).
And that which is to be manifested as an emergence (*unmajjana*) is for the purpose of realizing the existence of the appearance of a stable form through the eyes and other sense organs.
Showing that the opponent’s claim—that [the object] appears as the cause of those cognitions—is also possible even in its absence, he says: "by being the object of cognition" (*jñānaviṣayatayā*).
Previously, however, having closed one's eyes to this point (like an elephant), something else was stated.
Because this non-existence also appears in the form of that cause,
as is the case with the eye and so forth, according to the context.

Even if this [non-existence] were indeed an object of cognition, it would still not be its cause; so how can it be said that the appearance as having the nature of its cause is the same? To this he says: "And of a non-cause" (*ahetoś ca*).
This should be understood as before.
If, in your view, that which is called "non-existence" does not exist at all, then these cognitions of non-existence—

He asks, "What would they apprehend? and replies, "But for us... The phrase "following from the ripening of our own latent predispositions" (*svavāsanāparipākānvayā*) is a qualification used as a reason.

"Distinct from that" (*tadvyatireki*) means excluded from that; that is to say, it is devoid of that. "It would be touched" (*saṃspṛśyeta*) means it would be grasped; by way of its exclusion (*tatparyudāsena*), that is, by the exclusion of the limit of its cessation.
By stating that there is no existence for that which is not the object of the cognition "it is existent," you have accepted its nature as non-existent;

regarding this, he says—"And not of this" (*na cāsya*)—in order to refute one of the two positions: is it non-existent by way of its own nature, or is it non-existent by way of another nature? [He explains:
"by way of its own nature" means by way of a void nature that does not depend on association with any other entity. Of such a non-existent thing, there is no form whatsoever.
Furthermore, the simultaneity of existence and non-existence is never tenable;

for it is not the case that death occurs while one is still alive. Thus, the existence [of the object] is like a jar that has not yet fallen from its stand. Moreover, when destruction is brought about by disintegration (*dhvaṃsa*), is that destruction identical to the object itself, different from it, a false other entity, or of the nature of a void?

Regarding those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) therein, let there be a third object of conceptualization (*vikalpya*). Then, even if that exists, [the objection beginning with] "What [is the purpose]? (*kim iti*) and so forth—concerning the refutation and the avoidance [of that objection], as well as regarding repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*)—there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
The proponent says: "And from that follows an infinite regress" (82.6). [The opponent asks: "How so? [The proponent replies: "Because of the cessation of fuel and so forth.
The proponent of the established doctrine [replies]: "How so?"
The differentiation of those [effects] arises from the differentiation of their causes.
Demonstrating that this is observed everywhere else where there is a cause, he says "rice," etc. [of] a single entity that has a single taste.
This has been investigated here in brief;
however, since it is treated in detail in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*, those who prefer extensive treatments should understand it from that very source.
Intending to indicate that his own *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi* should also be consulted, he says: "and in detail" [82.14].

It might be argued: "By the statement 'it simply does not exist,' is it being asserted that its own-nature (*svarūpa*) is absent at the time of contact with fire and so forth, or rather that it persists [even then]?
It cannot be the latter, because that would entail the consequence of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*) and because it is not the meaning of the word.
Furthermore, if its non-existence were being asserted, the previously mentioned faults would follow."
This is not a fault;

for by this turn of phrase, it is demonstrated that even for that which exists during another's contracted time, at the very moment of its own arising, that form of the entity which consists in "nothing" [is present] in the second moment.
However, nothing is being positively enjoined.
For this very reason, he says: "Neither its non-existence nor anything else comes into being" [82.18].

[One might argue: "Let there be no agent of destruction such as contact with fire; what is lost to us if there is another cause? To this he replies: "The non-agency of that which is not a cause" [82.22]. Indeed, that [cause] is taught to be its agent.
That which, being antecedent, causes another thing to conform to its own positive and negative concomitances— just as the eye and other [senses] do for consciousness—

is a cause precisely by virtue of causing such conformity of positive and negative concomitance; for the definition of a cause is that in its presence the effect is present, and in its absence the effect is absent.

Furthermore, since there is no existence of anything whatsoever that possesses the nature of arising when fire and so forth are absent, how could causality—which is defined by agency—be applicable in the absence of such agency? This is the intention of the one who speaks thus.
[106] That which is not its object... S.
[107] Or this relatedness [108] belongs to that which has a single form [109]. S.
It should be applied as follows: "incapable of remaining even on the tip of a needle" refers to a mustard seed.
The connection is to be made according to the context: dependence upon other causes is the opposite of independence;
and by that [dependence], it is pervaded.
Regarding the phrase "its intrinsic nature": by the word "space" (*avakāśa*) in the verse, it is intended to mean a statement that is like space.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "anticipating a statement that has reached its proper occasion.
This should be understood in the same way for other similar usages.
That which comes from an example is "dārṣṭāntika" (pertaining to the example).
By the word *kuśūla*, a specific type of container made of clay and so forth is expressed.
That which has its initial abiding (*avasthāna*) therein is described as such.
Kaṃ S.
Just as in the case of states (*avasthā*), so too for the self (*ātman*), there would be a difference in its own specific nature (*prātisvikarūpa*) when those states differ.
To say that there is "somehow" (*kathaṃcit*)—that is, by some manner—a non-difference is merely a phrase whose meaning is faltering.
Precisely because of the difference in the body (*tanu*), the consequence of difference—the consequence of having a distinct nature—follows.
In the same way, it should be applied according to the context as "like that which abides in an undivided form" or "the consequence of non-difference.
Now, if difference and non-difference were absolute, then the fault just mentioned would indeed apply.
Anticipating the objection that there might still be some form of difference between those two and some form of non-difference, he says: "Of those two as well" (tayor api).
This refers to difference and non-difference; and to their states and the possessors of those states—namely, their respective natures—and to those two as well.
Even for that other form which is intended as the cause of non-difference from those two— the state and the possessor of the state—
if there were otherwise no difference whatsoever between those two and that other form which is the cause of non-difference, then there would be identity; this is the meaning.
And since that [entity] has a single nature characterized by non-difference, it is "thus" (tathā); therefore, from that [it follows].

The intention of one who says "difference and non-difference" is this: under the view of a single essence, there must be an entry either into the other form which is the cause of non-difference, or into those two—the state and the possessor of the state—by means of that other form which is the cause of non-difference.

In that case, if there is an entry [of the two] into a different form (*rūpāntara*) which is the cause of their non-difference, then because only the non-different form exists, there would be only non-difference between the state (*avasthā*) and that which possesses the state (*avasthātadvat*); thus, even the mention of difference would not occur.

Alternatively, if there is an entry of those two into that different form which is the cause of their non-difference, then only the state and that which possesses the state remain established; thus, non-difference is discarded.
If this is so, then let there be some kind of difference between that [form] and those two; thus he says: "of the different form" (*rūpāntarasya*).
"In some way, this [is established] by means of these two" is understood from the context.
"The basis for that" refers to the basis for the slight distinction of another form from those two;
as it was previously, so it is also for this other form.
That other [factor] is somehow the basis for their distinction.
This is the meaning: that other form has some kind of distinction from those other forms which serve as the causes for the distinction between the state and the possessor of the state;

otherwise, because it would be absolutely non-different from that single nature, there would be no distinction between the state and the possessor of the state, nor any other forms serving as the cause for such a distinction.
By the aforementioned reasoning, absolute difference and non-difference would both result.
Therefore, since some kind of difference from those [qualities] must necessarily be admitted for that [entity], another form must be accepted as the basis for that [difference] of the other form.
In the same way, this would apply elsewhere as well; thus, a single entity would possess an infinite number of forms.
With the words "Therefore... and so forth, he concludes the subject under discussion.
By the phrase "its sublation," he means sublation by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*).
By this, he demonstrates the following:
It is not that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), being a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is sublated; rather, it is a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) that is sublated.
This will be explained further below.
[112] There would be non-exclusivity (*anaikānta*), which is a lack of certainty (*aniścaya*).
[85.12] That it has the state of being a result of non-certainty means, in short, that it would be a cause of doubt.
[112] It would be inconclusive (anaikāntika). This very thing [85.14] is precisely the state of being both productive and non-productive.
The meaning is "of the substratum characterized by the dharma.
And this state does not produce a cognition distinct from the cognition of the effect, by which [it would be established] as having the characteristic of cognition.

With the intention that its capacity should be postulated because it is employed in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), he said [in the text]: "of that which is characterized by the absence of all capacity.
Regarding the phrase "from experience" (*anubhāvāt*):
since the suffix *śatṛ* is understood here in the sense of a cause, the meaning is "from the experience of sublation" (*bādhānubhavāt*).

Having established the absence of a general definition of valid cognition by stating that it must be "free from sublation" (*bādhavarjitam*) because of the existence of sublation, [the author] begins with the words "tatpratibhāsiniś ca" etc., in order to establish the absence of specific definitions as well.

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of a single form, how could there be a determination of reality (*tattvādhyavasāya*) for everyone?"—he speaks the passage beginning with "tasmād i" etc., showing through the guise of a conclusion that this [determination] is possible in quite another way.
By the word "similar" (*sadṛśa*), what is intended is uninterrupted similarity.
The meaning is that the state of another entity which is continuous and similar to it is the "cause of its uninterrupted connection.
This should be understood from the context as referring to cases such as hair that has been shaved and grown back again.
It refers to those whose hearts—meaning their minds—are "deceived by mere similarity of form," that is, rendered incapable of determining things as they truly are.

Now, [the opponent objects]: "If, according to your view, there were some such thing as 'similarity' (sādṛśya) consisting in the sameness of form, then those whose hearts are captivated by that alone would recognize [the object].
But this is not the case; so how can you say this? To this he replies: "And not... [na ce...].

This was stated because it has been explained in detail by such passages as: “Even though they are distinct, certain things—like the sense organs and so forth—are restricted by their own nature to accomplishing a single purpose, such as a single unifying reflection, the cognition of an object, and the like” (Pramāṇavārttika 3.72). Thus it was said.
Regarding those entities:
since all three types of evidence are established as valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is an independent reason (*svatantra-hetu*).
The rebuttal beginning with "by this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not certain," and so forth, follows from this.
Its status as a sublater does not occur so long as the invalidity of the recognition is not established;
otherwise, since its object would be sublated by this [recognition] itself, how could it possess validity such that it might act as a sublater?
And its invalidity is not tenable so long as the invalidity of this inference is not established through the proof of the validity of that [recognition].

Otherwise, one might suspect the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), thinking that validity would not be lost only if the definition characterized by "being free from sublation" (*bādhavarjitatva*) and so forth were possible; thus he says, "Nor also...

[87.10]. By using the word "inference" (*anumāna*) figuratively to intend the logical mark (*liṅga*), he states, "...because of the connection with its own probandum" [87.12], and so on. Alternatively, the word "of the mark" (*liṅgasya*) must be supplied; for if it were not stated, and sublation were possible despite something being endowed with the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that very definition would be undermined, resulting in a lack of confidence in all cases—this is his intention.

We do not say this; rather, being a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsā*), it stands by implication. "Not undergoing contradiction" means not undergoing sublation (*bādha*) by inference; "pervading" means embracing [the object].
"Perceiving" means ascertaining the reality of the oneness of the form—that is, the nature—by way of its generality.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the fruit is included;
this refers to that which is conventionally known by the term "conquered by the sun.
It experiences such a state.
[114] Because of similarity, S.
[115] S understands: Now, why was this stated as the reason for its being unestablished (*asiddha*)—namely, "And it does not occur anywhere in the subject (*pakṣa*)"? [88.19]
If this is so, then you have not understood for such a long time that [the reason] has the characteristic of being unestablished (*asiddha-lakṣaṇa*),
because the reason exists in that manner by way of its presence in the subject (*pakṣavṛtti*) and so forth.
You spoke correctly only if, at that time, you had not understood the intention of the one who said, "This reason is unestablished."
This is indeed his intention: recognition is a specific kind of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And that which is the object of conceptual construction is the object of language, because conceptual construction manifests an object conjoined with linguistic expression.
And that which is the object of a word is the object of convention (*saṃketa*),

because a real relationship of denoted and denoter has been excluded. Furthermore, since it is impossible to establish a convention regarding the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) due to [its] incapacity and futility, how could any entities exist as real things?
The self is the object of recognition;
therein lies its nature as that which is being recognized.

One might argue that whatever is recognized [as the same] possesses a single nature across the two times of the past and the future, just like "this" [present object]. However, because it is impossible to demonstrate this to the Tathāgatas, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished; thus, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Even though the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) has accepted the proof by way of bold assertion (*prauḍhavāditā*), he proceeds with the statement beginning with "na ca" [88.19] out of a desire to state another refutation;
or rather, he says "na ca" while gathering an additional refutation.
Furthermore, by stating "because of the absence of the nature of being a producer of cognition" [88.27], this very point is demonstrated.
If all things possessed the nature of being producers and that [nature] were dependent upon something else, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness; however, this is not the case.
The word *bheda* (difference) denotes a specific distinction.
The word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) does not exist [in the opponent's definition]. To the question, "What, then, follows for you in the present context?", he says: "In the same way" (*tadvat*).
It should be understood that the reason given—"because of those [factors] such as seeds"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the fundamental logical reason (*maula-hetu*).
The word *saha* is not intended by the Teacher to function in the sense of "simultaneous" (*yugapad*), but rather in the sense of "sharing a single object," like *sahodara* ("uterine brother").
Furthermore, as for the statement that "the syllable also performs a single function," why would this be explained in the section concerning the definition of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)?
Moreover, it is not the case that the mutual cooperation of entities is established merely through their simultaneous activity.
For otherwise, it would follow that even jars, cloths, and the like, while performing their respective causal functions at various times, would possess such a nature [of simultaneous action].
If it is asked, "How then does the Venerable Arcata explain the phrase 'when the auxiliary causes have the disposition to act simultaneously'?"—
this is not a fault.

For this is not an explanation of the word *saha* as meaning "simultaneously" (*yugapat*); rather, since the existence of a [permanent] cause is not admitted, the fact that things which perform a single function necessarily do so at one time is superimposed upon the intellect as a single object, and this actual state of affairs is merely restated. Therefore, it should be understood as: "among those whose nature is to perform a single function simultaneously."
However, the defining characteristic is precisely the performance of a single purpose, and not simultaneous performance, for even though the latter is necessarily present, it is subject to deviation.
The wise, moreover, support this according to the literal scripture, saying:
"Is this not a great gain?"
And there is no intolerance whatsoever;
by explaining "not at all" (*naiva*), he shows that the word *vai* is used for emphasis.
He asks, "What then is the function of the others in this regard? and replies with the words "by its existence" (*bhavanena*).
The connection should be made as follows: "If this employment of activity were ultimate, its status as a causal factor (*kārakatva*) would be lost.
When the question arises as to why this is so, the phrase beginning with "because of the effect" (*kārya*) and so forth should be applied.
"By way of metaphorical designation" (upacārāt) refers to "the state of being an agent," as that is the subject under discussion.
"In that manner" (tathā) means "like that.
"Precisely from that" (tata eva) means "merely by its own presence."
"From itself alone" means from form itself, independent of the operation of a cause. "Of the self" refers to the self that is the effect.
"Even before" means even prior to its birth.
Intending that there is no difference between form (rūpa) and that which possesses form, it was stated [in the text] that "it is characterized by the distinction of form.
Why is that? Because of its non-existence.
That in which something situated must produce an effect is intended here as the "locus of the effect" (kāryadeśa).
"And that intention, as well as [the seed] possessing it"—[this refers to the previous statement].

Now, one might object: "Since the capacity for all [seeds] to produce a sprout does not diminish, a sprout must necessarily be produced from multiple seeds. Anticipating the question of how this objection is refuted by one who speaks thus, he says: "This is the intention. [92.4]
The phrase "simultaneously from multiple agents" (yugapat kartṛbhyaḥ) is to be understood as before.

The opponent’s intention is this: once it has been stated, what exactly is to be understood? Since [the reason] "because of producing that which has such a nature" (tatsvabhāvasya jananāt) is inconclusive (anaikāntika), the same must necessarily apply to the fundamental [reason] as well. When the opponent has stated the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga)—that there would be no difference in the effect due to a difference in the causes—the author, fearing the question "How does this constitute a sublation (bādhaka) of that? says: "He thinks thus... (evaṃ manyate).
Thus,
because its nature is produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and because its nature is produced by multiple efficacious factors that have reached that particular state;
this refers to the effect’s non-differentiated self-nature, according to the context.
"Is it not so? and so forth says the opponent.
"If that is the case," says the proponent [at p. 332].

When it was stated that "that which arises from multiple [causes] must be manifold," this was said with reference to things of the same kind (*ekajātīya*), and not with reference to effects in general.
Because it is accepted that many things of different classes arise,
[the phrase] "a single agent" refers to an effect whose nature is non-differentiated;
this is the occurrence [of the effect] when that [agent] exists.
He says this with reference to your aforementioned enumeration:
because of the existence of the word "confusion" (*saṃkara*) in the statement regarding phenomena (*dharma*), [it implies] non-confusion, that is, the absence of confusion;
for this very reason, he says "mutually" (*paraspara*).

He begins with the words "tathā hi" [93.25] and so forth in order to demonstrate that there is a distinction [between cognitions] due to the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), in view of the effects cited by others.
"Sādguṇya" means being oriented toward [the object].
By the word "ādi" [93.26], the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth are included.

By the word "faculty" (*indriya*), a faculty impaired by conditions such as ophthalmia is intended, because otherwise erroneous cognition would not arise. By the inclusion of the term "only" (*mātra*), the exclusion of the object alone is intended;
however, light and so forth are not excluded, because in their absence, that [erroneous cognition] would not arise.
In the phrase "other than that," light and so forth should also be understood here.
Regarding the object of utility—that single produced consciousness—it does not differ; that is, multiplicity does not arise for that which is characterized by such a single nature.
The combination of the particles *kim* and *nu* constitutes a question;
alternatively, the word *nu* expresses deliberation (*vitarka*), while the word *kim* expresses inquiry.
The particle *vai* here functions as an address (*saṃbodhana*).

When it is accepted that, given the existence of multiple [causes], they possess a generative capacity through this [single effect], someone—bearing in mind the objection raised by Śaṅkarasvāmin—raises an objection with the words "But surely... (*nanu*) and so forth.
Desiring to avoid [the charge of] arbitrariness, he speaks while corroborating his point with the words of a preeminent Naiyāyika, saying "And he said... (*āha ca*).
And Śaṅkarasvāmin [says] that this is present in the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, for what reason? From what?
Because it arises from causes non-different from consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The word "m" [in the verse] is a qualification by way of being the cause.

He begins with the words "teṣām" and so forth in order to demonstrate that their differentiation arises from the differentiation of their respective intermediate causal complexes (*avāntara-sāmagrī*).
In the production of consciousness, consciousness itself is the appropriating cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

The eye and so forth are cooperative causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*). However, in the arising of a moment of visual consciousness, the eye is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), while consciousness and the rest are merely cooperative causes; this is likewise in other cases as well. Thus, one should observe the distinctness of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) by treating one factor as the material cause and the others as cooperative causes.
Regarding "of effects" (*kāryāṇām*), this refers to those things such as the moment of consciousness, the eye, and form.
Regarding "the nature of being awareness and so forth" (*bodharūpatāder*), the proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntin*) states this and so on.
The term "emulation" (*anukāra*) should be understood as derived from the root *kṛ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
And "imitation" (anukāraṇa) must be stated as the performance of an effect belonging to one's own continuum.
This will be made clear in the conclusion of this very [section].
Showing that imitation itself occurs by way of the imitator, he says: "For instance" (tathāhi).

Explaining the second characteristic, he says, "And by necessity" (*niyamena*). The term *samanantara* is to be understood as referring specifically to mental attention (*manaskāra*), because it is the subject under discussion; this is based on its etymological derivation as that which is both "equal" (*sama*)—insofar as it has the nature of cognition—and "immediate" (*anantara*)—insofar as it is uninterrupted. It should not be taken merely as a reference to the basis [of consciousness] by relying on scriptural authority alone, since only the characteristic of the appropriating cause (*upādāna*) is being stated here. Furthermore, the absence of the long vowel is to be understood from its inclusion in the *śakandhv-ādi* group.
The meaning is that there is no necessary operation of the eye and so forth;

for it is the eye that is under discussion as having a necessary operation. "By way of being produced" means: by way of the fitness of its own consciousness, which is the fitness of the producer—that is, the cause—of that [consciousness].
The meaning is "for the sake of producing knowledge.
Even though it serves as a qualification of the eye (*cakṣus*), its meaning remains exactly this. Here too, the word *samanantara* [is used].
This is the intended meaning.
Since the first of the two characteristics mentioned is difficult to understand, the author clarifies it under the guise of a summary, saying: "Therefore...

This is to be applied in response to the expectation: "From what does the very establishment of one's own continuum arise, such that it must be known as the cause for the production of effects falling within it?"
Regarding the phrase "that which has a single form" (*yad ekākāra*), the particle *iti* indicates a reason.
The meaning is: because it is produced by internal distinctions; that is to say, because it is produced by internal distinctions belonging to that very thing whose characteristics have been stated.

With the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he concludes the subject under discussion. By "of an effect belonging to a single class" (*kāryasyaikajātīyasya*), it is intended that plurality is accepted only with respect to effects in general; otherwise, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would not be established.
"Others [might argue]: 'Since you accept that [very point], it is established for you;
therefore, it is not appropriate to speak in this way. Anticipating this objection, he says: 'And not...
Thus, first of all, Bhaṭṭārcaṭa has formulated the definitions of the material cause (*upādāna*) and the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*).
Furthermore, some here say:
"These two definitions are not tenable because they are under-inclusive (*avyāpti*).

For instance, if that which, by being the basis for a cognition that apprehends a single form, is the cause for the production of effects falling within its own continuum, is called the 'appropriating cause' (*upādāna-kāraṇa'), [then the definition is too narrow]."
In that case, when water is produced from a moonstone (*candrakānta*), moonlight would not be the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
If, however, the moonstone possesses— along with the moonlight— the quality of being the cause for a single conceptual cognition (*ekākāraparāmarśapratyaya*) regarding the waters flowing forth,
by which means their establishment as a single continuum (*ekasantāna*) is achieved through that [moonlight], then [the moonstone] acts as the producer of effects belonging to its own continuum.
They might imagine the material cause to be like the moon;
however, it is not tenable for anything else to be its material cause.
Likewise, when fruit is produced from trees, the bark would not possess the status of being that material cause, as there is no distinction in its nature.
To what extent can it be illustrated? Only a mere indication has been shown here.
Regarding the second definition as well, its lack of pervasiveness (avyāpti) should be inferred by this very same reasoning;
for even Śakra could not demonstrate that moonlight and the like necessarily have their origin solely in fire.

If it is argued that such an arising exists, then since the eye and other [faculties] also necessarily exercise their activity toward the arising of such a consciousness, it would follow that they too possess that same nature; therefore, this is trivial. Furthermore, the definition of a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) is also flawed.
For it is only in the case of an entity that exists as a continuum (*saṃtāna*) that one might postulate for some thing the status of being a specific cause in relation to its prior state.

However, regarding the production of the very first moment, which does not depend on a continuum, how could such a statement not be reckless? Enough of this; here, however, is the resolution provided by those who are great.
This alone is to be enjoined.
[117] The reading "of a specific state" (*bhāvaviśeṣasya*) is also seen.

Regarding the term "both": because the causes that have entered into the midst of a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) are distinct and manifold, there is no difference in the effect, even though it belongs to a single class.

Unity [of the cause] is due to the difference in causes, because the cause characterized as a causal complex (sāmagrī) differs from other causal complexes. There is also a difference in the effect, meaning it differs from the effects of other causal complexes.
The word "tāvat" indicates sequence.

The potter [95.27] is a kiln-worker; things of a distracted nature [96.1], that is, things whose natures are not mutually concomitant, when combined with other causes, accomplish—that is, bring about—effects such as bricks and the like. When a lump of clay encounters causes such as a leather-worker and so forth, the effect such as a brick arises.
When a potter encounters other conditions such as a cutting tool and so forth, the result is salt (or similar substances);
when a thread is accompanied by other causes such as a weaver and so forth, the result is a cloth and so forth.
To the question, "What do those [causes] accomplish? he says: "other than that" (*tadanya*).

In relation to the lump of clay, they possess a nature distinct from the sprouts and so forth produced from seeds and other causes; and the pot-nature itself is indeed different from those [effects] which are accomplished by other causes that have reached a state of disjunction (*vyagrāvasthā*).

"Complete causes produce the effect," as in the case of the lump of clay, the potter, and the string; this is stated as an illustration of completeness (*sāmagry-upalakṣaṇa*), but it does not mean that these alone are the causes of the jar.
The same should be understood regarding the examples that will be presented hereafter.
Demonstrating precisely what has been shown, he says, "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

One might object: "If a lump of clay accompanied by a potter and other factors produces an effect that is no different from the effect produced by a lump of clay included within a different causal complex, then this example does not establish a distinction in the effect based on a distinction in the causal complex. Anticipating this objection, he says, "The potter and so forth" (*kulālādi*).
It produces that which is of the very same nature as itself—namely, that which has the nature of clay and the characteristics of a jar and so forth.
The agent previously mentioned as the "clay lump" (*mṛtpiṇḍa*) is connected here.
To the question, "Why does it produce something of a different nature? he replies: "Even from its own effect, such as a brick, and so forth. (96.7)
He asks, "For what reason? and says, "Of the mere [clay]" (*kevala*).
That clay lump whose nature is distinct from a mere [clay lump] is "such"; its state is "thatness" (*tattā*), and by that [it is so designated].
By the word "mere," only the absence of the potter and others is intended.

But it does not mean the exclusion of the accompaniment of other causes; rather, "from that effect" (tatkāryāt) means from the effect of the lump of clay accompanied by other causes. To the question, "From where does this distinct nature of his arise?", he says: "by its cause" (tatkāraṇena). This refers to the potter—meaning the cause characterized as the potter—who is in close proximity. By that cause, namely the preceding moment, a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is imparted, that is, produced, which is a specific form belonging to that [effect].
Thus it has been stated.
By this, the production of that which is not distinct [from its cause] as dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) is indicated;
and this qualification is made by way of its being the cause.
This is clearly evident in this sense:
even though the lump of clay is operative in both ways regarding the state of being the material cause (*upādānabhāva*),
because it acquires other auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*), the effect— which exists by its own nature— is indeed distinct from the effect produced when accompanied by those other auxiliaries.

Having established the status of being a producer, [the author], extending by analogy the capacity to produce an effect distinct from one produced with other factors to the potter and so forth— who, as a cooperative cause, functions in both cases solely through the mode of cooperation when another material cause is obtained— says: "In this way" (evam), that which [is produced] together with another material cause, [distinct] from the material cause characterized as a lump of clay...
Any other material cause (*upādāna*) accompanied by that [specific factor]—
such as one accompanied by a lump of clay— is indeed of a different character from it;
therefore, it produces an effect such as a jar that is entirely dissimilar to an effect produced by a material cause accompanied by something else.
Thus, [he] demonstrates the form of the collective meaning of the Master’s statement beginning with “just as from a lump of clay,” etc.;
then, with the words “In that regard,” etc., he now explains the meaning of the individual parts.
By the word *vughna*, [clay] vessels (*mṛṇmaya*)...

A specific type of covering is being described. Having formed a qualifying compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word *pṛthu* (broad) and that [covering], and having then established a determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*) such as "the belly and so forth of that," one should then form a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) meaning "that which has a shape like that, or like its [belly]."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of other specific parts of that [pot], such as the neck with its shell-like ridges (*kambugrīvā*), which belong to a different class. The connection [of the sentence] from the Sūtra is: "the very nature of that same pot becomes differentiated from the wheel and so forth," by virtue of its being essentially a particular configuration of clay (*mṛtsaṃsthānaviśeṣātmatayā*).
To the question "From what does the jar arise?", he says: "In the lump of clay.
This is because it has the nature of producing that [jar], meaning because its causal nature consists in producing the essence of the clay's configuration.
[The jar arises] because the jar possesses that form, meaning because it possesses the form of the clay's configuration.
If it is asked how those two can have the nature of producing that [cognition] even when they are entirely different from the collection of sūtras, he says: "independently of that" (*tannirapekṣe*).
By the word "that" (*tat*), the sūtra is referred to;
because of their distinct natures—that is, because of their having dissimilar natures—there is indeed a difference in nature from the state independent of that [sūtra].

When the question arises as to how these two [are distinguished], the phrase "of those endowed with the specificities imparted by the author of the Sūtra" (sūtrakāraṇopahitaviśeṣayoḥ) should be applied as a qualifying term in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
The mention of "three causes" (kāraṇatraya) is intended to indicate the specified causes; however, it does not mean that there are exactly three causes for a jar.

Rather, [the distinction is made] through their respective applications (*upayoga*), which are the operations of distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) directed toward the effect. Regarding one's own... [text ends].

The "particularities of being" (*bhāvaviśeṣāḥ*) are the specific natures (*svabhāvāḥ*) of effects; their "non-confusion" (*asaṃkaraḥ*) is their lack of intermixture. In that regard, if those [causes] such as the potter were each individually productive, then one might say that [the effect] is produced by the three aforementioned causes. Nevertheless, one might ask: how can this distinction—namely, that "this part of the effect arises from this [cause]" and "that part arises from that"—be established for an effect that is a single, undivided whole arising from everything? Anticipating this objection, he says: "And of that, each individual... and so forth.

[The opponent asks: "Let it be that the effect is produced by the entire causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as its cause; but how can the specific qualities residing within that [effect] be established as being produced by those [individual causes]? To this he says: "Each one of that kind... (96.27). In relation to a lump of clay and so forth, the fact that another [lump of clay] is of the same kind (*tajjātīyatva*) should be understood.

[40b] By this, he demonstrates the following: it is not the case that within a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), in relation to that very same effect which is an undivided whole (*akhaṇḍātman*), the production of each specific quality is restricted to being produced by that specific cause alone; rather, when there is an augmentation of this or that [cause], there is an augmentation of this or that [quality], and when this or that [cause] is removed, there is the removal of this or that [quality].
And because the cognition of the cooking [action] and so forth leads to the determination of oneness, they are established as having a single substratum; however,
it has been stated by the investigators of reality that those who engage in conventional usage do not analyze in this manner.
He asks, "What is the purpose of analyzing even those [causes] in this way? and answers with the words "yataḥ" [96.29].
That is, because of the analysis just mentioned. He asks, "Why do they accept even multiple causes? and answers with the words "paraspara-" [97.1].

For, in a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by succession, this is for the sake of establishing the existence of a causal totality capable of producing the desired effect, such as a sprout, through a sequence of effects in which excellence is mutually induced;
and this will be demonstrated below.
[118] Because their natures are distinct (*bhinnātmakatayā*).

"Wherever a form appropriate to it arises, that is its object"—this means "of that object," namely the jar. "From an object in another state" means from an effect produced by the acquisition of another auxiliary condition.
"Of this" refers to the effect.
By this, the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *kāryapadaviśeṣaṇa* in the root text—namely, *tajjanitaviśeṣabhedasya*—is shown as it should be formed as a *bahuvrīhi*.
[The phrase] “knowledge is fit to imitate that form” [is stated]; the word “not” (*na*) is understood from the preceding context, and thus the meaning is: “it is not fit,” or “it is not capable.”

Because the suffix *śānac* is prescribed [only] when there is a cause (*hetau*), its arising by the force of a meaning that lacks that specific form should be understood as stating the reason for the appropriateness of its conforming to that form.
Nevertheless, in response to the expectation of why it is not appropriate, he says: "because of error" (*bhrāntate*).

The intention is that there is no such thing as "absolute" (*aikāntikī*)— which others consider to be absolute— precisely because unity is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, "not absolute" means not certain (*aniścayavatī*).
Alternatively, the phrase "the state of having a manifold nature is not absolute" is connected with what precedes it.

Now, regarding the production of cognition, one might ask: do the sense organs and so forth—whose nature it is to produce [their effects] at various intervals as distinct specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)—cease their continuity entirely, such that they are described as performing the function of a single effect?
To this, he says: "And this... [98.6].

Now, if by the term "single causal complex" (*ekasāmagrī*) you mean the collection of causes that produces consciousness, then what has been said— that they lack continuity (*saṃtānatā*)— is already established.

Now, if it is argued that one [of two causes] is the material cause (*upādāna*) while the other is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), and thus they are called a "single causal complex" (*ekasāmagrī*), this too is not tenable;
for does that intermediate causal complex produce only a single moment that is both the material cause and its effect?
Or is it intended that the effect is not manifold?
Alas, even all of that is indeed only an effect (*upādeya*) in dependence upon its respective material cause (*upādāna*); thus, the fault remains as it was.
The meaning of the term "single causal complex" (*ekasāmagrī*) has already been explained; one need only apply effort toward understanding it.
When one [of two] substrata (*upādāna*) exists and the other cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) likewise exists, then only a single consciousness arises— namely,

that which has mental attention (*manaskāra*) as its substratum and the eye and so forth as its cooperative causes— but it is not the case that a momentary visual organ (*cakṣuḥkṣaṇa*) of such a kind arises;
rather, it is the visual organ as a substratum, together with mental attention and other cooperative causes, that exists [as the basis for the arising].
In this same way, the arising of a momentary instance of form and so forth should also be understood by oneself.

Here, the collective meaning is as follows: the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), consisting of the substantial cause which is attention (*manaskāra*) and the cooperative causes such as the eye, produces only a single effect.
However, when it produces another [effect] at that very time, it does not produce it while possessing that same nature.
What then? It consists of the eye as the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and mental attention (manaskāra) and so forth as the auxiliary causes (sahakāri-kāraṇa).
This should be understood in the same way regarding the production of moments of form (rūpa) and other [sensory objects].

Therefore, the distinction between their internal causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) has been established, and it was stated previously that there is a mutual differentiation among them; thus, everything is clear.
But why is this said only with reference to a single intended complex, and not with reference to the complex in general? To this he says: "But in the ultimate sense... [98.6].

"Included within that capacity" means that it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of the eye and other cooperative causes; and "wherein they are included by way of being the material cause" means wherein, in that causal complex, their activity occurs as cooperative causes.
That other causal complex [is its cause] by virtue of being a constituent part of that [complex].

Regarding the phrase "of another effect" (*kāryāntarasya*), this is said with reference to the moment [of consciousness] which possesses a substrate (*sopādeyakṣaṇa*); thus, that consciousness is indeed another effect of the eye. In the same way, for any other [cause], there is another [effect]; this continues because of the commencement of yet another effect of that [cause]. Thus, [the point is] "the performance of multiple effects. (3) *ra* (ca).
The remainder must be supplied; otherwise, in reference to what probandum would this ablative case express the state of being a cause?
To reinforce this very point, he says "just as" (yathā) while providing an illustration.

Then, by the recurrence of the word "one" (*eka*) in the phrase "even that which is produced from multiple conditions is one," the meaning is that even that which is produced from multiple conditions does not exist as a single entity.

The word "iti" [98.9] indicates the reason; the word "api" [98.10] expresses a logical possibility (*sambhāvanā*). Alternatively, the connection should be understood as follows: even if one accepts that there is a multiplicity of effects due to the multiplicity of causes from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no contradiction whatsoever.
He asks, "Why is there no impairment? and replies: "Of those included within that causal complex" (*tatsāmagryantargatānām*).
The phrase beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth is to be explained as before.
The particle *iti*, however, refers back to the aforementioned material causes (*upādānakāraṇa*) and auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*).
Therefore, this meaning is: "because of the multiplicity of causes characterized as previously stated.
Now, concluding the subject at hand, he says "therefore" (tataḥ).
"In general" (sāmānyena) means by relying on the mere fact of being an effect.

If it is asked, "What is the fault in the reason being a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established)?"—this has been analyzed by us at length in the *Dharmottarapradīpa* and in our own investigation of [the views of] our own school; so let this matter rest for now here.

By the word *dravya*, through the etymology "that which flows toward (*dravati*) or goes toward (*gacchati*) the modes (*paryāyas*)," a phenomenon (*dharma*) that is subject to transformation yet eternal (*pariṇāminitya*) is intended. And by the word *paryāya*, [it is intended] that which comes from all sides (*pari-samantād eti*) to the substance (*dravya*).
Thus, by this etymological derivation, they are *dharmas*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of contact (*sparśa*) and so forth is intended.

"The jar is the substance (*dravya*); color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest are its modes (*paryāya*)"—this is an example of substance and mode, which demonstrates the form of the difference in number; the second [example], however, demonstrates the difference in designation (*saṃjñā*).
Thus, the form of the distinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) has been shown. "Attachment to things" (*vasturāga*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, he states the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the distinction of effects (*kāryabheda*). The word "thus" (*iti*) refers back to the distinctions and non-distinctions mentioned immediately prior.

The opponent concludes with the words "these two alone," etc., [stating]: "That which is the non-distinct self (*ātman*) of the eye and so forth, which produces a single effect and serves as their commonality—
the fact that [the cognition] is produced from that [self] is what constitutes the non-difference of the nature of others in a general sense."
Having thus asserted the nature of being a substance (*dravyatva*), he now says—"First, the distinction of number" [99.7]—in order to demonstrate it specifically.

"Usage by way of plurality" refers to the employment of a word ending in the plural number; and the plural number [is applied] by the rule: "In the case of *yuṣmad* [when used] with a superior, [the singular is used] optionally."
By this, it is shown that the reason "because of the difference in number" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its being common to both sides.

It would follow that there is no cognition of "wholeness" (*kārtsnya*), which consists of the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). Alternatively, if that were cognized, it would follow that there is no cognition of "gravity" (*gaurava*), which is the object of the notion of venerability regarding the various states and the objects of those states.

Anticipating another objection to be addressed right here, he says: "If it is argued that [the word] *vrīhayaḥ* [is plural]... by means of the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.58]: "When a genus is denoted, the plural may optionally be used for a single entity.

Furthermore, by stating that "they do not differ in their nature as synonyms," if a difference in number were to be the proof for multiplicity, then the absence of such difference would likewise be the proof for unity.
Otherwise, that would be impossible;
yet it is not so. Therefore, it should be understood that the difference in number is not capable of proving multiplicity. Consequently, [it follows] from the difference in designation.
By this, it has been shown that the reason "because of a difference in designation" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its exclusion from the counter-example being doubtful.

Now, demonstrating that it is also inconclusive by virtue of being over-common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), he says: "And even in a single [entity]" [99.19]. Here, the previous fault should be understood through the "closing of the eyes like an elephant" (ignoring the point).
"Of the whole" [99.21] refers to the aggregate of property and property-bearer (*dharma-dharmin*) consisting of power and the possessor of power.
There are three [types of permanence]: of the property and the possessor of the property; of those that subvert them; and of those that express the properties. *Mātrā* means a trace.

Permanence as immutability (*kūṭasthanityatā*) is abiding in a single form at all times. Permanence through transformation (*pariṇāmanityatā*) is abiding while transforming into various successive states; and that [permanence] is accepted because of that.
[100.1] Transformational impermanence:
[100.2] of this substance, such as gold, which is transformationally impermanent; its "cutting off" (*cheda*) or destruction by way of that form, namely, by way of its successive states (*paryāya*).
The phrase "like the synonyms" is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
This is the permanence of transformation (*pariṇāma-nityatā*);
the permanence of immutability (*kūṭastha-nityatā*) is not possible in a substance that is distinct from its modes (*paryāya*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "In the alternative formulation" (*paryāye*).

Here, the reading "like immutability" (*kūṭasthanityatāvat*) appears correct according to the Tibetan version. Regarding the reading "in those whose transformation is differentiated" (*vibhaktapariṇāmeṣu*), the analysis of the compound is: "those for whom the transformation is differentiated."
The earlier commentators explained that the meaning is "divided" and "appointed" by virtue of being assigned to specific tasks;
even now, some who consider themselves scholars attempt to explain it in this very same way through their own reading.
This is most improper, because the word *vibhakta* has a different meaning.
For this word "divided" (vibhakta) does not denote something appointed by virtue of performing a specific function;
rather, it denotes something established through division.
Furthermore, what kind of lexical poverty is this, that he should employ such an inexpressive term, instead of saying "in transformations that perform specific functions"?

Moreover, every transformation produces a specific effect in relation to other effects; what, then, is the distinction of this transformation of cloth and so forth from any other, and who is its director? Why exert effort in such an irrelevant place? Therefore, this is a scribal error found in some manuscript.

However, the reading "vibhaktaparimāṇeṣu" (in those whose dimensions are distinct) is more appropriate. In that context, *parimāṇa* (dimension) is a specific quality (*guṇaviśe�ṣa*) that serves as the cause for the conventional usage of measurement.
This is stated according to what is established by others; furthermore, it is intended here as the produced [quality] called length (*dīrghatva*).
In that regard, those cloth-carpets and other items whose dimensions have been determined through division— that is, when they are spread out or lengthened—
cover something, support something, and bind something,
even though previously [that capacity] did not exist in anything at all.
In the sense of "existence" (*bhāva*), it refers to an effect that is currently arising (*utpadyamāna*);
and since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of "cause," it means that because something previously did not exist,
there is now the existence (*bhāva*) of something.
This is the meaning.
The reading "bhavet kāryam" (the effect would exist), however, is an inferior one.
For if every single moment included within that causal complex—which has acquired specific characteristics through mutual appropriation—arises as individually capable [of producing the effect].

Since consciousness and so forth arise [from it], that [cause] must necessarily possess either a nature that produces cognition or a nature that does not produce cognition; it cannot, however, possess a nature that produces both the one and the other, as these are mutually contradictory, which would entail the consequence of [the cause] being divided. With this intention, the opponent, raising an objection, says: "But surely... and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "How could there be the production of an effect other than that?", the intended meaning is as follows: "Entities possessing such-and-such a nature are born from causes possessing such-and-such a nature;
why then would cognition—which possesses that very nature—be ignorant, given that it is born from causes non-different from consciousness?"
(Pramāṇavārttika 2.251) Thus,
because they have the nature of performing multiple functions— that is, because they possess the form of producing multiple effects consisting of cognition—
of those moments, both those of the same class and others.

The existence of those [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, is the immediate cause of seeing; therefore, since one observes the effect characterized by consciousness in their presence, and because of the restriction that the faculty alone is the producer, why is this fault stated in that state? To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).

By this, he means that because there is doubt regarding the mere phenomenon (*dharma-mātra*), the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) is what is logically established here, not the exclusion of connection with another (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*).

Now, one might object: if consciousness produces matter with the same nature by which it produces consciousness itself, then that matter must necessarily possess the nature of cognition, just like that consciousness.

Alternatively, if it produces it with a different nature, then there would be the consequence of two contradictory natures. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not from this" (*na cāta*). This means: because [matter] does not have the nature of producing both consciousness and non-consciousness.
To the question "Why should this not be so?", he says: "Of the one alone" (ekasyaiva).

This refers to the specific excellence of the self (*ātmātiśaya*), which is a particular nature capable of producing consciousness or non-consciousness, attained through the power of its own causes and conditions.
By this, he demonstrates that it produces each [effect] by means of a single form; it is simply that this single form is such as to produce both consciousness and non-consciousness.

This is what is meant: by their own causes, all the moments included within that causal complex are brought to this state, namely, that they must produce an effect consisting of both cognition and non-cognition in the form of your [subjective] prior manifestation.
If that is so, then since pleasure and the like arise from causes non-different from consciousness, it follows that they must possess the nature of cognition and the capacity to establish suffering.

In this case as well, it can be argued that for one who experiences the moment of the arrival of a beloved son who had been away, a form of such a nature arises from its own collection of causes, by which consciousness, non-consciousness, pleasure, and other [states] are produced; thus, from a pure form, these [arise].

Regarding that, it has been refuted by us in the explanation of the specific [definition] that possesses a qualifier; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. One should observe the difference between what was stated previously—where the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) was disregarded in its formulation—and what is stated now, where the restriction is placed at the forefront.
That which is fit to be designated as "this" (*idantayā*) is "with demonstration" (*sanidarśana*).
That which obstructs the arising of another in its own location is "with resistance" (sapratigha);
this is the terminology of the Āgamas.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of two terms with distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) upon a single object; for it is impossible for those grounds to occur in one and the same thing, since those grounds are not compatible with it.
Regarding "dependence" (*apekṣā*): it refers to dependence on a single common benefit (*upakāra*), because it is established by logic that the benefit is non-different from that which is benefited.
Introducing the passage beginning with "Nor also... (*nāpi*) and so forth for the purpose of stating further points, he says:
"Why is there an absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)? He says 'by perception' (*pratyakṣataḥ*) in order to establish that very absence.
[The phrase] "precisely as a single nature" (*ekātmatayaiva*) means precisely as having the nature of light-form and so forth.

Since it is perceived in this way by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it has been shown by implication that direct perception is not the means for establishing the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them.

Regarding the inference by which the connection between the diversity of effects and the multiplicity of causes is established, that too should be understood as referring to individual specific causes contained within a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and not to causes in general, because a complex arises from a complex.
In this very context, gathering another fault, he says: "of one" (*ekasya*).

If we were to accept that a single entity possesses multiple natures on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), provided that we did not admit multiple activities by way of being both a cooperative cause and a material cause (*sahakāry-upādāna-bhāvena*), then it would have been stated as being the very nature of the subject (*dharmisvabhāvatayā*); it is with this intention that he has said so.
"Because it is precisely the multiplicity of natures in a single [entity] that must be examined" (i.e., *ekasyānekasvabhāvatāyā eva cintyatvāt*).
"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if that very thing by which it experiences multiplicity of nature were itself to be divided.
"But that is not the property-bearer (*dharmin*)"—this is the meaning of the word "for" (*iti*) in the context of the reason.

That which has a single effect despite being manifold is "that which has a single effect" (*ekakārya*); its state is "the condition of performing a single effect. The meaning is that this would not exist. The collective sense is: since the determination of the various modes of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) occurs by way of presenting the nature of that very effect, there is no single form (*ekarūpatva*) precisely because of that differentiation.

Now, one might object: "We do not say that a single [cause] produces many; rather, we maintain that in its complete state, each [cause] individually brings about each [effect]. Anticipating this, the passage beginning with "na caika... (and not one... should be applied first.
However, in response to the expectation of why it does not produce [the other], it should be applied later.

"Simultaneously" means at one and the same time. This is shown by the following: if, out of fear of this very fault, one were to maintain that they depend on the assistance provided by mutual appropriation, then since each individual [cause] would provide assistance for all those moments in reality, how could it be that a single [cause] does not produce multiple effects? Thus it has been demonstrated.
And then, with the words "and so" (*tataś ca*), because it is impossible for a single thing to perform multiple functions,
he says this— though its meaning was already understood— in order to state it explicitly:
the terms "one" and "many" are to be connected as appropriate.

The meaning should be understood as follows: because one [entity] is not admitted [to exist], it lacks multiple actions; and by the aforementioned principle, because multiple [entities] also lack a single action.
[Objection: But surely, it is intended that there is no mode other than the way a single [entity] performs multiple actions or the way multiple [entities] perform a single action?
If it is argued that it has been established that "the manifold indeed produces the manifold," and one asks how this is consistent, we say no;

for when multiple actions are admitted as falling within the scope of a single manifold causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there occurs the initiation of specific moments— both homogeneous and heterogeneous— by virtue of every [cause] functioning as either a material cause (*upādāna*) or a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*).
Because one accepts what is logically established, the objection that a single [entity] would result in multiple actions is resolved; thus, everything is clear.
The underlying sense is that if there were no cause, such a restriction would be impossible.
Furthermore, it is accepted that the effects of substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) are distinct.
With the intention of showing how one who is not insane could deny that a single thing, being of a single nature, can produce multiple effects, he says "in the substance," and so forth.
He states that even though there is a single nature, there is no single entity—namely, "of the nature itself.
Otherwise, if the nature were something other than the entity, then for that very entity, the nature would likewise [be distinct].

It should also be understood that this leads to the consequence of [the object] being a non-entity. Now, clarifying the intention with which he said, "How could one not be insane? [at 102.14], he says: "And if there were a single nature" [at 102.16].

For when a substance such as a tuft of cotton is, at the very moment of its production from a substance consisting of two tufts, by way of the maxim of the crow and the palmyra fruit (*kākatālīya*), [dispersed] by wind-blown cotton fibers and the like—

It becomes conjoined with another substance of very small dimension and acquires as its auxiliary cause an action that produces a disjunction born of disjunction, which is not counteracted by the conjunction that initiates the substance.

The intended meaning of this speaker is to be understood as follows: the Vaiśeṣikas must necessarily accept that the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of substance, quality, and action is a single entity— a dual-mass material substance such as cotton, as well as a quality called "conjunction of such a kind," and an action of such a kind, all of which perform their respective functions simultaneously.
Otherwise, at the same time that the effect-substance arises, color such as white would not arise in the effect;

rather, once the effect has arisen, it arises subsequently from the cause. For this very reason, yogis maintain that in a single moment the substance is without color, touch, taste, or smell. However, for that quality which is currently arising, its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is precisely that substance which has arisen immediately prior, and not the substance that is its [material] cause.

Thus, this has been established by us in some manner; however, the statement "and of a single action" can be established with reference to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and impression (*saṃskāra*), but not with reference to conjunction and disjunction (*vibhāga*).
For conjunction and disjunction do not arise simultaneously from any single action; rather, first there is disjunction, and from that, the destruction of the prior conjunction.
Immediately after that,
those who know the categories of reality understand the conjunction of the sense organs with their objects;
nor is this [conjunction] possible through logic alone.
This must be stated:
for it was precisely while remaining within the Vaiśeṣika system that this exposition was undertaken;
otherwise, why would one ask, "Does action exist? Does conjunction and so forth exist?"—on account of which such [a question] would be raised?
And for this very reason, he says, "by the wrath of Kṛtānta" [102.17].
Furthermore, what is under discussion is the investigation of an effect that occurs at the same time [as its cause], not one that occurs at a different time; so what need is there for further words?

Even if some clever scholars, while adhering to the Vaiśeṣika system, should attempt to justify this according to their own scriptures, let them do so as they wish—it would not cause us the slightest loss, but rather a great gain.

"Attainment" (*lābha*) means by way of its entirety (*kārtsnyena*), due to its being indivisible (*anavayavatvena*). The meaning is not that all things— whether of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of different classes (*vijātīya*)— should pervade it individually or collectively.
By means of discourse and investigation [103.1],
