[121] he says "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth [103.4], demonstrating that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)— being common to both sides— in the proof of non-difference regarding the non-distinction of place and time, amidst the distinctions of place, time, and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Explaining that there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he says: "Even intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvo 'pi*). The particle *api* is used to indicate acceptance.
Furthermore, the second *api* is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and should be understood as following the word "form-ness" (*rūpatā*).

Regarding the phrase "the nature of persistence and exclusion" (*anuvṛttivyāvṛttirūpatā*): the nature of persistence belongs to substance (*dravya*), and the nature of exclusion belongs to the modes (*paryāya*); these should be applied respectively.
The term "each" (*pratyekam*) should be understood as "with respect to each object" (*prativastu*), and not as "individually" (*pratyātma*).
For it is not the case that substance possesses the nature of exclusion, nor do the modes possess the nature of persistence.

Thus, the meaning is this: if, with respect to each individual thing, only the nature of persistence and exclusion were admitted for substance and mode, then there would be two distinct entities—like a jar and a cloth—characterized by a duality of mutually exclusive natures, rather than a single entity possessing a dual form.
This [conclusion] follows from the reason [stated].

Therefore, because there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because it is established by logic that this applies only to two distinct entities, the meaning is that the non-difference of intrinsic nature is thus proven.
Having accepted that recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) have that as their intrinsic nature, he says this; however, he now demonstrates that this very thing does not exist.

He says: "And not... (na cet), etc. Here, the intended cause for existence (*bhāvatva*) is the state of being the locus of that which persists and that which ceases, which will be clarified immediately below; therefore, because those two [action and agent] cannot possess that nature [of being the locus], how could their having that very nature not be tenable, such that this is said? He says: "By way of being an entity" (*bhāvatvena*), that is, by way of being an action (*kriyātvena*).
Because it depends on that which brings it about (bhavitṛ), that is, because it depends on the agent (kartṛ).
Or rather, whatever dharma possesses origination is a real entity (bhavitṛ) by its very nature; since it depends on that [agent], it is not [real] in terms of its own essence (tattva).
If unity [of the cause] were to follow from its performing a single effect, then multiplicity would likewise follow from its performing multiple effects;

otherwise, that [unity] would be untenable. Since this is neither desired nor logical, the intention is that this argument is also improper to state, as there is no sublation (bādhaka) in the case of the opposite; with this in mind, he says: "Even of one... [103.22].
The intention of one who says "even for a single [thing], many... and so forth should be understood as before.
Regarding "those that have been made and those that have not been made" (kṛtākṛtānām), this refers to those that are designated and those that are not designated.
When it is impossible for a single denotation to denote [all things], the fitness of the universe for that [denotation] is the logical reason (hetu).

Regarding the distinction of objects (*viṣayabheda*)—referring to the distinction between the expressed and the indicated objects of words due to their specific nature—it was just stated in response to one who asserts such a distinction. Furthermore, the intention of the author in stating "even in a single case" should be understood as before.

Having indicated the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) through the aforementioned formulation of speech by means of an ambiguous exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he now demonstrates that the reason "because it is the object of a single cognition" is a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
In order to explain this, he says, "And of many" [104.1].

Anticipating the objection of an opponent—"If one thing is not admitted to have two forms, how then can that single consciousness arise as both the nature of cognition (*bodharūpa*) and the form of blue?"—he says, "But rather...
"By way of having a blue reflection" means by way of having a blue form, in terms of its existence as a real entity (*vastu*).
By this it is shown that it is so described based on a distinction of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), but not because there is an actual duality of forms.
"Because of being coagulated" means because many parts have entered into one another.
And this is the reason for its variegated nature.
Refuting the very example, he says "For he... and so forth.
"He" refers to the one whose nature is the Man-Lion (Narasimha) manifested for the purpose of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Intending to show that the whole (*avayavin*) is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhitatva*), it was stated [at 104.8] that it consists of an aggregation (*saṃhāta*) of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Individually, they do not possess the form of Narasiṃha [as stated at 104.9].
The meaning is that [the example] lacks the substance of a man-lion (narasiṃha) everywhere because of the absence of the cognition [of it as such].
By this very fact of the absence of coalescence (saṃmūrcchita), the variegated nature (śabalarūpa) is not established; thus, it is shown that the example is devoid of the probans (sādhana).

Thus, the application of the term "part" (*bhāga*) is intended in the sense of an accumulation of unstable atoms, and not in the sense of a "constituent" (*avayava*) as established by others, because the commencement of a composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted. Now, let it be granted that a composite whole consisting of man and lion is produced from the parts of man and lion; nevertheless, since its variegated nature (*śabalarūpatva*) is not established, the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhana*). To demonstrate this through observation, he says: "And [it is] a different genus" (*jātyantaraṃ ca*).

For in those various states, because there is a cause for the recurring cognition that "this is that same man," there is the universal of humanity (*naratva-jāti*), which is denoted by the term "vertical generality" (*ūrdhvatā-sāmānya*);
and likewise, in those very states, because there is a cause for the recurring cognition that "this is a lion, a lion," there is the universal of lionhood (*siṃhatva-jāti*) of such a nature;
and distinct from these, in those various states, there exists a universal of such a nature which serves as the cause for the recurring cognition that "this is that same Man-Lion."
A universal (jāti) is to be understood as distinct from another universal.

Furthermore, the grammatical coreferential designation (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the phrase "that [is] it" (sa iti) should be seen as intended either to express the non-difference between the universal and its possessor, or to express them as a composite whole.

Moreover, because the system of the Digambaras is the subject under discussion, it is explained in this way; for they do not accept horizontal universals (tiryaksāmānya), and this will also be clarified later by Bhaṭṭārcaṭa.
Nor is it appropriate to postulate a horizontal universal (*tiryaksāmānya*) here,
because Narasiṃha is a single entity of such a nature, whereas a universal must subsist in multiple instances.
He demonstrates the very absence of a variegated form with the words, "For [the variegated] is indeed manifold," and so forth.

This is his intention: even if one were to set aside its state of being a mere coagulation and describe it as having a variegated form in some way through its manifold nature, nevertheless, because the absence of unity is established by logic, a single [entity] cannot be said to possess a variegated form;
for even so, the absence of unity is established by logic, and thus it cannot belong to a single [thing].
"The state of being variegated" would thus lose its very nature as the subject under discussion.
For one who necessarily desires variegation must also accept diversity (*vaicitrya*), that is, the state of having manifold forms; with this intention, he says: "For diversity... [104.11].
He states this with the underlying thought that diversity is the state of having manifold forms.
If a single variegated form is not tenable, then how does the world conceive that "this is variegated"? Anticipating this objection, he says "merely," and so forth.
Because one perceives a single effect due to its being apprehended by a single cognition, [it is designated as one].
And this is the reason for the single conventional usage;
furthermore, one could also read "by its own nature" (*tvena*).
But as for consciousness (vijñāna), S...
[124] The passage within the brackets has been repeated. [125] The passage within the brackets has been repeated.
Here, indeed, with respect to the real property (*vastvadharma*), there is the real possessor of the property (*vastvadharmin*).

Since the property (*dharma*) has already been rejected as ultimate through prior analysis of what is produced, the substratum (*dharmī*) dependent upon it is also excluded as being real; with this intention, it was stated, "because of the negation of both property and substratum" (*dharmadharmiṇor niṣedhāt*).
To demonstrate the aforementioned collection of points more extensively through his own verses, he says by way of another's voice: "And he said" (*āha ca*).
"Of one thing" (*vastuna ekasya*) is understood from the context.
The word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates the speaker's lack of conviction.
"Of those two" (*tayoḥ*) refers to substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*).
In this regard, first obstructing the notion that a difference in conceptual designation constitutes a difference in the object itself, he says: "Regarding the sense faculty" (*indriye*).
The actual nature of things (*vasturūpa*) is not at all the range or domain (*gocara*) of words.
Since even *apoha* is determined to be a real entity (*vastu*), he specifies it by saying: "that which appears in sensory cognition" (*indriyajñānanirbhāsī*).
By means of the plural number, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, for what reason?
This should be understood as a common worldly expression (*lokokti*);
it is a designation (*saṃjñā*), that is, a conventional term (*sāṃketika-śabda*), because of its differentiation from that.
For this very reason, it has been established in general that [things] are not the objects of words.

Furthermore, by means of negating the capacity of words to have real entities as their domain, the intention of one who establishes that differences in designations do not constitute a difference in the object is as follows:
if, on the contrary, words were in reality to have external objects—just as sensory cognitions do—it would necessarily follow...

"These [sensory faculties], being distinct from one another in form, would differentiate their respective objects—such as visible forms and so forth—just as the cognitions of the eye and other senses do.
He states the reason why things fall within their range with the words beginning "parame... [104.25].

The meaning is to be understood as follows: from the statement beginning with "when there is an intention to express the non-difference between the signifier and the signified," and from the sense established by such statements;
therefore, "having conceptualized objects" means having as their domain forms that have ascended into conceptual construction.
Therefore, if there were a difference based on a difference in names, it should be construed that the difference would belong only to the conceptually constructed.

To the question, "Does a difference in reality not exist when there is a conceptualized difference? he says: "a difference in exclusion" (*vyāvṛttibheda*). Making explicit what was already implied by the sense, he says: "not of the thing" (*na vastunaḥ*).
Now, are singular, dual, and plural merely the grammatical numbers, such that their difference would be called a "difference in number"? (The phrase *saṃkhyābheda* is repeated in the source).
And this is not so;
rather, number itself has forms such as unity and so forth, while the word is merely its designator. For this very reason, Pāṇini [states]: "The plural is used for many" (Pā. 1.4.21).
Thus he spoke.

This might indeed be so, provided that number—which is the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so forth—whether residing in a single substance or multiple substances, were not sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, such a thing simply does not exist.

However, because of conformity with such conventional designations (*saṅketa*), the very expression "one" and so forth is the basis for the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth; with this intention, it was said: "No other distinction of words is intended. [The reading enclosed within brackets has been repeated. Therefore, from that distinction of numbers consisting of a distinction of words, [it refers to] a conceptualized form—that which revolves within conceptual construction—but not to a real entity (*vastu*). This distant [phrase] is to be connected here.
In some way— whether in the form of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāya*) or otherwise—
the term "non-different" (*abhinnate*) refers to the determination (*avasaya*) of difference.
But from what is it established that this numerical difference consists in a difference of verbal expression?
And he says that it is non-differentiating: "of those" (yeṣām).

Here too, the phrase "by the intention to express the non-difference of the signified and the signifier," and so forth, should be understood as being indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ityādi*), since it has already been explained. [127] Distinctness (*vibhinnatā*).
Now, concerning the distinction of characteristics, he says "indestructible" [105.5]. Why? For what reason?
Because they are not of that nature [105.6].
The meaning is: "because of the imposition of contradictory properties.

Alternatively, the phrase "having that as their nature" (*tadātmakāḥ*) is a qualification used as a reason; thus, the sense is: "since they have that as their nature, why—on account of what—would they not perish when the substance does not perish?
By this, it is stated that because these two characteristics are incompatible in a single entity, the distinction between the characteristics is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Anticipating the objection of another who wishes to refute the fault already stated, he says: "They have perished" (naṣṭā).
These are synonyms.
The word "cedi" indicates the opponent's admission;
it is established by implication that this is in the form of a synonym (*paryāya-rūpeṇa*) and not in the form of the substratum (*dharmin-rūpeṇa*).
Refuting this, he says: "as a substance" (*dravya*).
Is there for them a nature other than their substantial nature?
The intention of the questioner is this: if they were to have a different nature, then due to that difference in nature, there would be no non-difference of nature [among them].
For this very reason, this is a question posed by one who desires to refute the Vaiśeṣika.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin), anticipating that the opponent—who perceives this fault—might deny its having another nature, says: "If not" [105.8].
To this, he replies: "Destruction" [105.8].
"In that way" (tathā) means by that manner.
The modes (*paryāya*) have perished in their mode-aspect, but not in their substratum-aspect (*dharmin*); thus, how can there be destruction of the self?
There is, however, a reading in some places as *no cet*.

In that case as well, it means: "if they have not perished in their mode-aspect by way of their substantial nature (*dravyasvabhāva*). And if the modes under discussion are connected with the agenthood [of the action of perishing], [then the argument holds].
Anticipating this objection, the proponent himself says: "Is there another nature for them? (i.e., *kim anyarūpatā teṣām*).
Since their nature as substance (*dravyasvabhāva*) has been stated, the meaning is: "Is there for them a different essential form (*svarūpa*) other than that nature of substance?"
The rest is the same as before.

Why do those without shame not accept that substance (*dravya*) has a form that persists, while the modifications (*paryāya*), which are subject to arising and passing away, possess identity with that substance?
In this regard, it was said concerning the modifications that are subject to passing away:
Now, with reference to Udayin, he says: "In the substance-self" (*dravyātmani*).

The term "modes" (*paryāyāḥ*) is understood by ellipsis, because "substance" (*dravya*) is what has been mentioned right here; therefore, by the word *tat*, there is a reference back to that [substance].

Thus, the meaning of this statement is as follows: even though difference is based on the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), for what reason are those synonyms (*paryāya*) said to have substance (*dravya*) as their essence?
To the question "Why is there indeed the superimposition of contradictory properties?", he says: "Because they arise subsequently while the substance-essence remains. (105.9–105.10)

The meaning is that because the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed [after a root] in the sense of "occurring after" (*paścād-bhāva*), there is simply a non-occurrence [of the effect] when that [cause] is accomplished;
the point is that this constitutes the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmādhyāsa*).

And by these two modes, through the removal of identity, since there is no connection between these [effects], which possess distinct forms, and that [cause], they could not possibly have that as their property (*taddharmatva*).

And then, while gathering other points to be stated right here as demonstrated by the author of the *Prakṛti*, he says: "What has come into being... [105.10]. Regarding that substance (*dravya*), what has come into being (*bhūta*) or been produced (*jāta*)?
The intention is that since substance and its modifications (*paryāya*) are of one essence, when the substance persists, the modifications also persist necessarily;
thus, nothing at all has come into being, because there is nothing existing apart from that [substance].
Anticipating the objection of another who does not understand his intention, he says "in the case of a difference" (*bhede*).
"Differences" (*bhedāḥ*) are synonyms (*paryāyāḥ*), for that which is expressed is a real entity (*bhūtam*) of that very nature. Wishing to refute this, he says "distinct" (*bhinnam*).
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis and should be understood as following the word *bhinnam*.
Regarding *abhede*, it means their identity (*aikātmye*). Regarding *etad*, it refers to the non-destruction of the substance (*dravyāvināśe*).
If it is argued that the modes (*paryāya*) perish in their mode-form but not in their substratum-form (*dharmirūpa*),
and while that [substratum] remains, the form of difference (*bhedarūpa*) becomes "existent" (*bhūta*), [the author] says "thus" (*evam*)—
thereby making explicit what was previously stated by implication— that this [position] is indeed incoherent: "it is both perished and not perished," and likewise [the rest].
[128] Anticipating the question of an onlooker who is unaware of the context— that "one" would thus follow as a logical consequence— the author says, beginning with "in the substance" (*dravye*),
etc. Since, by the reasoning already stated, the distinction between definitions (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is established, therefore (*tasmāt*).
Now, introducing the distinction between effects, he says: "In the effect" (*kārye*).

If there were a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those two due to the difference in their effects, then—such being the case, that is, when there is a difference in intrinsic nature—a difference in intrinsic nature must necessarily be accepted by one who desires [to establish] a difference; otherwise, the difference would not be established.

And since this is so, why is a distinction among effects—which accomplishes nothing—stated for the sake of establishing a distinction? Teaching the opponent this, he says: "Of the very intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvasyaiva*). One might object: "But surely a distinction among effects differentiates an undifferentiated intrinsic nature; thus, it does accomplish something and is indeed worthy of being adduced. So why is it said [otherwise]? Anticipating this, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

For this reason, the difference among effects does not differentiate that very [cause] which—due to the subsequent context—is of an undifferentiated nature arrived at its own cause, and which possesses the nature of arising subsequently;

for that [cause], having arrived through the power of its own causes, remains undifferentiated. This is because the suffix *śatṛ* (in *paścādbhavan*) is prescribed when used with a word denoting a cause (*hetu*), meaning "because of arising subsequently.
For indeed, a cause existing prior [to the effect] might produce a differentiated nature.
The intention is that it does not exist later.
To the question, "Even if it exists later, why is it not a differentiator?
he says: "Because of its intrinsic nature."

Now, one might argue: "Granted that the difference in effects may not alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) produced by its own causes, since alteration is impossible while that nature remains as it is; however, it will surely destroy that very nature. To this he says: "destruction" (*nāśa*). Furthermore, showing that if this difference in effects were to differentiate the intrinsic nature of those two, then this fault would indeed follow, he says: "absolutely" (*ekāntena*).
{p. 347} Those two are entities consisting of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāya*).

It might be argued: "This fault would indeed arise if, after the distinction had been apprehended through its own causes, there were subsequently a distinct nature for that very same thing which previously possessed an undifferentiated nature; for by the power of its own causes, that undifferentiated thing would not be the differentiator of those two, since it remains undifferentiated."
The intrinsic nature would not exist;
however, since there is indeed an undifferentiated intrinsic nature, there is also non-difference between those two. Thus he says, "And that" [105.22];
"that" refers to the undifferentiated intrinsic nature.
Regarding those two—substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)—for what reason?

Why, moreover, would that [oneness] not belong to them? He says: "By means of distinct [things]" (*vibhinnābhyām*); that is, by means of substance and mode which are mutually distinct, there could not be a conceptualized [entity] that is non-distinct, possessing a non-distinct nature.
"Of that," [means] "due to its division," that is, due to its distinction or difference;
for when there is difference, the relationship is one of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
And that [absence] is present here as an object of cognition.
Of those [entities], which are conceived as having a non-different nature consisting of substance and mode—
that third nature also, for the sake of establishing its non-difference, that is, for the sake of establishing the non-difference of the non-distinct nature of substance and mode.
A fourth alternative must be postulated; otherwise, it would follow that the three [moments] would be like iron rods—mere [unconnected] pieces—lacking any relation. This is the intended meaning.

In this way, for the fifth moment and so forth as well, by the phrase "the same situation," there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) which obstructs the determination of the lack of connection between things of distinct natures.
Now, one might ask: "Should the denial of the multiple natures that are observed be made out of fear of an infinite regress? To this he says: "And not... [105.27].
This objection might hold if one were to admit that even a single, undivided nature possesses a distinction from both substance and mode;
however, since there is indeed no such distinction, he says: "But absolute... [105.29].

One should supply the phrase: "If there were an absolute non-difference between the distinct substance and its modes due to their non-distinct nature, then their very distinction would be shattered—that is, dissolved.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of that one... [tadeke...].
Therefore, the meaning is that those two are not distinct from that single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, the passage beginning with "from two distinct [entities]" (*vibhinnābhyām*) may be explained differently:
the distinction of that which is non-different—that is, non-distinct—from the two distinct entities, namely substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*), would follow from its being identical to them.

And this is the intended meaning: if one accepts the identity (*tādātmya*) of substance and mode—which are imagined to have an undivided nature—then either that [identity] must be admitted to enter into them, or they must enter into it.

In that regard, if the imagined nature enters into substance and mode, then those two alone would remain established in their own form, but not that [nature]; how then could that [nature], being non-existent, be related to them?

"Is it not the case that this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while inhering in those two, does not experience their non-difference? Rather, for the sake of establishing their non-difference, is another distinct intrinsic nature not admitted? Anticipating this statement from the opponent’s intention, [the author] says "of those" (*teṣām*). Here too, setting aside further faults, he says "in that way" (*tathā*) while demonstrating an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Now, regarding the entry of substance and mode into that non-different nature, he says: "But [if it were] absolute," and so forth.
[Objection: Surely there is no non-difference between those two because they possess a non-different nature, such that this could be said.

But he says "of non-difference" (abhedasya) [106.1] to show that non-difference exists by its own nature. This refers to the acceptance (*aparityāge*)—that is, the acknowledgment—of the identity of substance and mode which is established by its own inherent force;
provided that this difference (*tasya bhedasya*) possesses an unfailing existence—that is, is real (*avitathābhāve satyatve*).
Since non-difference is what is to be established, it follows by implication that the statement establishing it must have a false object.
But why should difference and non-difference not be of a single nature? To this he says: "mutually... [106.3].

Since things whose nature consists in mutual non-existence are established through mutual exclusion, the existence of one is a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) while the non-existence of the other is a negation (*niṣedha*). Because that [negation] is the cause [of the former], there is no dual nature in terms of difference and non-difference.
If the superimposition of contradictory properties were the basis for establishing difference, [then this would not be the case].
It might be argued that difference and non-difference cannot coexist in a single locus;
however, fearing that this very [entity] would not serve as the basis for the determination of difference, he says: "and they consist of mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāvarūpāś ca).
By "contradiction" (virodha), the superimposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa) is intended.
By the word "distinction" (bheda), the establishment of distinction is intended;
and by the word "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa), the cause [of that distinction] is meant.
Therefore, the meaning is this: if the superimposition of contradictory properties is not accepted as a factor for the establishment of distinction, [then...]
In that case, it would not be so;
and how could it be so? And why should it not be accepted as such?

Even though they possess that very nature, they would not be distinct [if they were not]; for distinctions would have to exist because contradiction is a necessary factor for the establishment of distinction.
If it were destroyed by some other manner— that is, if the mode (*paryāya*) were destroyed—
how could the substance (*dravya*) be subject to destruction?
For it is the substance that perishes through the form of its modes.
But it is not accepted by those devoid of shame that [the entity] exists in the form of a substance;
why then is its destruction not also accepted in that same form?
The meaning is: why is its destruction not accepted in every respect whatsoever?
In response to the inquiry as to how a substance (*dravya*) is to be sought, he says "deceit" (*kūṭa*) while instructing;
"permanence" (*nityatā*) means stability (*sthiratā*). "Not firm" (*na dhruva*)...
Because the suffix -tva is prescribed by this [sūtra],

"va," the state of remaining in a form that has neither fallen away nor arisen, and which lacks prior or subsequent states, is "immutable permanence" (kūṭasthanityatā) among the various distinct modes (paryāya).
It has been indicated by implication as to why the permanence of transformation is accepted regarding substances.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, let there be the permanence of the immutable," he says: "If that [immutable permanence] were accepted" (tad-iṣṭau).
This means: if that immutable permanence were accepted.
Setting aside another fault here, he says this: "Why not? (kinne).

Just as a single universal, such as "gold-ness," is accepted as following through all successive stages, why—why is it not accepted—that there is a single [universal], such as "gold-ness" or "cow-ness," which follows all individuals across different locations and so forth?
Thinking, "We desire this as well," he says, "O Mother" (*jananī*).
*Jananī* means mother;
*prathamamaḍhā* means wife or spouse.

Now, if this is stated with the intention of referring to the universal of "womanhood" (*strītvasāmānya*), then acceptance itself is the answer; what kind of improper objection (*anupayoga*) is this? Furthermore, being a wife (*bhāryātva*) is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and not a universal. Otherwise, even for one who does not know the linguistic convention, those women—just like cows—would be intended as wives, and they would produce cognitions appearing as universals through that form.
"And this is not the case;
therefore, this is incorrect.
You have spoken well; however, the intention of the one who said this was simply not correctly understood.

This is indeed his intention: that femininity, existing in this wife by means of some form delimited by the [physical] substrate, does not make her a fit object for such enjoyment even without the self, since it must likewise exist in the mother due to the absence of any other form.
If this were the case, then that [universal] too would necessarily be of such a nature (i.e., multiple);
likewise, by this same logic of mutual dependence, it is unavoidable that the individual wife being spoken of here would also be of such a nature.
If this is so, why is unity not also attributed to Śābaleya, Bāhuleya, and others, on the grounds of their connection with a single universal such as "cowness"?
"Dear one acted kindly toward dear one"—this has been stated merely as an illustration by way of a joke; thus, everything is clear.

Having thus demonstrated that it is not logical for difference and non-difference to reside in a single substratum simultaneously, [the author] now considers whether they might indeed exist in such a manner.
Nevertheless, demonstrating that there is no liberation due to the aforementioned faults, he says: "And the faults mentioned regarding difference and non-difference.
For if substance and mode were absolutely distinct, they would be two separate things;
they would not be a single entity possessing a dual nature.

Likewise, in the case of the two states of gold and the earring, since they would not possess the nature of one another, there would follow the fault that the specific forms of the earring and the gold would fail to appear [in each other], and so forth.
Furthermore, on the position of non-difference, the previously stated capacity of a single entity to perform multiple functions would result in an unimpeded contradiction;
and the twofold nature accepted as consisting of substance and mode would be lost—such are the faults.
And since this is the case, it has been shown by implication that the admission of difference for a single entity is fruitless.
If both difference and non-difference were accepted, how could those faults not arise?
He says: "Those faults apply individually," meaning they do not arise in the aggregate because they arise in each individual part. Thus he says: "individually, those faults."
But is it not observed that faults which arise individually do not occur when they are in a state of combination? With this intention, the opponent says, "And molasses... [106.13].
Pure molasses is a cause of phlegm (*śleṣman*), while ginger (*nāgara*, *śuṇṭhī*) alone is a cause of bile (*pitta*).
However, why do those two faults not occur when these two are mixed? This is to be understood from the context, or an ellipsis must be supplied.
Regarding this, he states the underlying principle: "That has its root in that" (*tanmūlam*).

Due to the causal condition consisting in mutual proximity and reliance, and with that [proximity] as its material cause and cooperative condition, there arises something entirely different from the mere sugar-candy acting as the effect, and distinct from the mere ginger;
this is another substance called "sugar-candy-and-ginger" (*guḍanāgara*) which performs a specific purposeful action.
But it is not that this very same thing is both molasses and ginger; these two are two distinct substances.
That which is their source is the cause of that "molasses-and-ginger" [compound].

By this he means: this has arisen as a different substance that performs a specific causal function, such as removing phlegm, and therefore my fault—which applies to each individual component—does not apply here.
But for you, since both difference and non-difference—characterized as substance and mode—are precisely those two [concepts] combined, how could the faults that apply to both not arise?

Now, even if this were a distinct substance, one might still ask: "How is it that, despite being sweet and bitter, it does not produce phlegm and bile? Anticipating and refuting such an objection from a bystander, he says: "It is sweet..."
It is not conceivable that everything sweet is a cause of phlegm;
"it might be" is a phrase expressing possibility,
or it has the sense of capability.
But by what illustration is it improper to consider everything as being sweet? To this he says: "Just as... [106.15]. Because it is indeed a cause for phlegm (*kapha*), it is sweet (*madhura*).
This is the intended meaning.
By this, the reason "because of its sweetness" is shown to be a common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) one.
The words "all," "sharp," or "pungent" should be supplied as well as "not" and "it might be."
The illustration is to be explained as before. The intention regarding the Magadhan long pepper (*pippalī*) is that it lacks cold potency (*śītavīrya*).
By this, too, the intended meaning is to demonstrate that the reason "because of its pungency" (*kaṭukatvāt*) is a common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) one.

This substance called *guḍanāgara* possesses a sweetness entirely different from that of [ordinary] sugar, just as its pungency is entirely different from that of long pepper (*pippalī*). Therefore, when these two are combined, the occurrence of the two respective defects does not arise.

Furthermore, if this [objection] is refuted by demonstrating the absence of the defects inherent in each individual component within the state of their combination—as in the case of *guḍanāgara* and the like—then [the argument stands].

Then, in order to show that our own position is not undermined because one observes the existence [of those faults] even in their collective state despite their being individually produced, he begins with the words "individually" (*pratyekam*) and so forth.

Alternatively, he says "individually" in order to demonstrate the inconclusiveness (*sādhāraṇānaikāntikatva*) of the reason "because they are individually produced," which is intended to prove the non-existence of those faults in their collective state.

If that which is the cause, the basis, and the motive for a particular effect is, by its own nature, produced as a substratum that is inherently devoid of any other [causes], then why is it observed there to produce that effect?
By the use of the interrogative *kim* in the sense of censure, the meaning is: "Is it indeed observed [to do so]?"

For oiliness is observed to be the cause of phlegm (*kapha*), and heat is observed to produce bile (*pitta*); yet even when these two coexist, they are seen to perform their respective functions, as in the case of black gram (*māṣa*).
For this very reason, he cites "as in the case of black gram" [106.18].
Since black gram possesses both oiliness and a hot potency, it is of a dual nature and produces both effects characterized by phlegm and bile.

"Now, why is it that phlegm (*śleṣman*)—which is itself sweet—is not produced even from a sweet taste? And why is it that bile (*pitta*) is not produced from pungent long pepper (*pippalī*), such that what has been stated by us is contradicted by you? Furthermore, one might suspect the opponent's view that these two defects would not occur in the case of jaggery-food (*guḍānna*) and ginger (*nāgara*), even though they lack [those respective tastes]. Anticipating this, he says 'and depending on the capacity' (*śaktyapekṣañ ca*) in order to demonstrate the manner in which the observed fact is logically established."
Since that effect must arise from it, it depends upon the power of its own material cause; thus, it is "dependent on power" (*śaktyapekṣam*).
To the question, "Is that effect not based solely on qualities such as sweetness? he replies with the word "qualities" (*guṇa*), effectively accepting that very point.

That which has as its basis merely the quality (*guṇa*)—such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth—which is unconditioned by specific modes of conduct (*ācāra-viśeṣa*) and is purely a quality, is described as such; that is, it has no cause for it.
Even if an effect depends upon a capacity (*śakti*), since that capacity exists everywhere, the fault remains the same; thus he says "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).
Among those capacities, only a certain effect belongs to a certain [capacity] by way of being produced.

This point is as follows: although there is no difference in their sweetness, only certain things produce such an effect because they possess a specific nature arising from their own causes; not everything does so.

If it is asked, "From where does that cause derive its nature of producing that [effect]?"—the answer is that for its own cause, it likewise possesses that nature; thus, this is simply not subject to further questioning.
This is what is meant: for the fault of absolute distinctness and so forth, which would follow from mere difference, does not depend upon a specific capacity of difference;
nor can such a specific quality of difference even possibly exist in a state of conjunction, because it remains of that very same nature.
In this way, the fault of non-difference is also to be understood.
Therefore, just as an effect that is based solely on a quality occurs when that quality exists,
so too, how could those faults which are possible merely through difference and non-difference not occur when that [quality] is present?
Having accepted that these defects possess the nature of arising through both difference and non-difference, all this has been stated;

however, now, in order to demonstrate that their inevitability follows precisely from identity (*tādātmya*), the author—accepting that the production of defects in cases such as *guḍanāgara* (sugar and ginger) cannot otherwise be explained despite the opponent’s use of it as an example—says: "Because of the contradiction" (*virodhī*).
Of a contradictory thing such as a conch-shell and so forth;
"proximity" refers to that from which there is the birth of a defect whose origin is from that [proximity] which is devoid of the contradictory; it would not even exist.
Its nature consists of both difference and non-difference.
However, that fault does not cease even though it is undesirable in that case, whether there be difference or non-difference that has become its very nature;
the point is that this would entail the consequence of it not having that as its intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāvatva*).
Herein, the true reality of the matter is this: for a form that is being differentiated is "difference," and conversely, that which is the opposite is "non-difference."
And by the statement "those two would be distinct," etc., the fault is shown to consist essentially in that very nature [of difference];
likewise, even the performance of multiple effects is in reality of a non-different nature;
and any other refutation as well is in reality of the nature of both difference and non-difference.
"But if the distinction were one produced by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), let it be so; there is no damage to the subject at hand by that much.

This was stated in that [previous] view having accepted the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) in its different states; now, however, in order to show that that very [whole] does not exist, he says: "And the parts alone" (*bhāgā eva*).
That is to say, those very things intended as parts.
In ultimate reality, however, the meaning is that they are merely atoms (*paramāṇu*).
They are situated—that is, established—in various ways, characterized by their horizontal and vertical positions, and by their capacity for specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
That which possesses these is "possessing parts" (*bhāgavat*).
"Indivisible" means partless by its own nature;
by this, the non-perception of the object of vision is shown.
And the intended meaning is that, because of the absence of that [object], with what could there be any consideration of their difference or non-difference?

Now, one might ask: "If there is no single whole (*avayavin*), how can holding and pulling be possible? To this he says: "Mutually" (*anyonya*). These parts, because they depend on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), exist in dependence upon mutual causes; thus, while their forms remain situated in that way, when one is pulled or held, the same occurs for the others as well.
Showing that their existence in such a state is due not only to the power of visible causes but also to the force of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), he says: "And of the karmas" (*karmaṇāṃ ca*).
By the efficacy even of the karmas consisting of the unique volitions (*cetanā*) of worldly beings, they exist inseparably; that is, they do not exist with mutual distinction.
Anticipating the objection that it is improper to describe the efficacy of karma when it is not the direct cause, he says: "In the arrangement" (*sanniveśane*).
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because.
Since it is stated [in the Abhidharmakośa, 4.1], "The variety of the world is born of karma," he says that [beings] are produced by karmas.
By means of the common and uncommon karmas of those very sentient beings— meaning,
precisely because of the predominance of those karmas over them—
they are "non-participants," that is, they do not exist through partition.
Now, raising the objection as to how designations such as "this is one jar" could occur if there were no single composite whole (*avayavin*), he says: "And those [parts]" (*te ca*).
Those parts [are so designated] by some manner, such as their performing a single function.
But surely, when the word "one jar" arises, or in a cognition permeated by that word, something indeed appears as a unity.
And since that very particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is determined as being a particular characteristic, how can there be a denial of the non-different object? To this he says: "And not...
(*na ca*). Knowledge having the particular characteristic as its objective support is "knowledge of the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇajñāna*); [the negation applies] to that.

This is the intended meaning: if the object within the domain of words were a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it would appear in that very same way even in a cognition produced by the sense faculties.
But this is not the case, because there is an appearance of exclusion from both similar and dissimilar things.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single form to appear in different aspects despite a difference in the means [of apprehension]. Thus it has been said:
“From where does the form of a single thing appear as having diverse aspects? (Pramāṇavārttika 2.235).
If that is so, then let there be at least something single that is the object of verbal cognition;
thus, the non-existence of the one is not established in every respect. To this, he says: “Because it is indistinct,” etc.
Those very parts are thus perceived as having an indistinct form through the mere exclusion of heterogeneous elements.
This is the meaning: even in that cognition, those very parts are perceived without their internal distinctions being discerned, but there is not even a single thing over and above them.
And it should be understood that "they themselves" is stated in accordance with conventional determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Since that which is perceived as partless (*nirbhāga*)—beyond its constituent parts—is not apprehended, it falls within the scope of the conventional usage of non-existence;
therefore, from that [reason], [it follows that] those parts, which are expressible by synonymous terms.

[129] Furthermore, taking these [points] as indivisible (*nirbhāga*), he states another refutation according to the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*). Having first formed the compound *bhinna-doṣa-aṃśa* (that which has distinct faults and is a part), one should subsequently form a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *aneka*.

"Connection with that" (tadyogitā) means pervasion by that. This is the intended meaning: if that were composed of parts, then by one part it would pervade one distinct spatial portion, and by another part it would pervade another.
But a partless reality cannot possibly act in such a manner.
Now, it is indeed perceived that a single entity possesses parts located in multiple distinct places; regarding this, one need not inquire "what" or "how" this is by means of further deliberation.
And so it has been said:
[130] Of that which is without differentiation, [131] “That must be accepted exactly as it is perceived,” [131] as stated in the *Ślokavārttika*, Anumāna 186.

Anticipating the statement of another who holds such an intention, he says, "If [it is argued that it is known] through cognition" (*pratīteś cet*). Although the refutation has already been stated here—namely, that "it does not appear as a single entity in either non-conceptual or conceptual cognition," and so forth—he nevertheless sets that aside and states another refutation: "In destruction" (*dhvaṃse*).

[132] Regarding the phrase *kṣaṇadhvaṃsānu-...*: those synonyms which are perceived as possessing stability (*sthemāna*) or steadfastness (*sthairya*), because of their constant connection with the word "that" (*yat-tat*), how is it that they are considered to be characterized by momentary destruction (*kṣaṇadhvaṃsānubhāvinaḥ*)? From what [reason] are they so regarded?
Thus the construction should be understood.

By this he says the following: if you take cognition as your refuge, then how can things that are perceived in one way be followed [in practice] in another? Anticipating the opponent's reply, he says: "from another" (*anyataḥ*).
This is to be connected with the phrase "it is their opinion" (*tanmatā*), meaning "from another subverting means of valid cognition" (*bādhakāt pramāṇāt*).
In this context, that subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is "equal" (*sama*), meaning it is equivalent even here because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Even though subverting factors such as the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) have already been mentioned, he says "the two are certain" (*aikāntikau*) while showing yet another subverting factor:
because they are not other, that is, because they possess a single nature (*ekātmakatva*).
By way of their mutual interpenetration, these two would necessarily be either exclusively different or exclusively non-different;
this is certain (*dhruvam*), that is, established.
Now, even if they were of one essence (*ekātmye*), it would be only the modes (*paryāyāḥ*) that differ, not the substratum (*dharmin*).
And lest one should suspect that [the two] are not distinct, but rather [merely] synonyms, he says: "mutually" (*anyonyam*).
The intention is that because there exists the superimposition of contradictory properties—which subverts unity—distinction itself is certain and necessarily follows.
Anticipating the opponent’s argument that "even if they are non-different, this fault does not arise because their forms are distinct," he says: "of those two also" (*tayor api*).
The word "api" (also/even) is displaced; it should be understood as following the word "bheda" (difference).
Its meaning is that there is not only non-difference.
Regarding this, he says: "by which [it is known] by itself," and so forth.
Refuting even the non-difference indicated by the word "api," he says "[in the substance]" (dravye).
By "svabhāva," what is intended is "non-distinct svabhāva.
"Yannimittā" means that which has as its cause a non-distinct form.
To explain how it does not exist, he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

Therefore, from that single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if there were no distinction—that is, if they were to enter into the same intrinsic nature—there would be a loss of their own identity (*svātmahāni*); both the substantial form (*dravyarūpatā*) and the modal form (*paryāyarūpatā*) would be lost.

The meaning is "like that itself. By the word "of that" (*tasya*), the non-different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is referred to; by "from those two," the substance (*dravya*) and the mode (*paryāya*) are meant.
By the phrase beginning with "the substratum" (*dharmī*), he expresses the very plurality (*bahutva*) stated by the pronoun "those" (*te*).

If one postulates another, non-different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for those three— consisting of the two modes and that which is other than them— in order to establish their non-difference, then the same fault applies there as well. Furthermore, if one were to postulate yet another intrinsic nature,
there would be the aforementioned consequence, namely the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Citing another fault in this very context, he says: "The state of being a substratum (*dharmitva*).
To the question "How could this be so?", he replies: "Because of its dependence on that (*tattantratvāt*). This means: because of its dependence upon that [substratum].
In response to the inquiry as to why the body is dependent upon that [the self], he says: "Of the other two" (tad anyayoḥ).
Therefore, because difference and non-difference between substance and mode—which are distinct from that single nature—are rooted in it, their dependence upon it is to be understood.
Let it be, then, that it is such, and that the entity possesses a manifold nature.
And one cannot deny what is perceived on the grounds of infinite regress; thus he says, "nor is it so" (na caivam).
The word "ca" (and) means "because," [implying] that it is not understood in this way by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Concluding the section, he says, "therefore" (tena).
By this aforementioned collection of reasons, this doctrine of non-ascertainment (anaikāntavāda) is a fabrication of a fool, a fabrication of one who has set out upon a wrong path;
thus [the word] "iti" indicates the reason. "Enough with much talk" means there is nothing more to be said, because everything is fully established by this much alone—this is the intended meaning.
Since *avaśyam* means "the state of being necessary" (*āvaśyaka*) because it ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), one would expect the form to be *apṛthakkaraṇasyāvaśyakam*.
As for this usage—*yad idam āvaśyakam apṛthakkaraṇam*—which expresses a coreferential relationship (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), I do not know how it is justified; one must ask the great masters themselves.

Regarding conjunctions and disjunctions that are to be produced, the term "independent" (*anapekṣa*) means it is not a cause; this is intended with reference to the category of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and thus what is meant is merely that such a thing is not a cause.

It does not mean that because of the negation of a specific [quality], that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) possesses causality. Furthermore, by its lack of qualities (*aguṇatva*), it is distinguished from substance (*dravya*) and action (*karman*).
And by virtue of possessing generality (*sāmānyavat*), [the universal] is the cause of the particular universals (*sāmānyaviśe�șa*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
However, with respect to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*), what is intended is that it is not an independent cause, but rather a cause only when dependent [on other factors].
This state of dependence is not to be understood as dependence upon that which occurs at the final moment.
However, no entity whatsoever exists that is a cause while being entirely independent [of others], such that the statement "that which is independent is not a cause" would be appropriate.
Rather, the exclusion of a substance from being a quality should be understood by virtue of its temporal priority;

for example, the quality characterized as the conjunction of threads and a shuttle requires the cloth—which is posterior—to be produced when the conjunction of the cloth and the shuttle is to be brought about.

And just as, in the case of a bamboo stalk being split, a disjunction from another part is produced by the action of a constituent part, which—depending upon the subsequent destruction of the substance—produces a further disjunction of that active part from a location such as space; and just as this [latter] disjunction is not born of action but is indeed born of disjunction, as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas who accept "disjunction-born disjunction"—so too, because it is not the subject at hand here, it is not discussed.
However, by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "possessing qualities" (*guṇavat*), the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) is included.
By the word *codya* [108.28], a challenge (*codya*) formulated by a Buddhist should be understood according to the context; the analysis of the compound is "the refutation (*parihāra*) of that.
"This is ours" means "belonging to us" (*āsmākīna*).
The suffix *khañ* should be applied by the rule “*[yuṣmad-asmadbhyām anyatarasyām khañ]*”;
it is like the previously mentioned method of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*). The connection is that he explains [the point] by means of the mention of “insistence” (*nirbandha*).
The Pāṇinian sūtra (4.3.1), however, is different:
"those whose nature is to act together" (*sahakaraṇaśīlāḥ*) means "those whose nature is to act as one" (*ekakaraṇaśīlāḥ*).
Other conditions (*pratyaya*) that awaken latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as taste (*rasa*) and so forth, should be stated as appropriate.
"Dependent upon that" means dependent on that such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
"Of the other" refers to the non-conceptual [cognition] which has taste and so forth as its object.
"By way of being its material cause" (*tadupādeyatvena*) means by way of being the material cause characterized by consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Now, one might object: "Surely this single [result] produced from a collection of causes such as mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth has been shown; why has that which is produced from a single cause having entered into the midst of that causal complex not been shown? To this he says: "Other than that" (*tadanyat*). This should be understood as "produced from a single [cause]" meaning produced from a single cause independent of the other factors included within that causal complex.
However, nothing whatsoever exists that is produced by a single cause alone.
In this regard, there is the conceptual construction of mental fantasies and the like, which is produced by mental attention (*manaskāra*) independent of the eye and other [senses];
and there is the cognition of a double moon and the like, which is produced by a dyad consisting of the eye and mental attention, independent of the object and so forth.

This can be inferred from the very statement beginning with, "We perceive visual consciousness from the immediately preceding condition, which is consciousness," etc.; it is with this intention that he says, "it should be inferred by oneself" [111.13].
Now, one might ask: is there a specific function in each part such that there is a designation using the plural number? To this he replies: "and in relation to those produced from it" [111.17].
Because another causal complex possesses a different intrinsic nature, it produces a distinct effect;
this should be inferred by oneself in comparison with that which is not produced by it.
In response to the inquiry, "From what does that [matter] possess a difference in intrinsic nature? the passage beginning with "another effect" (*kāryāntara*) and so forth should be applied.

The term *upādāyarūpa* (derived matter) means that it exists depending upon earth and the other elements; it is a compound formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* class, meaning "mutually dependent" (*parasparādi*). Furthermore, by the opponent who was intent on speaking in reliance upon scripture (*āgama*), the very language of scripture has been restated.
Therefore, that which abides in its own nature is the basis of abiding; thus, it is the "basis for the abiding in its own nature.
For there must necessarily be something that acts as an obstacle to that which produces [change].
With the intention that [the substratum] is another entity denoted by the word "something else," he says: "in the production of another intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvāntarotpādane*) up to [line 112.19].
Now, one might object: "An *ādhāra* (substratum) is a benefactor (*upakāraka*), not a generator (*janaka*); so how can it be stated thus? To this he replies: "for not... (*na hi*) [line 112.27].
[The term] "of the elements" (*bhūtānām*) refers to earth (*pṛthivī*) and the others.
"It is said" (ucyate) should be understood as "it is stated according to the Vaibhāṣika school";
however, in the Sautrāntika system, there is no distinction between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative elements (*bhautika*).
"By delaying" (*kālakṣepeṇa*) means by a protraction of time.
"Coexisting with that" (tatsahabhāvini) is to be understood as "co-occurring with that which is to be benefited" (anugrāhyasahacāriṇi),
because it arises immediately after that,
due to the production of that specific excellence (viśeṣa).
Regarding that [entity] for which a specific modification is being produced:
how is it made known that its auxiliary cause is ineffective in that regard? He says: "by removing the obstruction to its capacity.
The particle *vai* is used here in the sense of "not indeed" (*na vai*), and by explaining it thus, he shows that the word *vai* functions as a restrictive particle.
It should be understood that this occurs when the possibility [of the probans being a reason] is established by the force of logic (*nyāya*).
For this very reason, he clarifies this with the word "logic" (*nyāya*).
By this, the author of the *Vārttika* has shown that in the term "cooperative cause" (*sahakārī*), the word "together" (*saha*) has the same meaning as "logic."
If it is asked, "How then does he explain the phrase 'acting together simultaneously'?"—
it has already been stated previously, so it is not repeated here.
"Of such a kind" means one who performs a single purposeful action.
The term *grahaṇam* (taking/mentioning) refers to that which is diminished by the intention toward an effect, characterized by moments such as coldness acting in conjunction with fire and so forth.
The word *yāvatā*, which is a particle resembling a form ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), follows in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*), or rather, in this particular sense.
"Accompanied by another" means conjoined with something else, persisting for only a moment—that is, remaining for only a moment.

Prior to that state, before it; and after, at a later time—separately, in a state devoid of that [conjunction], there is existence (*bhāva*), that is, being present (*sadbhāva*). Separateness (*pṛthaktva*).

Now, if production occurs from a cause that is already capable, then why was it just stated that "they are capable by their very nature" (svabhāvataḥ)? To this he replies: "according to the opinion of others" (paramate). [The word] *bhāva* means that from which the effect arises; thus, it refers to the cause. If it is asked, "Why did you not explain even that?"—[the answer follows].
No, for that would entail the contradiction of asking from what the capacity itself has arisen.

Furthermore, the statement "they maintain that the capacity arises from auxiliary causes" is made by resorting to the Mīmāṃsaka position; the Naiyāyikas do not accept this, such that it could be reconciled even by adopting their view, since they maintain that capacity consists precisely in the completeness of the auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-sākalya*).
And thus says the Jalpamahodadhi: "The completeness of auxiliary factors is the capacity of that which possesses them; their deficiency, however, is incapacity.
[137] He maintains that "capable" means powerful in the production of the intended effect.
I do not know how the formation of the word *āvaśyakajanana* was previously established.

It should be understood that its necessary productivity (*avaśyañjanakatvam*) was established by the passage beginning with "the state of being necessarily so" (*avaśyamo bhāvaḥ*) and ending with "I do not know" (*na jāne*), on page 354, line 8.
It appears that the reading conveying this meaning is missing here.

One should form a *dvandva* compound by combining "the granary," "the effort of the person who removes it," "the bringing to the field," "the scattering," and—by virtue of the context—"the scattering in the field"; subsequently, a *bahuvrīhi* compound should be formed with the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

The word *prakiraṇam* is an *auṇādika* derivative; it should not be regarded as ending in the suffix *lyuṭ* derived from the root *kṛ*. For if that were the case, since the guna substitution would not be prohibited, the form would result in *prakaraṇam*, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of its being grammatically incorrect (*asādhu*). “Having come together” (*sametya*) means having stood in a suitable location, having assembled—that is, having joined with the first [element]—together with the conditions (*pratyaya*) in the form of cooperative and material causes. Now, one might object: “Since the validity of recognition has already been refuted by the passage beginning with ‘Therefore, in those two states...’, why is this not a mere repetition?”
Thus he says: "And previously" (pūrvañ ca).
This too is the refutation of the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding objects of similarity;
it has already been stated, and its implication has already been demonstrated.

If so, for what purpose has it been stated again? He says: "But for the sake of detailed exposition" (*vipañcanārtham*). The word "but" (*tu*) shows the distinction of this explanation from the previous one. Regarding "internal" (*ādhyātmikeṣu*), that is, internal [factors];
he uses the word "first" (*tāvat*) in the sequence because it must subsequently be shown to apply to external factors as well.

"Capable of being delimited" (*śakyapariccheda*) means capable of being determined by way of its specific causal efficiency. From the perspective of a cause that is a condition (*pratyaya*) producing a cognition directly, without mediation—
when there is the production of that [cognition], or when there is the apprehension of mediation, that is, the acceptance of mediation and so forth.
To explain how it is not otherwise, he says "from something else" (*anyādṛśāt*).
For if it were to arise from something else, since it would be possible to designate even a cause that is of a different nature as a "cause," he specifies it as the "cause of production.

To explain how it is its cause, he says "that" (*tat*); [it arises] through those cooperative factors—the sense organs and so forth—which serve as the basis for mutual approach and other such conditions.
And it is capable of producing that consciousness in its own subsequent moment;

thus, because it initiates [consciousness] in that way, this demonstrates the causality of the complex consisting of the sense organs and so forth—which are specific supporting conditions such as mutual proximity—as the direct cause of consciousness.
This will be clarified immediately hereafter.
This should be understood as stated with reference to a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that possesses the capacity for projection.
How is it that change is impossible? To this he says: "mutually," etc.
Those causes which are capable of producing consciousness, and those [factors] such as the sense faculties—by means of their respective material bases (*upādāna*).
From that, there is the production of the sense faculties and so forth, which are capable causes;
this should be understood as a clarification of what was just mentioned. [140] *S* is missing here.

By explaining [the phrase] "because he was raised in comfort," the author shows that the term *sukhaidhita* ("raised in comfort")—which refers to the cause of a lack of application—is also, by implication, a qualification serving as the reason for the term *krīḍanaśīla* ("habitually playful"). Now, one might raise the objection: "The word *kṛta* means 'accomplished' or 'produced. What, then, has been accomplished by the Teacher here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is *kṛta*... [119.14].

Furthermore, it should be understood that by speaking in this manner, the absence of redundancy is demonstrated; for since this point has been stated more than once, it is appropriate— and indeed natural— to indicate "it is done, it is done," because if one were to have it repeated after it has already been refuted once, there would be a possibility of contempt and an occasion for derision, and because [the point] is already well-established.

Now, one might ask: what is the opponent doing that the proponent of the prima facie case (pūrvapakṣavādī) employs him again, such that it is said that "the proponent of the prima facie case causes him to act"? To this he replies with the words beginning "again" (*punar*).
"Thoroughly examined" (*nirloṭhita*) means investigated or determined.
As before, according to the intention of the Mīmāṃsakas, he explains that capacity (*sāmarthya*) arises from auxiliary factors (*sahakāribhyaḥ*).
The production of capacity (*sāmarthya*) and the non-production of that which possesses it [the entity].

Now, in order to lead the opponent to accept the invalidity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) by means of another method as well, [the author], preparing the ground, says: "Of that which is indeed fixed" (*vyavasthitasyaiva*).

And this is the intended meaning here: let there be the conceptualization of the production of capacity and so forth, insofar as one observes specific changes such as swelling or swelling further in the case of seeds and the like; however, it is not so in this case, because such [changes] are not observed.
"Of that which remains established without undergoing change" means its capacity,
namely the capacity for producing consciousness and so forth.
"For whom the distinction does not appear" refers to such a person.

Even if this distinction is not apprehended through direct perception, he says "from consciousness, etc. to show that the arising of its capacity, which is its very nature, is inferred from this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is certain that a capacity which was previously non-existent arises when the eye and other factors are present, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-arising [of effects], and because there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous production of successive effects such as consciousness.
"And that [cognition] is successive; this is the certainty.
"If it is so," says the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin).
"Unmodified" means having a single, uniform nature.
That which perceives the stone and so forth as distinct from—that is, devoid of—the aspect (ākāra) which is the manifestation of the capacity for the unprecedented (apūrva-sāmarthya);
for this very reason, it should also be understood as "unchanging. Alternatively, the word "or" (vā) is intended to indicate the impossibility [of the aforementioned].

"If it is accepted in this way, what is the harm? To this he says: "In that manner" (*tathā*), meaning "just like that. Regarding "capacity" (*sāmarthya*), it should be understood as adventitious capacity.
For capacity is of two kinds: inherent and adventitious.
Furthermore, a specific individual capacity (*prātisvikī śakti*) must necessarily be admitted;
otherwise, what answer could be given to the objection: "Why does even a fragment of stone not produce a sprout when in proximity to earth and other factors, just as a seed does?"—such is their view.

[Objection: But surely capacity (*sāmarthya*), characterized as an excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*), is something entirely different from those [factors]; so how can it be said that [the capacity] "is characterized by the proximity (*sānnidhya*) of the auxiliary conditions"? [Response: He says, "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
This is because no proximity characterized as nearness (*pratyāsatti-lakṣaṇa*) other than those [factors] already present is possible.

One should also understand that the phrase "characterized by the auxiliary conditions" (*sahakāri-pratyaya-lakṣaṇasya*) was stated by omitting the word "proximity" (*sānnidhya*), and that the expression "those very [factors]" (*te eva*) and so forth should likewise be understood in this sense.
Therefore, from the phrase "precisely because of this admission" (*ata evābhyupagamāt*), it should be understood as "because of the admitted [position]" (*upāgatābhyupagamāt*).
In the same way, by one who desires [this], it must be connected with the words "momentariness alone" (*kṣaṇikatvaiva*). For that very reason, S...
[142] For one who desires [the doctrine of] momentariness alone, this is the explanation of the word "since" (*yasmāt*): [143] because of this... [121.21] etc.
This is the view regarding the word "this" (*idam*) as being "of this" (*caitad*).
It is said that it is "made superior" (*uttarīkṛtam*) because it makes that which is unsurpassed itself superior.

Having raised the objection—"O, how great is the power of one who enjoins in such a way! What incapacity could you possibly have?"—he says "yadi nāma" and so forth in order to introduce the response. He states "na cātra" and so on to bring about the resolution.
"And here there is no intolerance on my part" [121.25], but rather "this thought of ours torments the mind" [122.3]; such is the connection.

Regarding the phrase "na cātra me," according to the view that it forms a single sentence with the words of the commentator, the term "asmākam" (of us) is used; for according to Pāṇini 1.2.59, "asmado dvayoś ca," the word *asmad* may take either the singular or plural number when referring to two.
By this [statement], it should be understood that the plural number is used for a single referent.
Thus, even though he speaks incoherently and is unworthy of honor, the expression of worship should be seen as intended for the conclusion [of the discourse].
"The manifestation of wretchedness" means, by implication, the disclosure of one's own misery to the person being addressed.
The word "hantaḥ" is used here in the sense of addressing someone who is inferior;
that is to say, because it possesses the property of being unwholesome (*apraśasta-dharmaka*).
That whose continuum (*saṃtāna*), or production (*prasūti*), or succession (*paraṃparā*) has departed or gone away is described as such.
By the word *iti* [122.3], the form of reflection (*cintārūpa*) is indicated.
Observing that the speaker employs the expression "this is true" (*satyam idam asti*) [122.10] when nodding his head, he describes the speaker's intention and says, "he asks" (*pṛcchati*) [122.13].

For this very reason, he says this: questioning a bystander, he asks, "Is it being asked by you whether [it] exists? (*kiṃ tvayāstitvena pṛcchyate*), and then [the bystander] asks, "What is that? (*kiṃ tat*) [122.13].
For this reason, [the term] "to be brought forth" (*āhārya*) follows from the context.
By the word "here" (*atra*), the form of the statement that is intended as existing—namely, the "proper statement" (*nyāyyavacana*)—is shown to result in a state of indifference (*audāsīnyāpatti*).
Therefore, demonstrating the nature of the proper statement as being shown to exist, he says again: "This too exists."
Anticipating the objection that "if this is so, since such a reasonable statement exists, our own position is indeed faultless," he says: "But rather...
(*kiṃtv i*). You must simply ask this which is about to be stated.

Intending the sense of a copulative compound in the singular (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*)—that is, the form that has ceased is non-productive and the form that has arisen is productive—he says "ceased and arisen" (*pracyutotpanna*), meaning "not having ceased" (*apracyuta*).
And it should be understood that its nature as stable and unitary is established precisely by its being unarisen.
Even when there is a difference— that is, even when there is a distinction between that which produces and that which does not produce—
of that difference in existence (bhāvabheda).

"Because it has the characteristic of a difference in intrinsic nature that is independent of another" means that it is not a difference in intrinsic nature that depends on another, but rather that which has the characteristic of a difference in existence (*bhāva*) by itself.
"This belongs to you" means *bhāvatkam*.
"Is attributed," "is applied," or "is assigned."

With the intention that if agency were [asserted] by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then even that which is intended [as the agent] would result in having that same nature, he says: "Even for these, agency is by way of another's nature" (*eṣām api pararūpeṇa kartṛtvam*).
If agency were by way of another's nature, then the other alone would be the agent.

However, its being such [an agent] would be equivalent to the saying, "Having reached the *harītakī* fruit, the deity causes one to purge"; with this in mind, he says: "Because there is no agency even by way of another's nature" (*pararūpeṇāpy akārakatvāt*).
Regarding this latter point, [the verse] "The nature of that is accompanied, not solitary," he says—
concluding the subject at hand— "Therefore... In some way, by whatever manner, there is no cessation of causal activity.
The meaning is that its own nature exists even prior [to the effect]. They might think:
"That which is its productive nature must be stable; and that is called 'productive' in which case the effect exists, but not necessarily that in which case the effect must invariably exist."
Because existence is common to all non-causes,
the effect would also [arise] from that non-existence.
Its function is simply this: that [the effect] would not arise [if the cause were absent].
But since it necessarily arises when that [cause] exists, what use is there for this [proof]?
Therefore, how can it be better to apply the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the production of the effect occurs even when its form is present?

To this it is replied: if a cause does not produce its effect even when all its states are identical—since, by virtue of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), its form remains unaltered, neither declining nor arising—then that cause would become independent (*svatantra*).
And in that case, the effect would not be its effect at all.
This was stated by Prajñākaragupta in the *Vārtikālaṃkāra*:
“If there were non-effectness even when the cause remains the same in all states,”
"It would be an effect independent [of anything else], and it would not be an effect in that case.
Furthermore, if there were dependence on a cause, that cause would necessarily produce that effect by force;
yet, even so, if [the cause] were non-existent, there could be no effect of it.

Therefore, the distinction of a cause from a non-cause must necessarily be stated as the very necessity of the effect [arising] from that [cause]. Now, one might object: "The distinction of this [cause] from a non-cause is simply that 'in the absence of that [cause], the effect does not occur.'"
For it is not the case that because its cause is absent, its effect does not exist; indeed, from what is this understood—that its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that [cause]?
For if [its non-existence were due to the non-existence of that...]

If, in the absence of that [cause], there were an absence of the absence of the effect—which is characterized by the presence of the effect—then its absence would be established as being necessitated by the absence of that [cause]. Otherwise, why could one not imagine that its absence is necessitated by the absence of something else that is considered not to be the cause? If it is argued that, even when that [cause] is absent, the effect may still exist, and therefore its absence is not necessitated by the absence of that [cause]:
This is the same even regarding that which is intended as a cause.

Therefore, just as the effect does not arise by itself while the cause remains in that very state due to its independence, so too its absence will not arise by itself for the very same reason of independence.

And that which does not exist by itself cannot be restricted by it; for if it were dependent on that cause, it would necessarily exist whenever that cause exists. Thus the author of the *Alaṃkāra* said:
"Even in the absence of that which is considered a non-cause"—this is the meaning.
