“[146] Even if that exists, if there is no occurrence, how can there be the state of having occurred when it is absent? [146] ‘Its non-existence is caused by the non-existence of that’—how can this be so? (Pramāṇavārttika-alaṃkāra, p. 74). Thus it is said.
Therefore, it indicates that the specific causal relationship—namely, that [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists and does not exist when that [cause] does not exist—necessarily occurs.
And thus, since the effect necessarily follows when the cause is present, how could there ever be a cessation of its activity?
Furthermore, it would also be logical that such an absence of the effect occurs by itself, precisely because it is without a cause.
However, it is not tenable to claim that an entity does not exist when its cause is capable, because an entity is dependent upon its cause. As it has been said:
"Indeed, the non-existence of things might occur by itself;
but since existence is dependent, how could it not arise from its cause?"
But surely, since the absence of the effect is independent, it is entirely logical that "it does not occur even when the cause is present.
If that is so, then how could the absence of the effect be caused by the absence of the cause? In that case, the effect would simply not exist by itself.
And one who does not exist by himself cannot be controlled by that [other];
therefore, he might as well not exist at all.
Consequently, there would be no purpose for him.

But when [the effect] must indeed arise as long as the cause exists, then even though there is a cessation by its own nature (*svarasanirodha*), because of the arising of successive moments, the very absence of that [cause] constitutes the cutting off of the continuum (*saṃtāna*); and the very absence of that [cause] is easily understood as the non-commencement of the moments that project the continuum.
Thus, the dependence upon a cause is established.

[147] "Its function" (*kāryam asya*)—*Pramāṇavārttika-alaṃkāra*, p. 74. By this, that [view] is also refuted which some have stated: that pervasion (*vyāpti*), being established in dependence upon both [the pervaded and the pervader], is defined with respect to the pervader through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—that is, when the pervaded exists, the pervader necessarily exists and not its absence; whereas with respect to the pervaded, it is defined through the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)—that is, the pervaded exists only in the pervader and not elsewhere.

In this way, although the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is also determined in dependence upon both [cause and effect], it is defined with respect to the cause by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*),
meaning that the cause exists precisely prior to the production of the effect and not its absence;

whereas with respect to the effect, it is ascertained in accordance with experience by means of the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), meaning that the effect exists only when the cause is present and not when something else is.

According to the principle stated, since [the effect] does not exist when that [cause] is absent, it follows that its status as an effect is non-existent; and because it is absent even when the nature [of the cause] is present, it cannot be its effect, for the relation of causality [requires] that [the effect] follow from that [cause].

Furthermore, for you who are establishing this connection, the experience of the primary cause is one thing, whereas the experience of that which has a figurative status as a cause—due to its being for the sake of that [primary cause]—is another; thus, it is simply of the nature of an experience of a figurative cause.

Moreover, just as one who does not accept the necessary existence of an effect when the cause is present must nevertheless accept that cause because of the occasional concomitance [of the effect], so too [is the case here].
Likewise, why is it that occasional absence (*vyatireka*) is not accepted—or even considered logical—as a cause?

Therefore, by one who desires a necessary relationship between cause and effect, just as a pervaded absence must be accepted, so too must a pervaded presence (*anvaya*) necessarily be accepted; otherwise, such [a relationship] would be impossible.
Furthermore, it is maintained that this entity produces the effect while in a state of association.
And what is the meaning of "producing"? Does the effect become connected with existence [already], or will it become so connected?
What follows from this?

If the latter position is held, then when that [cause] produces [the effect], the effect could never be the object of the notion "existent," because its connection with existence would have already been realized.
Alternatively, if...
Thus, at that time, there is an admission of two alternatives:
was this [entity] previously established with this very same intrinsic nature, or with another?
It cannot be with another.
Because it is impossible for a single entity to possess two natures;
and if it were to remain in that very same nature, then just as now, at that time too, the effect would necessarily be connected with existence. And thus, the original [position] would be undermined.
Why this insistence on an untenable position?
Furthermore, what is this "causality" of yours— is it merely prior existence, or is it existence that is necessarily prior?
If it were merely existence prior [to the effect],

then the refutation of a stable entity— which has been so well established as being a cause— would follow as a consequence. Alternatively, if it were existence only prior [to the effect], [the same fault would apply].
This [definition] is established only if momentariness is established;
but since that very [momentariness] is not established, how could this being asserted be tenable?
Let it be: what contradiction is there in prior existence itself being causality?

If it is argued: "But was it not already stated that even if the non-momentary could be established as a cause, its very non-rejection would constitute a great contradiction"? Alas! Is the existence of the non-momentary refuted by the Tathāgatas through the definition of the nature of a cause, such that the logicians have resolved to say this as well? To this, it is replied: [The text continues: It is said: "The non-momentary is not excluded from the state of being a cause; rather, it is excluded from the state of being a cause because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*). Therefore, since the non-momentary is not a cause, there is no contradiction [in our position]. If it is asked: "How can this be so?"—it is explained: "Because the capacity for causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of a cause, and that capacity is impossible for the non-momentary. If it is asked: "Why is that capacity impossible for the non-momentary?"—it is explained: "Because it is impossible for the non-momentary to produce an effect either successively or simultaneously. For if it were to produce an effect successively, it would follow that it is momentary, because it would be changing its nature at each successive moment. because they are established as being independent with respect to their own perishing.”

Whatever does not depend upon any other cause for the production of a particular state should be known as certain in that regard, because it arises from its own causes in such a manner; for a causal complex, when unimpeded, is indeed certain in producing its own effect.
Furthermore, all things that are born are independent with respect to their destruction.
(Tattvasaṃgraha 353–355), and so forth.

Furthermore, as for those who, in response to the fault thus demonstrated, claim they are able to establish this subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) according to their own scriptural tradition—we do not recognize them; rather, we consider them to be our very benefactors.

In that case, one might object: "The former teachers have stated that whatever exists uncreated is momentary; therefore, [if your view were correct], permanence would be undermined. Anticipating this, he says by way of a conclusion: "Thus, in this way," and so forth.

With the intention that there would be no restriction regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth for that which is causeless, he says: "because of the non-existence of that which possesses the property of being produced" (*kṛtakatvasya sato 'bhāvāt*).
[160] The reading *bahantaḥ* is also encountered.
[159] In this context, if the reading were *dviṣmaḥ*, then it would certainly be consistent.

[160] Regarding "of that which is unproduced" (akṛtakasya), the clarification of the term "in general" (sāmānyena) is provided by the phrase "in the case of the produced" (kṛtake). This is because [the former] is dependent upon that very nature, namely, dependence upon a perishable nature (vināśisvabhāva). The qualification "because of dependence upon a perishable nature" is made for the purpose of establishing it as a logical reason (hetu). [161] Thus, it is a specific qualification by way of its causal status.
Thus, the word "iti" indicates the reason.
Because non-dependence is the cause, its nature of being neither self-existent nor non-self-existent (or, its nature of being impermanent) follows from that.
The mention of "by itself" (*svataḥ*) should be understood as intending merely to exclude the operation of another cause for the establishment [of the cognition].
This is because it is understood from the context that the Master [Dignāga] considered what was to be expressed to be appropriate to state.
It should be understood that this occurs when a possibility has arisen through the force of reasoning (*nyāyabala*).
[161] Of those things that are dependent;
[162] by way of non-dependence; [163] of that which exists.

One might object: "Surely existence will be established for a non-momentary entity through its connection with *sattā* (existence); so how can it be appropriate to state, 'For power indeed... and so forth? Anticipating this, he says: "He thinks thus.
With the intention that "existence" (*sattā*) is accepted by them as that which makes the three categories of reality existent, he says: "The universal, etc. (*sāmānyādīti*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), particularity (*viśeṣa*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are included.
And if their existence in their own right (*svarūpasattva*) is asserted, why would this not apply to other things as well?
Furthermore, if there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), the fault is that if one is not established, both are not established.
Regarding those [entities], such as the son of a barren woman and so forth:

"the connection with existence belongs to that very thing" means that the capacity for purposeful action (*arthasāmarthya*) itself has emerged as the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*). This is precisely the reading [intended].
When the word *iti* expresses the reason, "purpose" (*artha*) is that which is sought; thus, "purpose" refers to burning, cooking, and so on, and "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is the efficacy toward that.

Because it follows that "that very thing has arrived as the characteristic of being" (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*), the reading "the connection with existence (*sattā*) belongs to that very thing" is a mistaken reading. For in this way, it would be stated without reason that the capacity itself (*sāmarthya*) is the characteristic of being; and where [would that be]?

Furthermore, it would not have been stated that "this is its capacity"; therefore, if one were to provide an explanation by supplying the word "tasmāt" (therefore), it would result in an undesirable complication. Anticipating another argument for this very point, he says: "And in this way," meaning by the manner that is about to be described;
[namely,] "thus, the characteristic of the existence of the capacity for the object."
Showing that very same point, he says "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
This means by another way [of interpretation], through the force of the meaning.
Having set aside the definition of existence according to the Mīmāṃsakas and others, he speaks in order to refute it even for the Digambara.
If they say this:
"A person experiences sorrow, joy, and indifference—each with its respective cause—regarding the destruction, arising, and persistence of a jar, a crown, and gold. [Āptamīmāṃsā 59]
“Without destruction there is no sorrow, without arising there is no joy, and without persistence there is no indifference; therefore, every entity consists of these three aspects.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:

"One who has undertaken the vow of *prāya* does not eat curd; one who has undertaken the vow of *dadhi* does not drink milk; one who has undertaken the vow of *agorasa* does not consume both. Therefore, an entity consists of three natures. [Āptamīmāṃsā 60].
To the question "How is this illogical?", he replies with the words "by way of permanence" (*ghrauvyeṇa*).
Because of the contradiction as a reason, it is impossible for these [three] to exist in a single substratum (dharmin); this refers to the meaning [of the word "these"].

By this, he states the flaw of the definition, namely its impossibility—referring to what was stated [above]: that which has the characteristic consisting of arising, passing away, and persistence is described as such.

The fault of being non-pervasive (*avyāpitā*) due to the consequence of the non-existence of arising, ceasing, and persistence should be observed; for it is not logical that there be a connection of those [three] with something else that is non-existent.
Otherwise, if one were to admit that [the cause] possesses a capacity unfit for producing its own cognition, by such a mode [of reasoning], [the argument would fail].

The point is this: if it were to produce its own cognition by way of a universal (*sāmānya*), then it would be established as an object, and not otherwise. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the non-establishment of substance (*dravya*) and so forth is intended.
In the term "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatva*), the locative case is used in the sense of existence (*sat*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of succession and simultaneity," it should be understood as "by way of the capacity for successive and simultaneous action"; otherwise, how could the causal property of being capable of producing an effect be pervaded by these two properties of the effect?
And how these two are properties of the effect will be clarified later by Bhaṭṭārcaṭa himself.

[164] If there were non-momentariness (akṣaṇikatve), existence— which consists in the pervasion of both the general property of "merely performing causal efficiency" and the specific properties of "performing it successively or simultaneously"— would be pervaded by successive and simultaneous performance;
otherwise, the specific would be pervaded by the general.
Just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* [tree] is pervaded by the state of being a tree,
the universal is not pervaded by the particular;
it is not as if the state of being a tree were pervaded by the state of being a *śiṃśapā*.
"How can this statement be made to appear coherent?

To this, [it is replied]: because of the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), there is the cessation of the two pervaders—namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇaśakti*) and the nature of being momentary (*kṣaṇikarūpa*)—due to the cessation of their respective properties of acting successively or simultaneously.
When one asks, "At what time does this cessation occur?", he says: "In the case of non-momentariness" (*akṣaṇikatve*), meaning when non-momentariness exists.
In that context, because of the non-momentariness [of the subject], the ablative case should be understood by implication as "from the exclusion of the counter-example" (*vipakṣāt*).
To the question, "How is there an exclusion of those two from that? he says: "Because of contradiction" (*virodhāt*).
"Because of contradiction" means "because of impossibility."
It is not, however, by virtue of one of the two contradictions defined in the treatises.

This is because by the word "contradiction" (virodha), non-occurrence (ayoga) is intended; therefore, for the Buddhist who pursues the establishment of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) through either succession or simultaneity for that which is non-momentary, even the non-momentary must be admitted as contradictory, since its cognition is invariably concomitant with the cognition of the contradictory.

The objection raised by Śaṅkarācārya, namely that "contradiction is established," has been refuted. Furthermore, regarding the position of non-conjunction (*ayoga*), we have already explained in detail in the *Viśeṣākhyāna* the refutations and counter-arguments as far as they are possible; therefore, one should look for them there. And by this [it is shown]: that which lacks conjunction with either succession or simultaneity possesses no causal capacity whatsoever.

It is like a lotus in the sky. Furthermore, it should be understood that when the non-momentary exists, there is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), which is to be seen as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the reason of existence (*sattva-hetu*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaye*).
And just as the fault of its basis being unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) does not occur, so too [it has been explained] by us in the *Catuḥśataka*...

Since that has been explained in the proof of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and in the detailed exposition (*viśeṣākhyāna*), it should be understood from those very sources. Regarding the two contradictory [properties], existence (*sattva*) and non-existence (*asattva*):
therefore, because of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), [this was stated] by the Buddhist (*saugata*). (Cf. Steinkellner 1963: [165])
In the *Saugata* [section of the] *Hetubinduṭīkālaṅkāra* [166], it says:
"Even though the non-momentary is contradictory" (cf. Steinkellner 1963: 8, fragment 6);
in the *Hetubinduṭīkālaṅkāra*, it says: "The momentary is contradictory to this."

[167] Regarding the phrase "because contradiction is established" (virodhasiddheḥ): in the statement from the *Hetubinduṭīkā-āloka* (HBTĀ), "The establishment of contradiction is precisely through succession and simultaneity" (virodhasiddhir kramayaugapadyābhyām eva), it is intended that succession and simultaneity are indeed properties of the effect (*kāryadharma*).
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: is the effect, such as a sprout and so forth, produced by the seed and so forth alone, or together with something else?

Regarding the production of the effect—that is, the arising of the effect—the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says "no" to those things that are remote, being characterized by remoteness in terms of intrinsic nature and so forth.
In both ways— that is, by way of the visibility or invisibility of that other mode— this author,
by explaining succession and simultaneity in the form of association with or dissociation from another effect, has clearly demonstrated that succession and simultaneity are properties of effects.
For this very reason, we have likewise explained that the performance of an action is pervaded by succession and simultaneity.

"Even in the absence of those two states" (tadubhayāvasthāvirahepi) means, according to the context, even in the absence of the states of being accompanied by or unaccompanied by other effects, such as the sprout and so forth.
"Becoming otherwise" (anyathābhavanam) means becoming in a different manner.
Let it be so.
To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "And of that...
By this, its nature as being perceptible is established.

Let it be so; however, because of the non-perception of the perceptible in a certain place and time, there may be the conventional usage of its absence in that [place and time], but since there is no prohibition against it in another place and time, how can there be an absence of other modes [of existence] there?
Anticipating the objection that [the argument] is established, he says:
"And of that," and so forth.

Regarding the negation of the sprout and other entities—that is, the production of the sprout and so on—being outside of two states, there is the exclusion of being outside of states both accompanied and unaccompanied by another effect.

When the negation of that [object] through a different mode is established by means of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), he states that the negation occurs when [the object] is absent— namely, "of certain [things]" (*kayościt*)—
in a place other than the one in question, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "even when it exists" (*bhāve 'pi*), there is no contradiction because the context refers to that [seed], such as the sprout and so forth.
To the question "In what state [does it exist]? In another place and so on?", he says "successively" (*krameṇa*) and so forth;
or else, "in the other," meaning in that which possesses the simultaneous existence of the sprout and so forth.
And this is a qualification by way of being a reason:
the intention here is that even [an entity] in another location and so forth must either possess that state sequentially, like this other location, or possess it simultaneously;
for its exclusion from both these states has been refuted.
And since this is so, there is no fault at all;

thus, for one who says "there is no injury whatsoever," the intended meaning is as follows: since it has been refuted that an effect could exist in two states at once in a single location, it must therefore exist at other times too with a nature perceived by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, how could it [exist] in another place and so forth?
Anticipating another alternative, he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*) while concluding the section:
"[of that which has the nature of an effect]. S. 168.

If it is objected: "Was it not just stated that it is precisely the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), and so forth? So how is it now said to be 'perception' (*pratyakṣa*) and so on?"—this is not a fault. For previously it was stated in that manner for the sake of a deluded cognizer, whereas now it is stated for one who is no longer deluded; what contradiction is there?

Regarding the phrase "of succession and simultaneity" (*kramayaugapadyayoḥ*), the meaning is "of succession and non-succession" (*kramākramayoḥ*); by the word "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*), which serves as an indicator for "at once," non-succession itself is meant.

Because this is what is intended to be expressed, otherwise it would be difficult to establish that they consist of mutual exclusion; therefore, in every case, the meaning of non-succession is the meaning of simultaneity.
For this very reason, we have restated simultaneity by means of the term "non-succession."
[The opponent asks:

"Is it not possible that the other alternative (*prakārāntara*) consists precisely in the negation of both? For by the negation of one, there would be the affirmation of the other, and thus its negation would follow. To this he replies: This is the intended meaning of the affirmation and negation—namely, that "it is not sequential" is itself the affirmation of non-sequentiality (*akrama*).

That too does not exist; therefore, its negation occurs at that very time. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between these two which share a common locus and exist simultaneously; thus, for such a thing, [the statement] "it exists" would mean its non-negation. However, the reading "tasyāpratiṣedha" (its non-negation) is incorrect.
Even a cause, in relation to its own effect, is indeed an effect; therefore, the term "cause" is employed [to distinguish it].
However, there is no utility for the mention of the cause here in terms of its being a causal factor,
because it is precisely the effect that must be considered as the impossibility of any other mode [of occurrence];
or rather, the mention of the cause is for the purpose of making known that "it is an effect when it is being produced by a cause," which is its actual nature (*vāstavam rūpam*).
The apprehension of that which is contradictory to what obstructs the negation—this is the doubt; explaining this very point, he says: "when [one thing] is being excluded" (vyavacchidyamāne).

"The establishment of the other" (itarasya vyavasthānam) means the establishment of that which is other than the mode being thus excluded. "The possibility of the reason" (sambhavaṃ hetoḥ) refers to its existence (sadbhāvam), according to the context.
The mention of "origination" (*saṃbhava*) is an illustration; by this, it should also be understood that one must show the pervasion (*vyāpti*) already established previously.

It should be concluded that the proof of contradiction (*virodha-sādhana*) itself has already proceeded by implication. Furthermore, the word "sublating" (*bādhaka*) should be supplied with the sense: "the sublating means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) for the perception of the non-contradictory (*aviruddhopalabdhi*)."

This suffix *ktvā* must be understood in relation to another action; otherwise, in relation to what action would this act of "showing" (pradarśana)—which indicates a prior time—be shown, such that this suffix could apply?

Furthermore, according to the literal sense of the rule, this suffix would erroneously apply to actions having different agents, because the act of showing is connected to the person [who performs it].
With the intention of referring merely to contradiction, he cites the example of "the sensations of cold and heat."

[169] "Surely, let an existent thing be pervaded by both succession and simultaneity with respect to its effect; nevertheless, a non-momentary entity will produce an effect either successively or simultaneously.
Anticipating the objection that, this being the case, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). [148.18]
"Because there is no distinction" means because there is no distinction from its prior state.
He clarifies this very point by way of an illustration: "as in the state of being a non-agent.
He says, "and the dependence on auxiliary causes," meaning that it produces [the effect] only when it possesses the required auxiliary conditions, and not otherwise.
And the connection is with the phrase "not to be proposed" (*anupanyasanīya*);
[the author] asks "Why? and says: "Because even of both kinds" (*dvividhasyāpi*).
Now, just as a single thing [produces] multiple effects located in different places from its own cause...

If it is argued that because [the cause] arises in such a way, its production of multiple effects at different times will be possible, and therefore how can there be an impossibility of successive action for a non-momentary entity? To this, we reply:
this is not so.
Regarding the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) therein, we have already provided our well-stated response; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.

If it is argued that the same fault applies because a sequence characterized by causality is untenable even in the case of momentariness, this too has been settled in that very place and is not stated here.
Furthermore, the phrase "of all" should be understood as referring to those occurring in the second and subsequent moments.

"At the very time of the single action" means at the very time of the action of the first moment. "Of that which has that as its cause" refers to the producer of the effect intended to arise in the second and subsequent moments;
the particle *eva* (only/just) is to be understood as following the word *bhāvāt* (from the existence).

And by this, he indicates the *prasaṅga* based on the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*): that whenever something is capable of producing a certain effect, it necessarily produces it at that time—just as the final causal complex does;
and that the non-momentary first moment possesses the very nature of producing the effect intended to arise in the second and subsequent moments.
Nor [does it produce them] simultaneously.
The phrase “the non-momentary produces effects” is connected [to the previous argument].
With the intention that the intrinsic nature by which it produced that effect persists in its own form, he says [further]: “because there would be the consequence of it producing it again” (148.22).
By this [reasoning] as well, whatever is capable of producing within a collection, that must produce it at that very time, just like the final causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*).

He demonstrates this very reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*): that a non-momentary entity, which is intended to be produced as a causal agent by virtue of being created, would persist into the second and subsequent moments.

Regarding these two demonstrated *prasaṅga*-reasons, and the corresponding *prasaṅgaviparyaya* (the contrapositives) which are to be inferred from their meaning, we have thoroughly investigated both the possible refutations and their resolutions in our work titled *Viśeṣakhyāna*.
"It must be understood from that very point" means that one should now understand the sense to be: "because there is no distinction in its non-productive form.
The consequence of difference follows because, by implication, there would be two forms—one capable and one incapable.
Adding another argument to this very point, he says: "And if it were eternal" (*nityaś cet*).
(The distinction between the two arguments regarding existence in prior and subsequent times is to be understood; the cause exists at a prior time and not at other times.

At one time—that is, within the single moment itself—since everything that is to be done would have been completed all at once, there would be an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and thus [the entity] would be non-existent.
The word "iti" here indicates the reason.
Concluding the discussion, he says "thus" (*evam*).
Furthermore, it is because of the consequence of that same activity.
The reading enclosed within brackets appears incoherent.
They are called *āyatanas* because they extend noble knowledge (*āryajñāna*).
And since these are both the eye and so forth, and they are *āyatanas*, they are thus [referred to].

Even for this proponent of internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), it must be stated that only that which is established by valid cognition (pramāṇa) can function as the subject (dharmin); otherwise, internal pervasion would remain unestablished.
Therefore, it should be understood that these sense-bases (āyatana), such as the eye and so forth, are indeed established by valid cognition.
It might be argued that the reason (hetu) called "existence" is employed to prove momentariness with the necessary certainty that "whatever exists is necessarily momentary."

Furthermore, this [reason]—proving that every entity is neither non-momentary nor momentary—is indeed contradictory (*viruddha*), because it proves the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyayasādhana*).
Thus, the Lion of Syādvāda stated in the *Vādanyāya*: "Every entity is manifold (non-absolute) because of its existence;
otherwise, how could there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)?"

And while explaining this, the commentator Kulabhūṣaṇa has both explained and established it as follows: "The entire world of moving and non-moving things—objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant—is taken as the subject (*dharmin*). Its property (*dharma*) is 'having a manifold nature' (*anekātmaka*), meaning its essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) is manifold; the state of being such is its 'reality' (*tattva*). This is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). 'Because of existence' (*sattvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*).

Otherwise, in the manner of the absence of having a manifold nature—that is, by way of the negation of the manifold nature of objects—the [capacity for] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is the effect (*kārya*)."
“From what [is it established]? From nothing whatsoever.
By this, he has demonstrated the supporting proof that sublates the opposite case (*viparyaye bādhakaṃ pramāṇam*), which is the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*):
“That for which there is the impossibility otherwise is accepted as the logical reason (*hetu*).”
"According to the principle that 'even two examples cited as evidence are not the cause [of the conclusion],' a non-momentary entity is therefore not able to produce an effect."
Because its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradicted by the impossibility of occurring either successively or simultaneously, even a momentary entity is not capable of producing an effect.
To explain: does the momentary entity possess the nature of producing an effect at the time of its own existence, or at another time?

If it were the first alternative, then it would produce [the effect] at that very moment; and if the effect were produced during its own moment of existence, the entire world would result in existing within a single moment. For instance, a cause would produce whatever effect it has not yet produced precisely during its own moment of existence, and since that [effect] would likewise be the cause of another, that too would produce its own effect at that very same time.
That cause also would have to produce that [effect] at that very same time, because it is the cause of another; and this same logic applies to all subsequent cases as well.
True, the cause produces the effect at the very moment of its own existence, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in producing that [effect].

If it is argued that the effect arises at another time, then the effect itself would have to arise at that very [other] time; for the arising of the effect while setting aside that specific time would be contradictory. Alternatively, if its arising is intended [to occur at that other time], there would be a contradiction regarding its arising immediately after [the cause].

For instance, even for an effect that arises from a cause capable of producing it, yet occurs at a different time and is indifferent to the assistance provided by its cause, there is this restriction of immediate succession:
"This is the effect of that, occurring immediately after its destruction. This [restriction] would be untenable.

Thus, although this destruction of the cause—called "dissimilar"—is ineffective, if the effect were nonetheless restricted to its immediate succession, then the causality of even a permanent entity would remain unimpeded.

For instance, just as in the case of a momentary entity whose nature consists in its own existence and its capacity for causal efficiency—even though such an entity exists, its effects do not arise at that very moment but rather at a later time; so too, why is it not the same in the case of a permanent entity, which, although always capable of producing those effects, has its effects arise only after long delays?
Furthermore, since there is no activity in the second moment, there is no distinction whatsoever between the non-momentary and the momentary, whether they exist or do not exist.

[172] Here, drawing in the previous phrase "at another time," the meaning should be understood as "when its arising at another time is desired. Even if the words of the shameless [opponent] are to be disregarded by the discerning, something is nevertheless said:
here, indeed, the causal efficiency of things does not result from the entry of an operation (*vyāpāra*), because an operation distinct from arising is logically untenable.
Nor is there simultaneous arising with the effect,
because it is impossible for two co-existent things— like the left and right horns [of an animal]— to act as cause and effect for one another;
for "that which is non-existent lacks capacity beforehand, and that which exists afterwards is of no use."
According to this principle, what then is the meaning? It is simply the state of being necessarily antecedent with respect to that which is subsequently connected with existence;
and for the effect as well, being produced by that [cause] consists simply in its being necessarily subsequent to it.
And this being so, what is the meaning of the statement that "an entity has the nature of producing an effect at the time of its own existence"?
Having first established the time of its own existence, the effect becomes connected with that existence;
likewise, what is the meaning of the statement that "it acts only at its own moment" (svalakṣaṇe)?
Because the effect exists immediately after [the cause], the cause exists prior [to it];
thus it has been said: "That which is arising (*bhūti*) is itself the action (*kriyā*)," and so forth.
And in this way, [it is established that] by a single stroke...
All that has been stated by the Digambaras is thus refuted.

Furthermore, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arises only for that which is momentary, those who proclaim that existence (*sattva*) proves nothing but momentariness are speaking of a contradiction; and when non-momentariness is the probandum (*sādhya*), these [Digambaras], while presenting this very proof (*sādhana*), are clearly like those who claim "it is only earth" (*mahīkā eva*).
"Because they deserve to have equanimity as their very nature.

Having thus explained the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the author of the *Vārttika*, desiring to explain the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), demonstrates the motive for stating that effect-reason and establishes the connection between the preceding and following sections with the words "Thus, therefore... and so forth.
"Dependent on that" (*tadgata*) means dependent on the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).

Why, then, are its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) not established in the same way as for the essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), such that the presentation of the scope of the effect-reason would be described solely for the purpose of removing the misconceptions of others? Anticipating this doubt, the passage beginning with "In the case of the effect-reason" (*kāryahetau*) and so forth should be applied.
Regarding those two, positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*):

if that is so, then the establishment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must be demonstrated; and since one asks why this is not stated in order to demonstrate it, the phrase "and of that" (*tasyāś ca*) should be supplied. That is, "of that," namely, the establishment of the causal relation.
Because the cause is proximate, he explains that [the effect] is "distinct from the cause. By "effect," what is intended is precisely the effect itself;
for the restriction that "it is only threefold" has already been established previously. For this very reason, the objection will later be raised: "Why is it only the effect?"
In the case of non-difference in meaning, due to the distinction in exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), there is another property (*dharmāntara*) consisting of an imagined exclusion;
this is the uncommon effect (*asādhāraṇa-kārya*). As Dignāga stated: "In all individuals, whether they are included or not..."
[173] Regarding the phrase "by the Teacher" (*ācāryeṇa*), it appears that this is an elaboration by Dignāga. [174] [The question is:
"How is the production of a recurring cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*) among all individuals [accounted for]?"
"This word marked with a query does not belong here, but appears to belong further on.
If it were placed immediately after 'agner iti', it might even be consistent;
yet there too, it appears that a general term has been omitted."
And thus, the meaning would be that a universal (*sāmānya*) is that which gives rise to a cognition that follows through all individual instances (*vyakti*).
Demonstrating its very existence in every respect, he says: "of fire" (*agner*).

Because this [fire-ness] is dependent upon fire, and because fire-ness pervades all fires, it is intended to be the cause of a following cognition; therefore, even common properties (*sāmānyadharma*) are intended to be indicative (*gamaka*), just like those [universals].

The status of "being made of grass" (*tārṇatva*) and so forth as particular properties (*viśeṣadharma*) is intended here because they are meant to be the causes of distinct cognitions (*vyāvṛttapratyaya*), due to their failure to pervade all fires;

it is not, however, intended to deny them the nature of universals (*sāmānyarūpa*) altogether, since they do serve as the cause for producing inclusive cognitions (*anugatapratyaya*) with respect to all fires made of grass and the like.
Furthermore, because the universal form is not contradicted in this case, otherwise— given that smoke is determined to have a nature produced by fire from grass and so forth—
there would be no inference of the specific [cause] such as grass-fire, since a particular form, being non-pervasive, cannot be an object of inference.

The meaning is that those particular properties (*viśeṣadharma*) would also have to be understood [as indicators], yet it is accepted that only the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of fire—such as fireness (*agnitva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), existence (*sattva*), and knowability (*jñeyatva*)—are to be understood.

Likewise, smoke’s general properties would also be indicators, like its particular properties; however, this is not accepted, for the meaning is that existence, knowability, non-earthiness (*apārthivatva*), and so forth, are not indicators.

If it is asked, "What is this specific property (viśeṣadharma) residing in smoke that has been made the example? we shall explain and define "smokeness" and so forth in the passage beginning with "by means of smokeness, whiteness, and so on. Now, one might object: "Since the capacity to indicate [the probandum] for the state of being an effect (kāryatva) arises solely by virtue of the single relation called 'existence when that [cause] exists' (tadbhāva), why is it said that [the inference] is 'in every respect due to the relation of produced and producer'? Anticipating this, he says "in the produced" (*janya*) and so forth. Demonstrating precisely the relation of produced and producer in every respect, he says "for instance" (*tathāhi*).
In the manner previously described, the status of fire-ness and so forth as general properties (sāmānyadharma) is to be understood.
All of this is stated through the conceptual construction of distinctions among properties (*dharmabheda-parikalpanā*):
that which exists in grass is "grass-fire" (*tārṇa*).
"Arising from leaves" is *pārṇa*;
this designation emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*), meaning "by virtue of being made of grass" (*tārṇatva*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: just as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) is called a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) because, by pervading all fires, it is the cause of a recurring cognition (*anugatapratyaya*), so too "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*) is likewise a general property.

Just as properties such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) are general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) because they serve as the basis for inclusive cognition due to being common to both fire and non-fire,
so too is "whiteness" (*pāṇḍutva*) a general property because it causes inclusive knowledge by occurring in smoke, mist, and so forth. Therefore,
how can these two be presented as the subjects (*dharmin*) of the example?
What you have said is correct;
one should simply exert effort toward awakening.

For in this context, it is precisely "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*)—the general property (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) which serves as the cause for the inclusive cognition pervading all individual instances of smoke—that is intended as a particular property (*viśeṣadharma*) by way of presenting a cognition that excludes [smoke] from what is of a different class.
Such objections as these have been refuted.

If it is argued that, this being the case, "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) is also a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*), and thus it follows that even a specific property of fire would be cognizable [by inference], we reply:
since such a specific property is accepted as being cognizable, there is no fault whatsoever.

However, there is no fault in this: while the specific particulars such as "being produced from grass" (*tārṇatva*) are indeed objects of cognition, the fact that smoke in general lacks a necessary connection (*apratibandha*) with them is what is being negated. Furthermore, the second objection—that the word "pale" (*pāṇḍu*), which denotes a unique property of smoke distinct from other classes, was not employed—is also refuted;
for that property expressible by this word is difficult to ascertain, and thus one does not say, "There is fire here because of its paleness. Thus, everything is perfectly clear.
The meaning is "by means of dharmas that are like intrinsic nature.
Regarding the phrase "another meaning": [it refers to the following].

As many as there may be external factors that are invariably concomitant with a portion of the cause, another meaning [is implied], but not by means of the entire text of the treatise; for the sentence would be incoherent either without this specific meaning or by means of the preceding meaning alone.

Regarding the phrase "it is connected" (*sambadhyate*), the connection is that "their effect is the cause"; thus, the meaning is "the effect," and it should be understood that what was stated in the previous commentary is not to be connected here in this current explanation.

In the previous explanation, since it would follow that the cause consists of those properties residing within themselves, such as "smokeness" (dhūmatva) and so forth, it must be connected [to the meaning] precisely because of the impossibility of such a connection;
thus, the previously stated point— that the effect is the cause of those properties residing in the cause— is what is being referred to here.
Regarding the question "By what intrinsic natures is the cause [constituted]?", one has merely closed one's eyes like an elephant; by pursuing this point, no subsequent statement will follow.
However, some here say as follows: "Once it has been stated, this must necessarily be explained, and not otherwise.
And this being so, what is the use of the previous explanation?"

Therefore, since it is entirely improper to establish the relationship between producer and produced in the absence of a restriction regarding its arising from that [specific cause], it is appropriate to explain it as follows: a cause consists of those factors established in the causal complex without which that effect does not come to be, and not others, because of the restriction that they alone constitute its effect.
But here, the resolution must be provided by those who are themselves experts in this matter.

Since the subsequent explanation follows upon the prior explanation, it is by means of that which comes later— the purpose for which the cause of all those factors dependent on a cause is established— that the factor (dharma) belonging to the portion of the cause is defined as the probandum (*sādhya*).
Having ascertained that, subsequently, by means of the "prior state"— that is, the previously explained meaning— as opposed to the meaning explained later,
he defines the property residing in the effect through the phrase "by as many [properties] as smoke-ness and so forth residing in itself," and determines it as the indicator according to the context.

As before, their paleness and their specific nature should be understood. The intention is that for others— who maintain that the relationship of indicator (*gamaka*) and indicated (*gamya*) arises by virtue of a conjunction with a form that is non-distinct in both cases—
it is to be grasped, that is, to be ascertained.

"Smoke-ness" is the qualifier of that [reason]; therefore, by the phrase "because of smoke-ness," when a qualifier such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is presented as the reason, since it would be a statement of a non-contributory factor (*asādhanāṅga*) due to being a qualified attribute that lacks capacity, how could earth and the other elements be grasped? This was indeed suspected by Bhaṭṭārcaṭa, yet it was not resolved; so what is the use of our labor here? That point should rather be understood from Dharmottara and others.

"Just as there is the relationship of producer and produced, why is there not likewise the relationship of the signified and the signifier? To this he says: "No" (na hi). Why is it that this is not so from the perspective of the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*), but rather from the perspective of certainty? To this he says: "For instance" (tathā hi). Now, one might object: since it was stated that positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) do not exist when there is a doubt regarding existence, how can it be appropriate to speak of non-existence (*abhāva*) in that context? Anticipating this, he says: "He thinks thus" (evaṃ manyate).
Thus it is said:
"The anthill is the head of Śakra.
Thinking this, he says: "How is it to be understood that everyone has such a birth? [155.17] Thus it should be viewed.

One might object: "Has this not already been stated—that a produced effect depends upon a cause, but not upon its being of such-and-such a nature? Since those two [natures] are accepted as being independent of a cause, what is the point of saying this? Anticipating this, [the author] provides the following refutation: "If there were no cause, there would be no distinction between these two in every instance of production," and so forth. This refutation will now follow.
Unable to tolerate the very idea that those two are independent of causes, he says, "No.
The term "dependent on that" (*tadapekṣā*) means dependence.
That specific kind of creeper which is denoted by the word *aparājita* should be understood as being designated by the word *sūrya*.

By the word *itara* (the other), one should understand the *latācampaka*—which grows in a specific region and has a form similar to the tree-campaka (*vṛkṣacampaka*)—and not that which is commonly known as the *bhūmicampaka*. For in the case of the latter, there is no similarity of form with the tree-campaka at all.
[The establishment of a momentary distinction arises] from some form or another, through the production of a single conceptual synthesis (*ekapratyavamarśa*) together with that [other].
Regarding the distinction between subtle intermediate classes by virtue of being a substratum, he asks:
"How can there be the establishment of a single continuum (*ekasaṃtāna*) when there is a difference in class? He replies with the word "all" (*sarve*). This means:
if [the continuum] were based solely on the non-interruption of cognitions of a single form...

At that time, the determination of another as being within the same continuum through its own appropriation would not be possible; and that [determination] must necessarily be stated, otherwise the determination of that which is intended to be the appropriation—as the producer of an effect falling within its own continuum—would not exist. With this intention, the opponent objects with the words "of the first" (*ādyasya*).

Conformity with the genus (*jātyanuvidhāna*) consists in the production, by means of some aspect in a certain manner, of a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) together with that [genus]. He supports this very point with the words beginning "For instance" (*tathāhi*).
The imitation of the specific varieties of *aguru* is the production of a recognition [of those varieties] by that smoke, due to its being accompanied by the fragrance of *aguru*.
The phrase "they indeed imitate" is understood; "those smokes" refers to the smokes of the wick.
To the question, "How is it known that these imitate those specific varieties? he says: "In that form... (tadrūpa).

Because smoke, together with fuel, establishes a single continuum by virtue of producing a single form of conceptual apprehension in some respect, it is designated as "fuel" itself in a coarse sense; however, in reality, its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) should be understood as a specific moist continuum contained within that [fuel], whereas the continuum belongs to the embers and so forth.
Since this has been determined by Dharmottara in the *Viniścaya-ṭīkā*, it should be sought from that very source.

"Prasaṅga" means that which is entailed or demonstrated; "atiprasaṅga" is an excessive prasaṅga. By this, the meaning here should be understood as "enough," that is, "do not be overly prolix. The reading enclosed in brackets is seen in some manuscripts, yet it does not appear correct.
Following Durveka, the reading should likely be "tad-rūpa-rasa-vīrya" and so forth.
Because that differentiation of effects, characterized by being non-similar, is absent.
Anticipating the objection from a bystander—asking how there can be a lack of causality for that differentiation if it does not arise even when [the cause] is present—he says, "For not... (na hi).
"In the absence of non-difference" (asaty abhede) means, by the context, in the absence of the non-difference of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Furthermore, when the question "How then can there be a difference? arises, the phrase "of the two causal complexes" (*sāmagryor*) should be supplied.

This refers to the context: first, regarding a difference characterized by dissimilarity that occurs when there is a difference between the two causal complexes; and second, regarding a difference that occurs even when there is no such difference in the causal complexes, characterized by their non-difference.

Non-difference means being suchness, that is to say, belonging to the same genus; because this is the basis [of non-difference], since difference exists in the case of rice (*śāli*), *kodrava*, and so forth, why is there no connection with the term "anywhere"? To this he says:
because those two causes are not the cause of non-difference, those two must also exist as non-different; thus the meaning is that even that is included within the subject (*pakṣa*).
Even when there is a difference in causes, [the effect] of rice, *kodrava*, and so forth, is not produced by that [difference].
He says that difference is not merely being of a different kind, but rather it is exactly thus: "without a cause" (*nimittam antareṇa*).

Since there is no distinction in the conceptualization—that is, in the conceptualization of difference—and since there is no distinction due to the absence of a cause, the remainder of the sense is: "why is it not also conceptualized in the case of another *śāli* grain? Or else, this is obtained from the context: "The non-difference of the cause is not the basis for [the object's] non-difference."

Nor is there a difference in cause; rather, it is precisely in this way that there will be non-difference. Thus he says: "The reason (*nimitta*) is... [in the context of] conceptualization—that is, the conceptualization of non-difference—because there is no distinction, even between śāli rice and kodrava grain, there would be non-difference.
"Why is this not postulated?"—this is as explained previously.
It might be argued: "This non-difference is based on the restriction of appearance, not on any other basis; so why is it stated thus? To this he says: "In appearance" (*pratibhāse*).
The difference of appearance is its being of such a kind (*tādṛśatva*).

Even though there is a difference [between them] in the ultimate sense, due to the similarity of their forms and so forth arising from the causes of error, and despite their not being identical, it should be understood that "it is not thus" because of the observation of their secondary characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, because this is a case of secondary characterization, even on the occasion of investigating their difference, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that they are different because of the difference in their appearances.
It must be stated that even though there is no ultimate difference [between things], a distinction in appearance is perceived due to some cause of error (*bhrāntinimitta*).

However, if in both cases the distinction and non-distinction of appearances were themselves based on further distinctions and non-distinctions of appearances, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding those as well; therefore, it is impossible to establish such a state even for the first two.
Thus, the fault must be shown regarding those two— difference and non-difference—
and regarding that intrinsic nature,
by means of those two, difference and non-difference.
That which is other than those [entities], their intrinsic natures, and their difference or non-difference, and which is that very relation—such is its conceptualization (*kalpanā*).

Regarding that [conceptualization], when there arises the expectation, "Whence does even that [relation] come from for them?", the acceptance of another relation is proposed; and when that too is questioned, the same answer is given, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
For one who says, "[It exists] by abiding in itself alone," if this entity were to enter into the intrinsic nature of those two, then only that [entity] would remain, but not those two.
Now, if their entry into that [substratum] were the case, then those two would remain there, but not that [entity itself].
Furthermore, while accumulating another fault in the very position of difference, he says: "And because of the lack of assistance" (*anupakārāt*).
If those two—difference and non-difference, characterized by being "such" and "not such"—which it [the substratum] undergoes, are themselves distinct, then they are separate from it.
"Remaining in that state" (*tādavastha*) means that which remains in that state— namely,
the state it was in at the time of perceiving its difference or non-difference.
Of that [164.2] entity which has intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*);
of that [164.6] being produced through another essential form;

from that very cause-power-attained [form], from some form that is both distinct and non-distinct, consisting of the particular (*viśeṣa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*)—in this context, the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) does not denote the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

It cannot be the meaning of the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) derived from the etymology "that which is divided" (*bhidyate*), because that would entail having the nature of being differentiated, which leads to the fallacies of non-connection (*ayoga*) and unestablished existence (*asiddhi*). Nor can it be the category-meaning of "particular," because the opponent intends by the word "difference" (*bheda*) that which applies to things such as atoms, space, and so forth, which are devoid of destruction and origination. Rather, even when there is connection with a single universal, it is a particular within that universal; [this refers to] those two.
Regarding the phrase "by way of dependence" (*apekṣayā hi*), this is an explanation of the original word *hi* found in that location, meaning "because" (*yasmāt*).
However, the author of the *Ṭīkā* [interprets] the word *hi* in the phrase "by way of dependence" (*apekṣayāhi*) as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
Alternatively, the word "hir" (for) should be construed with "tasya" (of that), meaning "because of which.

These two present participles (*śatṛ-pratyaya*) are to be understood as indicating cause. He asks: "Why is it not accepted for the sake of—[that is,] for the accomplishment or production of—the means (*sādhana*), i.e., the causes? Thus he says:
"Even from that which is dissimilar" means:
as it has been observed, in the manner it has been observed;
the sense is that an effect observed in a certain way must arise only from a cause observed in that very same way.

Even though the intended causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct [from others], that characteristic—namely, being similar in form to the effect produced by the intended causal complex—is present even in other [complexes].
Since there is no difference in the fact that they are all distinct from that [intended] causal complex, why would the effect produced by *any* causal complex not possess that characteristic?
Anticipating the objection that "in that case, the same fault remains," the opponent himself says: "of only some [causal complex]" (*kasyāścid eva*).
In this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the phrase "what kind of capacity" (*yādṛśī śaktiḥ*) is to be supplied.

Regarding the expression "by another name" (*nāmāntareṇa*), which means "by another designation" (*saṃjñāntareṇa*), he asks: "How could that very same thing be stated by another name? and answers: "of that which is distinct from it" (*tadvilakṣaṇasya*).
"Distinct from that" means distinct from the causal complex of fire and so forth.
That causal complex which is different from the causal complex of fire and so forth is what is to be understood by the word "that.

Because of the impossibility—that is, the non-existence—of that specific excellence of the nature (*ātmātiśaya*) of that non-distinct collection of causes such as fire, which is denoted by the term "potency" (*śakti*).

The collective meaning is that it is impossible for a collection of causes, such as those not consisting of fire and so forth, to possess the power of a causal complex (sāmagrī) such as fire and so forth. Even if there were a connection with a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) within its own nature, how could it have the form of fire and so forth? To this he says: "For that very [cause]... It produces smoke by way of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
It "imitates its own genus" by way of being the material cause (*upādāna-bhāva*); the meaning is that it produces [it] while conforming to its own kind.
Regarding the phrase "yadi ce" (if, moreover), the word *ca* has the sense of the word *tu* (but).

We designate that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) by the name "fire" and so forth, whereas you designate it by the name "Śakra’s head" and so forth; therefore, there would not be a dispute over the name "fire" alone.
To the question, "How then is there no dispute over fire itself, but rather over something else? he says: "because there is no difference in the object" (*arthābhedam*).
Having accepted the non-difference of the object, characterized by the capacity to produce smoke, [the author] speaks in that manner because he says "Śakra’s head" and so forth.
To the question, "How is it ascertained that smoke and the like are the effects of an agent? he says: "Atadrūpe... (not having that nature).
The cause, such as fuel and so forth, does not deviate from its effect.

In the view that depends upon moments, however, it should be understood that the cause, such as fuel and so forth, is momentary in nature. He demonstrates the form of non-deviation with the words "from that which is dissimilar to it.
The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*), meaning "it is established" or "it is accomplished."

Having explained the effect as a logical reason (*hetu*), he now wishes to explain non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). To demonstrate its origin from that [effect], he begins with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tad evam*) and so forth.
That which is "being produced" (*bhavat utpadyamānam*) is seen—that is, ascertained—"even once" (*sakṛd api*); this should be understood as even a single instance.
This is established through perception and non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) as they have been explained.
The logical justification for the restriction "only from such a cause" is the one just mentioned, which remains present in the mind.
Although the negation of arising from what is not of such a kind is understood through this restriction, the author states it explicitly by saying "not," thereby making it directly expressed.
The term "by pervasion" (*vyāptyā*) means by including all places and times.
[The author] now demonstrates that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is differentiated.

The meaning is: "in that [non-apprehension] which has been described as such, and which is qualified by visibility" (*dṛśyatva-viśeṣaṇāyām*). The intention is that the demonstration of the absence of other causes was stated previously.
The mention of "its own nature" (*svarūpa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it should also be understood as including "its operation" (*vyāpāra*).

For this very reason, since the operation is to be shown later, he will state that one who employs the word "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) in its sequence first demonstrates the nature of non-apprehension itself.
The word "only" (eva), however, is intended merely to refute misconceptions regarding the scope of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For if it were explained according to its literal sense, the passage beginning with "in that way" (*tathā*) which is to be stated later would be inconsistent.
Thus, by the words beginning with "for instance" (*tathā hi*), he demonstrates the misconception regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
And thus, in his commentary on the *Īśvarasena*, [Śāntarakṣita] presented this as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

One should understand that the non-transformation of the self into the form of the object of the cognition of the thing to be negated—that is, its not being the substratum for the cognition of that object, and its not persisting as the grasper of that [object]—is intended merely as the negation of its being the substratum for that cognition; and it is by establishing this very status as a distinct means of valid cognition through reliance on a different consciousness that he says, "For it is not... [167.13].
Whether it be perception alone or that which consists of inference—
of that [cognition], whether perceptual or inferential,
from that objective aspect (bhāvāṃśa).

If one asks, "By doing what, then, does that [cognition] receive the designation of a means of valid cognition for non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*)?", he says: "[producing] the aspect of existence" (*bhāvāṃśa*).
This suffix *-śatṛ* is to be understood here as having the sense of a causal agent (*hetu*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the cognition whose object is something else.

In the cognition produced by a sense faculty, that which appears therein is its object; because it acquires the status of being an object through the fact of generating the apprehension of that [object], the word "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) does not require the accusative case at the time of the grammatical formation of the term as a means (*sādhana*). It is for this reason that it is designated in such a manner. To address the doubt, "How then is that [object] established?", the author, describing the intention of the teacher himself, says: "from non-apprehension" (*anupalabdheḥ*).
If, upon reflection, the cognition "this ground is without a jar" does not exceed the knowledge "that jar is not here"—

because it is produced by the sense organ aided by the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)— then, being a perception arising from the sense-object contact characterized as the presence of a specific thing conjoined [with the sense organ] immediately following that knowledge, it is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a means of knowledge other than inference and the like.
Alternatively, this word *antara* has a specific meaning.
To the question, "What kind of entity is this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*? he says: "of non-existence" (*abhāvasya*).

This should be understood as "of that which has the nature of a void" (*tuccharūpasya*), meaning "devoid of the nature of a positive entity" (*bhāvarūpaśūnyasya*), and not as a mere state (*avasthā*).
The phrase "by [his] own view" is used because, according to that [author's] opinion, even non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*).
Now, one might object: "This is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called perception;

rather, it is the result in the form of a means of valid cognition belonging to the perceptual means of valid cognition known as sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*). So how can it be stated in this way? [To this we reply:]...
This is true;
however, this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is intended primarily as the result in the form of cognitions such as "negation" and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "consisting of determination" (paricchedātmaka): it is a "determination" (pariccheda) because one determines by means of it, and it is "consisting of that" (tadātmaka).
However, the determination [of the object] is simply the cognition of the appropriation and so forth.

Alternatively, by means of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) here intends the result itself; and for those who designate such a distinct result of the means of perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇaphala*), it is shown by implication that the perception from which this [result] arises is the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).
Thus, it is entirely pure.

Showing the indirect argument (*vakrokti*) directed against those very Buddhists, he says: "That very same [167.21]"—that is, the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) just mentioned, for the purpose of refuting that [view] of the opponents, the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthaka*), and those who act like teachers (*ācāryadeśīya*), and for the purpose of refuting their divergent conceptions (*buddhibheda*).
This is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions.
That which possesses the conditions for apprehension is indeed said to have "reached the conditions for apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

Anticipating the question—"What is that [condition] such that an object reaching it is described as such by the author of the Vārttika?"—he says "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) while demonstrating the intended meaning of "reaching the conditions for apprehension."

The connection should be made as follows: "The attainment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) has been explained in this manner by the author of the treatise elsewhere" [167.29].
The word *pratyaya* is to be connected with each [term].
[177] The causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) consists of light and so forth.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the prior consciousness;
the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is the eye and so forth; and that which is apprehended as an object, namely blue and so on, is the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
In response to the doubt as to why that which was formulated by the author of the treatise (*śāstrakṛt*) in such a manner has been explained elsewhere, he says: "The Naiyāyikas.
Demonstrating their very misconception, he says: "For they...

By stating that these are the perceivers of substances, [it follows that] wherever these exist, the cause for perceiving them is the substance itself; thus, these are the causes for the perception of the substance alone.
It has been shown that [perception] consists merely in non-apprehension;
otherwise, there would be no apprehension of absence (*abhāva*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
Nor is it the case that these do not exist, for the Naiyāyikas accept the apprehension of those two through their capacity to be conjoined and by way of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

"In this way, since the perception of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth is likewise accepted as occurring in such and such a manner"—to the question "From where is it known that their designation is thus?", he says: "Great" (*mahatī*).
And this is based precisely upon the tenets established within one's own system (*pratitantrasiddhānta*).
It should be understood that "speaking and so forth" means "explaining"; otherwise, what has been stated would be incoherent because it is a Vaiśeṣika sūtra.

This is its meaning: perception occurs in relation to that which is endowed with magnitude (*mahattva*) and is large, not in the case of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. If perception arises from magnitude, then why does it not also occur in the case of space (*ākāśa*), which possesses supreme magnitude? Anticipating this objection, [the author] stated "because of having multiple substances" (*anekadravyatvāt*) in order to exclude that possibility.
Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, since the state of possessing multiple substantial parts belongs only to a large composite (*avayavin*) and not to a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), this should be understood as intended to be a mere alternative definition (*lakṣaṇavikalpa*) showing that largeness and the state of having multiple substances are independent of anything else for their production.
That which has many substances existing as its constituent causes—that state [is "anekadravyavattva"].

Regarding the reading *anekadravyavattvāt*, since this belongs to the class of words beginning with *sarvadhana* (as it is included in the *ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *śatṛ* (the present participle ending *-vat*) should be understood as prescribed here by way of an exception to the prohibition against *bahuvrīhi* compounds; otherwise, the suffix *matup* would have been seen [prescribed]. Otherwise, since a *bahuvrīhi* compound is preferred for its brevity over a *karmadhāraya* with a possessive suffix (*mattvarthīya*), the formulation would have resulted in: "that which has many substances" (*anekaṃ dravyaṃ yasya sa tathā*), and then "that state" (*tadbhāvaḥ*), from which [the ablative] *anekadravyavattvāt* [would follow]. Thus, [the reading *anekadravyavattvāt*] is established.
But if the reading is *d* (i.e., *rūpād*), there is no difficulty whatsoever.

If perception were to occur in air (*vāyu*) as well—due to its magnitude (*mahattva*), its possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), or from either of these two factors—that [perception] would also apply there;
therefore, it was stated "from color" (*rūpāt*) in order to exclude that possibility.
[177] Following Durveka, the reading "hetusamanantare" and so forth appears correct. [178] Following Durveka, the reading should be "dravyāṇām upalambhakāny āha.

Now, one might object: since non-existence is established through the non-perception of that which is endowed with this "attainment of the conditions for perception" (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti), non-perception itself is indeed accepted by them as a logical mark (liṅga). To this he says: "And thus... [168.3].
"The [reason] is inconclusive," so say those very Naiyāyikas. Anticipating the question "Why is it inconclusive? and remaining within their own system, he says: "Even though... (saty api).
Demonstrating this very point through an illustration according to their own view, he says: "For indeed... (na hi).

[179] "They do not exist" means they are not present. The commentator— the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, Pakṣilasvāmin— states "because of being a sense faculty" (*indriyatvāt*) in order to demonstrate that very perception belonging to him through inference.
"Reaching its object" (prāpyakārī) means that having reached the object and conjoined with it, it produces cognition therein;
this should be understood as an explanation of the meaning, but not as a formal syllogistic argument (*anumānaprayoga*),
because the five-membered statement (*pañcāvayavavākya*) is not presented here.

Concluding the very statement regarding their lack of exclusivity (*anaikāntikatva*), he says: "Thus, in this way" (*tad evam*). Furthermore, the declaration of their lack of exclusivity should be understood according to the literal wording found in the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*.
But it is not as they explain it;

for they [the opponents], by qualifying "from form" (*rūpāt*) with "that which is designated as manifested" (*udbhūta-samākhyātāt*), intend to exclude the perception of the whole consisting of the visual rays.
To refute that, and to eliminate the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta-anupalabdhi*).
How is it for the purpose of refuting that? He says: "by perception" (*upalabdhi*).
[The word] "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) is supplied by implication.
If there is the possibility of deviation even when that [perception] is demonstrated, how is it refuted? He says: "for when... (*yadā hi*).

"How could there be any room for deviation?"—this is because of the context that "there is a non-perception of what exists by means of that [perception] which has reached the conditions for perceptibility. "Of that" refers to the non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perceptibility. Although the root text is printed as "they exist" (*bhavanti*), the reading "they do not exist" (*na bhavanti*) found in the commentary is correct.
[180] Refutation of that:

But surely, since the Naiyāyikas state that "attainment of the conditions for perception" (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti) refers to largeness and so forth, and since that too is faultless, why do you not simply say that very same "attainment of the conditions for perception"? Why, instead, do you express it otherwise out of mere self-conceit?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But [the qualities such as] magnitude," etc.
To demonstrate that very impossibility by way of the absence of a substratum, he says: "For not," etc.;
for (*hi*) means because.
A substance distinct from form and the other [sensory objects] does not appear in its own cognition.
To the question "How does it not appear?", he says: "by another aspect" (ākārāntareṇa);
that is, by an essence other than the essence of form and so forth.

To the question "By what [is this established]?", he says: "In its appearance" (*tatpratibhāse*). Since that which appears—namely, form (*rūpa*) and so forth—is what is called "appearance," its very own nature (*svarūpa*) is its distinction (*viveka*) or its exclusion (*pracyuti*) from that which possesses it.
By this, non-perception (*anupalambha*) is shown to be the means of establishing the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of the absence of that [other object].
Otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that even when a jar appears, there could be the establishment of the appearance of a cloth. Therefore [non-perception is necessary].
Now, having provisionally accepted substance, [the author], desiring to refute that largeness and so forth are the perceivers of it, says: "And not...

(*na ca*). Even when there is a connection with that—that is, even when there is a connection with largeness—the meaning is that, even though it has arisen from its own causes, it is of no effect upon that non-large substantial self.

One might object: "What is the need for a separate magnitude (*mahattva*) other than its own nature (*svarūpa*), since the cognition of that [object] also arises from that very [nature]? Anticipating this, [the author] says: "And it is not [perceived] by its own nature as non-magnitude" (*na ca svarūpeṇāmahata*). It should be understood that by this, the fault is shown in the very same position. Now, one might argue: "Even if it does not possess magnitude intrinsically due to its connection with that [magnitude], what is lost to us?
