Its apprehension will occur through the form of a magnitude that exists as a distinct entity. To this he replies: "By means of another's form" (*pararūpeṇa*).
"In the form of another, that is, of a different magnitude"—how is it non-erroneous? It is indeed erroneous;
the meaning is that it is an error because it takes the form of apprehending that [magnitude] where it does not exist.
It is called "upalambhaka" because it causes apprehension (*upalambhayati*). And this refutation has been stated by assuming [the existence of] magnitude (*mahattva*);
however, it is not [due to] the absence of magnitude.
It should not be said that there is no such thing as a "perceiver" here, nor that there is no perceiver of anything;
rather, it follows that form (*rūpa*) is the perceiver of a substance (*dravya*).

To the question, "Whence does its non-apprehending nature arise?", he says: "Of that too" (*tasyāpi*). This is to be connected with the phrase: "that form (*rūpa*) does not possess such a state of being an apprehender.
Furthermore, the meaning should be understood as follows: "apprehender" (*grāhaka*) means "it causes [an object] to be apprehended" (*grāhayati*); thus, its state (*bhāva*) is its essence (*tattva*).
Furthermore, he expresses the possibility through reasoning,
or he conjoins it with the logical consistency of equal agency.
To demonstrate the reason desired by the opponent, he says: "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*).

This means that when there is apprehension by way of its own specific individual essence (*prātisvikena ātmanā*), because of the proximity expressed as "of that," there is no manifestation of anything else;
for the substance-essence (*dravyātman*) is absolutely imperceptible (*atyantaparokṣatvāt*).
This is his intention: for it is logical that only form (rūpa) when being perceived is the perceiver, and not otherwise.
Moreover, that [substance] is not perceived in its nature as a substance (dravya), because that would entail the fallacy of the cognition apprehending it being erroneous.
Therefore, how can there be perception of a substance?

Nevertheless, we accept its suchness only if it were to appear as distinct from that; since this is not the case, he says, "of the nature of a substance" (*dravyarūpasya*), meaning of the essential nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpasya*).
This is because it is not perceived—that is, not apprehended—through its separation from that, which is to say, through its separation from the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpasvabhāva*).
And this refutation should be understood to apply to perception even when it is large.
Gathering another point to be stated on this very matter, he says: "And not...
He states the reason with: "Since..."
Being already produced as something that has acquired its own nature (*pratilabdhātmaka*), it is *tathatā*, which is to say, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
He says "and not" (*na ca*) because, although it is devoid of qualities at the moment of its arising, it will possess qualities in the second moment.
The intention is that even when its own substance is joined with a previous form, there is no destruction of its prior nature because it is non-momentary;
for [the consequence would follow] from the destruction of the previous form and the manifestation of another form.
[181] By means of another form, S.
[182] Of this, S:
But surely, when the prior form perishes, since that very thing has perished, and when another form manifests, since it is something else that exists, how [can there be continuity]?

If it is argued that "that very thing which previously had not attained the status of a substratum with respect to largeness and so forth may itself become the substratum," then let this be another fault for him; such is the intention [of the author], and thus there is no fault here.
Demonstrating that even in this case a substance cannot logically be the substratum with respect to largeness and so forth, he says: "And not... (na ca...).
The point is that even if the progenitor were likewise [the substratum], it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
and because the status of being a substratum through other modes such as "that which establishes" has been refuted elsewhere.
This is because purposeful action (arthakriyā) is untenable due to its contradiction with [the nature of] purposeful action.
And how that which is non-momentary cannot be conceived as performing a causal function either successively or simultaneously has already been explained above.

By the context of the phrase "of the inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇasya*), the meaning should be understood as "of this substance (*dravya*) which is the inherent cause with respect to largeness (*mahattva*) and so forth, and which is the object of perception. One might argue: "Even if, according to the principle just stated, its status as a substratum for that [quality] is not tenable, why could it not still be its inherent cause even while not being its substratum? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "yata" (since):
it means that which has emerged from itself, which is supported by itself, and which is mounted upon itself.
Let it then produce an effect that has emerged from itself.
He says "nor [is it]" (na ca) because it receives such a designation [as a cause].
"This" refers to the production of an effect that has been projected by itself.

This is its intended meaning: for an effect must be produced precisely by that which has already attained its own substantial existence (ātmasattva), and not by something whose form—such as magnitude and so forth—is merely being grasped.

Therefore, it must arise [simultaneously], because if the two co-existent things lacked the relationship of cause and effect, it would follow that they lack a cause; however, since they are momentary, they do not exist in the second moment, and thus there can be no production of an effect that has already arisen from itself— therefore, the phrase "nor is there subsequently the state of being a support" follows [from the previous argument].
The meaning is that there is no destruction of the form which serves as its substrate, as it has come into being from its own causes.
[183] Since there is an absence of a substrate, he asks how [the object] could be impossible even in its absence, and says: "Because... [169.6].
Thus, it is designated as "possessing multiple substances.

Furthermore, the absence of a substance [as a distinct entity] has just been established immediately following [the statement], "For there is no [substance] apart from color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth," and so on.
By that [phrase], "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), the meaning is: "of that which possesses such a state of having reached the conditions for perception."

Thus [169.11], the author of the treatise, namely the author of the *Vārttika*, intends by the word "non-existence" both non-existence itself and the conventional usage of non-existence; with this intention, he says: "and the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence" [169.13].

The intention of one who says "But that which... and so forth is as follows: if he intends to say that the conventional usage of non-existence is established by means of the non-apprehension of a pervader (*vyāpaka*) and so on, then [the author] replies: this is not so; for it is possible to express the subject (*viṣayin*) by means of its object (*viṣaya*), even by using the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*). Thus, by speaking in this way, he intends specifically a particular kind of non-apprehension.

By describing this function of non-apprehension as "the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension," the author of the *Vārttika* has, by implication, shown what is explicitly stated elsewhere;

demonstrating this as well, he says: "But that which is non-apprehension... and so forth, up to "...it should be understood as the cause for the negation of the conventional usage of 'existent'. (169.15–169.17)

In response to the expectation, "How, moreover, is it known that they intend for that to be the cognition of another object itself? the following should be applied: "Because of the statement, 'or cognition [is directed] toward another object' (vijñānaṃ vānyavastuni)" [169.21]. The meaning is: when it is intended to be expressed as residing in the agent (*kartṛsthatayā*). Now, in your own view, what is the *upadhi* (the condition or substrate)? He says, "There is some self by which this is spoken," [expressing this] with the words "and perceiving" (*upalabhamānaś ca*); here,
the particle *ca* is used in the sense of "this is evident" or in the sense of "because."
The intended meaning is that the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) arises precisely in this [self].

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the agent of the act of perception is called the 'perceiver' (upalabhamāna)? Then why is it said that the generator of perception is called such a perceiver? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is thus... (tathāhi).
Granted that this may be said, nevertheless, he says "and not" (*na ca*) to explain how the reality of the sense faculties and so forth is established;
"of another" (*anyasya*) refers to the self (*ātman*).
"Being a producer" means, by virtue of the context, "being a producer of apprehension.
Of the self— that is, of the eternal substance called the self—
[there is] the non-existence of causes for its arising, that is, for the arising of apprehension.
The meaning is that there would be no fixed rule that "the causes are only this many";
and if the causes were not fixed, one who seeks an effect would not be able to employ a specific cause.
To the objection that "in that case, he [the Self] must be the agent because he is the substratum," he replies: "Even the state of being a substratum... [170.11].
The meaning is that it is impossible for that eternal self to be a producer.

Since it exists for only a single moment of origination if it were momentary, there would be no duration distinct from that origination. Nor can there be an absence of falling for such a duration, because falling itself would be impossible; this is the sense.
"Why does it not fall? Because its non-falling is its stability," he says: "of that" (tasyāḥ).
Of that perception, because of the absence of gravity—that is, the absence of the quality designated as "gravity.
And that absence [of gravity] is due to the fact that, if cognition were of the nature of a quality, it would be devoid of qualities.

The qualitylessness of qualities follows from the statement, "Qualities are devoid of further qualities and are dependent upon substances. Furthermore, gravity is a quality, as stated in the passage, "Gravity is the cause of falling in water and earth"; therefore, there is an absence of gravity in that [ether]. To the objection, "Granted that it lacks gravity, why does it not fall? he replies: "Due to the absence of conjunction" (saṃyogābhāvāt).

If falling were to occur solely due to weight, then fruits would not remain on branches and the like; therefore, it is stated "in the absence of conjunction" (*saṃyogābhāve*). In the absence of conjunction—that is, in the absence of conjunction with the branch, the stalk, and so forth—[the fruit falls].
"The established conclusion" (*kṛtāntaḥ*) means the tenet (*siddhāntaḥ*); "because of inherence" (*samavāyāt*) refers to the fact that [the fruit] is perceived there due to inherence.
That "inherence" (samavāya) as well—
meaning that specific causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) or the relationship of the supported and the support (ādhāryādhārabhāva)— is possible for a permanent self; such is the sense.
Although a fall of cognition is not possible, one might still wonder whether it does not have a substratum; anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer within the very same previous position:
"And [it is] not [the case] for that which has the nature of not falling" (na cāpatanadharmikāyāḥ).
Furthermore, its having the nature of not falling was established immediately following [the discussion on] its lack of weight.

By this, he shows the following: let there be some substratum that acts as an obstacle to the falling of water and the like, which are by nature subject to falling; however, one should not inquire further whether even in that case there exists some "obstacle" (pratibandha) called such. But this does not apply to that which is not by nature subject to falling. Thus says the crest-jewel of the circle of authoritative scholars:
“An entity may be a substratum for water and the like by virtue of obstructing their movement;
but what is the substratum for qualities, universals, and actions, which are themselves devoid of motion?”
Thus it is said in [Pramāṇavārttika 1.70]:
"Also for another, even for the self (*ātman*),
there would follow the consequence of its existence— that is, the consequence of being its substratum."
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Of that," meaning of that inherence; "because of its being the same," meaning because of its being one.
For this very reason, he says: "by way of oneness" (*ekatvena*). "Of this" refers to *samavāya* (inherence).
"In the context" (*prakaraṇe*) means in the discussion or the introduction of the inquiry.
From that which is intended [170.25], namely from that which is prescribed by the treatise;
from "fit food" [170.25], meaning from what is worthy of being eaten;
as something other than that, the village cock [170.26] is distinct from that other thing, such as a Brahmin or the like [170.26].
The connection should be made as follows: "Even though it is edible, it is called inedible.
Since a point that is being established becomes easily understood through multiple illustrations, he states another illustration with the words "And just as...
(*yathā ca*). "In the context" (*adhikāre*) means in the introduction (*prastāve*).

In the same way, "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*) means "similar to that," namely, similar to the two things previously demonstrated, with respect to an object distinguished by the absence of the referent of the subsequent term; this is how one should connect [the phrase] "by that, the negative particle has existence as its object. Furthermore, this instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) should be understood as expressing a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*).
The meaning is that its object is merely the negation of the appearance of an existent entity (*bhāva*).
In response to the expectation of what kind of negative particle (*nañ*) it is, one should supply the word "grasped" (*āgṛhīta*).
Likewise, since the object of the negation has been entirely accepted as the referent of the subsequent term by way of a general affirmation (*vidhi-sāmānyena*), how then can this be?

Regarding the doubt that in the expression "it is to be known" (*jñātavyam*), this [negation] functions merely as a prohibition of the meaning of the subsequent term (*uttarapadārthapratiṣedhamātravṛtti*)—that is, a forceful negation (*prasajyavṛtti*)—whereas here it functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsavṛtti*) which refers to a similar entity qualified by the absence of the meaning of the subsequent term, he says: "Where... [171.4].
The connection is: "Where it is thus, there it has the nature of an exclusion (*paryudāsavṛttitā*)" [171.6].
The meaning is that the predominance of the injunction (*vidhi*) is established as having a positive form (*bhāvarūpa*) by virtue of being the primary thing to be expressed.

"Negation" (*pratiṣedha*) refers to the negation of such a subsequent referent (*uttarapadārtha*), which is grasped through implication (*arthagṛhīta*)—that is, suggested by the capacity of the injunction to establish a similar entity.
This is the portion of the injunction (*vidhibhāga*) where a referent such as a Kṣatriya is not expressed by its own word (*svapada*) as a self-designator; this is exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

It should be understood that [the term] refers to a sentence that conveys a meaning (*arthapratipādaka-vākya*), and not to an explanatory sentence based on a compound (*samāsanimitte anvākhyānavākya*); for since this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), such a [separate] sentence is impossible. Otherwise, just as in the case of "Bring the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣam ānaya*) and so forth, if the bringing of a Kṣatriya were intended, the usage "Bring a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇam ānaya*) and so forth would also undesirably follow.

As for the statement that "one who is not a Brahmin is called a non-Brahmin," this expresses the meaning only partially through absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), namely that he is not a Brahmin.
This is because even within an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there exists an element of absolute negation;
however, that sentence is not a restatement (*anvākhyāna*) intended to convey the full meaning of the compound.

One who makes a pot is a "pot-maker" (*kumbhakāra*); this is like [the term] *upakumbha*, meaning "near the pot," and so forth. If it is asked: "If it is not expressed by its own word, how indeed can it be expressed? [The answer follows:]...
We say it is by means of the word "other" (anya).

This is because the word "other" itself is employed there, and there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) when the meaning is thus stated, since the word "other," which expresses the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), is connected with another word ending in a case-suffix (*suvantena*). Applying this very definition, which was shown in general terms, to the present context, he says: "And [it is] a prescription (*vidhi*)," etc.
It should be understood that this refers to "by such a statement.

He says this so that its negation may be understood: "[because there is no cessation of the apprehension of what is intended to be expressed]. He then asks, "How, then, is it stated? and answers with "What then? [171.10].
To the question, "Why is it expressed by another term and not by its own term? he says: "Of the other term itself" (anyaśabdasyaiva).

Regarding the word "in the sentence" (vākya), it should be understood as "in the statement that explains the true meaning. Furthermore, when the expectation arises as to how there is the employment of another term even there, it should be connected with the phrase: "by relying on exclusion" (paryudāsāśrayeṇa).
This very point is demonstrated by the statement: "The non-apprehension [is] the apprehension of something else" (*anyopalabdhir anupalabdhiḥ*).
The particle *iti* indicates the form of the expression [of the term], and the negative particle *nañ* is shown to be compounded with a portion of a nominal stem (*subanta*).
Capability (*sāmarthya*) is a relationship characterized by mutual dependence;
this is the reason why there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) and not a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
The meaning is "grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "the non-apprehension of another is [itself] apprehension.
By the particle *iti*, the form of the syntactic unity is shown.

*Prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is a negation that occurs after having applied (*prasajya*) some meaning; that is, a negation made by first establishing the application, the presentation, or the context of some meaning, wherein the expressed sense is merely the negation of the subsequent term. The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.

[187] "The opposite of that" means the opposite of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) that was previously demonstrated. In order to demonstrate this very opposition for the sake of easy understanding, he says: "In that case, indeed," and so forth. For in that case, because the negation of the meaning of the subsequent member constitutes the meaning of the compound, it possesses predominance.

The "prescription" (*vidhi*) is the enjoining of some matter; it is understood through implication (*arthāt*), that is, by the force of the context. When there is a cognition of a prescription, one should understand that it occurs "by implication.

For instance, from the statement, "When [a case-meaning] is already expressed, the second and subsequent case-endings do not occur," it is understood—by implication, according to the rule that a specific prohibition is invariably concomitant with the understanding of the remainder—that [the endings] occur when [the meaning] is not already expressed.

The phrase "they do not see the sun" (sūryaṃ na paśyanti) is connected here with the finite verb *paśyanti* by means of the negative particle *na*, and not with the nominal ending; thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

That which is subject to negation, such as "seeing the sun," is expressed by its own term—that is, by its own designator—through the phrase "they do not see the sun. However, it should be understood that this refers to the explanatory sentence (*anvākhyānavākya*) which serves as the basis for the compound. This is because such a possibility exists in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation) within a compound. All of this can be understood from the context and so forth; thus, everything is clear.
[185] And of the injunction, S [186] not perception,
S [187] the opposite of this, S
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he now says "Thus, therefore," connecting it to the subject at hand;
"in reality" (*bhāvataḥ*) means from the perspective of the thing itself, that is to say, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*).

Regarding the "postulation of a relation" (*saṃbandhakalpanā*), that is, the postulation of some other real relation: when one is questioned as to how that relation, being a distinct entity, belongs to those two, one must postulate yet another [relation]; and since the same would apply there as well, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result, which is an obstacle to the establishment of the matter at hand.
"Similar to what was said" means "essentially as stated.
[188] However, the reading "due to the absence of a relation" (sambandhābhāvataḥ) is not correct;
rather, "the relation exists in reality" (sambandho bhāvato) is the proper reading, in accordance with the *Anuṭīkā*.
In that regard, when the question arises as to what kind of existent jar-form imparts its own aspect (*svākāra*) to that consciousness, it should be applied thus:
"of such a kind" (*tathāvidham*). This means that the form of the location, being of such a kind, is devoid of obstruction, distance, and so forth, by way of imparting its own aspect.
Clarifying this very point, he says "that" (tad); he demonstrates that within the nature of their own non-conjunction (saṃsargamātra), they are [non-different] within themselves.
"Whose words are to be heeded" means whose speech is worthy of being listened to.

Because cognition functions swiftly—that is, because it moves with extreme rapidity—there arises the conceit of simultaneity, the determination that "these have been grasped simultaneously. By stating this, it is shown by implication that while those objects standing before one, which possess equal capacity for perception, are actually grasped by cognition only in a sequential manner, they are nevertheless apprehended as simultaneous.
Because it would follow that everything exists in that way [as the object], and because it would follow that there is merely a conceptual construction of error.
The opponent considers that "cognition itself" is the action here.

How so? The proponent [of the Siddhānta] intends the sense that even in the case of perceiving a jar or similar objects situated in deep darkness—where an action must be performed—the lamp’s status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) remains unimpeded.

"Because of the difference in agents, since there is a plurality of agents in the form of perceivers such as Devadatta and others. To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "In that case, because of the unity of the agent. His intention is this: even if this single instrument exists, if there were a plurality of agents due to the plurality of objects such as jars and so forth—

If it is argued that the arising of multiple actions is described [in the case of a single agent], then by implication it follows that because the agent is one, the action must also be one; and consequently, the oneness of the action does not depend upon the oneness of the instrument. What, then, is the point of saying this? It might be argued as follows: "Just as there are many agents who are perceivers in that case, so too there are many instruments, namely the sense faculties."

And thus, because there is a multiplicity of instruments (*karaṇa*), there is a multiplicity of actions (*kriyā*) with respect to multiple objects; therefore, it is established that from the unity of the instrument follows the unity of the action.
This [position] is flawed, because when a lamp is burning, even though there is only one sense-faculty (*indriya*) or one lamp as the instrument, for all [of them]...

Because for those who act, there arises a multiplicity of actions from the moments of cognition whose objects are various things such as pots, the fault of being "inconclusive due to commonality" (*sādhāraṇanaikāntikatva*) is indeed unavoidable.
"In perishable things" (*viśarāruṣu*) means in things that have the nature of disintegrating.
His intention is this: one who, having already attained its own existence, subsequently undertakes some action independently is a "doer" (*kartṛ*).
And that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the accomplishment of an action is called the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Likewise, since an action arises as something distinct from the existent itself through its occasional connection with activity, and since the entire entity (*bhāva*) lasts for only a single moment,
how could it, having attained existence, act in such a way or be understood in such a way regarding the purpose of the action?
Regarding the phrase "intermediate state," he now states the specific refutation of both the momentary and the non-momentary with the words "And not...

(*na ca*). The qualifier "conforming to the positive and negative concomitance of all causal factors" (*sarvakārakānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyinī*) should be understood as being stated by way of a reason (*hetubhāvena*).
The example of having the property of being [distinct], such as color and taste, has been provided.
Now, in order to determine the meaning of the word "one" (*eka*) in the phrase "due to association with a single cognition," he says: "In that regard... [173.14].
"Comprehended by a single sense-field" means that even when [objects] such as visible forms are many, there is only a single sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) comprised within that one sense-field.

In the view that cognition is formless (*nirākārapakṣa*), the word "single" is used for the purpose of excluding numbers such as two or more; likewise, in the view that it possesses form (*sākārapakṣa*), the word "single" is used according to the doctrine of non-dual diversity (*citrādvaitavāda*).
The expression "with respect to each object" (*pratyartham*) is made using this coarse designation.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, within a single substance consisting of an aggregate of atoms, there arise—during the occasion of perception—only those cognitions that, for each individual atom, bear its form; these are the very same [cognitions] that arise when perception is considered in brief. And regarding this position, whatever objection [is raised]:
Both of these refutations have already been stated by us in the *Viśeṣākhyāna*, and thus are not discussed here.

Regarding the phrase "of the capacity" (*yogyatāyāḥ*), the meaning—given the context—is the capacity of the object to be negated and the location distinct from it to produce their respective cognitions. Those two things which have the nature (*śīla*) of being mixed together in a single cognition are described as such.

"By relying on the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*)" means by accepting the principle of universal inclusion (*aśeṣopasaṃhāra*). "By proximity" (*pratyāsatti*) means by resorting to the principle of proximity; this is the meaning.
To the question, "What possible proximity exists here between those two? he says: "In a single cognition" (*ekajñāna*).
Therefore, from that jar:

when there is the cognition of it, there is the non-perception of the characteristic of the knower; when there is its own nature, there is the non-perception of the characteristic of the known. Kumārila, the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika*, considers that "non-perception" in this context is simply the cognition itself as distinguished from those two, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and not the absence of their own nature—this is the remainder of the sense.
He thinks that since perception arises from duality when one intends to express its location in either the agent or the object, non-perception likewise results in duality by the same logic.

Anticipating the objection that "non-perception is appropriate only for the cognition of a place devoid of the jar, because it is that alone which is useful in the conventional usage of the absence of a jar, and not anything else," he says "just as... (*yathā...*) in order to demonstrate that there is no difference in the utility of both.

The counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is that which is intended to be negated; it depends upon the recollection of that [counter-positive]. Demonstrating this very point through the linguistic practice of cognizers, he says "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
If it is asked, "Since each one does not exist in the other, how can there be the true nature (*tattvārtha*) of the two?",
this is not so;
for in each one, the other must necessarily exist as its qualifier.

For instance, since I experience a cognition whose form is the bare location (*pradeśa*), even for one who employs the conventional expression "there is no jar," the location is indeed utilized as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that cognition.
Likewise, when one employs the expression "there is no jar" because this bare location is seen, the perception itself functions as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the location.
The particle *āhatya* is used in the sense of "at that very moment."
Regarding the three states of existence and non-existence,
the determination of their apprehension or non-apprehension is established respectively through their emergence and suppression.

Even though there is no difference in the substratum (dharmin) in terms of its essential form, a distinction between the two properties (dharmas) is accepted when there is a distinction between the properties themselves.
The phrase "our position" means that which is considered to be our established and settled view; "in that" refers to such a position.

Because it consists of both manifest and non-manifest natures—that is, because it has the character of being both manifest and unmanifest—both apprehension and, by virtue of the word "and," non-apprehension are maintained for those two, according to the context.

[189] Regarding this explanation, with the intention that the term *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) intended by the author of the Vārttika must be understood as emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*), he explains it as "the state of being a means" (*sādhanatvam*).
Furthermore, by the force of the word "cause of establishment" (*siddhihetutva*), the phrase "of something" (*kasyacid*) is obtained.
Because of that non-connection— that is, because of the impossibility of its being a cause for proof—
he says "and of non-existence" (*abhāvasya*) while adding another refutation here.

Having connected this to the consequence that there would be the constant production of the cognition "it does not exist" regarding non-existence, he states "not depending on auxiliary causes" (*anapekṣitasahakāriṇaḥ*) in response to the inquiry "whence is this?"

Thus, the qualifying term should be construed as being for the sake of providing a reason (*hetubhāva*). In response to the inquiry, "How does it have this very independence? it should be construed as "because it is that which cannot have any excellence added to it" (*anādheyātiśaya*). This is to be understood from the context, since it is the negation alone of that [object] that is under discussion, because [negation] lacks the capacity to be a means of accomplishment (*sādhanatva*).
Having stated one mode of the argument "because its proof is unestablished," he says "or else" (*athavā*) in order to demonstrate another;
that is to say, the proof itself, the establisher itself, the determiner itself. That both...
Because it would follow [from that premise], namely, because it would follow that there is the arising of the cognition "it does not exist";
[this is] the means of proof (sādhakatva).
Otherwise, [it would be so] in the manner of being conjoined with the nature of an existent entity (bhāvarūpa).
Because that is untenable; because that aspect of non-existence is untenable,
it is a state of being mixed with another form.

Since the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) is established even by another means without obstruction, what is the point of your effort in resorting to this particular position? Anticipating this objection from the opponent's side and describing the intention of the other, he says:
"He thinks thus" [177.9].
This continues with the sense that "one apprehends the absence of a jar through the apprehension of the absence of the cognition of a jar" [177.10–11].
Therefore, because there is the realization of the absence of a jar,
and following from the phrase "one realizes the conventional usage of the absence of a jar," it is stated that the direct apprehension is intended with reference to the bare location,
while the indirect apprehension is intended with reference to the cognition thereof.
And that absence of a jar is thus [established] through its removal (or non-existence);
for in this way, the common understanding of the world is accorded with, such is the meaning.
The opponent explains that because there is the cognition of the absence of a jar in the middle, [the cognition of the jar's absence] occurs even through a mediated succession (*pāraṃparyeṇa*).
Thus, the form of the object of consideration has been shown.
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the cognition of the bare location and to self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).
Anticipating a specific objection, the author himself offers a rebuttal, saying: "But surely it exists" (nanv asty eva).

Otherwise, by means of a mere negation—that is, through the non-perception of form as understood by that [negation]—there would be no apprehension of "the other," namely, that which is characterized by being either obstructed or unobstructed.
To the question, "What benefit is there in this being so?", the Sāṃkhya replies:

Showing the merit of his own position, he says "tathā" [178.18]; it should be construed as "tathā sahitī" (thus, together). The particle "hi" is to be understood in the sense of "because. It becomes the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of that object.
The meaning to be understood is that such is its very characteristic (*liṅga*) under these circumstances.
Because existence and non-existence are contradictory, their identity as a single essence is untenable; thus, its "nature of being void" (*tuccharūpatva*) means it has no form whatsoever.

With the intention that even that [non-existence] is nothing by way of another's form, he says: "because even that is of a void nature by way of another's form. This refers to that which appears in a conceptualization of emptiness, appearing as a conceptualization of mere non-existence.
Because it lacks that form— due to the absence of the form of the object to be negated—
it would likewise be contradictory; it would not be tenable.

Otherwise, even in its own nature (*svarūpa*), it would be of the character of being non-existent (*tuccharūpatva*). How, moreover, could there not be an absence of another thing in that case? To this he says: "For that which... (*yo hi*). "Another form" (*rūpāntara*) means a similar other form.
Because of the lack of that form (*tadrūpavirahāt*).

"What kind" means devoid of another form (*pararūpaśūnya*), that is, lacking the form of that which is to be negated. Or rather, by this object (*viṣaya*), there should be seen the designation of the subject (*viṣayin*)—that is, of the property being predicated (*vidhīyamānadharmasya*). It continues: "it is called *paryudāsa* (exclusion)."
Therefore, the cognition of that [object] from the intended form is the cognition of the absence of other forms. The word "not" negates what is under discussion.

In the phrase "in the cognition," the sense of the causative suffix (*ñic*) should be understood as being included; for otherwise, since it would be impossible for there to be capacity for cognition—that is, for making known—the non-cause, which does not produce [the cognition], could not bring about that cognition, given the context.
Regarding the phrase "of that intended form":
for if a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) were the indicator, then its capacity would have to be described as either being produced by that [entity] or as having the power to produce it.

However, since the negation of a distinct entity (*arthāntaraprasajyapratiṣedha*) is devoid of all causal capacity, it cannot be produced by that [entity], such that it could possess that nature; this is the meaning.
He says, "In identity" (*tādātmye*), because it must necessarily have that cause by which the statement "of that which has no cause" would be appropriate;
the sense is that this is because there exists another basis for non-deviation.
This is because it is not apprehended by that perception.

[192] Because of that apprehension, it might be argued as follows: if the non-existence of the jar, which is the contained object, is established by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its reality, then the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) must still be accepted for the sake of establishing its nature as being unconnected with the jar.
From that, its nature of being non-conjoined with a jar is established.

To this, one might raise the objection: "In that case, it follows that its lack of a substratum in relation to a jar must be negated by the means of knowledge consisting in non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*).
Anticipating this concern, [the author] begins with the words "For it is of two kinds," etc., in order to demonstrate how both of these are established from that very same source.
"This" (ayam) refers here merely to this location; only the place is intended to be expressed.
By virtue of having a nature excluded from that [other], [that is,] by virtue of having a nature excluded from a jar,
it does not have a single form consisting of a connection with the jar— that is, a form mixed with the jar.
And precisely by virtue of having a nature excluded from that, it is "possessing a jar," even though it is accompanied by a jar.
"Other than the jar" means that its being other than the jar in every respect constitutes one mode [of exclusion]. However,
the reading "possessing a jar" (*ghaṭavān*) is a scribal error.
He states the second type [of proof], beginning with "and merely" (*kevalaś ca*).
Regarding "merely" (*kevala*), it means that [the pot] is indeed something other than the pot itself.
— What is intended is that which is conjoined with it; clarifying that very state of isolation (*kaivalya*), he says: "with respect to the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ prati*).

When that location is apprehended through perception by means of its distinction from that [jar] and its distinction from the form of the jar, there is both the absence of the jar and the absence of the jar as a conjoined object.
Therefore, from that [it follows]: the non-confusion (*asaṅkara*) of things is their lack of confusion; for the word *saṅkara*, like the word *matsara*, is a term denoting a property (*dharma*).
Because it exists, for the sake of establishing that, for the sake of ascertaining that,
one relies on what is not accepted by others; "therefore" (*tadā*) is the break in the sentence here, meaning "in one's own cognition" (*svajñāne*) itself.
The phrase "because of the existence of another" (anyabhāvāt) demonstrates that its nature is precisely not admitted by others;
otherwise, if its nature as that [other] were dependent upon what is not admitted by others, it would be in that manner.
"And the fact that its absence is established by perception" follows from the context.
"At that very time" means at the time of accepting the identity (*tādātmya*) of those two; or rather, it should be construed as "at that very time, there is no establishment by perception."

Or, if one asks: "If that [non-apprehension] is relied upon without being accepted by the opponent, what then is the point of its being established by perception? the answer is "no. If one then asks: "Where, then, has it been stated? the reply is: "In the alternative position," which means:
in the position that accepts identity (*tādātmya*).

Explaining that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) itself is expressed by the word "inherence" (*samavāya*), he intends to show that smoke is indeed a probans based on conjunction. To the question, "Why then is it not stated by its own specific term? he replies with the words "In conjunction... (*saṃyoge*).
Because there is disregard for that designation (*vyapadeśa*)— that is, the state of being designated— by means of a form (*rūpa*) that is distinct from others;
or alternatively, because there is disregard for that designation, which is the expression by means of a distinct or different signifier (*vācaka*).
"Why, then, is *samavāya* (inherence) not mentioned at all? To this he says: "But for others...
Thus, first, Bhadanta Arcata explains it; others, however, say that his confusion of thought has arisen on an entirely inappropriate occasion.
For instance, [the argument applies] to smoke as the property-possessor (*dharmin*)—whether in its parts or on the mountain—or to the state of being smoke (*dhūmatva*).

Others maintain that smoke is not established as possessing fire by means of the reason "smokeness," but rather that smoke itself is the reason through its inherence in the same substrate (*ekārthasamavāyin*). Previously, he [the author of the Vārttika] demonstrated Uddyotakara’s view that "therefore, in this case, smoke alone must be the subject (*dharmin*): 'This smoke possesses fire because it is smoke,'" but now, having forgotten that very point, he explains it thus, making even the author of the Vārttika an object of contempt.
"He brings about" (āpādayati)—what can we say to this?
Of the other, namely smoke;
"that" refers to S.

[194] By the passage beginning with "Is it not the case... (*nanu ce*) and so forth, the author first challenges the subject under discussion; then, by the passage beginning with "It is true... (*satyam*) and "by means of the consequence of impermanence" (*prasaṅgato 'nityatvenetyādi*), he offers a rebuttal. By this, if someone—through an adherence to the view of Īśvarasena—desires any one of these relations between the presence of another thing and its absence, [the author] demonstrates that such an absence does not exist.
That [objection] is first refuted by what has been explicitly stated;

furthermore, by implication, those Naiyāyikas who think: "We do not describe a relationship of signifier and signified between these two, but rather that the absence of a jar is cognized through a perception produced by the contact of a qualified object with its qualifier" are also addressed.

Furthermore, since there is no relationship between the existence of another thing and its non-existence, the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva) is untenable; thus, even the mention of a perception arising from that [existence of another] is refuted, by which means the claim that non-existence could be determined through it is discarded.
It should be understood that the absence of a relationship between the existence of another thing and its non-existence has been demonstrated with this intention.
In order to avoid the charge of redundancy regarding this very point, he says: "For previously...
(181.11). It was stated [previously] because it had already been explained by the passage beginning with "of that [object], whose form is not mixed with anything else" (181.11).
The phrase "another perception" (pratyakṣāntara) (181.12) should be understood in relation to cognitions such as those of loss and so forth.

Furthermore, the relationship is not defined solely by the qualifier-qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya) relation. Nor can it be said that another relationship must be sought for the [qualifier-qualified] relationship itself, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of accepting a seventh category— since it is not included among the six categories—

or of the disappearance of the relations of conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya), given that the qualifier-qualified relation is established between the staff and the bearer of the staff, as well as between a genus and its possessor.
And because [the definition] cannot withstand such investigations as "What is the cow? and "What does it do?", which serve as its qualifiers?

Thus, this demonstration of the resolution of the objection and the avoidance of redundancy should be seen at the beginning when an objection is raised by one who is urged with haste and has not yet understood the meaning of the text to be explained; otherwise, this would appear only after the commentary on the section demonstrating the absence of connection.
[195] Therefore, the spatial parts (*pradeśāvayava*) are of the nature of substance (*dravyātmānaḥ*), having the essential character of substance (*dravyasvabhāvāḥ*).
There are exactly nine; that is, they are delimited by the number nine, characterized as earth, water, fire, air, space, direction, time, self, and mind.
Thus Praśastakāra said: "In this regard, substances—earth, water, fire, air, space, direction, time, self, and mind—are declared to be exactly nine, designated by general and specific names."
By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), there is the understanding of possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) and being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Regarding that,
he says “and not” (*na ca*) because, in that case, since non-existence exists in the substance precisely in the form of a quality, [the aforementioned properties would follow].

In that substance, there are twenty-four qualities: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, weight, fluidity, viscidity, momentum, merit, demerit, and sound.
And this [sound] is not one of those twenty-four qualities, such as color and the rest, which are non-existents.
If it is argued that it will therefore exist there in the form of karma, he says: "Nor even... (*nāpi*).
The phrase "it exists in the form of karma" (*karmarūpatayā vartate*) is understood to carry over from the previous context.
To the question "Why does it not exist? he says: "In the five... (*pañcasu*).
Because it is not included among the five types of action characterized by throwing upward, throwing downward, contracting, expanding, and moving;
[the author] asks, "How is it not included therein? and replies, "Because it lacks those characteristics.
Furthermore, what is the characteristic of action, the absence of which is being stated for it? He replies, "[It is] a single substance... and so forth.
The meaning is that because the description emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*), there is a single substance [as the substratum].

By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the following properties are indicated]: connection with the state of being an object (*karmatva*), momentariness, subsistence in corporeal substances (*mūrtadravyavṛttitva*), being produced by gravity, effort, and conjunction, opposition to conjunction which is its own effect, being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction, and being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*).
The qualities of being the originator of effects inherent in both self and other, not originating things of its own genus, and originating substances are thus established.
To the objection that it might therefore exist there in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, he says: "Nor also...
The word "also" (*api*) includes the inclusion of particularities (*viśeṣa*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
To the question "Why does it not exist in that way?", he says: "In its form" (*tadrūpe*).

The intention of one who speaks thus is as follows: the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed that which pervades all its own objects, consists of non-difference, and is the cause of the cognitions of multiple occurrences and continuities; yet this [particular] is not so.
Furthermore, those things existing at the ends are "ultimate" (*antya*), because they distinguish their own substrata.

The remaining [qualities] reside individually in each of the eternal substances— which are devoid of destruction and origination, namely atoms, space, direction, time, and the self— and they are the causes of the cognition of absolute exclusion;
however, this [quality in question] is not so.

"Inherent relation (*samavāya*) is the cause of the notion 'here' for things that are inseparably established and stand in the relation of supported and supporter; however, this [relation in question] is not of that nature.

Because of the acceptance of that—namely, because of the acceptance of that conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—the five categories, namely substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity, possess the state of being inherent, which is to say, they are the substrata of inherence.
"Even in the absence of a location"—that is, even in the absence of a specific designated place—"the non-existence of a jar is possible.

By this, it is shown that [non-existence] does not follow the presence of a spatial locus (*vyatirekānanuvidhāna*). And by the statement "nor does it have a distinction for each respective object," it is shown that it transcends the properties of other effects.
"Due to the difference of the related entities" means because the related entities— such as a jar, a cloth, and so forth— are distinct, manifold, or otherwise different.
"In the case of difference" means when distinction, multiplicity, or otherness is being sought.
The consequence of that is the consequence of [the distinction between] fear [and its absence].
This was stated immediately prior.

Now, are not the word and the object here the primary [entities], consisting of the signifier and the signified? Likewise, it is the generalities of word and object—constructed by the intellect—that possess the nature of signifier and signified, and not the specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*) of word and object.

And since the relationship of producer and produced between those two—the word and the universal of the object—is not possible, one might wonder how such a statement was made. Anticipating this objection and intending to state a qualification, he says, "Even though...
and "between the word and the object."
The intended meaning is "of those that have become the signified and the signifier.

Regarding the phrase "having the nature of a universal constructed by the intellect": for one whose mental impression (*vāsanā*) has been instilled by previously awakened linguistic conventions, there arises a cognition [in the form]:

"This very same thing is what I previously apprehended as the signifier; this very same thing is what was perceived as the signified. This occurs through the distinction between the word and the object perceived at the time of the convention.
It arises as it cognizes its own form; that imagined nature which is the universal (*sāmānya*) is not intended here as a specific [particular].

"Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) means: with respect to the basis (*nibandhana*), that is, the seed (*bīja*), of conceptual construction (*utprekṣā*), which is to say, of synthesis (*samākalanam*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*).
For it is precisely from the experience of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound that the universal (*sāmānya*) of the expressive word [arises].
The meaning is that there occurs a conceptual construction (*utprekṣā*) by means of that.

Through that medium—namely, by way of raising the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the seed-word for the conceptual construction of the general term denoting the expressive word—the "other entity" (*anyabhāva*), which is the state of being merely a location and so forth, [is apprehended].

And by this [passage beginning with] "even previously," as well as by [the passage beginning with] "even though that intention exists," [it is shown that] even when there is its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the cognition does not arise].
The procedure for that has been shown.

Since the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is untenable when there is a distinction between things yet no causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) exists, he says that it is "mediated by that" (*taddvāraka*).
Now, if it is asserted that whenever something is the basis for the establishment of another, there must necessarily be a relationship such as causality between them; [then...]
"In that case, the sense-faculties such as the eye would not be the basis for the apprehension of their own objects, such as visible form," thinking thus, the opponent asks: "How then?
The proponent replies: "Mutually...
By this, he demonstrates that although those two are simultaneous, there is nonetheless a direct relationship of cause and effect between them.
He says that it will be exactly the same for these two as well: "Not so" (naivam).
Here, in the case of establishing the absence of one thing through the presence of another, what was just mentioned does not apply.
Why is this so? He says: "Because of the existence of another" (*anyabhāve*).
This is because of their non-connection (*tadayogāt*), that is, because of the impossibility of arising from the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryutpādāyogāt*).

And why is there no connection? Because if non-existence were to arise from something, it would attain the nature of an entity (*bhāvarūpatāprāpteḥ*), which entails the loss of its status as such [i.e., as non-existence]. Furthermore, without the non-existence of the jar, it would entail the impossibility of a momentary state similar to that specific location-moment [existing there].
And it should be seen as follows:

having demonstrated that various things he stated were improper due to his boldness of speech, [the author], now showing that his current statement is irrelevant to the subject at hand, says: "And of that characterized by the relation of mark and marked... [184.2]. How so? Regarding the sense-faculty (indriya) S... [196]
But it is not "the mere absence of a jar," because that is the subject under discussion.

He demonstrates this very point of "mere-ness" by stating that [the absence] has not attained the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*), that is, the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) of any substratum (*dharmin*).
This is because there is no other substratum apart from the form of the bare location; "of another" means of something other than the form of the bare location.
Because the locus (*dharmin*), which is the substratum of the logical mark (*liṅga*), is absent; and therefore, for anything else,
the qualification "restricted by place, time, and substance" is applied by way of its being the cause.

The thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement of that which is to be proven. Desiring to avoid [the fallacy of] "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, he qualifies it by saying, "also by way of exclusion" (*vyāvṛttito ’pi*).

By stating "a mere location" (*pradeśamātra*), the opponent has shown that the reason (*hetu*) is the generality of being a location (*pradeśatvasāmānya*), while the locus (*dharmin*) is a specific location.
[198] Its place and time are not fixed;
as for that which is "pure" (*kevala*),
it should be understood as belonging to the same class as the jar situated in front, because that alone is the subject under discussion.

With the intention that it must necessarily be understood because it functions as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), like a logical mark (*liṅga*), he says: "in the cognition of the mere location (*pradeśa*) which has become the logical mark" (*liṅgabhūta*);
here, as before, one should also observe that it constitutes a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
Therefore, from the mere location which has become the logical mark (*liṅgin*).
The third [ablative case], characterized by "having been thus," occurs through the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).
The reading "by means of not knowing such intentions" (*tathāvidhābhiprāyānabhijñatayā*) is clear; it refers to not knowing the intentions according to the expression.
But in the reading *tayā*, there is great difficulty;
for it would imply a lack of understanding of the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*),
since [the object] is a cognizable (*prameya*) and thus something yet to be proven (*sādhya*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is no contradiction in the case of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), nor in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka school.
These distinctions, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, arise from the cognition of the other [term] and from the cognition of the aspect of non-existence.
"In its conjunction" (*tatsaṃyoge*) means when there is a connection with that sense faculty (*indriya*) by which the object is to be perceived.
But as for the phrase "that which is thus perceived," it follows from the context;
that [perception] has non-conjunction as its cause, meaning it has the lack of connection with the sense faculty as its cause,
because "cognition" is the subject under discussion.
Or rather, that kind of cognition is not caused by non-connection—in this context, not caused by non-connection with the sense faculties—due to the force of the argument.

Anticipating the objection, "But since there is a difference between the two positive aspects (bhāvāṃśau), how can the Teacher have stated that 'it is simply the existence of something other than that'?", he says: "He thinks as follows" [188.15].
"[Because of the deficiency of that form]" [188.17] means because of the absence of the form of a jar.
The deficiency of that form is the deficiency of the form of the jar. In its absence— that is, in the absence of the deficiency of the form of the jar—
there is the existence of that other entity, such as a location and so forth, distinct from the jar.

And thus, [188.20] even when that [cognition] has the mode of being the form of a jar, the non-existence of the jar is not established even in the portion consisting of non-existence, because it would have the nature of the jar; this is the sense.
"The conjunction with that" [188.24] means precisely the conjunction with the existence of another thing.
"By me while reflecting" is present in the mind;
"to be ascertained" means to be known.
It would not be established.

It is distinct from all the three worlds, excluded from all categories of objects, characterized by non-confusion and certainty, possessing a thoroughly bewildered form, a form in which all aspects are being doubted, and an indeterminate form.
"One who has jaundice" (*kāmalin*) is one in whom jaundice exists;
"the absence of its discernment" (*tatparicchadābhāvaḥ*) means the absence of the discernment of that very absence, such as the ground and so forth, which is present before him.
It is of an indistinct form (*sammugdhākāram*).

But surely, since this conventional practice regarding something seen in a certain place is for the purpose of attaining or avoiding it, how is the explanation in the present context—that it is "for the purpose of avoiding what has not been seen"—not sheer rashness? For there can be no seeing of what has not been seen.
Or perhaps "seeing" here is merely an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa)?
If it is argued that one should also consider [the phrase] "due to non-perception" (*adarśanāt*),
that is flawed,
because the investigation has been undertaken precisely regarding whether perception itself manifests in a mixed or unmixed form.

If worldly activity were for the sake of avoiding the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), then activity for the sake of avoiding thorns and the like would not exist; rather, it would be solely for the sake of attainment.
Furthermore, the accomplishment of human goals, characterized by all forms of rejection and acquisition preceded by right knowledge, would not be possible.
You have exerted yourself well in this regard, yet you have simply failed to apply your mind correctly to the intended meaning of the terms "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*).

For by the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) pleasure is intended here, and by the word "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), its opposite, pain. Thus—when there is this worldly activity characterized by engagement, which, upon seeing some object that is a cause of pleasure, proceeds toward the attainment of a pleasure that was previously experienced through the power of consciousness or through memory and so forth in a certain place; and when there is that worldly activity which, upon seeing a cause of pain, proceeds toward the avoidance of a pain that was previously experienced—

It would not possess the characteristic of cessation, because every act of perception would have a completely indistinct form, as its objects would everywhere consist of both causes of pleasure and causes of suffering.
And for this reason, it has been determined: "Having understood the means for achieving pleasure and pain, those who desire to act accordingly [proceed]. Enough with further elaboration.

He asks: "Of what nature is that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) for that purpose? He replies: "Characterized by engagement and withdrawal" (*pravṛttinivṛttilakṣaṇa*). A connection should be made according to the respective order [of the terms].
Otherwise, [it would be] in the manner of not appearing as a mixed form, of this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By means of two cognitions (*jñānadvaya*) consisting of direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
It should be understood that "para" refers to the Mīmāṃsaka.
Even if such an admission has been made, he asks what the result is and says, "And thus" (tathā ca).
This is to be seen as stated [previously]: by means of the dharma called the transformation of cognition (jñānapariṇāma), in accordance with what is heard in scripture.

Because of such statements as, "Non-existence here is free from being another entity, like non-apprehension," it is said that even another entity—provided its form possesses a corresponding capacity—is accepted as being [of the nature of non-existence].

However, the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will not take the form of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as you have proposed; therefore, he says, "[only] of that which has a corresponding form of capacity.
The meaning is that otherwise, its nature as the non-existence of that [entity] would be untenable.

It might be argued that even so, there will still be a distinction due to the lack of association with a single cognition; to this he replies: "of that which has a form possessing equal fitness" (tulyayogyatārūpasya) and "only of that which is associated with this cognition" (etajjñānasaṃsargiṇa eva).
Otherwise, the very state of having a form possessing equal fitness would not be established.
And if that were absent, there could be no determination of the presence of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin); such is the intended meaning.
Likewise, the object to be attained (*upeya*) is to be understood through the absence of means of valid cognition (*abhāva-pramāṇa*).
This is because of the knowledge of that [object], namely, the knowledge of that entity which possesses a nature incompatible with it and which is associated with it alone.
Proving this very point, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

How can there be a determination of anything through non-existence? Since both absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and relative negation (*paryudāsa*) are devoid of any defining characteristic (*nirupākhyatva*), how could there be a delimitation of something? Its being the cause of that [determination] means it is the cause of delimitation. [It is] precisely another entity (*bhāvāntara*).
[203] Of that single... [204] Of a single cognition—thus, at the time of such an admission; [191.10] "at that time."
By the phrase "of anyone at all" (*kasyacid api*), he restates the root text's "of anyone at all.
By saying "he states that very thing," the Teacher indicates that he is expressing precisely what was intended by the term "of anyone at all" in the summary verse.
By the word "of that" (*tasya*), he explains the meaning of the root word "of that" (*tasya*) as referring to the absence of the perception of water.

Regarding the phrase "of something other than that," while explaining the root [of the argument], he says: "[also] from that. Why, then, is it explained as "from that water, of something else such as fire," and not by merely prioritizing its negation?
Anticipating the Master’s intention in presenting these two [alternatives], he says, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), in order to describe it through a particular turn of phrase.

Therein, regarding the definition "or consciousness of another object," if that [definition] were accepted, the term "non-transformation" (*apariṇāma*) would imply the admission of the cognition of another object; that is to say, because its nature consists in that—namely, because its nature consists in the cognition of another object.
Therefore, lest the transformation of the self be established as distinct [from it], the definition [is stated] as "or consciousness [is the cognition] of another object," according to the context.

Now, he begins to explain the collective meaning of the root text beginning with "of anything whatsoever" (*kasyacid api*) with the words "and therefore, of anything whatsoever" (*tataś ca kasyacid api*).
By the word "sthāpana," deep sleep is intended.
For one who is overcome by deep sleep, there occurs an incapacity for perceiving objects.

If everything were well-established for another [observer] by virtue of that [sleeping person's] perspective through the fact of being "other," then the Master would not have presented the state of obstruction and so forth as a logical consequence; such is the intended meaning, and he demonstrates this by including the mention of "obstruction" and the rest.
It should be understood from what is being said:
"in another way" means by a manner other than our intended *pradhāna*;
"it would not remain" is explained as meaning "it proceeds."
"In that case, one should indeed set out; one should simply undertake the departure in order to achieve purposeful action"—to this he says, "nor even" (*nāpi*).

He explains the meaning of "one should not set out" by saying "one should not proceed" (*na pravarteta*). He begins to demonstrate this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). Then... S.
[206] Knowledge indeed—S;
therefore, when there is the non-existence of anything other than what has been perceived once, knowledge arises, and thus it is called "other.
It is so called because of that nature, namely, by way of appearing as the form of all things unmixed with one another.

Because that other entity, which is perceived as such, cannot be designated as "the cognition of the absence of another," since that is impossible; and because the apprehension of the absence of another is impossible.

Furthermore, the alternative conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that follows—the meaning being the conceptualization of affirmation (*vidhi-vikalpa*)—is not the means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva-pramāṇa*); this is to be understood as following from the previous context.
A vehicle (*vahana*) is a boat (*vahitra*); "by those mounted upon it" refers to those who have ascended it.
"Of that itself" means from the perspective of the self which functions as all remaining categories of existence. "That" refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Relying on its validity" means relying on the validity of non-existence (*abhāva*).
"By its very nature" means by its own cause.
"Of that" refers to the means of valid cognition called non-existence.
"From itself" means from its own essence, as opposed to another essence.

The exclusion (*nivartana*) from others is the delimitation (*vyavacchedana*) of that which is being apprehended; this follows by implication, because there would otherwise be the consequence of delimiting that [object] itself, or the consequence of delimiting the nature of another. It functions by excluding all else other than its own nature. In response to the inquiry, "How can it be said that it perceives through its own nature? it should be connected [to the answer]: "Because it conforms precisely to such an intrinsic nature."
Regarding the word *upalabhamāne* [196.14], since the suffixes *śānac* and *śatṛ* are prescribed in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), this should be understood as a causal term.
The phrase beginning with *anyadeśe* [196.15] is an explanation of the deviation from suchness (*tathātvapracyuti*).
Since the root text beginning with *tathābhūtād* [196.24] is absent, he states the effect (*kārya*).
"By the conceptualization of non-existence" means "by the conceptualization of the means of valid cognition that is non-existence," as is clear from the context.
This should be understood because the object itself is used to designate the subject.
And furthermore, it continues: "there is nothing else of such a nature.

Therefore, from non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), there arise the conceptualizations of affirmation and negation; it should be understood that these occur according to the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), consisting of both affirmative conceptualization and [negative conceptualization].
Or rather, [it refers to] the deficiency...?
It has been stated that from the direct [perception] of one thing and by the power of the other, there arises a pair of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consisting of affirmation and negation.
Regarding the phrase "for that purpose" (*tadarthāt*): the meaning is that it is a state of conceptualization because it is distinct from both identity and difference.
Because that basis by which the intended object is not established as being other than that [object] is common [to both], this should be applied in response to the expectation:

"How does it indicate the absence of any other mode? [The phrase] "of that which is contradictory to it" [means] of that which is contradictory to what is delimited by that [delimiting factor], and which is established through the exclusion of that [intended object].

This means "of that which is not mixed with it. In response to the expectation of why the proof of the twofold nature of every object that is opposed to it is established, one should connect the text by stating: "because the pervasion of everything by its otherness is established. Otherwise, the formulation "it is of this nature" (S) would not be correct.

[208] Therefore, for one who says that "it is simply the operation of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) [198.6]," the underlying intention is this: when the functioning of that very same single means of valid cognition is reflected upon, it is established as follows.
"Because of that nature" means because its form is not commingled with anything else.

"In accordance with the thing" (*yathāvastu*) means without overstepping the reality; this should be understood as being stated by way of an investigation into the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the pervasion of everything is established through the observation of that [object] and what is other than it.
By the word "iti," the form of the principle (*nyāya*) just mentioned is shown.
The state of having no other assistance for the effect is to be understood with reference to effects of a single kind.

Duality (*dvaita*) is the state of being two (*dvitā*); this is established from that [text]. It must be understood that the cognition indeed perceives [the object], and at the very time it establishes [the distinction], it differentiates that which lacks that form as being separate from it.
Otherwise, the occurrence of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) would result in an impossibility.
In response to the inquiry as to how the absence of any other suffix is established in this case, he says: "In its opposite," and so forth.
At the very time of establishing [the rule], S...

"Based on a single means of valid cognition" (*ekapramāṇanibandhanām*) is intended to mean based on perception alone or based on inference alone; it does not mean that the opponent also accepts this as being based on multiple means of valid cognition such that it would be excluded by this [term]. For he accepts it as being based solely on the means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*). The connection is: "the exclusion of that [object] which is being perceived from its own nature."

Anticipating the objection, "Since the root text (*mūla*) states 'of that other self' (*tadanyātmanaḥ*), how can you explain it as 'the state of being that other self' (*tadanyātmatāyāḥ*)?", he says: "Because the designation has the abstract quality (*bhāva*) as its primary sense.
[The word *avacchidyate* means] it is excluded (*vyavacchidyate*).
That realization is restricted to that single form;
and it would possess both that location and that time.
Furthermore, its "location" should be understood as being stated with reference to what is conventionally established in the world.
But a material entity does not occupy a single location within another material entity.
If this is not so, how [is it possible]?
It should be understood that the "establishment of non-existence" refers both to the establishment of the conventional usage of non-existence and to its cognition by one who is deluded.
For one who is not deluded, the conventional usage of non-existence is established through perception alone;
this will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
To show that very non-perception as it has been described, he says: "of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility" (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya).
And the phrase "due to non-apprehension" (anupalambhāt) must be repeated.
Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence: "because of the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension.

Now, one might ask: what kind of non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension is it, from which its establishment follows? To this he says: "in that which is similar to it" (tattulye).
That which has as its nature (rūpa) or essential character (svabhāva) a capacity equal to that of the object to be negated with respect to the production of its own cognition— that is,
the perception of such an object, which possesses the property of being perceived by the perceiver— is its "self" (ātman);
the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of making this point clear.

Alternatively, the word "perception" (*upalambha*) may denote mere cognition; this is then conjoined with the phrase "by means of that which is being perceived in the form of a capacity equivalent to it. It is from such a non-perception [that the absence is established]. If it were explained otherwise, the expression "of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya*) would be incoherent.
But not by mere non-perception in general; this is the meaning.
To the question, "Is it possible even for one who speaks thus, such that this is said? he says: "As others have said.
This is to be construed as follows: "For the sake of understanding the existence of a real entity, in that form of a real entity where the five means of valid cognition do not arise."
That which has five members is called "pañcaka";
the suffix *kan* is applied here by the rule “*saṃkhyāyā atisadattāyāḥ kan*”.

It is then to be understood as a subsequent *karmadhāraya* compound: "the pentad that is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇapañcaka*). And when it is said that "it does not arise," this refers to a case where, among the five means of valid cognition, even one [of them]...
The meaning is that "it is not born.
To the question, "How is there no arising of that when the object exists? he says, "even though [the object] exists" (*saty api*).
Furthermore, by virtue of the context, the apprehension of that object also functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
This should be construed as follows: "Because it is equal in its lack of connection with that non-existence.
[210] Of that which is of the nature of an entity—that is, of the nature of an entity consisting in perception—[210] and of the nature of another entity (anyabhāva).

From what [source] does it follow that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*)? He says: "Because of the apprehension of the object consisting in the existence of another" (*anyabhāvaviṣayopalabdheḥ*).

Why [is this said]? He asks generally; [why is it said] again? He asks specifically. That "existence of another" (*anyabhāva*) is that existence of another characterized by the bare locus (*kevalapradeśa*), which is [apprehended] by the characteristic of perception—that is, by the characteristic of sensory perception (*indriyajapratyakṣa*).

And this should be understood as stated with the intention that, because for the most part the world perceives only this ground, it realizes "there is no jar here" by way of the cognition [of its absence]; thus,

the statement "established by non-perception" (*anupalambhena siddha*) is to be understood as a factual restatement (*vāstavānuvāda*) of that very perception, since it has the nature of the non-perception of that [jar], and not as a demonstration that the perception itself has the nature of non-perception—
otherwise, it would not be relevant to the present context.

The meaning is that one should establish the conventional usage of "absence" (abhāvavyavahāra), not the absence itself, because that [absence] is already established at the very time of perceiving the bare location.

Now, one might object: "The conventional usage of absence is to be established by non-perception, yet this location is not such [a case of non-perception]. To this he replies: "With reference to the action residing in the object" (*karmasthakriyāpekṣayā*).
The meaning is that, in view of the fact that perception resides in its object (*karmastha*), the nature of "the existence of another" is established by the exclusion of that [perception].
