One who is unable to initiate the conventional usage of non-existence through direct perception must, in this system, be called "deluded. Furthermore, regarding his comprehension, the term "comprehension" (*pratipatti*) must refer to a specific portion of the conventional usage of non-existence, characterized either as cognition or as practical application.
When that [object] is being proven, the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it should be understood as other than that [proving];
the collective meaning is that one establishes it for a deluded cognizer, but not for one who is undeluded.
To the question, "Then what is the basis for the linguistic usage of non-existence regarding one who is undeluded?", he says: "But as for him... [yas tv i].
Enough of this incidental digression.

Regarding this very topic, Dharmottara has stated: "Even a clear perception restricted to the form of that [object] alone is not capable of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*), for non-existence is always subject to the fallibility of non-perception (*anupalambhavyabhicāra*) due to the possibility of the existence of beings that have never been seen."
And he intends to show that when the qualification "being visible" (dṛśyatva) is required, it results in nothing other than non-apprehension (anupalabdhi).
However, as to how this should be answered, we have already examined it in detail in our own investigation of the internal school (svayūthya-vicāra); therefore, one should look for it there.
[211] -pekṣāyām S.
Although non-apprehension is of many kinds, it should nevertheless be understood that the term "threefold" is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental types.
"With qualification" means it exists together with a qualification, namely the characteristic of having attained the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*).

Likewise, regarding the phrase "of the nature of the non-apprehension of the cause and the pervader" (*kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhilakṣaṇasya*), this refers to that which consists of the knowledge of a location devoid of the cause and the pervader, which is the very definition of those two.

The phrase "of those whose relation is established" [204.3] is appropriate because it refers to the root text’s mention of "the cause and the pervader. Similarly, regarding the expression "upon seeing such a state" [204.10], this means that when one thing is seen through the sight of another, and likewise when one thing is not seen through the non-sight of another— provided that repetition is performed without qualification— one acquires that [cognition] just as in the case of the cognition of "scratchability by iron" based on "earthiness," and so forth.

Because those two consist of doubt regarding the cognition of an object distinct from that [object], it must be stated that the non-existence of those two—the cause and the pervader—is characterized by uncertainty. Showing this very point to some extent through a verse by Vidarbha, he says: "But for a person... [67b] 1puruṣasya tv i[204.11].

The meaning of the phrase "coincidence by chance" (*yadṛcchāsaṃvāda*) is as follows: just as in the case of the amla fruit, even though its transformation into a different state—such as the acquisition of a bitter taste through processing (*saṃskāra*) and so forth—is possible, there is nevertheless a coincidence due to the observation of their constant association; so too will it be in the case intended here.
A "connection" (*pratibandha*) must be stated as a relation (*sambandha*), not as a state of being tied to that [relation] as is the case elsewhere.

Because [otherwise] there would follow the consequence that the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)— as expressed in the passage beginning with "of the probandum and the probans"— is untenable;

and because when the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and the desired [logical] operation are established, the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the two pervaders arises, even though it depends on the observer’s perception of all things as possessing the probans and thus possessing the probandum, and of those possessing the absence of the probandum as possessing the absence of the probans.
This should be understood as the proper method (*nyāya*), the general approach (*prāya-prakāra*), which is the covering of the earth by means of mere footwear;
the mention of "Naiyāyika" here should be understood according to the intention of the older Naiyāyikas.

However, modern [logicians] declare that the positive-negative (anvaya-vyatirekin) [reason] has five characteristics, while the purely positive (anvayin) and purely negative (vyatirekin) [reasons] have four characteristics each; thus, when "the Naiyāyikas" are mentioned in a general sense, their specific doctrine would be understood.
Since number, being a quality (guṇa), is dependent upon a substance (dravya), he says: "[of the reason-substance]."

The phrase "unrestricted by the number one" is an explanation of the meaning of the very expression "devoid of a counter-reason" (*pratiheturahitāyām*). A "counter-reason" (*pratihetu*) is a reason that establishes the opposite of the probandum;
"devoid of such" means that it does not deviate from what is contradictory to that which is intended to be proven.
Likewise, the previously mentioned statement that "knowability is another property" follows here.

The refutation of the probandum-property by means of the aforementioned subverting evidence (*bādhā-pramāṇa*) occurs when that probandum is absent. The particle *vata* is used in the sense of "indeed" or "furthermore."
By the term "two machines" (*yaṃtra*), given the context, it refers to the two types of machines characterized as the attractor and the extractor.

It is just as if some curious person were to marry a certain ascetic to a third gender—bearing the form of a woman but unfit for sexual union—who is designated by that very name; and then, under that pretext, he requests from him a son or the fulfillment of some purpose. This [case] is similar to that.

Thinking that [the fallacy consists in] stating the probandum (sādhya) regarding the subject (dharmin) while presenting a reason (hetu) that is devoid of inseparable connection (avinābhāva), the Master, preceded by a rebuke of others, says: "He marries a eunuch. Having cited the root text, he demonstrates its application to the present case by saying: "In that... [etc.].

In that subject (*sādhyadharmin*), it is "devoid of the capacity to prove the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmasādhanaśaktivikala*), meaning it is lacking the power to manifest the property to be proven. And that deficiency exists because one does not accept its being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitā*) with that [property] therein.
This explanation of the meaning of the words should be understood by means of this reflection.
Having established the meaning of the term, explaining it in that very way, he says: "to be married" (*pariṇāyya*).

By the word *pariṇāyya*, the indication of its connection [to the father] is characterized; that is to say, such a son, characterized by that [connection], is sought (*mṛgyate*), entreated (*prārthyate*), and requested (*yācyate*).

One might ask: "But surely a reason (*hetu*) that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) elsewhere may still manifest the probandum (*sādhya*) in that specific case; what, then, is this mockery? To this he says: "Not so" (*na hī*). This is to be understood as being stated in the following formal argument (*prayoga*): "Whatever is water has a salty taste, like seawater; and this [lake] water is not from the sea."
By way of saltiness— that is, by way of the salty taste. Water is sought among the primary elements because it is observed as such when brought about by its causes.

"Unsublated property" (*abādhitadharma*) means that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is not contradicted. "Of that which falls under it" (*tannipatasya*) refers to that which is subject to the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*).
The sense is that when the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is absent, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) must necessarily also be absent.

"Of that state" means of the state of the probandum (*sādhyabhāva*). "Precisely for this reason" means precisely because of the absence of the probandum when there is a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*). "Even in its absence" means even in the absence of the operation of the subverting proof; it follows from the context that this refers to the absence of the probandum.
The opponent speaks [at 209.2] while demonstrating the capacity of the reason (*hetusāmarthya*).
In response to the inquiry, "How does he demonstrate the capacity of the reason?", the phrase "therein, otherwise-ness" (*tatrānyathātva*) should be supplied.

By saying "showing" (*darśayan*), since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in the sense of a causal agent (*hetau*), the meaning is: "because he demonstrates otherwise-ness as being uncontradicted therein."
"For the sake of its establishment" means for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*).
That object for which it is to be stated for that purpose is the domain of the application of the reason (*hetu*).
In that regard, "otherwise than the object" refers to *S*.
The word *vai* signifies "tolerance" (*akṣamā*). Regarding what is said, such as "non-sublation is the non-perception of sublation," the meaning there is that it is "tolerated.
However, the combination of the particle *kiṃtu* and the particle *iti* constitutes a question.

In the phrase *tasyāḥ*, the suffix *-iti* has the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*); since fear is the cause for the ablative case according to the rule "the source of fear is the ablative," this is the fifth case (ablative) used in the sense of an ablative.
By the word *kāku* here, a particular arrangement of speech is intended.

With the intention that even in the absence of the interrogative particle *kiṃ*, it is the *kāku* itself, accompanied by a nod of the head, that reveals the question, he explains [the text] as "he asks.
The opponent, intending to say that this has already been stated because "non-contradiction" (*abādha*) is defined as the non-perception of sublation (*bādhā*), says: "This has indeed been said."
For what purpose is it employed? It is a "reason" (hetu) by virtue of its functional capacity.
It is for the sake of determining non-existence—that is, for the sake of determining ultimate non-existence.
It is for the sake of subverting that which is doubted—that is, for one in whom doubt has arisen.
By the cessation of cognition—that is, by the cessation of the subverting cognition—there is the subversion of the probandum.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of that which is contradicted by inference and so forth. The description of these, such as that which is contradicted by perception, is for the purpose of demonstrating their essential nature.

Because of the impossibility of its existence—that is, because of the impossibility of its being an object due to the non-occurrence of the proving means of knowledge, namely inference—the meaning is what was stated: "The reason is excluded from having no locus."
Is the reading "kiṃ yathā bādhāvinābhāvayoḥ" (as in 213.9) the more appropriate one?
However, when the reading is devoid of the word *kiṃ*, the question of one who speaks thus with a nod of the head should be understood as having the following intention:
"How so?—just as in the case of sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). S.
The definition of that [reason] is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). It consists of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Furthermore, because the word *lakṣaṇa* does not retain its gender when it is not part of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is here designated by its own inherent gender.
Since even a contradictory [reason] is a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) when its reverse is established, it was stated with that intention: "and because of the reverse" (*viparyayasya ca*).
"Establishment of existence" (*bhāvasiddhi*) means the establishment of reality (*tattvasiddhi*), because [otherwise] that would be impossible.
"Demonstrated by the intended singularity" (*vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvapratipādita*) means demonstrated by the term "intended singularity" (*vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatva*).
Regarding the phrase "of that which is preceded by" (*pūrvakasya*), this is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*).

Here too, even though it possesses other forms such as being sublated (*bādhitatva*), it was demonstrated for the purpose of being applied to what precedes. The term "lacking valid means of cognition" (*niṣpramāṇika*) is a qualification used as a reason (*hetubhāvena*).
"That" (sa) means "that very same thing," which is what is intended to be expressed.

To the question, "Why is it that its counter-argument has been refuted? he says: "When such a thing"—that is, when there exists some subject (dharmin) in which a probandum of that kind, characterized by specific qualities as they actually are, is possible.
"Then, 'non-deviating' means non-deviating from the probandum (sādhya).

Regarding the phrase 'among those who reject the authority of the Veda' (vedaprāmāṇyanirākartṛṣu), it is intended that this applies even to the context of perception and so forth, because of the lack of correspondence with them, and so on—as Kumārila states in the *Vārttika*:
'The injunctions concerning the relationship between heaven and sacrifice are false...'"
"Because there is no connection with the object for them, even though they have the authority regarding perception and so forth," and so on (*Ślokavārtika* 2.26).

However, in the *Ślokavārtika*, the statement "because it does not convey an object known through perception and so forth, like such statements of the Buddha and others" refers to those who preceded the author of the *Vārttika*, namely the earlier Buddhists (*uttarādharma saugataiḥ*).
"Counter-reasons" (*pratihetavaḥ*) refers to such arguments as "because they are produced by causes free from defects," and so forth.
As Kumārila said:
"The cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is produced by [causes] devoid of defects."
Because it is produced by causes, like the cognition derived from a logical mark, authoritative scripture, or the senses.
“[Ślokavārttika 2.184],” and so forth.
Because that cause arises,
even by mere abuse [217.20], that is, by mere speech in the case of the prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He says, "of those who maintain the doctrine of a single number," so that for no one would there be any cause at all.
The connection with this passage by the Master—"the cause of the error of right knowledge is accepted"—is to be understood through the preceding text of the Master.
Thus, the relationship of this passage by the Master, "the cause not being demonstrated," should be established.
In no way is there a cause for exclusion; by no means does it possess the nature of being a cause for the exclusion of either permanence or impermanence.

This is because its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with those two have not been established, and it was stated only with a specific intention (*abhiprāya*).—S.
*Hetutvam* (the state of being a cause).

"Raising his arm" means stretching out his upper limb; "uttering a *phūtkāra*" means emitting the sound *phūtkāra*. By some—namely, Īśvarasena, Jinendrabuddhi, and others—it is said that this is "not to be concealed," meaning it is not to be obscured.
According to the Mīmāṃsaka school, uninterrupted bliss is to be designated as heaven (svarga);
liberation, however, is apavarga.
And that [liberation] is held to be of many kinds due to differences in philosophical systems.

Showing that the union with heaven and liberation occurs precisely by relying on the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), he says: "For it is thus" (*tathāhi*). Alternatively, by saying "or by relying on the view of the Mīmāṃsakas," he states another position: "from the cultivation of the Vedānta" means from the cultivation of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*);
"by one of a certain kind of wisdom" means by one possessing excellent wisdom (*praśastaprajña*).
This application should also be understood from the context even in the case of a joke (*upahāsa*).

Explaining that "whatever capacity this [reason] previously possessed has been 'unbolted' (*utkīlita*)— that is, removed— by demonstrating that [capacity]," [the author means] that the capacity of the proof belonging to the reason characterized as audibility has been unbolted, i.e., removed.
He shows that this refers to the root text as stated.

Now, one might object: "Are not those objects and those persons displaced from such prosperity by means of a counter-argument (*pratihetu*) through the presentation of a contrary form, and not by that [original] reason? Why then is it said that 'those objects are displaced from the perfection of permanence and those persons from the perfection of heaven and liberation'? [To this he replies: 219.8. If you ask why this is so...

This is true; however, because he himself brought about that very prosperity which now exists, when it is being lost, he remains indifferent—unlike another person of the same kind who would cry out "Save those things! Save those men! as if in a state of agitation, speaking with gasping breath and looking toward his own life.

If you argue that there is no fault because we intend to displace that [reason] from its position— just as one might employ a counter-reason (*pratihetu*)— then all this must be stated by removing the term "counter-reason" and substituting the term "non-sublation" (*abādha*) in the definition, even though the refutation beginning with "because it is impossible in reality" applies to the case where the object is not sublated.

Therefore, we must now consider this very point: do you intend by "the state of having a non-contradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) the fact that contradiction is impossible in reality, or rather that contradiction does not appear even at that time?
And if it is the latter, is it so only for [the proponent] himself, or for others as well?
Furthermore, in that case, is it so only at that specific moment, or both [at that time and at other times]? Please explain.

By raising such alternatives as whether [the reason] belongs to others at that very time or at another time, and by applying refutations accordingly in all cases, those who have undertaken the refutation of the self have discarded the qualification of the reason— characterized by recognition— that was intended to establish the self.
Furthermore, if the qualification "uncontradicted by others who also desire victory" is applied, then in every case one should offer a counter-argument in this very same manner.
That definition is the definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
However, it is the cognition itself that is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) and the reflexive suffix (*tvatpratyaya*).
Establishing this very point, he says: "For thus... (*tathāhi*).

"Independent" (*svatantra*) means precisely independent of the object to be expressed (*vācyavastu*). "It would result in nothing at all" (*anarthapratilambha eva syāt*) means that there would be no attainment of the object (*arthapratilambha*) whatsoever.
Regarding this universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*):
if it is thus the case that only the external object possesses causal efficacy, then what is the point of this effort? To this he says: "In the probandum" (*sādhye*).

How, then, can there be the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), or the nature of being an effect and so forth, for those universal forms mounted upon conceptual construction which, in ultimate reality, do not touch upon any external constituent parts?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "precisely its nature as that" (*taddharmatām eva*). This means its very nature as that, namely, the nature of an external object;
[that which] resides in the external.
That is to say, having the nature of being excluded from that;

following after [the objects], and because they do not perceive their difference, they determine— on the basis of a non-existent ground— the various exclusions (*vyatireka*) such as "producedness" and "impermanence," which are multiple forms even within a single object,
as well as oneness, the universal (*sāmānya*), which is a recurring form.
The meaning is that the mutual exclusion (*vyatireka*) between those two and the distinction from the subject (*dharmin*) are demonstrated by the fourfold formulation of the reason (*hetu*).
This should be understood as stated for the purpose of establishing the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
In order to establish its concordance (*saṃvādakatva*), he says: "Regarding the object" (*vastuni*).
"Regarding the object" means with respect to the thing to be proven (*sādhya-artha*).
"Indirectly" (*paramparayā*) means by way of being connected to that which is connected [to the ultimate object].
In order to justify the designation of "effect" and so forth, he says "the effect, etc. [221.5].

Because they are reached by way of the perception of the effect and so on, and because they are determined as being such in reality, those very things are the basis for the designation of "effect" and so forth; this follows from the context.
And the phrase "the basis for designation by that" should be understood as a designation similar to the instruction: "O King, this is not the proper place for the sense-faculty.
Recalling [this], S...
[218] Based on the designation of marks such as the effect (kārya) and so forth, [the opponent argues that cognition has the form of an external mark].

Having refuted that cognition possesses the nature of an external mark, [the author], while also refuting its possession of the nature of a universal form (sāmānyākāra), says: "And it appears as conceptual construction" [221.7].
Of that which "appears as conceptual construction" [221.8].
And by explaining that "the universal form is indefinable," he intends for exclusion (*apoha*) to have a false nature.
This is because that form—the form consisting of the exclusion of non-trees—is, upon investigation, unreal in nature; it is a reflection within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Since it is impossible to perceive the reflection of exclusion as distinct from the form of the conceptual construction, just like a reflected image, or rather, by this turn of phrase, even the form of the intellect is likewise superimposed as an exclusion.
By this, it has been shown that [the universal] is the denotable object (*vācya*).
To the question, "How is its establishment as having the nature of a universal (*sāmānyātmatva*)? he says: "Because... (*yasmād*).
The phrase "of that which is determined (*adhyavasitasya*)" through persistence (*anuyāyitayā*), mentioned previously, is supplied here.
"Even for such a thing, why is there not the nature of conceptual construction?
And likewise, why is cognition not the form of the logical mark? To this he says: "And in that case" (*tathātve ca*).
"In that case" (*tathātve*) means in the state of being a persistent follower (*anuyāyitve*).
The nature of conceptualization (*vikalparūpātmatā*) is the nature of the specific characteristic of conceptualization (*vikalpasvalakṣaṇātmatā*).

Regarding what is under discussion (*prakṛtāyām*), that is, what is currently being treated; "form" (*rūpam*) is precisely what is being designated—namely, such a form of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is what is being designated.
From conviction (*pratyaya*), that is, from firm belief (*saṃpratyaya*).
Of the wheel of the reflected image of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibimba-cakra*),
which is determined (*vyavasita*).
[221] The nature of conceptual construction; [222] its own form is manifested;
[223] because of the resulting conviction.
It was stated "with respect to the ultimate [view], of the knower" (pramātuḥ);
likewise, "[of] conjunction, inherence, and so forth," and "[of] light, mental attention, and so forth."
This was stated with reference to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*).

For it is not the case that when those [reasons] are non-existent, this entity [the probandum] does not exist; if what is to be proven were not present there, then—by way of the perception of a thing that is invariably concomitant with it—there would be no cognition of it at all.
And if there were no inherence of magnitude and so forth in the mark, such as smoke,
and if there were no conjunction of that [mark] with the sense organ, then there would be no perception at all regarding that object.

And when that [mark] is absent, no cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) arises; likewise, it should be understood that even in the absence of light, there is similarly no arising of the cognition of the possessor of the mark.
Thus, it should be understood that when attention (manaskāra) is absent, there is an absence of the excellence of attention.
And, as before, there is the non-arising of the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
The reading should be "niścayo 'pi" (there is also certainty); although in some manuscripts the reading is "niścayo hi," in that case the word *hi* should be understood in the sense of *api*.
"Because it is a particularity of that" means because it is a particularity of cognition.
Regarding "of this," namely of the certainty, he asks: "By its presence in the similar class (sapakṣa)? and answers: "In the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)."

Regarding the phrase "qualified by that which is the absence in all dissimilar instances" (*sarvatra vipakṣe yo 'bhāvas tadviśiṣṭena*): what is it that exists in all dissimilar instances? He says: "in similar instances" (*sapakṣa*).
That entity whose characteristics and causes are identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*) is "qualified by that.

Now, one might object: since the presence and absence in similar and dissimilar instances are based respectively on perception and non-perception, they are already mutually qualified; so what further distinction is stated here? Anticipating this, he says: "this... [etad].

"It has been stated" means that those two are ascertained through the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and not by means of observation and non-observation; this is the implied sense.
"Of such a kind" means "possessing pervasion. "Ascertained" refers to the object of the proof of identity and origination— that is, the object of the establishment of identity and origination.
Of those very two, namely existence and non-existence;
it is "projected," that is, made manifest.
Since there is no existence distinct from arising, he explains that whatever existence there is, that is arising.

The designation of that which has the characteristic of non-existence—by means of its dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and by relying on the characterization of an entity as distinct from it—is established; thus they attain fitness for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). "Of everyone" refers to persons.
And thus, the intention is that everyone would be an omniscient seer without effort. To this, he replies: "It is not so," connecting this with the word "iti" (thus).
He says "of the indicator" (*jñāpaka*) because the "mark" (*liṅga*) is the subject under discussion.
"By the Teacher" means by Ācārya Dignāga.

With the intention that the author of the *Vārttika*, while describing the fruitfulness of grasping what was determined by the author of the *Sūtra*, has here shown his own approval, [the author of the *Ṭīkā*] treats this as the word of the Teacher and says, "And here by us," and so forth.
"Existence in such a manner" refers to positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"In the absence of that [reason] everywhere, there is necessarily an absence [of the probandum]"—the preceding phrase must be supplied here.
Therefore, the passage beginning with "from which" (*yataḥ*) and so forth [refers to] the subject matter (*vastuka*).
The opening of the *Mūla* has not been commented upon here because it is easily understood;

however, its meaning should be understood as follows: since the determination of these two—existence and non-existence—occurs through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the establishment of the being of those two, existence and non-existence, is dependent upon that; this is for the purpose of making known this point.

Regarding the phrase "it was made a definitive statement": anticipating the objection—"How can we say this when the author of the *Vārttika* is once again condensing the meaning of the term 'definitive' as composed by the teacher Dignāga?"—he says, "by us. This means "by us" in the sense of what was composed by the Teacher, that is, by the Teacher who is the author of the *Sūtra*.
By the statement, "Because [the inclusion of the term] 'ascertainment' (niścita) is desired by us," he shows the Master’s intention in this way:

that if this is indeed what we desire, then it has already been stated by us ourselves. Thus, for the time being, the explanation appears to be given by him; furthermore, this is its meaning—for this purpose: {p. 409} For this purpose...

The author of the *Sūtrasamuccaya* [states]: "And by me, in the *Viniścaya* and other works, the term ‘ascertained’ (*niścita*) was employed. With this intention, the Master, the author of the *Vārttika*, used the word ‘by us’ (*asmābhiḥ*) to convey the sense of ‘by the two of us. To the question, "By which grammatical rule is the plural number applied to two referents? we reply that it is by the rule: "And for the two words *asmad* and *yuṣmad* [the plural is used when referring to two]."
The reading "ato 'pi nyāyāt" (for this reason as well) is correct; however, "ata eva nyāyāt" (for this very reason) is a scribal error.
The phrase "of cognition" (*jñānasya*) follows from the context of "because it has been apprehended" (*pratipannatvāt*).

The sages (*munayaḥ*)—such as the *pratyekabuddhas* and others—are so called due to their engagement in the silence (*mauna*) of body, speech, and mind. Their Lord and Teacher is the Buddha, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), because he is preeminent through his abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*). Because he protects (*tāyitva*) by means of having attained the culmination of that [abandonment], his "way" (*naya*) is his method (*nīti*), his teaching (*pravacana*). His established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is his tenet (*siddhānta*). By this [verse], [the author] [establishes] the meaning of the teaching, such as "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary," and so forth.
